# Unit I: First Principles — What Is Time?

---

## Unit Introduction

There is a peculiar kind of knowing that defeats itself the moment you try to articulate it. You can ride a bicycle, but explaining the precise neural and muscular sequence that keeps you upright is another matter entirely. You can recognize a face in a crowd, but you cannot describe the algorithm you use to do it. Time is like this — only more so. You have never, not for a single moment of your conscious life, been outside of it. You know it from the inside with an intimacy nothing else approaches. And yet, if someone asks you what it *is*, you will find yourself reaching for words that slip away.

This is not a sign of intellectual failure. It is the first indication that time is philosophically deep.

Augustine of Hippo, writing in the fourth century, gave the most honest formulation of the problem that anyone has ever managed: *"What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to one that asks, I do not know."* (Augustine, *Confessions*, XI.14.17) The sentence is funny, paradoxical, and exactly right. It locates the problem with surgical precision. The difficulty with time is not that we lack experience of it — we are saturated with experience of it — but that our experience resists conceptual capture. Time keeps sliding between our fingers the moment we try to hold it still long enough to examine.

This unit is about getting the problem clearly in front of us before we attempt to solve it. That sounds modest, but it is genuinely difficult work. Philosophy moves badly when it rushes past the question toward an answer. The history of the philosophy of time is littered with theories that are ingenious but answer a slightly different question from the one they were supposed to answer — or that dissolve the question rather than answer it, which is sometimes useful and sometimes merely evasive.

We will begin, in Chapter 1, by asking what kind of question "What is time?" actually is. Is it a scientific question, a conceptual question, or something else? We will examine the methods available to us and think carefully about the relationship between philosophical and physical inquiry into time — a relationship that is cooperative but irreducibly tense. Chapter 2 then turns to the ground floor of human experience: the pre-theoretical intuitions, linguistic structures, and cultural frameworks through which time first becomes visible to us before philosophy gets to work on it.

The goal of this unit is not to answer the question of what time is. That would be premature. The goal is to equip you to ask it well. Asking a philosophical question well is more than half the battle — and it is a battle that most people lose by charging in too quickly.

**A note on what to expect.** The chapters that follow are demanding but not technical. They require no background in physics or formal logic, only the willingness to think slowly and carefully about things you ordinarily take for granted. That kind of thinking is harder than it sounds. We are accustomed to passing over the obvious because it is obvious. Philosophy asks you to stop and look at it. Prepare to find it strange.

---

*Unit I comprises Chapters 1 and 2.*

## Chapter 1: Approaching Time Philosophically

---

### Chapter Introduction

Every inquiry has to start somewhere, and the best place to start is with the question itself: not with answers that have been given, not with the history of the problem, but with the raw difficulty that makes the question interesting and hard. This chapter is about situating ourselves before we begin to move.

"What is time?" sounds like a question with a simple answer — or at least a question for which the resources of modern physics might furnish one. After all, physics deals with time in every equation it writes. Surely physicists know what time is? The uncomfortable truth is that they do not — not in the sense that would satisfy a careful inquiry. Physics uses time; it does not explain it. It tells us how time relates to space, to velocity, to energy, to gravitational fields. It tells us that time is measurable, that clocks can disagree, that the rate of temporal passage is not absolute across different reference frames. All of this is profound and important. But none of it answers the question that Augustine was asking, which is the question we will be asking in this book: not *how does time behave* but *what kind of thing is it*? Not the physics of time but the *nature* of time.

This distinction is not merely verbal. The question of nature is a philosophical question, and it requires philosophical tools: conceptual analysis, careful attention to what we must presuppose in order to say anything at all, the willingness to follow an argument wherever it leads even when it leads somewhere uncomfortable. This chapter introduces those tools and explains why they are needed.

We begin (Section 1.1) with the observation that time is puzzling in a distinctive way — not just unknown but resistant to easy framing. Section 1.2 introduces the methods of philosophy and explains what they can and cannot deliver. Section 1.3 takes up the relationship between philosophy and physics: when do they compete, when do they cooperate, and who has the final word? Section 1.4 provides a preliminary map of the terrain — the different sub-questions that fall under the heading of the philosophy of time — so that later chapters are navigated with a sense of where each fits in the larger picture.

By the end of this chapter, you should feel both the genuine difficulty of the subject and the genuine power of the tools available to address it. The aim is not intimidation but preparation.

### Section 1.1: Why Time Is Philosophically Puzzling

---

#### Section Introduction

The first step in any philosophical investigation is to resist the temptation to already know the answer. Time is so deeply woven into ordinary experience — we talk about it constantly, plan around it, fear it, mourn its passage — that it can seem self-evident. But self-evidence is a philosophical trap. The most obvious things are often the hardest to understand, because we have learned to use them without examining them.

This section works to make time strange. That is not an end in itself, but it is a necessary beginning. We need to feel the puzzlement before we can properly formulate the question, and we need to formulate the question before we can make progress toward an answer.

Three distinct sources of puzzlement are identified in the subsections that follow: the gap between experience and articulation that Augustine identified; the multi-dimensional nature of time as simultaneously experiential, physical, and metaphysical; and the curious gap between our ordinary temporal talk and what any systematic theory will have to say. Together these set the stage for the methodological discussions that follow in the rest of the chapter.

#### 1.1.1 — Augustine's Confession: The Problem Stated

---

The most famous sentence in the entire history of the philosophy of time belongs not to a scientist or to a professional philosopher but to a North African bishop writing in the late fourth century. In Book XI of the *Confessions*, Augustine of Hippo asks, with a directness that no subsequent writer has improved upon:

> *"What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to one that asks, I do not know."*
> (Augustine, *Confessions*, XI.14.17, trans. Chadwick 1991: 230)

The sentence is worth pausing over. It is not a confession of ignorance in the ordinary sense — Augustine is not saying he has never thought about time or that he lacks the relevant vocabulary. He is saying something more precise and more disturbing: that the pre-theoretical, lived familiarity we all have with time does not translate into theoretical understanding. There is a gap between *knowing how* to use something and *knowing what* it is. We know how to use temporal concepts fluently; we deploy tenses every time we speak; we remember the past and anticipate the future without any sense of theoretical difficulty. But as soon as we try to formulate what we mean — as soon as we try to say what time *is* — the concepts that seemed solid become elusive.

This is not a problem peculiar to the fourth century. It has recurred in every subsequent period of philosophical reflection on time. Aristotle, who gave the first systematic philosophical treatment of time, began by cataloguing a set of *aporiai* — puzzles or difficulties — that show why time is hard to place within ordinary ontological categories (Aristotle, *Physics*, IV.10, 217b29–218a30). He asked: Does time exist at all, given that its two apparent parts — the past and future — do not exist, and the present is a dimensionless instant that vanishes before it can be grasped? And yet time seems clearly to exist in some sense — we measure it, order events by it, plan around it. Something that does not exist at all could hardly be so practically indispensable.

The same puzzle appears in a different guise in the philosophy of physics. When physicists write down the equations of mechanics, relativity, or quantum theory, they include a variable *t* that represents time. But what does that variable stand for? One way of putting the problem is this: in physics, time appears as a *parameter* against which other quantities are measured, but the nature of that parameter — what kind of thing it is, whether it flows, whether the past and future are equally real, whether there is an objective "now" — is not settled by the equations themselves. The equations work whatever the answer to those questions turns out to be (Maudlin 2012: 5–12). Physics uses time without explaining it.

##### The Gap Between Use and Understanding

There is a philosophical tradition that treats this gap — between competent use and theoretical understanding — as the central method-revealing feature of philosophical problems. Wittgenstein, who was preoccupied throughout his career with the difference between using a word correctly and understanding it, put the general point like this: *"We are under the illusion that what is special, profound, essential in our investigation resides in its trying to grasp the incomparable essence of language."* (*Philosophical Investigations* §110, trans. Anscombe et al. 2009). His suggestion — not always helpful, but illuminating here — is that philosophical puzzlement often arises when we take words out of their ordinary working environments and ask them to do something they were not built for.

This diagnosis partly applies to time. We use temporal words — "before," "after," "now," "past," "future," "duration," "earlier than," "later than" — with perfect fluency in ordinary life. The puzzlement arises when we try to step back and ask what these words *pick out* in the world. Do they pick out properties of events? Relations between events? Features of our own mental representations? Something else entirely? The very fluency of ordinary temporal talk can disguise the fact that these are not settled questions.

But Wittgenstein's therapeutic approach — which would dissolve rather than answer the question — is ultimately insufficient here, for a reason that will become a recurring theme in this book. Time is not only a feature of ordinary discourse; it is a feature of the *physical world* that our discourse is trying to describe. The question "what is time?" is partly a question about language, but it is principally a question about nature. When physicists tell us that time passes at different rates in different reference frames, or that time may have had a beginning, or that the equations of quantum gravity seem to eliminate time as a fundamental variable, they are making claims that go beyond the analysis of ordinary usage. The philosophical question of what time is cannot be dissolved by attending more carefully to how we talk; it must be answered, at least in part, by attending to what the world is like.

##### Why the Puzzle Is Distinctive

Not all philosophical questions have this character. Many philosophical questions — about the nature of justice, or the conditions for knowledge, or the analysis of causation — are primarily questions about concepts, where careful attention to how we use terms will do most of the explanatory work. The philosophy of time has a component of this kind, but it also has a robustly metaphysical and empirical component that makes it distinctive.

The puzzle of time is distinctive in at least three ways. First, time is *existentially unavoidable* in a way that many other philosophical topics are not. You can bracket the question of the existence of numbers or the nature of universals and live your life without feeling the gap. You cannot bracket time. Whatever answer we give, it has to coexist with the fact that you experience yourself as moving through time, that you remember a past and anticipate a future, and that this structure of experience is not optional. Any theory of time that cannot accommodate the phenomenology of temporal experience — or that requires us to dismiss it as wholesale illusion — owes us an account of why we should accept such a radical conclusion.

Second, time is *scientifically fundamental* in a way that creates genuine constraints on philosophical theorizing. Unlike questions about justice or knowledge, the question of what time is has answers that are partly constrained by the best physics we have. A theory of time must be compatible with the physical facts about time — about its relationship to space, its role in causal structure, its topology, its apparent asymmetry. Philosophy cannot simply ignore what physics tells us.

Third, time involves what we might call the *coincidence of the subjective and the objective*. Time is not only something in the world that we study from the outside; it is the medium of our own experience. We are in time in a way we are not in space — we can step sideways but we cannot step temporally. This creates a peculiar reflexivity: any account of time must account not only for time as a feature of the world but for our experience of being in it. The phenomenology of time and the physics of time cannot be kept in entirely separate compartments.

##### Augustine's Own Answer

It is worth noting that Augustine's confession of ignorance is followed by a sustained and brilliant attempt to answer the question he has so memorably posed. His answer — that time is a *distentio animi*, a stretching or extension of the soul — is the first great phenomenological account of time in Western philosophy, and it anticipates, in striking ways, some of the most sophisticated treatments of temporal experience in the twentieth century. We will examine it in detail in Chapter 8. For now, the important point is simply that Augustine's puzzlement is not the last word; it is the right first word. It names the problem correctly. The philosophy of time begins in honest acknowledgment of what we do not know.

#### 1.1.2 — Time as Simultaneously Experiential, Physical, and Metaphysical

---

Part of what makes time so difficult to pin down philosophically is that the concept does not belong to any single domain of inquiry. It is not purely a matter for physics, nor purely a matter for phenomenology, nor purely a matter for metaphysics. It sits at the intersection of all three, and the theories that emerge from each domain place different — and sometimes conflicting — constraints on what a satisfactory account must look like.

Understanding why this is so is essential preparation for the investigations that follow. This subsection traces each of the three dimensions of the problem and begins to map out how they relate to one another.

##### Time as Experienced

Consider first what it is like to live in time. Right now, as you read these words, you are not merely processing a static array of information. You are doing something irreducibly temporal: reading is a sequential activity in which earlier words inform the understanding of later ones, in which sentences accumulate meaning over their duration, in which anticipation of what comes next shapes the comprehension of what is happening now. Language itself, and therefore thought itself insofar as it is linguistically structured, is temporal through and through.

But the temporal character of experience goes deeper than that. You experience yourself as continuous — as the same person who read the previous paragraph, who had breakfast this morning, who was a child two decades ago. This sense of continuity, of being a self that extends through time, is not a belief you hold as a result of inference; it is a basic feature of experience, or at least of what philosophers call *the structure of the given*. You experience yourself as coming from a past and moving toward a future.

This experiential dimension of time has attracted sustained attention from phenomenologists — philosophers who take the structures of experience as philosophically primary. Edmund Husserl, in his *Lectures on the Phenomenology of the Consciousness of Internal Time* (1928/1991), argued that our experience of time is not produced by passively receiving a sequence of atomic moments and then mentally arranging them into an order. Rather, we experience time through what he called *retention* and *protention*: a just-passed impression remains phenomenally present (retained) as the next impression arrives, while a not-yet-arrived impression is anticipated (protended). Consciousness is always already temporally extended, even in what seems like an instant of present experience. The notes of a melody are not heard one by one and then assembled into a sequence; they are heard as flowing, each note retaining a trace of the one before and anticipating the one to come (Husserl 1991: 27–42).

This phenomenological account is rich and important, and we will examine it carefully in Chapter 26. For now, what matters is the observation that experiential time has its own distinctive features — features of flow, of the structured present, of memory and anticipation — that any adequate philosophy of time must somehow accommodate.

##### Time as Physical

Meanwhile, physics has developed its own account of time, and it is dramatically different from the picture suggested by experience. In Newtonian mechanics, time is absolute and universal: there is a single, uniform temporal flow against which all events in the universe are coordinated, and all clocks that are not interfered with measure the same thing (Newton 1687/1999: 408–415). This fits relatively well with common experience.

Einstein's special theory of relativity shattered this picture. According to special relativity, simultaneity is relative to a reference frame: two events that are simultaneous as measured in one inertial frame may not be simultaneous as measured in another. There is no observer-independent fact about which events are happening "now" across different locations (Einstein 1905; Minkowski 1908/1952). Time dilation is real: a moving clock runs slower than a stationary one, not as an illusion or a measurement artifact but as a physical fact. Two twins who age at different rates due to differential motion will return from a journey genuinely different ages (Maudlin 2012: 47–76).

General relativity goes further still: the rate of time's passage is affected by gravity. A clock deeper in a gravitational well runs slower than one higher up. This is not a theoretical prediction with no practical consequences; GPS satellites must account for this effect or their location calculations drift by kilometers per day (Ashby 2002).

And the most radical challenge comes from attempts to unify quantum mechanics with general relativity. In the Wheeler-DeWitt equation — one of the central equations of canonical quantum gravity — time does not appear as a fundamental variable at all. The wavefunction of the universe is timeless; time, on some interpretations, must emerge from something more basic (DeWitt 1967; Barbour 1999: 229–271). Whether this is the last word on the physics of time remains deeply contested, but it reveals that even the physicist's conception of time is far less settled than it might appear.

##### Time as Metaphysical

Between the phenomenological and the physical sits a set of distinctively metaphysical questions — questions about what kinds of things exist, what properties they have, and how they relate to one another — that neither experience nor physics alone can settle.

The most fundamental of these concerns *what times there are*. Are only present things real, with past and future things having no genuine ontological status? This is the view called *presentism*. Or do past, present, and future things all exist equally, the "present" being merely the time we happen to be at — just as "here" names the place you happen to be, with no implication that other places are less real? This is *eternalism* or the *block universe* view. Or is there a growing ontological totality — the past and present are real, the future is not yet, and time genuinely grows as new events occur? This is the *growing block* view (Broad 1923: 66–84).

These options are not distinguished by physical predictions — the physics is, to a significant degree, neutral between them — and they are not resolved by the phenomenology of experience, since experience is consistent with several of the views. They are purely metaphysical questions about the fundamental ontological structure of the temporal world.

Other metaphysical questions about time include: Does time have a direction, and if so, what grounds it? What is the relationship between time and causation? Does change require time, or does time require change? Can there be time without events? Is the universe's temporal structure discrete or continuous? Could time have a topology different from a simple linear order — circular, branching, or closed?

##### The Intersection and Its Tensions

What is important to grasp at the outset is that these three domains — experiential, physical, and metaphysical — are not sealed off from one another. They interact and constrain each other in complex ways, and a recurring challenge throughout this book will be to keep the interactions clear.

Consider one example of the tension. Our experience of time presents it as *flowing* — as having a direction, a "moving now," a genuine passage from past through present to future. This is one of the most vivid and pervasive features of temporal experience. But many philosophers and physicists hold that physical time is static: the block universe, if correct, contains no objective flow, no moving now, no genuine becoming. If this is right, then the experienced flow of time is in some sense an illusion generated by the structure of consciousness — it is not a feature of time itself (Price 1996: 12–14; Callender 2000).

Whether this conclusion should be accepted — whether physics really does mandate a static conception of time and whether the phenomenology of flow must therefore be debunked — is one of the deepest and most contested questions in the entire field. It will occupy us in Unit V, Unit VII, and Unit VIII. For now, the point is simply that the question cannot be answered by attending to one domain alone. You cannot settle it by phenomenology, because the phenomenology might be misleading about metaphysics. You cannot settle it by physics, because the physics underdetermines the metaphysics. And you cannot settle it by pure conceptual analysis, because the question has empirical components. You need all three tools, and you need to be careful about how they interact.

#### 1.1.3 — The Gap Between Ordinary Talk About Time and Theoretical Accounts

---

When you say "I'll meet you in an hour," nobody is confused. When you say "that was a long time ago," your listener understands immediately. When you say "things were better then," or "the future is uncertain," or "she died before he was born," you are communicating temporal information with perfect efficiency. Ordinary temporal language is rich, flexible, and in constant practical use.

But look more closely at some of the things we say — really look at them — and they begin to seem stranger.

##### The Vocabulary of Temporal Experience

We speak of time as something that *passes* or *flows*. We say "time flies," "how quickly this afternoon has gone," "the years seem to slip by faster as you get older." These idioms treat time as something that moves — presumably relative to some fixed reference point. But relative to what? In ordinary spatial motion, when we say a train moves, we mean it moves relative to the track or the earth. When we say time passes, what is time moving relative to? If everything is in time — every event, every process, every observer — then there is nothing *outside* time relative to which it could be measured as moving. The notion of time's flow threatens to be incoherent, or at least deeply obscure (Williams 1951: 464–465; Smart 1949: 483–484).

We speak of the present as a kind of *location* — where we are in time. "I'm stuck in the present," someone might joke. "If only I could see the future." This spatial metaphor — the present as a place, the future as somewhere we haven't yet arrived — is so natural and so pervasive that it is difficult even to notice that it *is* a metaphor. And like all metaphors, it can illuminate some aspects of a phenomenon while obscuring others. In space, you can move in any direction you choose. In time, there seems to be only one direction available to you. In space, other places are simultaneous with where you are — they exist right now, even though you are not there. In time, the future does not exist yet (at least according to some views), and the past no longer exists. The spatial metaphor breaks down at exactly the points where temporal experience is most distinctive.

We speak of the past as *fixed* and the future as *open*. "What's done is done." "Anything could happen." This asymmetry — the immutability of the past versus the indeterminacy of the future — is one of the deepest features of ordinary temporal thinking. And yet from the standpoint of physics, it is puzzling. The fundamental laws of physics (with minor exceptions we will discuss in Chapter 18) are time-symmetric: they work equally well run forwards or backwards. Nothing in the laws singles out a direction. The asymmetry between past and future — the sense in which the past is fixed and the future open — must therefore come from somewhere else: from the initial conditions of the universe, from thermodynamics, from the structure of causation, from the nature of agency. Where exactly it comes from is, as we will see, one of the deepest questions in the entire field.

##### The Problem of Tense

Perhaps the deepest divergence between ordinary temporal talk and theoretical accounts concerns *tense* — the grammatical feature of language that marks events as past, present, or future. When I say "the meeting *is* happening," I mean something different from "the meeting *was* happening" and different again from "the meeting *will* happening." Tense is not merely a grammatical convention; it is how we express something about the temporal position of events relative to the moment of utterance.

But many philosophers of time — those who favor the B-theory, which we will examine closely in Chapter 14 — argue that tense is in a significant sense a *misleading* feature of language. Their claim is that the real temporal structure of the world consists entirely of *tenseless* relations: the fact that event A is earlier than event B, or that B is later than A, or that A and B are simultaneous. On this view, there is no fact of the matter about which events are *now* happening, independent of a perspective. "Now" is like "here" — it picks out a position relative to the utterer, not an objective feature of the world. The proper way to describe temporal reality, they argue, is in terms of these tenseless before-and-after relations, with no irreducible use of past, present, or future (Mellor 1998: 1–20; Russell 1903: 469–471).

This view is philosophically coherent, and there are good reasons to take it seriously. But it is deeply revisionary. It implies that ordinary temporal talk — all that rich, practical, phenomenologically saturated talk of the past and future and present — involves a form of systematic distortion when taken at face value. It implies that the "nowness" of the present is not an objective feature of time but a perspectival feature of the mind. That conclusion may be correct, but it should not be adopted lightly, and it certainly should not be adopted before we have examined the alternatives.

##### Two Models of the Problem

There is a useful way of thinking about the gap between ordinary talk and theoretical account that will be helpful throughout this book. We can distinguish between two models of what philosophy of time is trying to do.

On the first model — call it *descriptive metaphysics* (a phrase borrowed from Strawson 1959) — the goal is to articulate and systematize the conceptual scheme implicit in ordinary temporal talk and thought. What does it presuppose about the structure of time? What commitments does it carry that might be made explicit? On this model, the intuitive conviction that the present is special, that the past is fixed, that time flows in a particular direction — these are *data* that a theory of time must accommodate or explain away.

On the second model — call it *revisionary metaphysics* — the goal is to arrive at the *true* account of temporal reality, even if this requires departing significantly from ordinary intuitions. On this model, ordinary temporal talk may embed systematic errors: perhaps time does not really flow, perhaps the present is not objectively special, perhaps tense is not a real feature of the world. Science and rigorous argument, not intuition, are the guides.

Both models have their defenders, and both have their dangers. The descriptive model risks making intuition too authoritative, ignoring the possibility that our pre-theoretical picture of time might be seriously wrong. The revisionary model risks an overconfidence in its ability to derive metaphysical conclusions from physics, ignoring the genuine evidential weight of how time appears to us from the inside.

The best approach — and the one this book will attempt to model — holds both commitments in productive tension. Ordinary temporal talk is taken seriously as data; departures from ordinary intuitions require genuine justification; and the goal is an account that does justice to both what time is like in experience and what the best available physics and metaphysics tells us it is.

### Section 1.2: The Methods of Philosophy Applied to Time

---

#### Section Introduction

Philosophy is sometimes described as the discipline that lacks a method. Scientists run experiments, mathematicians prove theorems, historians consult archives. What do philosophers do? The question is not entirely unfair, but the honest answer is that philosophers use a cluster of methods — some shared with other disciplines, some distinctive — and the choice of method matters enormously to the results you get.

In the philosophy of time, four methods are particularly important: *conceptual analysis* (examining what our temporal concepts mean and what they presuppose), *intuition pumps and thought experiments* (using carefully crafted hypothetical scenarios to test and develop theories), *reflective equilibrium* (the iterative process of bringing intuitions and principles into coherent alignment), and *naturalistic and revisionary approaches* (letting science constrain or even revise philosophical conclusions). This section introduces each of these and, crucially, begins to assess their limitations — because in the philosophy of time, the limitations of methods are at least as instructive as their successes.

#### 1.2.1 — Conceptual Analysis

---

The classical project of conceptual analysis is as old as Socrates: to take a concept we use fluently in practice — courage, knowledge, justice — and articulate the necessary and sufficient conditions for its application. What must be true for something to be an instance of knowledge? Plato's *Theaetetus* suggests: justified true belief. What must be true for someone to count as courageous? The analysis proceeds by proposing a definition and then testing it against cases — including, especially, counterexamples that expose where the proposed definition goes wrong.

Applied to time, conceptual analysis asks: what does it mean for something to be temporal? What distinguishes a temporal sequence from a non-temporal one? What must be true for two events to stand in the relation "earlier than"? What are the conditions under which we would say a particular moment is *present*?

##### What Conceptual Analysis Can Accomplish

At its best, conceptual analysis achieves two things. First, it makes *implicit commitments explicit*. When we say "the meeting was before the lecture," we are committed to a relation between two events that is asymmetric (if A is before B, then B is not before A), irreflexive (nothing is before itself), and transitive (if A is before B and B is before C, then A is before C). These are logical properties of the relation of temporal precedence, and they constrain what a theory of time must look like. They are commitments we had all along; conceptual analysis just surfaces them.

Second, conceptual analysis can identify *tensions and inconsistencies* in our ordinary thinking. Consider the following cluster of ordinary temporal beliefs: (a) only the present is real; (b) the past was once present; (c) the past is gone. These three seem individually compelling, but they pull against one another in subtle ways. If only the present is real, and the past is no longer present, then the past is not real — which seems to conflict with (b), which attributes reality to the past "when it was present." Conceptual analysis makes this tension visible, so we can decide whether to resolve it by revision, by contextual disambiguation, or by adopting one of the metaphysical theories we will examine in Unit V.

##### The Limits of Conceptual Analysis

The method has two important limitations in the philosophy of time.

First, there is the problem of *concept empiricism*: our temporal concepts may be shaped by features of our specific perceptual and cognitive architecture in ways that do not reflect the metaphysical structure of time itself. The concept of a "present moment," for instance, may be shaped by the width of our specious present (approximately 2–3 seconds) rather than by anything metaphysically fundamental. If so, analyzing the concept of the present may tell us more about human temporal cognition than about temporal reality. We will return to this point in Chapter 27.

Second, there is what Quine (1951) called the challenge to the *analytic-synthetic distinction*: the sharp line between claims that are true in virtue of meaning (analytic) and claims that are true in virtue of the world (synthetic) may not be as clear as the method of conceptual analysis assumes. If there is no sharp line, then "conceptual truths" about time may be partly empirical — revisable in light of new evidence. This does not destroy the method, but it does chastening. Conceptual analysis is not a way of arriving at necessary truths that are immune to empirical revision; it is a way of making our current commitments explicit so that they can be held up to scrutiny.

##### Conceptual Analysis in Practice: The Case of "Earlier Than"

Consider a concrete example. The concept *earlier than* seems to have the following features: it is a two-place relation between events; it is asymmetric, irreflexive, and transitive; it is total or at least dense; and it is connected to causation (causes are earlier than their effects) and to memory (we remember earlier events, not later ones).

Now, special relativity tells us that the relation *earlier than* is not, in general, frame-independent. Whether A is earlier than B depends on the reference frame of the observer. Does this mean our concept of "earlier than" is confused or incoherent? Or does it mean that what we ordinarily call "earlier than" is really a composite of different relations (proper-time ordering, causal precedence, simultaneity-relative ordering) that come apart in the relativistic regime?

The answer shapes everything. If our ordinary concept of "earlier than" is irrevocably committed to frame-independence, then special relativity shows that concept to be inapplicable to physical time — and the correct concept of temporal ordering must be the frame-relative one. If instead our ordinary concept is neutral between frame-dependent and frame-independent versions, then we can accommodate relativity without concluding that our pre-theoretic temporal concepts are mistaken.

This is not a merely verbal question. Which answer we give affects what we think special relativity shows about the *nature* of time — about whether the present is objective, whether presentism is coherent, whether the passage of time is real. The methods of conceptual analysis and of physics must cooperate to answer it.

#### 1.2.2 — Intuition Pumps and Thought Experiments

---

One of the distinctive contributions of analytic philosophy to the practice of inquiry is the systematic use of thought experiments. Thought experiments are carefully constructed hypothetical scenarios designed to elicit intuitions about how a concept applies or how a principle holds. They are not idle speculation; they are precision instruments for probing the structure of our commitments.

The philosopher Daniel Dennett, who has written extensively about thought experiments, coined the term "intuition pump" to describe them — sometimes approvingly, sometimes as a mild warning. An intuition pump can illuminate genuine features of the conceptual landscape, but it can also be constructed in ways that generate misleading intuitions, smuggling in assumptions that bias the result (Dennett 1991: 37–39). The best philosophers of time have been both prolific users of thought experiments and appropriately vigilant about their limits.

##### Classic Thought Experiments in the Philosophy of Time

**The Twin Paradox.** Albert Einstein's special theory of relativity, developed in 1905, is richly illustrated by a thought experiment that became one of the most famous in all of philosophy and physics: the twin paradox. Imagine two twins, Alicia and Bruno. Alicia boards a rocket and travels at a very high velocity to a distant star and back. Bruno stays home. When Alicia returns, she is younger than Bruno — measurably, genuinely younger. This is not a psychological effect; her cells have divided fewer times; she has aged less. Time passed more slowly for the moving twin.

This thought experiment functions simultaneously as an illustration of a physical consequence and as a philosophical provocation. If Alicia's time and Bruno's time can diverge, in what sense is there one shared objective time? If different frames have different temporal rates, can there be an objective "now" that applies to both twins simultaneously? The thought experiment forces you to feel the puzzlement at the foundations of temporal physics.

**The Eternal Return.** Nietzsche's thought experiment of the Eternal Return (presented most dramatically in *Thus Spoke Zarathustra* and in a note from *The Gay Science*, §341) asks: what if every moment of your life, in every detail, recurred infinitely many times? Could you affirm such a thought, or would it be intolerable? Philosophically, the thought experiment is also a probe of circular temporal topology: if time is literally circular, then every event recurs identically — yet what would the identity of an "earlier" and "later" occurrence mean when the recurrence is perfect? It tests both our concepts of identity through time and our commitments about the topology of time.

**Gödel's Rotating Universe.** In 1949, Kurt Gödel published a mathematical solution to Einstein's field equations describing a universe that rotates as a whole. In such a universe, there exist closed timelike curves — paths through spacetime that loop back to their own starting point. Gödel himself drew a striking philosophical conclusion from this: if such a universe is *physically possible*, then the flow of time and the objective present cannot be fundamental features of physical reality, even in our actual universe. The thought experiment (here backed by actual physics) is a test of how much weight we should place on our intuition that time flows (Gödel 1949: 558–560). We will examine Gödel's argument carefully in Chapter 22.

##### What Thought Experiments Test — and Can Mislead About

Thought experiments are at their best when they test the *consistency* and *applicability* of concepts: do they extend cleanly to unusual cases? When they conflict with firm intuitions, that conflict is evidence that something is wrong with the concept, or with the theory, or with the design of the thought experiment. The task is to determine which.

Thought experiments are at their worst when they rely on *unexamined background assumptions*. Consider the classic "grandfather paradox" of time travel: a time traveler goes back in time and kills her grandfather, so that she was never born, so that she could not have gone back. The thought experiment is supposed to show that backward time travel is impossible. But on examination, the argument depends on background assumptions about personal identity, causation, and the topology of time that are themselves contested. Recognizing this does not show the paradox is harmless; it shows that what seems like a simple intuition is actually a tangle of commitments that need to be unwound separately.

##### A Methodological Principle

Here is a principle worth taking seriously throughout this book: *a thought experiment's evidential weight is proportional to the firmness of the intuition it elicits and inversely proportional to the complexity of the background assumptions it requires*. A thought experiment that generates a very firm, nearly universal intuition — and that does so without requiring the reader to accept contested background assumptions — is highly evidential. A thought experiment that depends on complicated stipulations and generates an uncertain or divided intuition is less so.

By this standard, Zeno's paradoxes (examined in Chapter 3) score very high: they generate firm intuitions about the impossibility of infinite divisibility traversal, and they do so from very simple premises. Their resolution has therefore required genuine conceptual work over two millennia. The grandfather paradox scores lower: it generates a moderately firm intuition, but it depends on assumptions about temporal topology and personal identity that, once examined, undermine its apparent force.

This does not mean we should ignore thought experiments with complex background assumptions — only that we should use them as occasions to examine the assumptions, not as quick knockdown arguments.

---

#### 1.2.3 — Reflective Equilibrium

---

Imagine you are trying to work out your ethical commitments. You have some considered judgments about particular cases — it is wrong to torture innocents for entertainment; it is admirable to help strangers in distress. You also have some general principles — perhaps "maximize welfare" or "respect persons as ends." The method of *reflective equilibrium*, introduced by John Rawls in the context of moral theory (Rawls 1971: 46–53) and extended to epistemology and metaphysics, describes the process of moving back and forth between particular judgments and general principles, adjusting each in light of the other, until you arrive at a coherent and stable system.

The starting point is always this: when the principle conflicts with a firm particular judgment, you have a choice. You can revise the judgment (concluding that your initial intuition was mistaken) or revise the principle (concluding that the principle is too strong). The method provides no algorithm for choosing; it requires judgment about which commitments are firmest. The goal is a state of coherence — what Rawls called "wide reflective equilibrium" — in which principles and particular judgments are mutually supporting, neither flatly inconsistent nor merely accidentally related.

##### Applying Reflective Equilibrium to the Philosophy of Time

The method of reflective equilibrium applies directly to temporal inquiry, and it disciplines the use of thought experiments. Consider the following constellation of commitments:

**Intuitions about particular cases:**
1. The present moment is special — uniquely real — in a way that past and future moments are not.
2. Events in the past happened; they are fixed and nothing can change them.
3. Events in the future are open; whether they happen depends on what we and others do.
4. The temporal distance between two events — how long ago, how far in the future — is an objective fact.

**General principles candidates:**
P1. All times are ontologically equal: the past, present, and future are equally real.  
P2. Only present things exist.  
P3. The past and present exist; the future does not yet.  
P4. There is no observer-independent fact about simultaneity.

Intuition 1 conflicts with P1. If all times are equally real, why does the present feel uniquely special? Perhaps, P1's defenders say, because we are *at* the present — just as a place feels special when you are there, not because it is objectively special. Intuition 2 supports both P1 (the past is real, so fixed) and P2 (the past was real when it was present — now it is gone, which is why it is fixed). Intuition 3 conflicts with P1: if the future is equally real, it is "already there" and its being open seems illusory. Principle P4 conflicts with intuition 4: if temporal distance is objective but simultaneity is not, how do we measure distance from one event to another?

Reflective equilibrium asks: given all these conflicts, what should be revised? The B-theorist (who adopts something like P1 and P4) concludes that intuitions 1 and 3 are systematically misleading — they reflect our perspectival position in time, not its objective structure. The presentist (who adopts P2) accepts intuition 1 at face value but faces serious challenges from P4. The growing block theorist (who adopts something like P3) splits the difference but faces the epistemological challenge of knowing which block we are at the edge of.

This is genuine philosophical work, and it has no algorithmic resolution. Different philosophers weight their commitments differently, and the debate is live.

##### The Discipline the Method Provides

What reflective equilibrium provides, importantly, is a *discipline*: it prevents both the pure rationalist move of simply deducing conclusions from axioms (ignoring the weight of intuitions) and the pure intuitionist move of simply insisting on intuitions (ignoring theoretical pressure). In the philosophy of time, both moves are tempting and both are mistakes.

The pure rationalist move is tempting because the physics is elegant and the metaphysics is amenable to formal treatment. It is easy to feel that the block universe — with its clean four-dimensional geometry — is simply *obviously* correct, and that anyone who insists on an objective present is just confused. But this is to give too much weight to theoretical elegance and too little to phenomenological data. The experience of the present as uniquely real is not a trivial or negligible datum; it is an extremely pervasive, detailed, and compelling feature of the human situation.

The pure intuitionist move is tempting because our temporal experience is so vivid and immediate. It is easy to feel that the block universe must be wrong because we *know* time flows — we feel it. But this is to give too much weight to phenomenology and too little to physical theory, which has repeatedly surprised us by showing that things are structured very differently from how they appear.

Reflective equilibrium keeps both pressures in play. It is the method of theoretical humility: willing to revise either theories or intuitions, but only under genuine pressure, and with eyes open about what is being abandoned.

---

#### 1.2.4 — Naturalistic and Revisionary Approaches

---

The methods discussed so far — conceptual analysis, thought experiments, reflective equilibrium — operate primarily within the space of concepts and intuitions. They start from what we ordinarily think and work to make it coherent. But there is a long tradition in philosophy that is skeptical of this starting point: perhaps ordinary concepts and intuitions are too anthropocentric, too parochial, too limited by our evolutionary and cultural inheritance to serve as reliable guides to the deep structure of reality. On this view, philosophy should be *naturalistic* — taking its cue from science — or even *revisionary* — willing to abandon ordinary concepts wholesale if they conflict with our best theoretical understanding.

In the philosophy of time, naturalistic and revisionary pressures are especially acute, because physics has so dramatically revised what we thought we knew about time. This subsection examines what these approaches consist in and where they lead.

##### Naturalism in the Philosophy of Time

The naturalistic approach to time, most prominently associated with Willard Van Orman Quine and developed in different ways by philosophers like David Lewis, David Albert, and Tim Maudlin, holds that philosophical theories of time must be *continuous* with — and ultimately constrained by — our best scientific theories. Philosophy and science are not two separate enterprises with separate subject matters; they are part of a single ongoing inquiry into the nature of reality, differing in degree of generality rather than in kind (Quine 1969: 126–127).

For the naturalist, what Newton's mechanics tells us about time, what Einstein's relativity tells us about time, and what quantum gravity (when we have a coherent version) tells us about time, are all data that any adequate philosophical theory of time must accommodate. Philosophy cannot arrive at truths about time by *a priori* reasoning alone; it cannot simply deduce the structure of time from the armchair. The armchair is useful for conceptual work, but the empirical content of our temporal concepts must ultimately be answerable to physics.

This does not mean that philosophy simply reads off metaphysics from physics, which would be naive. As we saw in subsection 1.1.2, physics underdetermines metaphysics: the same physical theories are compatible with multiple metaphysical interpretations. What naturalism requires is not that philosophy take physics' dictates as final, but that it take physics seriously as evidence — that philosophical theories which conflict with well-established physics are suspect, and that philosophical theories which are best motivated by physics are, other things equal, preferable.

##### The Revisionary Impulse

The *revisionary* approach goes further than naturalism. The revisionary metaphysician holds that ordinary concepts of time — the flow of time, the objective present, the fixity of the past — are not merely incomplete but positively mistaken, and that a proper philosophical and scientific account will require replacing them.

J.J.C. Smart, writing in the 1950s, articulated perhaps the most direct version of this view: the concept of time as flowing, as having a "river of time" that carries us from past to future, is incoherent — there is no sense that can be made of it; it should be abandoned, not analyzed (Smart 1949; 1980). D.H. Mellor, in a series of important papers and books culminating in *Real Time II* (1998), argued that tensed facts — facts about what is past, present, or future — are not real features of the world but are systematically reducible to tenseless facts about temporal relations. Nothing is "really" present; "present" means nothing more than "simultaneous with this utterance."

These revisionary views have important implications. If they are correct, then a large portion of what ordinary people think about time is wrong. The "nowness" of the present, the "passage" of time, the "openness" of the future — all of these are illusions, projections of our cognitive structure onto a static four-dimensional manifold. Whether this conclusion is correct is one of the central disputes of the philosophy of time and will occupy much of this book.

##### The Case for Taking Ordinary Intuitions Seriously

One should not capitulate to revisionary pressure without strong reasons. Ordinary temporal intuitions are not merely psychological curiosities; they are the data that any theory of time must ultimately answer to. The world appears to us as temporal; the appearance of temporality is the most pervasive structural feature of experience. A theory that explains away this appearance must offer an account of why it appears — and that account must be both empirically and philosophically convincing.

Moreover, revisionary arguments often conceal dependencies on the very intuitions they claim to revise. When Smart argues that the concept of temporal flow is incoherent because flow requires a second temporal dimension against which the first can be measured, he is relying on an intuition about what flow consists in (involving a rate) to argue that temporal flow is incoherent. If the ordinary person's concept of temporal flow does not involve a rate — if it is a different kind of phenomenon from spatial flow — then Smart's argument misses its target. Identifying these hidden dependencies is a large part of what careful philosophical work in this area consists in.

The lesson is methodological: revisionary arguments are worth taking seriously, but they must be scrutinized as carefully as the ordinary intuitions they challenge. Revision must be earned.

---

### Section 1.3: Philosophy and Physics — Complements or Competitors?

---

#### Section Introduction

Perhaps the most practically urgent methodological question in the philosophy of time is this: what is the relationship between what philosophers say about time and what physicists say about it? Are these two independent inquiries that can proceed in isolation? Are they competitive claims about the same subject, so that one must win and the other lose? Or are they genuinely complementary — addressing different aspects of the same phenomenon, with each depending on and informing the other?

The answer matters enormously for how you read this book. If physics has already answered the questions of the philosophy of time, then much of what follows is merely historical. If physics is irrelevant to those questions, then much of what follows in the physics chapters (Unit VII) is mere background. Neither extreme is right. The relationship is complex, productive, and irreducibly tense — and understanding its character is itself a significant philosophical achievement.

This section examines three aspects of this relationship: when physics settles philosophical questions; when philosophical questions go beyond anything physics can settle; and the "two-way street" by which philosophical analysis informs how we interpret physical theories, and physical results constrain and motivate philosophical hypotheses.

#### 1.3.1 — When Physics Settles Philosophical Questions

---

There is a temptation, especially among scientifically minded philosophers, to think that philosophy is merely "pre-science" — the confused early stage of an inquiry that, once properly formalized and subjected to empirical test, becomes science and leaves philosophy behind. On this view, philosophical questions about time are provisional questions that were asked before physics had the tools to answer them, and now that those tools exist, the questions are answered.

There is something to this view, and it would be intellectually dishonest to deny it. Physics has settled some philosophical questions about time. Let us be specific about which ones.

##### Genuine Philosophical Progress from Physics

**The question of absolute versus relational time.** From Aristotle through Newton, a central question was whether time is an independent entity (a kind of container in which events occur) or whether it consists entirely of relations among events. Newton defended the first view; Leibniz attacked it; the debate seemed philosophically intractable (see Chapter 10). Einstein's special relativity did not *definitively* settle this question, but it decisively changed its terms. Without a preferred frame of reference, there is no fact of the matter about what is happening "at the same time" at distant locations — a result that removes one of the most compelling motivations for absolute Newtonian time. The relational character of temporal facts has been substantially vindicated (Maudlin 2012: 60–68).

**The eternity of the world.** For much of the Western philosophical and theological tradition, the question of whether the world (and time) had a beginning was both philosophically and theologically live. Kant thought it was antinomial — neither answer could be established by reason alone. Modern cosmology has transformed this debate: we have compelling empirical evidence that the universe had a beginning roughly 13.8 billion years ago, and the best current models describe what that beginning was like (at least down to a Planck time of ~10⁻⁴³ seconds). This does not close every philosophical question about temporal origins — quantum gravity may revise the picture, and the question of *why* there was a Big Bang remains open — but it rules out the eternalist answer in its simple classical form.

**The universality of temporal flow.** Newton's assumption of a single universal time — the same for all observers, everywhere — has been decisively refuted. Different observers, moving at different velocities or occupying different gravitational fields, genuinely experience different amounts of time passing. This is not a theoretical nicety; it is measured every day by GPS satellites (Ashby 2002). Any philosophy of time must accommodate this fact.

##### What This Means for Method

The lesson is not that physics is sufficient for philosophy of time. It is that philosophical theorizing about time cannot proceed in empirical isolation. A philosophical theory of time that requires universal Newtonian simultaneity, or that requires the world to be eternal, or that requires all observers to share a single temporal experience, is not merely philosophically inadequate — it is *false*, ruled out by the evidence.

Philosophers of time must therefore be scientifically literate. They do not need to derive tensor equations, but they need to understand what the equations say and what they imply for temporal structure. A philosopher who argues confidently for presentism without engaging seriously with special relativity is like a philosopher who argues about species without knowing what Darwin established. The engagement is not optional.

---

#### 1.3.2 — When Philosophy Must Go Beyond Physics

---

If physics settles some philosophical questions about time, it equally fails to settle others — and these are often the ones that matter most for the philosophy of time. The incompleteness of physics as a guide to temporal metaphysics is not a temporary deficiency that better physics will remedy; it is a structural feature of the relationship between empirical science and metaphysical interpretation.

##### The Underdetermination Problem

The core issue is *underdetermination*: multiple, incompatible metaphysical interpretations are consistent with the same physical theory. This is not a new observation; it was articulated clearly by Pierre Duhem in the context of classical physics (Duhem 1906/1954) and has been extensively studied in contemporary philosophy of science. Applied to time, it means that the same physical equations — the same predictions, the same empirical tests, the same observational consequences — are compatible with metaphysical theories that disagree profoundly about what is *real*.

The block universe interpretation and the presentist interpretation, for instance, give identical physical predictions. Both are consistent with special relativity, with the measured rate of clocks, with the entropy gradient, with every physical experiment ever performed. They disagree about whether the past and future *exist*, about whether there is an objective "now," about whether the universe is fundamentally static or dynamic. These are metaphysical disagreements that physics, by itself, cannot settle.

This is not because physics is insufficiently developed; it is because the question "which times are real?" is not a question about observable phenomena. Observational equivalence holds between the block universe and its alternatives in principle, not merely in practice.

##### Questions Physics Does Not Address

Several major questions in the philosophy of time are, in this sense, beyond physics:

**The ontological status of times.** Are past, present, and future events all equally real? Or does only the present exist? Physics uses a four-dimensional formalism, but the formalism does not *assert* that all four dimensions are equally real; it simply uses them as coordinates. The metaphysical question of what is real is a further question that the formalism leaves open.

**The phenomenology of temporal experience.** Physics has nothing to say about what it is *like* to be in time — about the peculiar character of the experienced present, the phenomenal difference between the lived now and the remembered then, the feeling that time flows. These are questions about consciousness and experience. Even a complete physics of temporal structure would leave these questions untouched, just as a complete physics of light and surface reflection leaves untouched the question of why red *looks* the way it does to a conscious observer.

**The direction of time as normative vs. descriptive.** Physics describes the thermodynamic arrow of time — entropy tends to increase in one direction. But the question of whether this makes that direction the "true" direction of time, whether there is something wrong with the other direction, whether the future is "really" open in a way the past is not — these are normative or interpretive questions that no amount of thermodynamic data settles (Price 1996: 1–16).

**Personal identity through time.** What makes you the same person who was here yesterday? This question about persistence through time — which we examine in Unit IX — depends on philosophical considerations about what constitutes a person, what makes a person the same person, how memory and psychological continuity contribute to identity. Physics has no account of persons; it deals with physical configurations, not persons. The philosophy of personal identity through time therefore requires distinctively philosophical tools.

##### The Danger of Physics-Imperialism

There is a form of intellectual overreach that might be called *physics imperialism* in the philosophy of time: the assumption that any philosophical claim that cannot be settled by physics is thereby confused or meaningless. This assumption has been influential — it is a descendant of logical positivism — but it is wrong.

The most direct argument against it: physicists themselves must interpret their equations, and interpretation is a philosophical activity. When Niels Bohr said the wavefunction should not be taken to represent a real physical state, and when Hugh Everett said it should, they were engaged in philosophical interpretation of a physical theory. When Barbour says quantum gravity shows time is unreal, and when Smolin says it shows time is the most real thing, they are engaged in philosophical argument about the implications of physical results. Physics does not automatically interpret itself. Philosophy of physics is genuinely necessary — not merely decorative.

---

#### 1.3.3 — The Two-Way Street: Philosophy and Physics in Dialogue

---

The relationship between philosophy and physics in the study of time is best described not as subordination in either direction but as a genuine *dialogue* — a two-way exchange in which each discipline contributes to and is constrained by the other. This dialogue has a long history. It produced Leibniz's critique of Newton, Mach's critique of absolute space and time, the neo-Kantian interpretation of special relativity, and the contemporary debate over what quantum gravity implies about temporal ontology. Understanding its structure helps us navigate the material that follows.

##### Philosophy Informing Physics: The Leibniz-Mach Tradition

The first direction of the exchange is philosophy constraining physics. Philosophers and philosophically minded scientists have repeatedly identified conceptual problems with physical theories that motivated theoretical revision.

Leibniz's critique of Newton is the paradigm case. Leibniz argued, on philosophical grounds (the Principle of Sufficient Reason and the Identity of Indiscernibles), that Newton's absolute time was metaphysically unjustified: if the world had been created one hour earlier, occupying the same absolute times plus one hour, there would be no difference in the relations between events — hence no reason to prefer one hypothesis over the other, hence no fact of the matter about absolute temporal position (Leibniz, Fifth Letter to Clarke, 1716). This philosophical critique was mathematically vindicated by Einstein two centuries later: special relativity eliminates the preferred temporal frame that Newton required.

Ernst Mach pressed an analogous critique against Newton's bucket argument. Newton claimed that the rotation of a bucket (relative to absolute space) was revealed by the concavity of the water's surface — proving that absolute space is real. Mach argued (on philosophical grounds of empirical meaningfulness) that the result could equally be interpreted as rotation relative to the fixed stars — the totality of matter in the universe (Mach 1883/1960: 271–284). Mach's Principle directly influenced Einstein's development of general relativity, in which (in a partial sense) the distribution of matter determines the inertial structure of spacetime.

In both cases, philosophical argument identified a tension or unjustified assumption in a physical theory, motivating theoretical development.

##### Physics Informing Philosophy: The Relativity Tradition

The second direction of the exchange is physics constraining philosophy. When physical theories are well-confirmed, they place genuine constraints on what philosophical theories can coherently maintain.

The relativity of simultaneity in special relativity is the clearest case. If there is no observer-independent fact about whether two spatially separated events are simultaneous, then any philosophical theory that requires an objective global present — a set of events that are all "happening now" — is in tension with the physics. Hilary Putnam drew the most direct conclusion: special relativity, together with plausible assumptions about the relationship between reality and the present, implies that all events in spacetime are equally real — the block universe. This argument (Putnam 1967) has been contested (Stein 1991; Zimmerman 2008), but it demonstrates the direct relevance of physical results to metaphysical conclusions.

Similarly, the discovery that entropy increases in one temporal direction — and the subsequent development of the statistical mechanical explanation of this increase — places constraints on philosophical accounts of the arrow of time. Any account of temporal direction that makes the thermodynamic arrow a mystery, or that denies that thermodynamic processes have an asymmetric temporal structure, is in tension with the physics.

##### The Indispensability of Interpretation

There is a further, deeper sense in which the relationship is two-way: physics cannot be understood without philosophical interpretation, and philosophical interpretation is constrained by physical theory. This is not a defect of physics; it is a structural feature of any theoretical enterprise.

When we say that special relativity "implies" the relativity of simultaneity, we are already interpreting: the equations of the Lorentz transformation relate coordinates, not necessarily facts about what exists. The inference from the coordinate transformation to the metaphysical conclusion that there is no objective simultaneity requires a philosophical premise about the relationship between coordinates and facts. Different philosophers make different choices about that premise and reach different metaphysical conclusions.

When we say that quantum gravity "suggests" that time is not fundamental, we are again interpreting: the Wheeler-DeWitt equation has no explicit time variable, but this may mean that time is not fundamental, or it may mean that the equation is expressed in a convenient formalism, or it may mean that our classical concept of time fails to apply at the quantum gravity scale while time as such remains real. Choosing between these interpretations is philosophical work.

This is the two-way street in its fullest form: physics and philosophy are neither independent nor in a relationship of simple authority, but are engaged in a continuous, mutually correcting dialogue. Philosophers of time who ignore physics are working with one hand tied behind their back. Physicists who think their equations automatically resolve philosophical questions are misreading what their equations say. The productive zone is the interface — and much of this book lives there.

### Section 1.4: A Map of the Terrain

---

#### Section Introduction

Every inquiry benefits from a map — not a final chart of fully explored territory, but a rough schematic that shows where the main regions are, how they connect, and which paths lead between them. The philosophy of time is large enough that it is easy to lose one's sense of the whole while working through a particular part. This section provides the orientation.

Four major regions of inquiry constitute the field: the *metaphysics of time* (ontological and structural questions about what time is and how it is structured); the *philosophy of physics of time* (questions about what physical theories imply about the nature and structure of time); the *phenomenology and psychology of time* (questions about how time is experienced and represented); and *time in ethics, identity, and existence* (questions about how temporal structure bears on practical and existential concerns). These regions are not sealed compartments; their questions interact, and some of the most interesting problems sit precisely at their boundaries.

#### 1.4.1 — Metaphysics of Time: Ontology, Topology, Direction

---

The metaphysics of time is the oldest and most central region of the philosophy of time. It asks questions about what time *is* at the most fundamental level — questions that are partly conceptual and partly ontological, and that connect to the broadest issues in general metaphysics.

##### The Ontology of Time: What Exists?

The most fundamental metaphysical question about time concerns which times exist. Three main positions have dominated the debate:

*Presentism* holds that only the present moment is real. The past has ceased to exist and the future does not yet exist; only what is happening now is real in the full, unqualified sense. This view has intuitive appeal: when you reach for an object, the past position of the object is gone and its future position does not yet exist; only its current position is there to be reached for.

*Eternalism* (the "block universe" view) holds that past, present, and future are all equally real — they are all "there" in the four-dimensional spacetime manifold, distinguished only by their temporal positions, not by any difference in ontological status. The present is to time what "here" is to space: the position you happen to occupy, not a privileged location in the metaphysical order of things. This view is strongly suggested by the spacetime structure of special relativity.

*The growing block theory*, proposed by C.D. Broad (1923), splits the difference: the past and present are real (they have "grown" into existence), but the future is not yet real. Time grows from a fixed beginning toward an open future.

Each of these positions generates its own philosophical difficulties, which we examine in detail in Unit V. The ontological question connects directly to questions of change, persistence, and identity — for what it means to persist through time depends on what times there are to persist through.

##### The Topology of Time: What Structure Does It Have?

Beyond the question of which times exist, there are structural questions about how times relate to one another — questions about the *topology* of time. These include:

*Linearity vs. circularity.* Is time ordered like a line (with a definite before-and-after everywhere) or like a circle (so that events eventually recur)? If time is circular, then every past event is also a future event, which has radical implications for causation and identity.

*Discreteness vs. continuity.* Are there ultimate, indivisible temporal atoms, or can time always be further divided? Quantum gravity suggests that time may be quantized at extremely small scales, but no definitive answer is available.

*Boundedness.* Does time have a beginning, an end, or both? The Big Bang cosmology suggests a beginning; physics makes no decisive prediction about an end. Kant thought the question was antinomial — unanswerable by pure reason.

*Branching.* Can the future branch into multiple distinct trajectories? Some interpretations of quantum mechanics suggest it can. This has implications for both the metaphysics of possibility and for the analysis of free will.

##### The Direction of Time: What Grounds the Arrow?

The laws of fundamental physics are (with minor exceptions) time-symmetric: they work equally well run forward or backward. Yet time as we experience it has a clear direction: the past is fixed, the future is open; entropy increases, not decreases; causes precede effects. The question of *what grounds this asymmetry* — what makes one direction of time special — is one of the deepest problems in the field, sitting at the intersection of physics and metaphysics. It is examined in Unit VI.

---

###### References

- Broad, C.D. *Scientific Thought*. London: Kegan Paul, 1923.
- Sider, Ted. *Four-Dimensionalism: An Ontology of Persistence and Time*. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001. Ch. 2.
- Le Poidevin, Robin. *Travels in Four Dimensions: The Enigmas of Space and Time*. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003. Part II.

#### 1.4.2 — Philosophy of Physics of Time

---

The philosophy of physics of time is, in a sense, the newest region of the field — not because the questions are new, but because the physical theories that frame them are. This region asks how the discoveries and formalism of modern physics bear on the metaphysics, ontology, and phenomenology of time. It requires philosophers to engage seriously with the content of physical theories, and physicists to engage seriously with the conceptual and interpretive issues their theories raise.

##### Special Relativity and the Geometry of Time

Special relativity (1905) replaced the Newtonian picture of absolute, universal time with a four-dimensional spacetime in which time and space are interwoven. The philosophical implications are substantial: temporal relations between distant events become frame-relative; the "present moment" loses its claim to objective universality; and the notion of a "block universe" — all events equally real in a static four-dimensional manifold — becomes the most natural interpretation of the theory's formalism.

The central philosophical question raised by special relativity is whether it *requires* the block universe interpretation, or merely *permits* it. Different answers yield different positions on the metaphysics of time. This debate, examined in Chapter 21, is the deepest single intersection of physics and metaphysics in the philosophy of time.

##### General Relativity and Dynamical Time

General relativity (1915) makes time dynamical: the rate of time's passage varies with the gravitational field, and the global temporal structure of spacetime depends on the distribution of matter. This raises philosophical questions that go beyond special relativity: what does it mean for time to be "curved"? Can time have exotic topological features — loops, branches? Does general relativity permit the physical possibility of time travel? What does the Big Bang singularity say about whether time had a beginning?

##### Thermodynamics and the Arrow

The second law of thermodynamics — entropy increases over time — is the most direct physical expression of time's asymmetry. Yet the microscopic laws are symmetric. Explaining this asymmetry is partly a physical problem (which David Albert 2000 addresses by positing a "Past Hypothesis" about the universe's initial conditions) and partly a philosophical one (whether the Past Hypothesis is explanatory, what explanatory success requires here, how probability enters the picture). This discussion spans Chapters 18 and 23.

##### Quantum Mechanics and Quantum Gravity

Quantum mechanics raises distinctive questions about time's role in physics: time is not an observable in standard QM; the measurement problem involves questions about when collapse occurs; some interpretations suggest that temporal structure at the fundamental level is very different from what classical physics assumed. And the search for a quantum theory of gravity — which must reconcile the dynamical time of GR with the parametric time of QM — has led to suggestions that time might not be fundamental at all, but emergent from a more basic non-temporal structure. These are among the most exciting and unsettled questions in contemporary philosophy of physics, examined in Chapters 24 and 25.

---
