If tenseless discourse is fundamental — if all temporal facts can ultimately be expressed in terms of permanent "earlier than" relations without any essential reference to a present moment — then the world, as described by physics, is a four-dimensional block of events, none of which is objectively present, past, or future. The sense of a moving now would be a kind of cognitive illusion, a perspectival artifact of conscious experience rather than a feature of objective reality.

If tensed discourse is fundamental — if there is no way to eliminate the essentially perspectival, present-oriented character of temporal talk — then the world has a genuine "now" built into it, and the A-series is as real as the B-series. The flow of time is not an illusion but a feature of the world's own structure.

This is not a merely verbal question. It matters to how we understand agency, consciousness, and the asymmetry between past and future. It matters to whether our practices of hoping, regretting, and planning are tracking something real about the difference between the future and the past. Getting this right is one of the central tasks of the philosophy of time.

---

**Key terms introduced:** A-series, B-series, tensed discourse, tenseless discourse, tense logic (Prior), token-reflexive analysis, A-theory, B-theory.

#### 2.3 Temporal Indexicals: "Now," "Then," "Yesterday," "Soon"

---

##### The Peculiar Logic of Context-Dependent Terms

"I am here now." This sentence, David Kaplan famously observed, is necessarily true: any utterance of it will be true (Kaplan 1989: 509). The speaker of the sentence is, by definition, wherever they are speaking from, at the moment they are speaking. And yet the sentence tells us nothing specific. It does not identify any particular person, place, or time. Its necessity is somehow empty — a formal property of how the words refer, not a deep metaphysical truth.

*Indexical expressions* are words and phrases whose reference shifts systematically with features of the context in which they are used. "I" refers to whoever is speaking; "here" refers to wherever the speaker is located; "this" refers to whatever object the speaker is indicating. These are *context-sensitive* terms: their semantic value is not fixed by meaning alone but by meaning together with context.

Temporal indexicals work in the same way. "Now" refers to the time of utterance; "yesterday" refers to the day preceding the day of utterance; "soon" picks out a time in the near future relative to the utterance time; "then" refers to some contextually salient time that is not the time of utterance. Understanding how these terms work — and why they raise special puzzles that purely spatial indexicals do not — is philosophically illuminating.

###### Kaplan's Framework

The most influential theoretical treatment of indexicals is David Kaplan's (1989). Kaplan introduced a systematic distinction between two kinds of meaning: *character* and *content*.

The *character* of an expression is a rule that, given a context, determines what the expression refers to in that context. The character of "I" is the rule: "refers to the agent of the context." The character of "now" is: "refers to the time of the context." Characters are constant across contexts — the rule never changes.

The *content* of an expression, by contrast, is what it contributes to the proposition expressed by a sentence in a particular context. When I say "now" at noon on May 20, 2026, the content of "now" is the time 12:00 PM, May 20, 2026. Content varies across contexts.

This two-level semantics allows Kaplan to explain several interesting features of indexicals. It explains why "I am here now" is true in every context (its character guarantees this), yet not necessarily true in the sense that might be metaphysically significant (the proposition it expresses is a contingent one). It also explains why indexical sentences cannot simply be replaced by their non-indexical equivalents without loss. "The lecture is happening now" and "The lecture is happening at 2:00 PM on May 20, 2026" express different propositions even if they are simultaneously uttered at 2:00 PM on May 20, 2026. The first is context-sensitive; the second is not (Kaplan 1989: 493–501).

###### "Now" vs. "Here": An Asymmetry

Spatial and temporal indexicals behave similarly in many ways. But there is a philosophical asymmetry between "now" and "here" that has attracted significant attention (Perry 1979; Sider 2001: 11–13).

Consider the spatial indexical "here." My current location — wherever I happen to be — is not metaphysically special. There is nothing philosophically distinctive about the place I happen to occupy: every place is on an ontological par. The specialness of "here" is purely perspectival: it is special to me, in my situation, but there is no sense in which my current location is *objectively* special or privileged.

Now consider "now." According to the folk conception — and, as we saw in the previous subsection, according to A-theorists — the present moment *is* objectively special. It is not merely the moment I happen to occupy; it is the moment that *is real*, the locus of existence, the place where the becoming is happening. On the A-theory, "now" picks out a genuinely privileged moment in the history of the universe in a way that "here" does not pick out a privileged place.

If the A-theory is right, "now" is not merely an indexical like "here." It refers to a property — *presentness* — that is distributed unevenly across time, present at some times and absent at others. The reference of "now" tracks this distribution. But "here" does not pick out anything analogous: there is no spatial analogue of presentness that distinguishes my current location objectively from all others.

On the B-theory, by contrast, the temporal case collapses back to the spatial case: "now" is just like "here," an indexical that picks out a time perspectivally, without any objective privilege. The asymmetry between temporal and spatial indexicals that the folk picture encodes is, on the B-theory, merely psychological — a feature of how temporally bound consciousness relates to a symmetrical temporal reality (Mellor 1998: 34–38).

This is a philosophically live dispute, and the linguistics of temporal indexicals is directly implicated in it.

###### The Semantics of "Yesterday" and Temporal Adverbs

While "now" raises the deepest metaphysical questions, the broader family of temporal indexicals is philosophically interesting for other reasons.

"Yesterday" does not merely pick out a time relative to the utterance; it picks out a *day* — a structured period, not an instant. This temporal granularity is philosophically interesting: temporal indexicals do not simply refer to points on a continuum but to temporally structured units (days, weeks, seasons) that are culturally and pragmatically significant. The structure of temporal indexical reference reflects the structure of human temporal experience, which is organized by the rhythms of natural cycles (light and dark, seasonal change) and social institutions (work weeks, fiscal years).

"Soon" and "recently" are *vague* temporal indexicals: they pick out a range of times without sharp boundaries, and the range shifts with context. "I'll be there soon" means something different in the context of a five-minute walk than in the context of an interstellar journey. This vagueness is not a defect; it is a practical resource. Human temporal planning and communication operate at many scales, and context-sensitive temporal vocabulary allows speakers to calibrate their claims appropriately without specifying exact quantities.

John Perry's work on indexicals and self-locating beliefs adds another dimension to this picture (Perry 1979). Perry argued that indexical beliefs — beliefs expressed using "I," "here," "now" — are irreducibly first-personal: they cannot be captured by any description that does not essentially refer to the agent's current context. A person who knows all the objective (B-series) facts about the world may still wonder, "Is *now* the time at which I have an appointment?" — and this question is not answered by any B-series fact. The temporal case generalizes this to "When is *now*?" — a question that presupposes a kind of self-location in time that no purely objective temporal description captures (Perry 1979: 3–21; also see Lewis 1979 on centered worlds).

###### What Temporal Indexicals Reveal

The linguistic study of temporal indexicals reveals two things of philosophical importance.

First, temporal language is essentially perspectival. Even if the world, in itself, is a B-series — a four-dimensional array of events ordered by permanent "earlier than" relations — temporal *discourse* is oriented toward a present. We speak from a now, looking backward to a past and forward to a future. This orientation is not merely optional or conventional; it is built into the grammar and semantics of natural language.

Second, the question of whether this orientation is a *cognitive fact* about speakers or a *metaphysical fact* about time itself is not settled by the linguistic data alone. The data are compatible with the A-theory (the orientation tracks objective presentness) and with the B-theory (the orientation reflects the perspectival character of context-sensitive reference). Linguistics sets the puzzle; philosophy must work to solve it.

---

**Key terms introduced:** indexical expression, character (Kaplan), content (Kaplan), temporal indexical, presentness, perspectivalism, self-locating belief.

### Section 3: Time in Myth, Religion, and Culture

---

#### Section Introduction

Philosophy did not invent the problem of time. Long before anyone wrote the word "metaphysics," human beings were constructing elaborate accounts of time's structure, origin, and meaning — accounts embedded in myth, ritual, cosmology, and theology. These accounts are not merely historical curiosities or pre-scientific approximations to the truth. They are repositories of genuine wisdom about time's phenomenological, social, and cosmological dimensions, and they reveal the range of ways in which the question of time's nature has been — and can be — approached.

This section surveys three areas of cultural time-thought. The first concerns cyclical time: the conception, found in Hindu cosmology, ancient Greek philosophy, and Mesoamerican calendar systems, that time does not run from a unique beginning to a unique end but rather repeats, loops, or revolves. Understanding cyclical time is philosophically important both because it represents a genuinely different temporal metaphysics and because it poses sharp challenges to intuitions about identity, freedom, and historical meaning that Western linear temporality takes for granted.

The second concerns the linear temporal frameworks embedded in the Abrahamic religious traditions. Creation, redemption, and eschatology — the beginning, middle, and end of sacred history — construct a framework in which time has a direction, a purpose, and a terminal point. This theological conception of linear, directed time had an enormous influence on Western philosophy's assumptions about temporal structure, and understanding it is essential for understanding why Western philosophy of time has the shape it does.

The third offers a brief and necessarily selective survey of non-Western temporal frameworks: Aboriginal Australian Dreamtime, Lakota temporal concepts, and Ubuntu's relational conception of time. The aim is not comprehensive ethnographic coverage but philosophical alertness: a reminder that the assumptions of Western academic philosophy about time are not universal human assumptions, and that other frameworks may illuminate aspects of temporal experience that the Western tradition overlooks or suppresses.

Throughout, the emphasis is philosophical rather than historical or anthropological. We are not primarily concerned with whether these accounts are historically accurate or scientifically defensible. We are concerned with what philosophical options they represent — what they take for granted, what they deny, and what they notice that other frameworks miss.

#### 3.1 Cyclical Time

---

##### Time That Comes Back Around

Imagine that the year 2026 is not merely similar to 2025, not merely the same type of year with the same kind of seasons and rhythms, but *literally the same year* — that history is not a line extending forward from a past that recedes and a future that approaches, but a great wheel, and that the events of this year are destined to recur, exactly as they have occurred, through an infinity of revolutions. This is the idea of cyclical time: not merely that nature is periodic, but that history itself returns.

The idea strikes most Western readers today as strange, even absurd. But it was held, in various forms, by many of the most sophisticated thinkers of the ancient world. Understanding why it was taken seriously — and what philosophical questions it forces into the open — is an important part of understanding the philosophy of time.

###### Hindu Cosmological Time

The most elaborately developed cyclical temporal cosmology is found in Hindu philosophical thought, particularly in the Puranas and in the speculative cosmology of the Mahabharata. The basic unit of cosmic time is the *kalpa*, a day of Brahma lasting 4.32 billion years. Each kalpa is divided into fourteen *manvantaras* (periods of Manu), each of which is itself divided into seventy-one *mahayugas*, great cycles of four ages (Lochtefeld 2002: 343–344).

Each *mahayuga* consists of four *yugas* of declining virtue and increasing suffering: the Satya Yuga (the golden age of perfection), the Treta Yuga, the Dvapara Yuga, and the Kali Yuga (the current age, characterized by conflict and spiritual decline). At the end of the Kali Yuga, the cosmos is destroyed and the cycle begins again. One kalpa is a day of Brahma; the god's night is an equal period of dissolution. The complete lifespan of Brahma — 100 divine years — is itself followed by a period of total dissolution before a new Brahma appears (Eliade 1954: 113–115).

The scale of Hindu cosmological time is staggering, and it was philosophically productive: it allowed Hindu thinkers to take the immensity of geological and cosmic time seriously long before Western science had the tools to do so. But the metaphysical significance of the cyclical structure goes beyond scale.

In a cyclical cosmology, the question of ultimate origins does not arise in the way it does in a linear cosmology. There is no first moment, no initial creation ex nihilo. Every beginning is a re-beginning, every creation a re-creation. The problem of what existed "before" time started — which is a genuine puzzle for linear cosmologies with a first moment — simply does not arise.

###### Ancient Greek Eternal Return

The idea of temporal cycles also appears in ancient Greek thought, though in a more philosophical and less mythological guise. The Stoics held that the universe passes through a series of great cycles, each beginning with the emergence of the cosmos from fire (ekpyrosis), passing through the familiar history of the world, and ending with the conflagration (ekpyrosis again) in which all things are dissolved back into fire, only to re-emerge in exactly the same form (Long and Sedley 1987: 274–276).

The Stoic eternal recurrence is not merely that similar events will occur again; it is that the *very same* events will occur, because the cosmic cycle is governed by the same rational principle (the *logos*) throughout. Socrates will drink hemlock again, in exactly the same circumstances, in the next cycle. The cycle is a literal repetition, not merely an analogy.

Friedrich Nietzsche revived and radicalized this idea in the nineteenth century under the name of the *Eternal Return of the Same* (Nietzsche 1974: §341). For Nietzsche, the thought that everything will recur eternally is a test of one's relationship to life: can you live in such a way that you would will the eternal recurrence of all your choices? The idea is less a cosmological claim than a psychological and ethical one — but it draws on the ancient philosophical picture.

###### Mesoamerican Calendar Systems

The Aztec calendar system illustrates a different form of cyclical time. The Aztec calendar interleaved two cycles: a 260-day ritual calendar (*tonalpohualli*) and a 365-day solar calendar (*xiuhpohualli*). Every 52 years, the two cycles aligned, producing what is sometimes called the Calendar Round — a period after which the same combination of day-name and year-name recurred (Clendinnen 1991: 21–24).

The end of each 52-year cycle was a time of collective anxiety among the Aztecs: would the sun rise again? Elaborate ritual (the New Fire ceremony) was performed to ensure the continuation of the cosmic order into the next cycle. Time was not a neutral background medium; it was a charged, dangerous, and potentially finite resource. The cycles of the calendar were the joints of a temporal structure that could fail.

The Maya possessed an even more sophisticated calendrical system, including the Long Count that measures time in units extending to millions of years — a system sufficiently precise to predict astronomical events with remarkable accuracy. The famous "Maya 2012 apocalypse" misrepresented a genuine feature of the Maya temporal framework: the completion of a 5,125-year cycle (*b'ak'tun*), not a predicted end of the world, but a transition between cosmic periods (Coe 1994: 63–67).

###### Philosophical Implications of Cyclical Time

What philosophical questions does cyclical time raise?

**Personal identity across recurrence.** If history literally repeats, in what sense is the Socrates of the next cycle *the same person* as Socrates in this one? He has the same properties, the same experiences, the same history — but no continuous causal connection to his "previous" instantiation. This is a hard question for the standard accounts of personal identity. Psychological continuity requires memory, and there is no memory across cycle-boundaries. Physical continuity requires an unbroken causal chain, and the conflagration breaks all such chains. Perhaps the cycles produce type-identical but numerically distinct individuals — but then Nietzsche's "eternal return of the *same*" becomes the eternal return of the *similar*, which is far less philosophically provocative.

**Freedom and fatalism.** If every event that occurs in this cycle has occurred in exactly the same form in infinitely many previous cycles and will occur in infinitely many future cycles, then the notion of genuine individual choice seems strained. What was there to choose, if your "choice" has been fixed through all the cycles? Linear time, by contrast, makes room for novelty, genuine alternatives, and historical uniqueness. The connection between linear time and meaningful freedom is not coincidental.

**The problem of temporal origin.** One powerful argument for cyclical time is that it avoids the cosmological regress: what happened before the first moment? In a linear time with a genuine beginning, this question has no answer (or requires appeal to a timeless cause). Cyclical time dissolves the question by eliminating the first moment.

**The measure of cosmic significance.** In a cyclical cosmos, no event is historically unique. What happens, happens again and again. In a linear cosmos with a beginning and an end, events can be singular, unrepeatable, and therefore (in a sense) supremely significant. The monotheistic sense that history is *going somewhere* — toward redemption, toward consummation — depends on the linear picture. Cyclical time, by contrast, embeds events in a structure that minimizes the significance of any particular moment.

These implications are genuine and deep. The choice between cyclical and linear temporal frameworks is not merely a question of cultural preference; it is a question about the structure of reality that has consequences for identity, freedom, and meaning.

---

**Key terms introduced:** kalpa, yuga, mahayuga, eternal recurrence, Calendar Round, cosmological cycle, temporal origin.

#### 3.2 Linear Time and the Abrahamic Traditions

---

##### Creation, Redemption, and the End of History

The idea that time has a unique beginning, a directional middle, and a final end — that history is an irreversible narrative with a plot and a terminus — is not a neutral or universal assumption. It is a deeply specific theological and cultural inheritance that Western philosophy has absorbed, often without acknowledgment, from its Jewish, Christian, and Islamic background. Understanding this inheritance is essential for understanding why the Western philosophy of time has the shape it does: its preoccupation with creation ex nihilo, its treatment of temporal passage as morally and metaphysically significant, and its assumption that the question of time's ultimate structure has a single determinate answer.

###### Creation Ex Nihilo

The opening words of Genesis — *Bereshit bara Elohim* ("In the beginning, God created") — are among the most philosophically charged words ever written. They assert that there was a beginning: a first moment before which nothing existed except God. The universe was created at a specific time, by a divine act, and has been running ever since.

This doctrine of *creatio ex nihilo* — creation out of nothing — poses immediate philosophical challenges. What was God doing before creation? Augustine's answer — that there was no "before," because time itself was created with the universe — is philosophically sophisticated and, as we shall see, anticipates aspects of modern cosmology (Augustine, *Confessions*, XI.13.16; XI.30.40). Time is not a container in which God existed waiting to create; time is itself part of the created order.

The philosophical implications are significant. If time has a genuine beginning — a first moment with no prior moment — then temporal experience has a directionality that is not merely conventional. Time runs from creation forward. Events are historically unique: they occur once, not as part of an infinite cycle. And the universe as a whole has a narrative shape: it is going somewhere, not merely cycling.

###### Eschatology and Directed History

Jewish, Christian, and Islamic accounts of time are not merely cosmological (about how time began) but eschatological (about how time will end and what it all means). The Hebrew prophetic tradition conceived history as a series of divine interventions — covenant, exile, return — oriented toward a messianic future. Christian theology added the belief that the decisive event of history — the Incarnation and Resurrection — had already occurred, dividing time into a pre-messianic before and a post-messianic after (Cullmann 1962: 17–23, 63–66). Islamic thought placed the Quran and the career of the Prophet at the culminating moment of prophetic history, with the Day of Judgment as its end point (Izutsu 1964: 129–137).

What all three traditions share is the sense that time is *directed* — it has a telos, an end toward which it moves. Events in history are not mere occurrences but *meaningful episodes* in a narrative that is moving toward a goal. This conception of meaningful, directed time is one of the most powerful ideas in Western culture. It shapes the way Western historians write history (as progress, or decline, or redemption), the way Western ethics understands moral responsibility (as tied to a temporally extended narrative of a life), and even the way Western science frames the question of cosmological evolution.

###### The Philosophical Legacy

Augustine's treatment of time in *Confessions* XI is the most philosophically profound confrontation between the Abrahamic conception of linear created time and the Greek philosophical tradition (Augustine, *Confessions*, XI.4–31). Augustine is acutely aware of the problem: if God exists outside time, and created time with the universe, then questions about "what came before" or "why did God wait so long" are malformed — they presuppose a temporal framework that applies to the created order but not to God.

This leads Augustine to a genuinely original philosophical position: time is not a feature of the external world but a "distension of the mind" (*distentio animi*). The past exists as memory, the future as anticipation, and the present as attention — all three as psychological modes of a consciousness that is stretched, distended, across the span of its experience (Augustine, *Confessions*, XI.26.33–XI.28.38). This is one of the earliest and most sophisticated phenomenological accounts of time, anticipating Husserl by fifteen centuries.

The Abrahamic linear-temporal framework also bequeathed to Western philosophy a distinctive set of *problems* that Greek philosophy had not posed in the same way:

- The problem of the first moment: Can time have a genuine beginning without an infinite temporal regress?
- The problem of eternity: Is God's existence simply very long (sempiternally), or is it genuinely outside time (timelessly)?
- The problem of divine foreknowledge: If God knows the future, is the future fixed? Does this threaten free will?
- The problem of eschatological time: What happens to time at the Last Day? Does time end, or does it transform into eternity?

These problems — all generated by the intersection of Abrahamic theology with Greek philosophy — set the agenda for much of medieval philosophy and continue to reverberate in contemporary discussions. Boethius's treatment of divine eternity in the *Consolation of Philosophy* (Boethius, *Consolatio* V.6, trans. Relihan), Aquinas's discussion of God's sempiternity versus timelessness (*Summa Theologica* I.10.1–4), and Plantinga's and Stump and Kretzmann's modern treatments all trace back to this fundamental collision (Stump and Kretzmann 1981; Leftow 1991).

###### The Legacy for Secular Philosophy

Even in the post-theological context of modern secular philosophy, the linear Abrahamic framework has left deep traces. The idea of historical *progress* — that events in human history form a narrative moving toward a better condition — is a secularized form of eschatological thinking, visible in Kant's philosophy of history, Hegel's dialectic, Marx's historical materialism, and the liberal theory of democratic development (Löwith 1949: 1–20). The very idea of philosophical *modernity* — a decisive break with the past — is a secularized application of the theological idea of a turning point in sacred history.

Understanding that Western philosophy's dominant temporal framework is rooted in specific theological commitments is not to say that the framework is wrong. Linear time may well be closer to the truth than cyclical time. But it does mean that the framework is not self-evidently universal — it needs to be argued for, not assumed — and that confronting genuinely different temporal frameworks, as the next subsection does, is not merely an exercise in multicultural awareness but genuine philosophical work.

---

**Key terms introduced:** creatio ex nihilo, eschatology, directed history, telos, divine eternity, sempiternity, distentio animi (Augustine).

#### 3.3 Indigenous and Non-Western Temporal Frameworks

---

##### Beyond the Western Default

Philosophy of time, as it is taught in Western universities, proceeds largely within a Greek-Christian framework. Time is linear (or is argued to be). It has a direction (or is argued to have one). The present moment is unique (or is argued to be). These are taken to be the default positions from which inquiry begins. Alternative views are considered as departures from the default — exotic positions that need special motivation.

But this framing is culturally specific, not universal. Different cultures and intellectual traditions have developed temporal frameworks that are genuinely distinct from the Western linear model — not because they are primitive approximations to a truth the West has discovered, but because they are exploring different aspects of temporal experience, different features of time that are genuinely present but tend to be suppressed or ignored within Western conceptual frameworks. Surveying several such frameworks briefly is philosophically important, even if our treatment here must necessarily be introductory.

A word of caution is in order. These are living traditions, and summarizing them briefly risks distortion, reduction, and appropriation. The goal here is philosophical alertness — an expansion of the range of options under consideration — not ethnographic comprehensiveness. Readers are encouraged to follow the further reading to encounter these frameworks in their full complexity.

###### Aboriginal Australian Dreamtime

Among Aboriginal Australian peoples, the temporal framework most fundamental to cultural and spiritual life is often translated into English as the "Dreamtime" or the "Dreaming" — though these English terms are acknowledged to be inadequate approximations (Swain 1993: 17–22). The Aranda term *Altyerre* (and equivalent terms in other languages) refers to a founding creative period — a time of immense formative power — that is not simply past, not simply a historical epoch that has concluded and receded.

This is the crucial philosophical point: the Dreaming is not experienced as past in the Western sense. It is not over; it is *continuously present*. The ancestral beings who shaped the landscape, created species, and established the patterns of human life are not merely historical figures who existed in a remote past. They are ongoing presences whose formative power is still active in the land, in ritual, in social structure, and in the relationship between human beings and country (Strehlow 1947: 15–17; Rose 1992: 38–42).

This gives rise to a temporal ontology that is fundamentally different from the Western linear model. In Western linear time, past, present, and future are mutually exclusive: what is past is no longer present. But in the Aboriginal framework, the founding time is simultaneously original and contemporary — it *underlies* the present rather than preceding it in a linear sequence. The landscape itself is a temporal document, not a record of past events but an ongoing expression of the Dreaming's continuous creative power.

Philosophers have noted interesting parallels between this framework and certain strands of Western philosophy of time. Mircea Eliade argued that many archaic cultures treat sacred time as a periodic recovery of the founding time — a return to the beginning that does not abolish but regenerates the present (Eliade 1954: 34–37). David Bohm's distinction between the *explicate order* (the unfolded, sequential temporal world of everyday experience) and the *implicate order* (the enfolded, timeless ground from which explicate events unfold) has been noted as bearing structural similarities to the Aboriginal framework, though such comparisons require care (Bohm 1980: 172–177).

###### Lakota Temporal Concepts

Among the Lakota peoples of North America, time is understood in close relation to the structure of community, kinship, and the natural world. The Lakota word *wicasa* (man, person) implies a relational identity — a person is constituted by their relations to family, to land, to the community of the living and the dead — and this relational constitution extends across time (Deloria 1999: 45–52; Vine Deloria Jr., *Spirit and Reason*, 1999).

Past and future are not simply absent in Lakota thought, but their significance is not primarily governed by linear succession. Ancestral figures are experienced as present in ceremony, in the landscape, in dreams and visions; they are not merely remembered but encountered (Powers 1977: 57–62). The ceremonial cycle embeds temporal experience in natural rhythm — the Lakota calendar is organized by the cycles of the moon, the migrations of animals, and the passage of the seasons — rather than in a linear historical narrative with a beginning and end.

What is philosophically interesting about this framework is its emphasis on *relational* time. Time is not an abstract container in which individuals are located; it is a medium of relationship — between the living and the dead, between human beings and the rest of the natural world, between individuals and the community across generations. This relational ontology of time resonates with aspects of process philosophy (Whitehead 1929), where temporal reality is fundamentally constituted by relations among events rather than by substances persisting through time.

###### Ubuntu and Relational Time in African Philosophy

The concept of *Ubuntu*, widely developed in Southern African philosophical traditions, is often glossed with the phrase "I am because we are" (Ramose 1999: 49–54; Shutte 1993: 46–50). Ubuntu is, at root, an ontology of personhood: one is not a self-contained individual who happens to enter into relations with others, but a relational being whose very existence is constituted by community and by what one has received from others.

Temporally, Ubuntu implies a conception of time as fundamentally *communal*. The past is not merely over; it persists in the community as a living inheritance of values, practices, and relationships. The ancestors are not simply dead; they are active participants in the community's life, addressed in ritual, consulted in decision-making, honored in ceremony (Mbiti 1969: 20–25). And the future is not something toward which individuals project themselves autonomously; it is a horizon of communal becoming in which individual destinies are bound up with communal ones.

John Mbiti's distinction between what he calls the "African time sense" and the Western linear model has been influential, though also contested. Mbiti argued that traditional African time is primarily constituted by *events* rather than abstract temporal units — that time is "created" or "made" by events, and that the future in the Western sense (the domain of not-yet-existing events) has little substance in African temporal thought (Mbiti 1969: 16–28). Critics have argued that Mbiti overstates the case and may have been unconsciously imposing a colonial framework that renders African thought as temporally deficient rather than as expressing a different set of priorities (Deng 1971; Wiredu 1996: 39–41).

The philosophical point, stripped of the contested ethnographic claims, is this: a conception of time organized primarily around events, community, and relationship, rather than around abstract linear succession, is not incoherent. It reflects a set of emphases — on the persistence of the past in community, on the relational constitution of persons, on time as saturated with meaning rather than neutral and homogeneous — that deserve serious philosophical engagement.

###### The Philosophical Import of This Survey

This survey has necessarily been brief and selective. The aim has not been comprehensive ethnographic coverage but a demonstration that the folk conception familiar to Western-educated philosophy students is not the universal human starting point. Cyclical time, Dreamtime, relational time — these are not naive approximations to the Western linear model but genuine philosophical alternatives.

Three lessons for the philosophy of time follow:

First, the assumption that time is linear and homogeneous is an assumption that needs to be argued for, not merely assumed. The Greek-Christian-Newtonian framework has enormous explanatory resources, but so have the alternatives, in their own domains.

Second, features of temporal experience that the Western framework tends to suppress or marginalize — the persistence of the past in the present, the relational constitution of temporal identity, the non-linear character of sacred or foundational time — are features that a complete philosophy of time should be able to accommodate or explain away.

Third, the philosophy of time, like all philosophy, benefits from comparative breadth. If our only touchstone is a single cultural tradition, we are unlikely to notice the assumptions that tradition builds into its very starting points.

---

**Key terms introduced:** Dreamtime (Altyerre), Ubuntu, relational time, ancestral presence, event-based time, temporal ontology.

### Section 4: Pre-Scientific Accounts of Natural Time

---

#### Section Introduction

Philosophy of time did not originate in libraries. It originated in the fields, on the rivers, at sea, and on the open plains — wherever human beings looked at the sky and asked: how do I know when I am? The measurement of time precedes its philosophical analysis by millennia. Long before anyone argued about the nature of temporal passage, farmers were calculating planting seasons, navigators were tracking stars, priests were predicting eclipses. The philosophical reflection on time grew out of this practical engagement with natural cycles and was transformed — fundamentally, irreversibly — by one technological invention: the mechanical clock.

This section traces two episodes in the pre-scientific history of time that have lasting philosophical significance.

The first concerns astronomical and seasonal time: the origin of time measurement in the observation of periodic natural processes — the rising and setting of the sun, the phases of the moon, the annual return of the stars. This is not mere history; it raises the philosophical question of the relationship between time and the processes used to measure it. Is time identical with natural periodicity, or is it something independent of natural cycles that those cycles reveal? The Aristotelian and Newtonian answers to this question differ sharply, and examining the pre-philosophical basis of time measurement illuminates why the question arises at all.

The second concerns the mechanical clock and its philosophical legacy. The invention of the mechanical clock in the medieval period — and the proliferation of reliable clocks through the early modern period — transformed time from a natural feature of the lived environment into a quantitative, homogeneous, measurable medium. This transformation had profound consequences for the philosophy of time. It made possible a new conception of time as a kind of number — a grid imposed on reality from without — and raised the question, still live today, of whether the clock *discovers* time or *constructs* it.

These episodes are not merely historical. They illuminate the pre-theoretical commitments that any sophisticated philosophy of time needs to engage.

#### 4.1 Astronomical and Seasonal Time

---

##### Time Before Clocks

Go outside on a clear night, away from city lights, and look up. The sky is moving — or rather, the Earth is rotating, but the effect, from your perspective on the ground, is that the stars wheel across the sky in great arcs, rising in the east and setting in the west. If you watch the same star on successive nights, you will find it rising approximately four minutes earlier each evening — a consequence of the Earth's orbital motion around the sun. Over the course of a year, the sky cycles through its entire celestial cast.

This is free, publicly available information, legible to anyone patient enough to observe. And for most of human history, this was the only clock available. Time was not something you read off a device; it was something you read off the sky, and off the landscape, and off your own body.

###### The Origins of Time Measurement

Archaeological evidence of systematic astronomical observation extends at least to the Neolithic period. Stonehenge (built in phases from ca. 3000–1500 BCE) was oriented to the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset — evidence of precise solar observation used, almost certainly, for agricultural and ceremonial timing (Hawkins 1965: 112–125; Ruggles 1999: 70–76). The Antikythera mechanism, a remarkable ancient Greek computational device (ca. 150–100 BCE), could predict the positions of the sun and moon, calculate eclipse cycles, and track the dates of athletic festivals (Freeth et al. 2006: 587–591). In Mesopotamia, Babylonian astronomers from at least the seventh century BCE maintained detailed records of planetary positions and used mathematical models to predict astronomical events (Neugebauer 1969: 97–122).

What all these astronomical practices shared was the use of *periodic natural processes* — the daily rotation of the Earth, the monthly cycle of the moon, the annual orbit of the Earth around the sun — as temporal measures. Time was reckoned by the repetition of celestial events.

###### Sidereal vs. Solar Time

The distinction between *sidereal* and *solar* time is philosophically instructive, because it reveals that even at the most practical level of time measurement, there is more than one "natural" measure of time, and these measures do not perfectly agree.

*Sidereal time* is measured relative to the fixed stars — specifically, relative to a reference direction pointing toward the distant stellar background. A sidereal day is the time it takes the Earth to rotate 360° relative to the stars: approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds.

*Solar time* is measured relative to the sun. A solar day is the time from one solar noon to the next: approximately 24 hours. Solar time differs from sidereal time because the Earth is also orbiting the sun: by the time the Earth has completed one rotation relative to the stars, it has moved slightly along its orbit, so the sun appears to have shifted position relative to the stars, and the Earth must rotate a little more before the sun returns to the meridian.

This four-minute discrepancy accumulates: over a year, sidereal time "gains" one full day relative to solar time. For practical purposes — agriculture, daily life — solar time is more natural, because it tracks the cycle of daylight and darkness that governs human activity. For astronomy — tracking the fixed stars, determining the sidereal positions of celestial objects — sidereal time is more natural.

The existence of these two natural measures of time raises a philosophical question: which is the "real" measure of time? Is there a fact of the matter about how long a day "really" is, independent of which natural process we use to measure it? Newton's absolute time provides one answer: real time flows uniformly, and both sidereal and solar time are imperfect approximations to it. Leibniz's relational view provides a different answer: there are multiple legitimate temporal measures, none more "real" than the others, because time just is the set of temporal relations among events, and there is no unique natural measure that all others must match.

###### Time, Periodicity, and Aristotle

Aristotle's definition of time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after" (Aristotle, *Physics* 219b1–2) was, in part, a philosophical articulation of the practical consensus that time is measured by motion. For Aristotle, the most natural and regular motion — the rotation of the celestial spheres — provided the standard against which all other temporal measures were calibrated (Aristotle, *Physics* 223b12–20).

But Aristotle was not merely endorsing the practical astronomical tradition. He was raising the philosophical question: what is the relationship between time and the processes used to measure it? Is time *identical* with the celestial motion, or is it something independent that the celestial motion reveals?

Aristotle's own answer is subtle. He holds that time is the *number* of motion — not the motion itself, but the measurable feature of motion that makes it possible to say "how long" a motion took. The celestial rotation is the preferred measure, but it is not the only possible measure; it is preferred because it is the most uniform, the most continuous, and the most universally observable. We will examine this in detail in Chapter 5.

###### Implications for Philosophy of Time

Two philosophical implications of the astronomical tradition deserve emphasis.

First, the dependence of time measurement on periodic physical processes raises the question of whether time could exist without such processes. If all motion stopped — if the universe were instantaneously frozen — would time still pass? Aristotle's answer was no: time without motion is impossible (*Physics* 218b21–219a2). Newton's answer was yes: time would continue to flow even if the universe were entirely static, because absolute time is independent of all physical processes.

This debate about the relationship between time and its physical measures is not merely academic. It bears directly on questions in modern physics about whether time is a fundamental feature of reality or an emergent property of more basic physical processes — a question that remains unresolved in quantum gravity (Barbour 1999: 1–10).

Second, the natural origins of time measurement remind us that time, as initially encountered by human beings, was not a neutral, homogeneous, mathematically precise medium. It was saturated with qualitative significance: the season for planting and the season for harvest, the time of festival and the time of mourning, the dangerous days and the propitious ones. The quantitative, homogeneous conception of time that dominates modern thought is a historical achievement — as we shall see in the next subsection — not a discovery of what time always already was.

---

**Key terms introduced:** sidereal time, solar time, astronomical period, periodic measure, temporal measure, Aristotle's definition of time.

#### 4.2 The Mechanical Clock and the Objectification of Time

---

##### A Device That Changed Everything

In the last decade of the thirteenth century, large mechanical clocks began to appear on the towers of European churches and civic buildings. The earliest recorded mechanical clock in Western Europe was installed at Milan in 1335; by the mid-fourteenth century, such clocks were common in major Italian, French, and English towns (Landes 1983: 58–60). These were not merely convenient devices for telling the time. They were — gradually, subtly, and then with increasing speed — engines of a transformation in how human beings experienced, conceptualized, and organized temporal reality.

The historian David Landes, in his magisterial study *Revolution in Time*, argued that the mechanical clock was among the most consequential technological inventions in human history, not because of what it did to time but because of what it did to *thought about time* (Landes 1983: 1–7). The clock made time into something that could be divided, counted, possessed, bought, and sold. It made time *scarce*. And in so doing, it made possible a particular conception of time — as a homogeneous, quantitative, fungible medium — that had not previously been available.

###### From Qualitative to Quantitative Time

Before the mechanical clock, time was primarily *qualitative*. Time was the time for something — the time for planting, for praying, for sleeping, for working. It was structured by natural rhythms (light and dark, seasons) and social institutions (liturgical hours, market days, feast days). The length of an "hour" was not fixed: the canonical hours of medieval monastic life divided daylight and darkness into twelve hours each, so that summer hours were longer and winter hours shorter. Time was embedded in activity and context; it was not an abstract container waiting to be filled.

The mechanical clock changed this. Its escapement mechanism — the gear-and-detent system that converts continuous mechanical force into discrete, equal time intervals — produced a new kind of temporal object: the equal, regular, context-independent unit. An hour was now always the same duration, regardless of season, location, or activity. Time became *homogeneous*: one hour was intrinsically the same as every other hour, differing only numerically.

This transformation had far-reaching consequences. Equal-unit time made possible the precise scheduling of labor — and therefore the wage economy, in which workers are paid by the hour rather than by the task (Thompson 1967: 56–97). It made possible navigation by chronometer, since determining longitude requires knowing exact time (Sobel 1995: 3–15). It made possible the coordination of the industrial revolution, which depended on the precise synchronization of machines, workers, and transportation networks. In short, the quantitative, homogeneous, clock-measured time was not discovered; it was *produced* — by a particular technology, in a particular cultural context, serving particular social and economic interests.

###### Does the Clock Discover Time or Construct It?

Here is the philosophical question the history of clocks raises in its sharpest form: is the equal-unit time produced by the mechanical clock a discovery of something that was always there — the genuine structure of time, previously approximated only crudely — or is it a *construction*, a particular way of carving up reality that serves human purposes but does not simply read off objective temporal structure?

The Newtonian absolutist says: discovery. Absolute time flows equably and uniformly; the mechanical clock, by producing equal intervals, is approximating the genuine structure of absolute time better than the irregular rhythms of natural processes do. The clock is more accurate, not merely more convenient.

The relationist says: the question "is the clock accurate?" only makes sense relative to some standard, and standards are human choices. There is no clock-independent fact about whether two intervals are "really" equal. The mechanical clock imposes an equal-interval measure on temporal experience; it does not reveal a pre-existing equal-interval structure. The homogeneous time of the clock is a social and technological artifact, not a metaphysical discovery.

Lewis Mumford, in his influential cultural history of technology, put the point memorably: "The clock, not the steam-engine, is the key-machine of the modern industrial age" — not because of what it measures, but because of what it creates: the concept of time as a neutral, homogeneous medium that can be allocated, optimized, and exchanged (Mumford 1934: 14).

A more nuanced view is available. The mechanical clock is both discovery and construction. It discovers something real — the approximate uniformity of many natural processes — and it constructs something new — the cultural practice of treating time as a fungible commodity. These two aspects are not mutually exclusive. The clock reveals temporal structure that was genuinely there (the approximate regularity of mechanical oscillation), while also imposing a social and conceptual framework that was not simply "given" in pre-clockwork temporal experience.

###### Philosophical Implications: Time as Measure

The history of clocks illuminates several philosophical issues that recur throughout this book.

**The relationship between time and its measures.** If the equal unit of the mechanical clock is a construction rather than a discovery, this raises the question: what makes one time measurement system better than another? The answer, presumably, is that a better system is one that coheres better with the rest of our physics — one that gives simpler, more unified laws of nature. Philosophers of physics call this the criterion of *simplicity* or *theoretical coherence*, and it is the criterion that physicists actually use when they define the second in terms of atomic oscillations. The "correct" measure of time is the one that simplifies physics (Poincaré 1898: 1–13; Dummett 2000: 497–499).

**Time and power.** The sociological observation that the mechanical clock served the interests of capital — giving employers control over workers' time — raises a more radical philosophical question: are our temporal concepts, including the apparently neutral concept of equal, homogeneous time, embedded in structures of social power? This question connects the philosophy of time with the sociology of knowledge and critical theory (Thompson 1967; Adam 1990: 1–25; Fabian 1983). The answer is almost certainly yes, in part — but this does not mean that temporal concepts are *merely* ideological. The capacity to identify the ideological dimensions of a concept and the capacity to identify its genuine cognitive content are not mutually exclusive.

**The phenomenology of clock time.** Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger both argued, in different ways, that the clock-time of the modern world — abstract, homogeneous, quantitative — is a derivative and in some sense impoverished mode of temporal experience, a far cry from the rich, qualitative, lived time of immediate temporal consciousness (Husserl 1964: 21–35; Heidegger 1962: 456–472). This phenomenological critique of clock time is an important counterweight to the Newtonian tendency to treat clock-time as simply the *real* time that other measures approximate.

These implications will recur throughout this book. For now, the key point is that the folk conception of time — including its implicit picture of a homogeneous, measurable, linear medium — is not a neutral given. It is historically shaped, technologically mediated, and philosophically loaded. Recognizing this is not a reason to abandon it. It is a reason to examine it carefully.

---

**Key terms introduced:** mechanical clock, escapement mechanism, equal-unit time, homogeneous time, quantitative time, clock-time vs. lived time, construction vs. discovery, atomic second.

### Chapter 2 Exercises

---

#### Comprehension and Analysis

**Exercise 1.** Explain, in your own words, the distinction between the *container view* of time and the *relational view* of time. For each view, give one reason in its favor and one difficulty it faces. Then explain how Newton and Leibniz would differ on the following question: "If all matter in the universe were destroyed, would time continue to pass?"

**Exercise 2.** The folk conception of time includes the claim that the past is fixed and the future is open. Critically assess this claim. What does it mean for the future to be "genuinely open"? Could the openness of the future be merely a feature of our ignorance (we don't know what will happen) rather than a feature of reality (what will happen is not yet settled)? What would be at stake in choosing between these interpretations?

**Exercise 3.** McTaggart distinguished the A-series from the B-series. Consider the sentence "The lecture *was* interesting." Is this an A-series statement or a B-series statement? Justify your answer. Now consider: could this statement be *translated* into a tenseless B-series statement without loss of meaning? What does the token-reflexive analysis say about this? Do you find that analysis convincing?

**Exercise 4.** Summarize the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis in both its strong and weak forms. Explain what Malotki's research on Hopi showed, and what it failed to show. Does the cross-linguistic variation in grammatical tense tell us anything about the *metaphysics* of time, or does it only tell us about the *grammar* of particular languages? Argue for a position.

**Exercise 5.** Kaplan distinguishes the *character* of an expression from its *content*. Explain these two concepts using temporal indexicals as your examples. Why does Kaplan say that "I am here now" is necessarily true? Is this the same kind of necessity as "Water is H₂O" or "2 + 2 = 4"? Explain the difference.

**Exercise 6.** Compare and contrast two of the following temporal frameworks: (a) Hindu cyclical cosmology (kalpas and yugas), (b) Abrahamic linear eschatological time, (c) Aboriginal Australian Dreamtime. For each framework you discuss, identify at least one philosophical question about time that the framework either raises or resolves differently from the default Western linear model.

**Exercise 7.** What is the philosophical significance of the distinction between sidereal time and solar time? How does the existence of these two natural time measures bear on the debate between Newton's absolute time and Leibniz's relational time?

**Exercise 8.** Discuss Lewis Mumford's claim that the mechanical clock — not the steam engine — is the key machine of modernity. Do you agree that the clock has changed not just how we measure time but how we conceptualize it? What philosophical issues does this raise about the relationship between technology and temporal experience?

---

#### Critical Thinking

**Exercise 9.** The folk conception of time includes the belief in an "objective moving present" — a present moment that is objectively distinguished from past and future, and that *moves* through time. Critically assess this belief. What would it mean for the present to be *objectively* distinguished? Is there a coherent version of this view? What is the main challenge it faces (consider the "how fast?" problem)?

**Exercise 10.** A critic argues: "The discussion of non-Western temporal frameworks in this chapter is culturally relative — it implies that there is no fact of the matter about whether time is really linear or really cyclical; it's just a matter of cultural perspective." How would you respond to this objection? Is it possible to take indigenous and non-Western frameworks seriously without collapsing into cultural relativism about time? Write a structured argument for a position.

---

#### Lab Exercises

**Lab 1: Timing Without a Clock.** Go to an outdoor location (a park, a backyard, or a window with a clear view). Without using any clock or phone, estimate: (a) what time it is now (time of day), (b) how much time passes between two chosen events (e.g., the time it takes you to walk a certain distance, or the time between two observations). Then check against a clock. Record your estimates and the actual values. Reflect: what information did you use to make your estimates? What does this reveal about the pre-clockwork resources human beings have for temporal orientation? Write a brief (one page) reflection connecting your observations to the philosophical discussion in Section 4.

**Lab 2: Temporal Indexical Observation.** For one full day, keep a log of every temporal indexical expression you encounter (in conversation, on your phone, in written text): "now," "today," "soon," "yesterday," "later," "recently," "in a moment," etc. Count how many you encounter of each type. Then: (a) Identify three cases where the reference of the indexical would have been ambiguous to someone hearing it out of context. (b) Identify one case where the indexical was used to express something that a tenseless B-series statement could capture fully, and one case where you think it could not. Write a one-page reflection on what the pervasiveness of temporal indexicals in everyday language suggests about human temporal cognition.

**Lab 3: Circadian Rhythm and Temporal Orientation.** For three consecutive days, at the same time each day (e.g., on waking), before checking any clock, write down: (a) your best estimate of what time it is, (b) how rested or tired you feel, (c) how much time you feel has passed since you fell asleep. Then compare your estimates to actual clock times. Are you closer on some days than others? What factors seem to affect your accuracy? This exercise explores the relationship between *felt* time — the temporal experience of consciousness — and *clock* time. Reflect: does your biological sense of time constitute evidence that time is "really" something beyond mere clockwork? Connect your observations to the distinction between lived time and clock time discussed in Section 4.

### Chapter 2: Further Reading and Bibliography

---

#### Annotated Further Reading

**Adam, Barbara. 1990. *Time and Social Theory*. Cambridge: Polity Press.**
Adam provides a wide-ranging sociological and philosophical analysis of time, examining how temporal concepts are embedded in social structures, economic systems, and natural rhythms. Particularly good on the difference between clock-time and the multiple, overlapping temporalities of lived experience. An important corrective to overly physics-focused approaches to time.

**Augustine of Hippo. *Confessions*, Book XI. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.**
Book XI of the *Confessions* is the foundational text for phenomenological approaches to time. Augustine's discussion of the "distension of the mind," of what God was doing before creation, and of the psychological modes of past, present, and future is philosophically original and inexhaustibly rich. Read it slowly.

**Boroditsky, Lera. 2001. "Does Language Shape Thought? Mandarin and English Speakers' Conceptions of Time." *Cognitive Psychology* 43: 1–22.**
One of the best empirical studies of the weak Sapir-Whorf hypothesis. Boroditsky compared how English speakers (who tend to use horizontal spatial metaphors for time: ahead/behind) and Mandarin speakers (who also use vertical metaphors: up/down) conceptualize temporal relations. Her findings suggest that language use can prime and activate particular ways of thinking about time, even if it does not determine them.

**Dahl, Östen. 1985. *Tense and Aspect Systems*. Oxford: Blackwell.**
A systematic typological study of how languages encode tense and aspect. Essential for understanding the cross-linguistic evidence about temporal grammaticalization. Dahl's data show both the considerable variation and the underlying universals in how human languages handle temporal distinctions.

**Eliade, Mircea. 1954. *The Myth of the Eternal Return: Cosmos and History*. Translated by Willard Trask. Princeton: Princeton University Press.**
Eliade's argument that traditional and archaic cultures understand sacred time as periodic return to the founding creative time, not as linear historical succession, remains the most important scholarly treatment of cyclical time. Read critically but read it: the account of "strong" versus "profane" time raises genuine philosophical questions.

**Kaplan, David. 1989. "Demonstratives." In *Themes from Kaplan*, edited by Joseph Almog, John Perry, and Howard Wettstein, 481–563. Oxford: Oxford University Press.**
Kaplan's foundational paper on indexicality. Dense but rewarding. The character/content distinction is introduced here, along with the formal semantics of indexical expressions. Chapter 17 of this paper ("Logic of Indexicals") is particularly relevant to temporal indexicals.

**Landes, David S. 1983. *Revolution in Time: Clocks and the Making of the Modern World*. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.**
The definitive scholarly history of timekeeping. Landes traces the mechanical clock from its origins in medieval Europe through the marine chronometer to the quartz and atomic clocks of the twentieth century, and argues throughout that changes in timekeeping technology are inseparable from changes in how people think about time.

**Leibniz, G. W., and Samuel Clarke. 1956. *The Leibniz-Clarke Correspondence*. Edited and translated by H. G. Alexander. Manchester: Manchester University Press.**
The primary source for the Newton-Leibniz debate about absolute versus relational time. The correspondence is accessible, philosophically rigorous, and historically important. It is also a model of philosophical debate: both sides argue carefully, and neither simply talks past the other. Read all five letters.

**Malotki, Ekkehart. 1983. *Hopi Time: A Linguistic Analysis of the Temporal Concepts in the Hopi Language*. Berlin: Mouton.**
The meticulous refutation of Whorf's Hopi claims. An extraordinary piece of sustained linguistic scholarship, though not light reading. Even if you only read the introduction and conclusion, you will come away with a clear sense of why Whorf was wrong and what linguistic evidence about temporal cognition can and cannot establish.

**Mbiti, John S. 1969. *African Religions and Philosophy*. London: Heinemann.**
Mbiti's influential account of traditional African time concepts, organized around the claim that time in many African cultures is primarily event-constituted and oriented toward the past. The work has been contested but remains essential reading for anyone interested in non-Western temporal frameworks. Read alongside Wiredu (below) for critical context.

**Mellor, D. H. 1998. *Real Time II*. London: Routledge.**
The most systematic and rigorous contemporary defense of the B-theory of time. Mellor argues that all tensed facts can be accounted for in terms of tenseless "earlier than" relations, and that the appearance of an objective present is a feature of how temporal experience represents reality, not a feature of reality itself. Demanding but essential.

**Prior, Arthur N. 1967. *Past, Present and Future*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.**
Prior's foundational exposition of tense logic. The first chapter, "Time and Tense," is relatively accessible and provides the best introduction to Prior's reasons for thinking that tensed discourse cannot be eliminated in favor of tenseless discourse.

**Whorf, Benjamin Lee. 1956. *Language, Thought, and Reality: Selected Writings of Benjamin Lee Whorf*. Edited by John B. Carroll. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.**
Whorf's own writings, including the essays on Hopi and on the relation between language and thought that sparked the Sapir-Whorf debate. Essential for understanding what Whorf actually claimed, rather than the sometimes caricatured version in secondary sources.

**Wiredu, Kwasi. 1996. *Cultural Universals and Particulars: An African Perspective*. Bloomington: Indiana University Press.**
A critical and philosophically sophisticated perspective on African philosophy, including a critical reassessment of Mbiti's temporal thesis. Wiredu argues that many claims about distinctively "African" time are overstated and may encode colonial assumptions about African thought as pre-rational. An important corrective that does not abandon the genuine philosophical interest of non-Western temporal frameworks.

### Chapter 2: Important Concepts

---

**Folk Conception of Time**
The implicit, pre-theoretical picture of time that structures ordinary temporal cognition and practice. The folk conception is not a theory anyone explicitly adopts; it is the background framework presupposed by everyday temporal talk, planning, memory, and expectation. Articulating it carefully is a genuine philosophical task.

**Knowledge-How vs. Knowledge-That**
A distinction introduced by Gilbert Ryle. Knowledge-how is practical competence — the ability to do something skillfully. Knowledge-that is propositional knowledge — the ability to state that something is the case. Most ordinary temporal competence is knowledge-how that outstrips the corresponding knowledge-that; this gap is what produces the Augustinian puzzle about time.

**Container View (Absolute Time)**
The view that time is a medium or vessel in which events are located, existing independently of those events. Even if no events occurred, time would still exist and "flow." Isaac Newton's absolute time is the paradigm case: it "flows equably without relation to anything external."

**Relational View**
The view that time consists entirely of the temporal relations among events — simultaneity, succession, duration — and has no existence independent of the events that stand in those relations. Leibniz is the paradigm defender; time, on this view, is a feature of how events relate to each other, not a container over and above them.

**A-Series**
J. M. E. McTaggart's term for the ordering of events by the dynamic, one-place properties of being past, present, or future. A-series properties are not permanent: what is now future will become present, and what is now present will become past. The A-series is associated with temporal flow and the objective present.

**B-Series**
McTaggart's term for the ordering of events by the fixed, permanent, two-place relations of "earlier than," "later than," and "simultaneous with." B-series relations do not change: if the Battle of Thermopylae is earlier than the Battle of Actium, it is always earlier. The B-series is associated with the static, four-dimensional "block universe" picture.

**Grammatical Tense**
The systematic, obligatory encoding of temporal location into the morphological structure of verbs. Tense differs from aspect: tense locates an event in time relative to a reference point (usually the time of utterance), while aspect describes the internal temporal structure of the event (completed, ongoing, habitual, etc.).

**Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis (Linguistic Relativity)**
The hypothesis, associated with Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, that the language one speaks shapes or determines the thoughts one can have. The strong version (language determines thought) has been largely discredited. The weak version (language can influence or facilitate certain ways of thinking) retains some empirical support and remains philosophically relevant.

**Tensed vs. Tenseless Discourse**
The distinction between temporal statements whose truth value changes over time (tensed: "the meeting is happening") and statements whose truth value is permanent (tenseless: "the meeting is earlier than the lecture"). Tensed discourse seems to presuppose an objective present; tenseless discourse does not. This grammatical distinction maps onto the A-theory/B-theory debate.

**Token-Reflexive Analysis**
A semantic analysis of tensed statements, associated with Reichenbach and Mellor, on which "the event is happening now" means approximately "the event is happening at the same time as this utterance token." The analysis eliminates the need for objective A-series presentness; what appeared to be a claim about objective nowness turns out to be a claim about a B-series simultaneity relation.

**Tense Logic (Prior)**
A formal logical system, developed by Arthur Prior, that treats temporal operators — "it was the case that" (P) and "it will be the case that" (F) — analogously to modal operators. Prior's tense logic provides a rigorous semantic framework for tensed discourse and embodies a commitment to the reality of the A-series.

**Indexical Expression**
An expression whose reference shifts systematically with features of the context of utterance. Temporal indexicals include "now," "then," "yesterday," "soon," and "recently." Following David Kaplan, we distinguish an indexical's character (the rule by which it picks out a referent relative to a context) from its content (what it contributes to the proposition expressed in a specific context).

**Cyclical Time**
The conception of time as repeating in great cycles rather than running from a unique beginning to a unique end. Found in Hindu cosmology (kalpas, yugas), Stoic eternal recurrence, and Mesoamerican calendar systems. Raises philosophical challenges about personal identity across recurrence, the coherence of historical uniqueness, and the problem of temporal origins.

**Creatio Ex Nihilo**
The theological doctrine that God created the universe out of nothing, implying that time itself has a beginning. Central to the Abrahamic religious traditions, this doctrine raises philosophical questions about what "before" the creation means, about the structure of eternity, and about divine foreknowledge versus temporal openness.

**Dreamtime (Altyerre)**
Among Aboriginal Australian peoples, the founding creative time of ancestral beings — not simply past but continuously present and active in the land, ritual, and community. Philosophically, the Dreaming represents a temporal ontology in which founding time underlies rather than precedes the present, challenging Western linear models.

**Homogeneous Time**
The conception of time as a uniform, quantitative medium in which all units are intrinsically equal and in which no moment has qualitative significance in itself. This conception was made practically salient by the mechanical clock. Contrasted with qualitative or lived time, in which temporal units have intrinsic differences in significance, texture, and meaning.

**Sidereal vs. Solar Time**
Two natural measures of time: sidereal time is measured relative to the fixed stars (Earth's rotation with respect to inertial space); solar time is measured relative to the sun (Earth's rotation with respect to the sun). They differ by approximately four minutes per day due to Earth's orbital motion. The existence of multiple natural measures of time raises philosophical questions about which (if any) reflects "real" time.

**Distentio Animi (Augustine)**
Augustine's term for the "distension of the mind" — the stretched, extended character of conscious temporal experience. Past, present, and future are not external realities but modes of attention: memory, attention, and anticipation, respectively. Augustine's account is an early and sophisticated phenomenological analysis of time consciousness.

### Chapter 2: Important Researchers and Thinkers

---

**Isaac Newton (1642–1727)**
English mathematician, physicist, and natural philosopher. Newton formulated the doctrine of absolute time in the *Scholium* to the *Principia Mathematica* (1687), arguing that time "flows equably without relation to anything external." His absolute time was theoretically productive for classical mechanics, providing a unique, universal standard against which all motion could be measured. The doctrine was challenged in the eighteenth century by Leibniz and eventually overturned — or at least severely qualified — by Einstein's special theory of relativity in 1905.

**Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716)**
German philosopher and mathematician, co-inventor (with Newton) of calculus. Leibniz articulated the relational theory of time in correspondence with Samuel Clarke (1715–1716), arguing that time consists entirely of relations among events and has no existence independent of them. His arguments turned on the Principle of Sufficient Reason and the Principle of the Identity of Indiscernibles. Leibniz also contributed fundamental work on the logic of relations and on the nature of substance, both of which bear on the philosophy of time.

**J. M. E. McTaggart (1866–1925)**
British idealist philosopher at Cambridge. His 1908 paper "The Unreality of Time" introduced the distinction between the A-series and the B-series — one of the most influential conceptual contributions to analytic philosophy of time. McTaggart argued that the A-series is essential to genuine time (because only it captures temporal passage) but self-contradictory, and therefore that time is unreal. Although his conclusion is widely rejected, the A/B distinction he introduced remains fundamental.

**Arthur Prior (1914–1969)**
New Zealand logician and philosopher. Prior invented modern tense logic, developing a formal semantic framework for tensed temporal discourse modeled on modal logic. His work, especially *Time and Modality* (1957) and *Past, Present and Future* (1967), gave rigorous formal content to A-theoretic commitments and demonstrated that the dispute between tensed and tenseless temporal discourse could be investigated with precision. Prior was a passionate defender of the philosophical significance of the open future.

**David Kaplan (1933–)**
American philosopher of language at UCLA. Kaplan's work on indexicality, especially his paper "Demonstratives" (1989), provided the standard semantic framework for context-sensitive expressions including temporal indexicals. His distinction between character (the rule for reference relative to context) and content (what is contributed to a proposition in a specific context) is essential for understanding how "now," "then," and other temporal indexicals function, and why they raise special metaphysical issues that purely descriptive terms do not.

**Benjamin Lee Whorf (1897–1941)**
American linguist and insurance investigator (his day job). Whorf's studies of the Hopi language led him to formulate the strong version of linguistic relativity — the claim that language determines thought. His claims about Hopi temporal concepts were enormously influential in mid-twentieth-century linguistics and anthropology. Subsequent research, particularly Malotki's detailed study, showed that Whorf had misanalyzed the Hopi language, but his work stimulated productive debate about the relationship between language and temporal cognition that continues today.

**Ekkehart Malotki (1938–)**
German-born American linguist and Arizona State University professor, specialist in Hopi language and culture. His monumental *Hopi Time: A Linguistic Analysis of the Temporal Concepts in the Hopi Language* (1983) systematically refuted Whorf's claims about Hopi temporality, documenting extensive temporal vocabulary and grammatical resources in Hopi that Whorf had overlooked. Malotki's work stands as a cautionary tale about inferring metaphysical conclusions from inadequate linguistic data.

**David Landes (1924–2013)**
American economic historian at Harvard. His *Revolution in Time: Clocks and the Making of the Modern World* (1983) is the standard history of timekeeping from antiquity to the twentieth century. Landes argued that the mechanical clock was among the most transformative technologies in human history, not simply because it measured time more accurately but because it produced a new conception of time as a homogeneous, quantitative medium susceptible to rational management. Essential reading for understanding the relationship between technology and temporal experience.

**Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE)**
North African bishop and theologian, author of the *Confessions* and *The City of God*. Augustine's treatment of time in *Confessions* XI is among the most philosophically profound ever written. He argued that time is a "distension of the mind" (*distentio animi*), with past, present, and future understood as modes of psychological orientation rather than external realities. He also developed the most sophisticated early response to the question "what was God doing before creation?" — arguing that the question is malformed, since time itself was created with the universe.

**Mircea Eliade (1907–1986)**
Romanian historian of religions at the University of Chicago. His *The Myth of the Eternal Return* (1954) remains the foundational study of cyclical and primordial time in archaic and traditional cultures. Eliade argued that sacred time in traditional societies is fundamentally different from profane historical time — it involves a periodic return to the founding creative time, not merely a repetition of similar events. His work is essential context for understanding the range of temporal frameworks across human cultures.

**Lewis Mumford (1895–1990)**
American cultural critic and historian of technology. Mumford's *Technics and Civilization* (1934) included an influential analysis of the mechanical clock as the key machine of modernity — not for what it measured but for the cultural transformation it produced, making time into a commodity subject to rational allocation and exchange. His critique of clock-time as an impoverished abstraction from the richness of lived experience anticipates later phenomenological analyses.

**John Mbiti (1931–2019)**
Kenyan philosopher and theologian. His *African Religions and Philosophy* (1969) proposed a distinctive analysis of traditional African time sense, arguing that time in many African cultures is primarily event-constituted rather than abstractly linear, and that the future (as a domain of not-yet-existing events) has little substance.
