### Chapter 3: Important Concepts

---

**Flux Doctrine (Heraclitus)**
The view that everything is in a constant state of change — that no thing remains the same from one moment to the next. Not a claim that nothing can be identified or known, but that identity persists through change at the level of structure and proportion (the Logos) rather than at the level of material composition. The river is the same river but never the same water.

**Logos (Heraclitus)**
The rational principle, measure, or account that governs the universal flux. Not a separate divine being outside the world, but the immanent rational structure of reality itself — the law of measure and proportion that determines how opposites cycle and how change is regulated. Everything occurs "according to the Logos," though most people fail to understand it.

**Unity of Opposites**
A central Heraclitean theme: opposites (hot and cold, wet and dry, day and night, life and death) are not simply exclusive of each other but constitutively related — each requires and passes into the other. The cosmos is constituted by the tension between opposites held in unity by the Logos, like the opposing forces in a bow or a lyre.

**Way of Truth / Way of Seeming (Parmenides)**
The two paths of inquiry in Parmenides' poem *On Nature*. The Way of Truth follows the argument that Being is one, unchanging, and without plurality or temporal structure. The Way of Seeming describes the world of ordinary experience — change, plurality, temporal succession — which is characterized as mere appearance, not genuine knowledge.

**Being (Parmenidean)**
For Parmenides, Being (*to eon*) is the only genuine reality: one, continuous, undivided, unchanging, without beginning or end, "like a well-rounded sphere." Being cannot not-be, cannot be divided, and cannot change. The argument depends on the principle that non-being is strictly impossible — it cannot exist, be thought, or be spoken.

**Non-Being and the Parmenidean Prohibition**
Parmenides' claim that non-being (*to mê eon*) is strictly impossible: it cannot exist, be thought, or be talked about. This prohibition on non-being underlies the entire Parmenidean argument, because change, plurality, and temporal structure all seem to require reference to what is not (what was but no longer is; what is not here but is there). The prohibition generates the Eleatic denial of time and change.

**Eleatics**
The school of philosophy associated with Parmenides and his followers (including Zeno) in the Greek city of Elea (southern Italy). Characteristic Eleatic doctrines: Being is one and unchanging; plurality and change are illusory; the senses are unreliable guides to reality; reason alone reveals the truth. The Eleatics set the agenda for subsequent Greek philosophy of nature.

**Dichotomy (Zeno)**
The first of Zeno's paradoxes of motion: to move from A to B, you must first reach the midpoint; before that, the quarter-point; before that, the eighth-point; and so on without limit. The journey consists of infinitely many sub-journeys, and infinitely many sub-journeys cannot be completed. Therefore motion is impossible. The paradox targets continuous conceptions of space and time.

**Achilles Paradox (Zeno)**
Achilles (fast) races a tortoise (slow) with a head start. At each stage, by the time Achilles reaches where the tortoise was, the tortoise has moved on. The tortoise always maintains a positive lead. Therefore Achilles can never catch the tortoise. Mathematical response: the infinite series of "catching up" intervals converges to a finite total time.

**Arrow Paradox (Zeno)**
At any instant, the arrow occupies a region of space exactly equal to its own size — which is what it means to be at rest. At every instant the arrow is at rest. If time is composed of instants and the arrow is at rest at every instant, the arrow never moves. Targets the composition of time out of durationless instants.

**Stadium Paradox (Zeno)**
Three rows of bodies moving relative to each other in a discrete spacetime. The relative velocity of two rows moving in opposite directions is twice the absolute velocity of each; but in a discrete spacetime, twice the absolute velocity might require half a spatial or temporal atom, which is impossible. Targets discrete conceptions of space and time.

**Instantaneous Velocity**
The concept, introduced with calculus by Newton and Leibniz, of the velocity of an object at a single durationless instant: defined as the limit of the ratio of distance to time as the time interval shrinks toward zero. Allows us to say that a moving object has a definite velocity at each instant without requiring that any displacement occur at that instant. The standard modern response to the Arrow paradox.

**Atomism (Leucippus, Democritus)**
The cosmological theory that reality consists of indivisible, eternal, homogeneous particles (atoms) moving through void. Atoms differ only in shape, arrangement, and position; macroscopic change is produced by the combination and separation of atomic configurations. Atomism affirms the reality of void (contra Parmenides) and explains temporal change through the eternal motions of unchanging atoms.

**Void (kenon)**
For the Atomists, the empty space through which atoms move. Void is "nothing" in the sense of being without material content, but it is real in the sense of being causally efficacious: it is what makes motion possible. The Atomists' insistence on the reality of void was a direct response to the Parmenidean prohibition on non-being.

**Principle of Sufficient Reason (Leucippus)**
The principle that nothing happens without a reason or cause: "Nothing happens for no reason; all things come from reason and necessity." Applied to temporal structure, this implies causal determinism: the sequence of events is causally necessitated by prior states. An early formulation of the deterministic picture of temporal causation.

**Great Year (Pythagorean)**
The period of cosmic time after which all celestial bodies return to their original positions. The Great Year represents the complete cycle of the cosmos — the fullest temporal expression of the mathematical harmony governing the heavenly spheres. It connects Pythagorean mathematics to cyclical temporal cosmology.

**Harmony of the Spheres**
The Pythagorean doctrine that the motions of the planets and stars produce a celestial music, with speeds in mathematical ratios corresponding to musical intervals. The cosmos is a mathematical harmony expressed in temporal cycles; the temporal structure of the heavens is an expression of the same numerical ratios that govern musical concords.

**Metempsychosis (Pythagorean)**
The doctrine of soul-transmigration: the soul is immortal and passes through many bodies across many lifetimes, gradually purifying itself until it achieves release from the cycle of rebirths. Implies a temporal structure for the soul that is much longer and more complex than a single human lifespan — a multi-lifetime temporal trajectory toward eventual transcendence of temporal existence.

### Chapter 3: Important Researchers and Thinkers

---

**Heraclitus of Ephesus (active ca. 500 BCE)**
One of the most original and difficult thinkers of antiquity. Heraclitus argued that everything is in a state of flux, governed by a rational principle (the Logos) that maintains measure and proportion through constant change. His river fragments (DK 12, 49a, 91) introduced the philosophical problem of identity through change. He also pioneered the idea that opposites are constitutively related rather than simply exclusive — a principle that influenced the Stoics, Plato, and (via Hegel) the entire tradition of dialectical philosophy. His work survives only in fragments, preserved by later writers.

**Parmenides of Elea (active ca. 480 BCE)**
The most philosophically rigorous of the Pre-Socratic thinkers, and one of the most important philosophers in the entire tradition. His poem *On Nature* contains the first sustained deductive argument in Western philosophy: from the principle that Being is and cannot not-be, Parmenides argued that Being is one, unchanging, undivided, and eternal. Change, plurality, and time are mere appearances, accessible to opinion but not to genuine knowledge. Parmenides forced subsequent philosophy to be precise about the concepts of being, non-being, and change, and his challenge shaped the entire subsequent Greek philosophical tradition.

**Zeno of Elea (ca. 490–430 BCE)**
Student and intellectual ally of Parmenides, celebrated for the four paradoxes of motion: the Dichotomy, the Achilles, the Arrow, and the Stadium. Zeno's strategy was indirect: rather than arguing for Parmenidean metaphysics directly, he showed that ordinary conceptions of motion, continuity, and extension are internally incoherent. His paradoxes have been discussed for twenty-five centuries; they remain philosophically and mathematically productive, having influenced the development of calculus, the foundations of mathematics (infinitesimals, infinite series), and contemporary philosophy of physics.

**Leucippus (active ca. 450 BCE)**
Co-founder, with Democritus, of ancient atomism. Leucippus is credited with the claim that "nothing happens for no reason; all things come from reason and necessity" — an early formulation of the Principle of Sufficient Reason. He proposed the existence of void (against the Eleatics) as the medium of atomic motion, and argued that matter consists of indivisible, eternal atoms. Almost nothing of his own writing survives; he is known primarily through Aristotle and Theophrastus.

**Democritus of Abdera (ca. 460–370 BCE)**
The most prolific and systematic of the atomist philosophers. Democritus developed the full atomist cosmology: atoms differing in shape, arrangement, and position; void as the medium of motion; macroscopic change as atomic rearrangement; the soul itself composed of fine, spherical atoms. He was a polymath who wrote on ethics, mathematics, music, and a wide range of natural phenomena. Like Leucippus, he left no complete surviving texts. His atomism influenced Epicurus, and through him the Roman poet Lucretius, whose *De Rerum Natura* is our richest surviving source for ancient atomist thought.

**Pythagoras of Samos (ca. 570–495 BCE)**
One of the most influential and most elusive figures in the history of philosophy. Pythagoras founded a semi-religious philosophical school, the Pythagoreans, devoted to the study of mathematics and its cosmic significance. He is traditionally credited with the discovery of the mathematical ratios governing musical harmony (though the historical accuracy of specific attributions is uncertain) and with the doctrine of metempsychosis (transmigration of souls). He left no writings; our knowledge of his views derives entirely from later sources. His conviction that mathematical structure underlies all of reality — that "all is number" — proved extraordinarily influential on Plato, on Neoplatonism, and on modern mathematical physics.

**G. S. Kirk (1921–2003), J. E. Raven (1914–1980), and Malcolm Schofield (1942–)**
Authors of *The Presocratic Philosophers* (1957; revised ed. 1983), the standard English-language sourcebook for Pre-Socratic philosophy. Their collaborative work provides authoritative Greek texts, translations, and philosophical commentary for all the major Pre-Socratic thinkers. Indispensable for any serious study of the philosophers discussed in this chapter.

**Hermann Diels (1848–1922) and Walther Kranz (1884–1960)**
German classical scholars who compiled *Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker* (first published 1903; 6th ed. 1951–1952), the standard collection of Pre-Socratic fragments. The "DK" numbering system used throughout this chapter — and throughout scholarly work on Pre-Socratic philosophy — derives from this compilation. A is used for testimonia (reports about thinkers), B for genuine fragments.

**Gregory Vlastos (1907–1991)**
American philosopher and classical scholar, one of the most important twentieth-century interpreters of ancient Greek philosophy. His work on the Pre-Socratics, Socrates, and Plato is distinguished by its combination of rigorous philosophical analysis with deep classical scholarship. His essay "Zeno of Elea" in the *Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (1967) is the best brief philosophical treatment of Zeno's paradoxes.

**Bertrand Russell (1872–1970)**
Though primarily known as a twentieth-century analytic philosopher, Russell's treatment of Zeno's paradoxes in *Our Knowledge of the External World* (1914) and elsewhere represents an important tradition of bringing mathematical precision to bear on ancient philosophical problems. Russell argued that the calculus of infinite series, properly understood, dissolves Zeno's paradoxes completely — a view that has been influential but also contested.

**Wesley Salmon (1925–2001)**
American philosopher of science whose book *Space, Time, and Motion* (1980) provides one of the most careful modern treatments of Zeno's paradoxes and their relationship to theories of continuity and motion. Salmon's analysis of the Stadium paradox is particularly useful.

## Chapter 4: Plato on Time and Eternity

---

### Chapter Introduction

Plato (428–347 BCE) is the first philosopher to give a sustained, systematic account of time as part of a larger theory of reality, and his account in the *Timaeus* has exercised a defining influence on the Western tradition's way of framing the relationship between time and eternity. To understand Plato on time is to understand a whole philosophical picture — one that encompasses cosmology, metaphysics, epistemology, and theology — and to understand that picture is to understand many of the concepts and distinctions that have structured philosophical discussion ever since.

The central text is the *Timaeus*, a cosmological dialogue written in roughly 360 BCE in which a character named Timaeus (a Pythagorean philosopher from Locri, Italy) delivers a long account of the creation of the universe. The dialogue is a creation myth — but it is a philosophical creation myth, designed not merely to tell a story but to illustrate how the rational mind makes sense of temporal existence in relation to eternal truth.

The *Timaeus* is a difficult dialogue — Plato himself calls it a "likely story" (*eikôs logos* or *eikôs mythos*: *Timaeus* 29d, 59c), meaning a plausible account of a domain that does not permit the kind of strict demonstration available for mathematics. The physical world is the realm of becoming, not being; our best account of it will be probable, not certain. This epistemic humility about the physical world is not weakness but a reflection of Plato's fundamental distinction between the realm of eternal, unchanging being (accessible to knowledge) and the realm of temporal, changing becoming (accessible only to belief).

The chapter is organized around four interconnected themes.

First, we examine the *Timaeus* cosmogony itself: the figure of the Demiurge (the divine craftsman), the eternal model (the Living Being), and the creation of the ordered cosmos as an imperfect but genuine likeness of the eternal model. Understanding why the world was made and what it was made from gives the context for Plato's account of time.

Second, we examine Plato's famous definition of time as "a moving image of eternity" (*Timaeus* 37d) — one of the most beautiful and most philosophically dense sentences in the entire tradition. What does it mean for time to *image* eternity? What is the relationship between the numerical structure of time (measured by the celestial motions) and the eternal model it images?

Third, we examine the distinction between *aion* (eternity) and *chronos* (time) — two Greek words for temporal matters that Plato deploys with philosophical precision. Understanding this distinction requires understanding Plato's metaphysical hierarchy: the Forms, the Demiurge, the created cosmos, and the *Receptacle* — the strange, third kind of thing that underlies all temporal becoming.

Fourth, we turn to epistemological questions: what does Plato's temporal ontology imply about the possibility of knowledge? Can we have genuine knowledge (*episteme*) of temporal things, or only opinion (*doxa*)? And how does the famous doctrine of recollection (*anamnesis*) give time a role in the soul's relationship to eternal truth?

A note on method: throughout this chapter, citations to the *Timaeus* follow the standard Stephanus pagination, using Donald Zeyl's translation as the base text (Plato 1997).

---

*Chapter 4 comprises four sections. Chapter-end resources include exercises, further reading, key concepts, and key researchers.*

### Section 1: The Timaeus Cosmogony

---

#### Section Introduction

The *Timaeus* begins in the middle of a conversation — we are told that Socrates had the previous day given an account of the ideal city, and now Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates have gathered to respond with an account of the origin of the cosmos. Timaeus speaks first, and what he delivers is not a refutation of anything but a construction: a full-scale account of how the universe came to be, what it is made of, and why it has the temporal structure it does.

The cosmogony is explicitly presented as a "likely story" (*eikôs logos*) rather than a demonstration (*apodeixis*). Plato is clear that the physical world, being in the domain of becoming rather than being, can only be described with probable accounts, not strict knowledge (*Timaeus* 29c–d). This epistemic humility is part of the philosophical content: the story of creation is as accurate as any story about a temporal, changing world can be.

The heart of the cosmogony is a distinction between three kinds of things: the eternal model (the Living Being, the Form of all forms), the Demiurge (the rational craftsman who looks to the model and makes the cosmos in its likeness), and the product (the created cosmos, a temporal image of the eternal model). Understanding each of these — and their relations to each other — is essential for understanding Plato's philosophy of time.

This section has two subsections. The first examines the Demiurge: his nature, his motivations, and the role he plays in the cosmogony. The second introduces the relationship between the eternal model and its temporal copy, leading into the discussion of time as a moving image.

#### 1.1 The Demiurge

---

##### Why Was the World Made?

Before asking what time is, Plato asks why the world exists at all. The answer given in the *Timaeus* is among the most philosophically remarkable in all of ancient thought: the world was made by a divine craftsman who looked at an eternal model and fashioned the best possible temporal likeness of it, motivated simply by goodness.

Here is the key passage:

"Let us therefore state the reason why the maker of this universe of change framed it at all. He was good, and what is good has no particle of envy in it. Being without envy, he wished everything to be as like himself as possible. This is the supremely valid principle of becoming and of the ordered world, as we shall do well to believe on the testimony of men of insight. God, wishing that all things should be good and so far as possible nothing imperfect, and finding the visible universe in a state not of rest but of inharmonious and disorderly motion, reduced it to order from disorder, as he considered that order was in every way better than disorder." (Plato, *Timaeus* 29d–30a, trans. Cornford 1937: 33–34)

Several features of this passage repay close attention.

###### The Demiurge's Nature

The Demiurge (*dêmiourgos* — literally "craftsman" or "artisan") is not the omnipotent creator-god of Abrahamic theology. He is a *craftsman*, not a creator ex nihilo: he works with pre-existing material (the *Receptacle* or *chora*, discussed in Section 3) and looks to a pre-existing model (the Living Being). His creativity is not unlimited production from nothing but the rational imposition of order on prior disorder.

This matters philosophically. The Demiurge is constrained: by the nature of the model (which he cannot violate, only approximate) and by the nature of the material (which resists complete ordering). The result is not a perfect reproduction of the eternal model but the best possible temporal likeness of it, given the constraints of material and change. Temporal reality is genuinely good — genuinely ordered, genuinely intelligible — but it is imperfect goodness, imperfect order, imperfect intelligibility compared to the eternal original.

###### Goodness Without Envy

The reason for creation is the Demiurge's goodness. He lacks envy (*phthonos*): there is nothing in him that would want to keep goodness to himself or to withhold it from things that could partake of it. A less good maker might have been satisfied with a static, isolated perfection. The Demiurge, being entirely good, wants the good to be shared, to be expressed, to be realized as fully as possible in the material domain.

This is a remarkable claim. It makes creation an expression of the diffusive nature of the good — the principle that goodness, by its very nature, wants to spread and share itself. This principle — that the good is self-diffusive — became one of the most important ideas in Neoplatonist philosophy (Plotinus, *Enneads* V.1.6; V.2.1) and was later taken up by Christian theology in accounts of divine creation. Creation, on this view, is not an arbitrary act or a response to divine need but an expression of the essential nature of goodness.

For the philosophy of time, this has an important implication: time, as the medium of the created temporal cosmos, is not evil or defective in its nature. It is imperfect by comparison with eternity, but it is genuine and good — a real (if incomplete) expression of the eternal good. This distinguishes Platonic temporal ontology from purely dualistic views that see the temporal world as simply bad or illusory.

###### The Model: The Living Being

What model does the Demiurge look to? It is "the Living Being," the eternal Form that encompasses all the intelligible living forms (*Timaeus* 30c–31a). The Living Being is the most perfect and comprehensive of the Forms — an intelligible totality that contains within itself the formal principles of all living things.

The Demiurge makes the cosmos in the likeness of this model — as "one visible living thing that embraces all the visible living things within it" (*Timaeus* 30d, Zeyl trans.). The cosmos is a *living animal* (the Greek *zôon* means both "living creature" and "animal"), not a dead machine. It is alive, it is rational, and it is temporal because it is made in the likeness of an eternal model that it can only imperfectly reproduce.

###### Why Not Simply Make an Eternal World?

A natural question arises: if eternity is better than time, why didn't the Demiurge simply make an eternal world? Why make something temporal at all?

Plato does not address this question explicitly, but the answer is implicit in the account. The Demiurge makes the cosmos from pre-existing material (the Receptacle), and material — by its very nature — is subject to change. The Receptacle is the medium of becoming, of spatial location and material realization; it is not the medium of eternal, changeless being. A temporal material world is the only kind of world that can be made from material at all. Eternity is the condition of pure, immaterial being; anything material and physical is, by necessity, temporal.

This connects to a deep theme in Plato's metaphysics: matter is the source of imperfection, instability, and temporal change; form is the source of intelligibility, stability, and approximation to eternity. A perfectly material world cannot be eternal; a perfectly eternal being cannot be material. The created cosmos is a compromise — the best possible material image of the eternal model — and time is the medium of this compromise.

###### The Cosmogonic Myth and Philosophical Interpretation

Scholars have debated whether the creation narrative in the *Timaeus* should be understood literally (as describing an actual act of creation at a specific time) or metaphorically (as a way of analyzing the structural features of the cosmos without implying that there was a first moment). Aristotle took Plato to be a literal creationist; Speusippus and Xenocrates argued for a metaphorical reading; the debate continues in modern scholarship (Vlastos 1964; Sorabji 1983: 268–283).

For the philosophy of time, the question is significant: if the creation is literal, then time has a genuine first moment and was genuinely absent before. If it is metaphorical, then the account is saying something about the *structural* dependence of temporal order on eternal being, not about a temporal origin. In either case, the central philosophical claim — that time is ontologically dependent on and derivative of eternity — stands.

---

**Key texts:** Plato, *Timaeus* 29d–30a, 30c–31a, 37c–38c (Zeyl trans. in Cooper 1997).

#### 1.2 Time as a Moving Image of Eternity

---

##### The Most Beautiful Sentence in the Philosophy of Time

At *Timaeus* 37d, Plato gives what is arguably the most celebrated definition of time in the entire philosophical tradition:

"So he [the Demiurge] began to think of making a moving image of eternity: at the same time as he brought order to the universe, he would make an eternal image, moving according to number, of eternity remaining in unity. This is, of course, what we call 'time.'" (Plato, *Timaeus* 37d, trans. Zeyl)

The sentence deserves slow, careful unpacking. Every word is doing philosophical work.

###### "A Moving Image"

The Greek word for "image" is *eikôn* — from which the English "icon" is derived. An eikon is not a copy in the degraded sense of a counterfeit; it is a *likeness*, a representation that genuinely participates in or reflects the nature of what it represents. A portrait of a person is an eikon: it is genuinely like the person (it represents their features), even though it differs from the person in being flat, static, and not alive.

Time is a *moving* image — *kinêton tina aiônos eikona* — not a static one. This is essential. Eternity is the realm of stable, unchanging being; you cannot make an image of it that is also unchanging, because that would be another eternal, not an image. The image must be temporal — it must move, change, cycle — and yet in its motion it must genuinely represent the structure of eternity.

Think of a rotating clock hand. The hand moves in a circle, returning periodically to its starting point. In this motion, it approximates the unchanging completeness of a circle — returning to the beginning, recreating a whole, cycling through all its positions. The completeness of the circle is timeless; the clock hand's traversal of it is temporal. The hand's motion is a temporal image of the circle's timeless completeness.

This is, roughly, what Plato means by time as a moving image of eternity: the cyclical motions of the celestial bodies — the sun, moon, planets, and stars — cycle through their positions, returning periodically, and in this periodicity they approximate the timeless completeness of the eternal model.

###### "Of Eternity Remaining in Unity"

The eternal model remains in unity — *menontôs aiônos en heni* — it does not move, does not change, does not spread itself across time. Eternity is whole, complete, self-identical. Time, by contrast, proceeds "according to number" — sequentially, one moment after another, spreading out what is in eternity simultaneously concentrated in a single, undivided whole.

Consider the number 1 as an analogy. The number 1 is simply 1 — complete, whole, undivided. Now suppose you want to represent 1 in base 10 notation by adding fractions: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... converging to 1. The process is infinite; 1 itself is complete and simple. The infinite series "images" 1 in the sense that it approaches it, approximates it, takes it as its limit — but it spreads out over infinitely many terms what 1 simply is all at once.

Time is like the infinite series; eternity is like 1. Time approximates eternity by proceeding sequentially through what eternity encompasses all at once. The temporal cosmos cycles through its seasons, its astronomical periods, its Great Year — and in doing so, it approximates the completeness of the eternal model. But it can never fully achieve it: there is always another cycle ahead, always another moment not yet arrived.

###### "Moving According to Number"

The phrase *kat' arithmon iousan* — "moving according to number" — gives Platonic time its mathematical character. Time is not just any motion; it is *numbered* motion. The celestial bodies move according to precise numerical ratios; their periods can be expressed as numbers; the Great Year is the period after which all the numbers come back into alignment. Time, in this sense, is the mathematical dimension of the temporal cosmos's movement toward its eternal model.

This connects to the Pythagorean inheritance in the *Timaeus*. The Demiurge, in constructing the World Soul (the intelligent animating principle of the cosmos), uses mathematical ratios — the same ratios that govern musical harmony — to structure its composition (*Timaeus* 35a–36d). The World Soul is literally a mathematical structure; its motion produces the celestial orbits; and the orbits produce time. Time is therefore mathematically structured at its very foundation.

For Plato, this mathematical character of time is not a contingent feature; it is what makes time genuinely representative of eternity. The eternal Forms are objects of mathematical knowledge: they have precise, necessary structure, accessible to reason. Time approximates them by having a mathematical structure of its own — a structure that can be known by reason, not just perceived by the senses.

###### The Asymmetry Between Eternity and Time

Several important asymmetries follow from Plato's definition.

**Ontological asymmetry.** Eternity is more real than time. The eternal Forms — including the Living Being — are the originals; the temporal cosmos is a copy. Copies are ontologically dependent on originals; they exist insofar as and because the originals exist. Time therefore depends on eternity ontologically, not the reverse.

**Epistemic asymmetry.** Knowledge of eternal things is stable, certain, and accessible to reason. Knowledge of temporal things is unstable, merely probable, and accessible primarily to perception. This is why the *Timaeus* account of the cosmos is a "likely story" — because its subject matter (the temporal, material cosmos) does not support the kind of certain knowledge that mathematics or philosophy of Forms can provide.

**Evaluative asymmetry.** Eternity is better than time. The goal of the Demiurge was to make something as good as possible; the constraint was the material, which is inherently temporal. Time represents a genuine good — it is the best possible temporal approximation of eternity — but it is imperfect goodness by comparison.

###### Philosophical Assessment

Plato's definition of time as a moving image of eternity is one of the most influential and most debated in the history of philosophy. Its strengths include: it gives time a positive ontological status (not mere illusion but genuine image); it connects temporal structure to mathematical necessity (time is not arbitrary, it is governed by numerical ratios); and it explains the cosmological significance of astronomical cycles (they are the most visible expression of time's approximation to eternity).

Its difficulties are equally notable. The notion of "imaging" eternity is metaphorical and needs unpacking: in what precise sense does numerical, cyclical motion represent timeless being? The account seems to imply that temporal passage is, in some sense, a defect — an inability to be all at once — rather than a positive feature. And the close identification of time with celestial motion raises questions: what happens to time if the celestial bodies stop moving? Is time simply identical with those motions, or are the motions merely the measure of something else?

These questions were taken up with great energy by Plotinus in the Neoplatonist tradition and by Augustine, each of whom developed sophisticated responses to the Platonic account.

---

**Key texts:** Plato, *Timaeus* 37c–38e, 35a–36d (Zeyl trans. in Cooper 1997).

### Section 2: Eternity vs. Time

---

#### Section Introduction

Plato's philosophy of time cannot be understood apart from his account of eternity. The two concepts are defined in relation to each other: time is what eternity is *not*, and yet time is what it is precisely because it *approximates* eternity. To understand what it means for time to image eternity, we need to understand what eternity is.

The Greek philosophical tradition distinguishes two ways in which something can be "without temporal limitation." Something is *sempiternal* if it exists at all times — if it has always existed and always will exist, but within time. The sun, on a certain picture, might be sempiternal: it has existed since the universe began and will exist until the universe ends. Something is *eternal* in the stronger sense if it exists *outside* time altogether — not "at all times" but in a mode of being to which temporal predications (before, after, duration) simply do not apply.

Plato's Forms are eternal in the stronger sense. They are not just very old; they are not temporal at all. The Form of Beauty does not have a duration; it is not located in time at all; it has not existed since some particular moment and will not cease to exist at some future moment. Its being is radically different in kind from temporal being.

This section examines two aspects of Plato's eternity-time distinction. The first concerns the Greek terms *aion* and *chronos* and what Plato intends by them. The second concerns the ontology of the realm of *becoming* — why temporal existence is ontologically inferior to eternal existence — and what this implies for Plato's system.

#### 2.1 Aion vs. Chronos

---

##### Two Greek Words for Time

Philosophical vocabulary is never entirely innocent, and the Greek vocabulary for time repays careful attention. The two primary Greek words for time are *aion* and *chronos*, and their relationship is philosophically significant in the *Timaeus* in a way that is easily lost in translation.

*Chronos* is the ordinary Greek word for time: the time of the clock and calendar, the time that is measured and counted, the time in which events occur and are located relative to each other. It is the time of ordinary human experience — the time that divides past from present from future, the time that is measured by the motions of the sun and moon, the time that can be "wasted" or "saved."

*Aion* has a more complex semantic history (Onians 1951: 200–228). In Homer, *aion* means something like "vital force" or "life span." In the fifth-century lyric poets, it can mean "lifetime" or "generation." But in philosophical usage — beginning decisively with the *Timaeus* — it acquires the meaning of *eternity*: not endless duration, but a mode of being that is categorically distinct from temporal existence.

In the key passage of the *Timaeus*, Plato uses *aion* for the eternal model and *chronos* for its temporal image. The sentence at 37d reads: "he decided to make a moving image of *aion* ... this is what we call *chronos*." The distinction is explicit and deliberate.

###### What Makes Aion Different from Endless Chronos

The crucial question is: what exactly is the difference between (a) *aion* as *eternity* — a mode of being utterly outside time — and (b) *aion* as *endless time* — an infinite temporal duration?

Plato's answer is in the grammar of the eternal. The eternal model, Plato says, "was and is and will be" — but wait, Plato immediately corrects himself: "only 'is' applies to it in strict truth; 'was' and 'will be' are forms of time that have come to be" (*Timaeus* 37e, Zeyl trans.). The past tense ("was") implies that something is no longer; the future tense ("will be") implies that something has not yet come to be. Both carry a reference to a present moment relative to which they are defined. And the eternal has no relationship to a present moment — it is not "now" rather than "then"; it simply *is*.

The distinction, then, is between:

(a) **Eternal being (aion)**: Being that is wholly present to itself, not distributed across time, without before or after in its own nature. The word "is" applies to it, but "was" and "will be" do not. It is not that it exists at all times; it is that it exists in a mode to which temporal location is inapplicable.

(b) **Temporal existence (chronos)**: Existence that is distributed across time, in which the past is gone, the future not yet arrived, and the present is a brief transition between them. The words "was," "is," and "will be" all apply to temporal things, shifting in their application as time passes.

This distinction anticipates the medieval philosophical debate about the nature of divine eternity. Boethius, in the *Consolation of Philosophy*, draws the contrast in terms that are explicitly Platonic: eternity is not the *whole* of an infinite life spread out through time, but the *simultaneous* possession of a complete life (*interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio*) — all of it at once, not extended over time (Boethius, *Consolatio* V.6, Relihan trans.). The contrast is between a *tota simul* eternity (all-at-once) and a sempiternal existence (existing at all times in sequence).

###### The Forms and Their Timeless Existence

The Forms — the eternal, unchanging objects of Platonic knowledge — exist in the mode of *aion*. The Form of Beauty is not beautiful *now* (as opposed to being ugly yesterday or tomorrow). It is simply, unqualifiedly beautiful — at all times, outside of time, in a mode of being to which temporal qualifications do not apply. It is not in time at all.

This is why knowledge of the Forms is not temporal knowledge. When you genuinely know that the sum of the angles of a Euclidean triangle equals 180 degrees, you are knowing something that is true regardless of when you know it, that does not change over time, that does not depend on any particular moment of temporal existence. Mathematical truths are timeless in this sense; and for Plato, mathematical knowledge is a model for knowledge of the Forms in general.

The philosopher who achieves genuine knowledge of the Forms has, in that moment of knowledge, a direct cognitive relationship with the eternal — with *aion* rather than *chronos*. This is not a merely academic accomplishment; it is, for Plato, a transformation of the self, a moment in which the soul turns away from the temporal, changing world and toward the eternal, unchanging reality that underlies it.

###### Aion in Later Philosophy

The *Timaeus* distinction between *aion* and *chronos* was enormously influential. The Neoplatonists — particularly Plotinus in the *Enneads* — developed it into a full metaphysical hierarchy. For Plotinus, Eternity (*aion*) is a property of Nous (Intellect or Mind) — the eternal intellectual activity of contemplation in which all the Forms are simultaneously present and active. Time (*chronos*) is a property of Soul — the World Soul's perpetual, sequential activity that cannot grasp all the Forms at once but cycles through them, producing temporal succession (*Enneads* III.7).

This Neoplatonist development takes up the Platonic insight that time is the Soul's way of approximating Intellect's timeless completeness — a temporal spread-out of what is, in Intellect, gathered up in a single, atemporal act of knowing.

---

**Key texts:** Plato, *Timaeus* 37c–38b (Zeyl trans.); Boethius, *Consolatio* V.6 (Relihan trans.).

#### 2.2 Becoming and the Ontology of the Image

---

##### Why Temporal Existence Is Ontologically Inferior

Plato's metaphysics is hierarchical. Some things are more real, more good, and more knowable than others. The Forms are at the top: fully real, fully good, fully knowable. The temporal world of becoming is at the bottom of the ontological scale (above pure formlessness, but well below the Forms). Understanding why Plato places temporal existence so low in the hierarchy is crucial for understanding his philosophy of time.

###### The Divided Line

In the *Republic* (509d–511e), Plato introduces the famous image of the *Divided Line* to illustrate his epistemological and ontological hierarchy. The line is divided into two major sections: the Intelligible (the realm of the Forms, known through reason) and the Visible (the realm of images and ordinary objects, known through perception and belief). Each major section is in turn divided into two sub-sections, giving four levels in total.

In ascending order:
1. **Images** (reflections, shadows): the lowest level of the visible realm. Known through imagination or conjecture (*eikasia*).
2. **Ordinary visible things** (animals, plants, artifacts): the level of ordinary perceptual objects. Known through perception-based belief (*pistis*).
3. **Mathematical objects** (numbers, geometric figures): the lower level of the intelligible realm. Known through hypothetical reasoning (*dianoia*).
4. **The Forms** (including the Form of the Good): the highest level. Known through pure rational insight (*noêsis*).

Temporal things — the things that come to be and pass away — fall at levels 2 and possibly 3 of this hierarchy. They are genuine objects of perception-based belief; they are real enough to be seen, touched, and interacted with. But they are not objects of the highest knowledge; they are not fully real; they are more like images of Forms than like Forms themselves.

###### Why Temporal Things Are Ontologically Inferior

The reason temporal things are ontologically inferior is that they lack the stability, unity, and self-identity that full reality requires. Consider a beautiful face: it is beautiful now, but it was not beautiful in infancy and will not be beautiful in extreme age. It is beautiful only *to some* observers and under some conditions of light and angle. It is beautiful in one respect (the eyes) and not in another (some feature that does not please). In all these ways, it falls short of the Form of Beauty, which is beautiful always, to everyone, in every respect, unconditionally (Plato, *Symposium* 211a–b).

The same applies to all temporal predicates. A temporal thing is F at one time and not-F at another. A Form is simply F, without temporal qualification, without exception, without the hedging that temporal predication requires. The Forms "always are" (*aei onta*) what they are; temporal things "come to be" (*gignomena*) what they temporarily are, and they pass away.

This instability — the characteristic of temporal things — is what makes them less real, less good, and less knowable than the Forms. Reality, for Plato, is a matter of *what you can count on*: the Forms can always be counted on to be exactly what they are; temporal things cannot.

###### The Image and Its Original

The metaphysics of the image (*eikôn*) is philosophically subtle. An image is not an illusion; it is not nothing. The reflection of a tree in still water is a real image — it is really there, it has real properties, it can be seen. But it is ontologically dependent on the tree: if the tree were destroyed, the reflection would vanish. The tree can exist without the reflection; the reflection cannot exist without the tree.

Temporal things stand to the Forms as images stand to originals. They have genuine existence — they are really there, they have real properties — but they are ontologically dependent on the Forms that they image. They exist *because of* and *by participation in* the Forms. A temporal beautiful thing is beautiful insofar as it participates in (shares in, imitates, images) the Form of Beauty.

And crucially: as images, temporal things have the defects of images. A shadow of a tree looks like the tree but lacks its texture, color, three-dimensionality, and life. A temporal beautiful thing approximates the Form of Beauty but lacks its stability, universality, and necessity. The defects of images — imprecision, instability, context-dependence — are the defects of temporal things.

###### Temporality and Opinion

This ontological hierarchy has direct epistemological consequences. The *Republic*'s Divided Line indicates that perception-based belief (*doxa*) — opinion — is the cognitive state appropriate to temporal things. We do not *know* (in the strict Platonic sense) temporal things; we form beliefs about them, beliefs that may be accurate and well-justified but that can always turn out to be wrong because their objects can always turn out to have changed.

This is not a counsel of cognitive despair. Plato does not say that beliefs about temporal things are worthless or that we should ignore the temporal world. He says that the cognitive achievement appropriate to temporal things is belief, not knowledge; and that beliefs about temporal things, however accurate, do not achieve the stability and certainty of genuine knowledge of the eternal.

The practical implication is that the philosopher should not confuse accurate perception of temporal things with genuine understanding. Understanding requires knowledge of the Forms; knowledge of the Forms is not temporal. The philosopher who mistakes a beautiful face for the Form of Beauty has mistaken an image for an original — and, for Plato, this is not only an intellectual mistake but a moral and existential one: a life lived in pursuit of temporal beauties, rather than eternal Beauty, is a life oriented toward the inferior rather than the superior, toward becoming rather than being.

###### Philosophical Assessment

Plato's ontological hierarchy has been enormously influential and enormously contested. The standard objection — the "Third Man Argument" that Aristotle raised and that appears in Plato's own *Parmenides* — questions the coherence of the participation relationship: if a beautiful thing is beautiful because it participates in the Form of Beauty, what makes the Form of Beauty itself beautiful? Another Form? And then another? (Plato, *Parmenides* 132a–b; Aristotle, *Metaphysics* 990b17–991a8.) This regress threatens the whole framework.

More relevant to the philosophy of time is the question of whether temporal existence is really as defective as Plato suggests. Is it true that we cannot "count on" temporal things in the way we count on mathematical truths? Many philosophers, including Aristotle, have thought that temporal existence has its own kind of reliability and its own kind of knowability — that science of temporal, changing things is possible, even if it differs from mathematical knowledge. We will examine this in Chapter 5.

---

**Key texts:** Plato, *Republic* 509d–511e, 476d–480a; *Symposium* 211a–b; *Timaeus* 27d–28a (Cooper 1997).

### Section 3: The Receptacle and Becoming

---

#### Section Introduction

The cosmogony of the *Timaeus* involves not two but three fundamental principles: Being, Becoming, and a third that is philosophically the most puzzling of all — the *Receptacle* (*chora*, sometimes *hupodochê*, "that which receives"). Plato introduces the Receptacle in *Timaeus* 48e–52d, in a second creation account that supplements the first by introducing the material dimension of the cosmos.

The introduction is striking. Plato says that when the first account was given (of the Demiurge, the model, and the cosmos), he was "omitting" the Receptacle — a "third kind" (*triton genos*) alongside Being and Becoming. Now he must address it, even though it is difficult to talk about and resistant to ordinary forms of predication.

The Receptacle is the "nurse of becoming" (*Timaeus* 49a): it is the medium in which the images of the Forms appear, the material substrate that receives impressions from the eternal model. It is not itself a Form; it is not any particular kind of thing; it is the precondition of all temporal, material existence.

Understanding the Receptacle is important for the philosophy of time because it is the *material* dimension of temporal existence — the side of the temporal world that is not explained by its participation in Forms but that provides the *where* and the *when* of temporal things: their location in space and time.

This section has a single subsection examining the Receptacle in detail.

#### 3.1 The Receptacle (Chora)

---

##### The Third Kind

The Receptacle (*chora* — literally "space" or "room," though in the *Timaeus* it functions as more than just physical space) is introduced by Plato with unusual philosophical caution. It is "difficult and vague" (*argalepê kai amydra*); it is known "by a kind of bastard reasoning" (*logismô tini nothô*); it is "perceptible to a sort of perception that is illegitimate" (*Timaeus* 52b, Zeyl trans.). These warnings are themselves philosophically significant: the Receptacle is at the limit of what Platonic philosophy can handle with its normal tools.

Here is Plato's main description:

"It is invisible and characterless, all-receiving, partaking in some very puzzling way of the intelligible and very hard to catch: we shall not be wrong if we call it the receptacle and, as it were, the nurse of all becoming and change." (*Timaeus* 49a, Taylor trans.)

What is being described here? Let us work through the main features.

###### "All-Receiving" and "Characterless"

The Receptacle is *all-receiving* (*pandechês*): it receives all the impressions of the Forms. Think of it as a wax tablet that receives the impressions of seals: the wax itself has no shape of its own, but it takes on whatever shape is pressed into it. The Receptacle is the "wax" of the cosmos: it has no inherent qualities of its own, but it can receive and display the characteristics that correspond to the Forms.

It is *characterless* precisely because it receives all characters. If the Receptacle were, say, hot by nature, it would resist receiving "cold" — the Form of Cold could not appear in it. If it were blue, the Form of Red could not fully appear. To receive all qualities equally, it must be intrinsically colorless, temperatureless, textureless. It must be a kind of pure receptivity, without any positive nature that would interfere with the reception of Form.

This creates a philosophical puzzle. If the Receptacle has no positive character, what kind of thing is it? Is it a *substance* (a thing in the Aristotelian sense)? It does not seem to be: it has no essential properties, no natural kind. Is it a *property* or *accident*? No, because it is the *substrate* of properties, not a property itself. Is it simply *space* — the spatial extension in which things are located? This is tempting (and *chora* does mean "space"), but the Receptacle seems to be more than just space: it is the *material* dimension of temporal existence, the *stuff* out of which temporal things are made, not just the place in which they are located.

###### The Gold Analogy

Plato illustrates the Receptacle with an analogy to gold (*Timaeus* 50a–b). Suppose a goldsmith makes many different shapes — animals, vessels, tools — out of gold. When asked "what is that?" referring to the gold that takes all these shapes, the best answer is "gold" rather than naming any of the particular shapes, since the gold persists through all the transformations. The shapes come and go; the gold remains.

The Receptacle is like the gold: it is what persists through all the transformations of the temporal world. As the Forms impress themselves on the Receptacle, temporal things appear and disappear — like shapes being made and remade in the gold. The Receptacle is the permanent, characterless substrate of all this change.

The analogy is illuminating but imperfect. Gold is a specific substance with specific properties (it is yellow, heavy, malleable). The Receptacle has no such properties; it is gold stripped of all its qualities, leaving only pure material receptivity.

###### The Receptacle and Space-Time

Modern readers have naturally wondered about the relationship between the Receptacle and modern concepts of space and time. The *chora* is clearly spatial — it provides the *where* of temporal things, their location. But it also seems to be temporal — it provides the *when*, the medium of temporal change.

Julia Annas (1975: 116–119) and others have argued that the Receptacle is better understood as something like a *spatial substrate* (a "space" in the modern sense) into which Forms are projected. But Harold Cherniss (1954) and later scholars have argued that the Receptacle has a temporal as well as spatial dimension — that it is the medium of *becoming* in general, not just spatial location.

This question has been taken up in modern physics. In relativity theory, spacetime is a four-dimensional manifold that provides the "container" for all events — somewhat analogous to the Receptacle. And in some interpretations of quantum field theory, the vacuum (the ground state of quantum fields, which is not "empty" in the ordinary sense) plays a role analogous to the Receptacle: it is the characterless substrate from which particles appear and into which they disappear. These parallels are suggestive but should not be over-stressed; Plato is not doing physics.

###### "A Kind of Bastard Reasoning"

Perhaps the most interesting feature of the Receptacle's description is Plato's claim that we know it "by a kind of bastard reasoning" — by an illegitimate, not-quite-rational mode of cognition. Why?

The Receptacle cannot be known as the Forms are known (by pure rational intuition), because it is not an intelligible Form — it has no positive rational structure for the intellect to grasp. It cannot be known as ordinary sensible objects are known (by perception), because it has no perceptible qualities. It is known only by a kind of inference from what we observe: we see temporal things changing, and we infer that there must be a substrate — something that receives the changing impressions — even if we cannot directly observe or rationally grasp it as such.

This is philosophically important: it reveals the limits of Platonic epistemology. The Receptacle is necessary to account for the material, spatial, temporal character of the world — but it resists both the intellectual gaze (which requires a positive Form to grasp) and the perceptual gaze (which requires perceptible qualities to detect). It is at the margins of the Platonic system, a necessary but recalcitrant element.

###### Philosophical Significance for the Philosophy of Time

The Receptacle's relevance to the philosophy of time is threefold.

First, it shows that temporal existence is not merely a degraded copy of eternal existence; it also has a material dimension — the Receptacle — that the Forms alone cannot account for. Temporal things are constituted by both Form (the intelligible structure they instantiate) and the Receptacle (the material medium in which they are realized). The material dimension introduces an irreducible element of contingency, instability, and particularity.

Second, the Receptacle is the "nurse of becoming": it is what makes temporal change possible. Forms do not change; the Demiurge does not change. What changes is the pattern of Form-impressions in the Receptacle. Temporal change is change *in* the Receptacle — a succession of different patterns appearing in the same underlying characterless medium.

Third, the Receptacle raises one of the deepest questions in metaphysics: what is the relationship between form and matter, between intelligible structure and physical realization? This question will preoccupy Aristotle (who transforms it into the hylomorphic framework of form and matter), medieval philosophy (in discussions of prime matter and substantial form), and modern philosophy (in discussions of abstract versus concrete objects and the mind-body problem).

---

**Key texts:** Plato, *Timaeus* 48e–52d (Zeyl trans. in Cooper 1997).

### Section 4: Time and Knowledge

---

#### Section Introduction

Plato's philosophy of time is not only a metaphysics — it is also an epistemology. The sharp ontological distinction between eternal being (the Forms) and temporal becoming (the perceptible world) has direct implications for what we can know and how we know it. The realm of becoming, being ontologically inferior, is also epistemically inferior: it is the object of opinion (*doxa*) and belief (*pistis*), not of genuine knowledge (*episteme*).

But this raises a set of fascinating and difficult questions. Does it follow that we cannot have *any* genuine knowledge of temporal things? What about memory — our knowledge of the past? What about the soul's relationship to its own temporal existence? And what is the significance of the *Meno*'s doctrine of recollection (*anamnesis*), which suggests that genuine knowledge is not acquired through temporal experience but recovered from a pre-temporal condition?

These questions connect the metaphysics of the *Timaeus* to the epistemology of the early Platonic dialogues, particularly the *Meno* and the *Phaedo*. Together, they reveal a picture in which temporal experience plays a paradoxical role in knowledge: it is both the obstacle to knowledge (because temporal things are unstable and changing) and the occasion for knowledge (because temporal experience of particular beautiful or just or good things can trigger the soul's recollection of the eternal Forms).

This section examines the epistemological dimension of Plato's philosophy of time, focusing on the Divided Line (*Republic*), the doctrine of recollection (*Meno*, *Phaedo*), and the implications for the soul's temporal and eternal status.

#### 4.1 Knowledge, Eternity, and Recollection

---

##### Can We Know Temporal Things?

Plato's answer to the question "can we know temporal things?" is nuanced and sometimes appears contradictory. The strong answer, suggested by the *Republic*, is no: knowledge (*episteme*) is of the unchanging, and temporal things change, so they can only be objects of opinion (*doxa*). The more nuanced answer, suggested by the *Meno* and *Phaedo*, is that temporal experience can be the occasion for genuine knowledge — not because the temporal things themselves are known, but because encountering them triggers the soul's recovery of knowledge it already has from a pre-temporal condition.

To understand this position, we need to examine both the *Republic*'s epistemology and the doctrine of recollection.

###### The Divided Line and Temporal Knowledge

In the *Republic*'s Divided Line (509d–511e), Plato assigns different cognitive faculties to different levels of reality:

- *Noêsis* (intellectual intuition, dialectic): the highest cognitive state, directed at the Forms, including the Form of the Good.
- *Dianoia* (mathematical reasoning): the cognitive state of the mathematician, using hypotheses and diagrams.
- *Pistis* (perception-based belief): the cognitive state directed at ordinary perceptible things — animals, plants, artifacts.
- *Eikasia* (conjecture, imagination): the lowest cognitive state, directed at images and reflections of perceptible things.

Temporal things — the perceptible objects of ordinary experience — fall under *pistis*. We form *beliefs* about them, beliefs that can be more or less accurate, more or less well-justified. But *pistis* is not *episteme* in the strict sense: it is not knowledge of the necessary, the unchanging, the eternal. It is tracking the world as it temporarily is rather than grasping how things must be.

This seems to imply that science of temporal things — natural science, including what we would call physics, chemistry, and biology — cannot achieve the status of genuine knowledge in Plato's strictest sense. And indeed, the *Timaeus*'s "likely story" acknowledges this: the best cosmological account is probable, not certain, precisely because its subject matter is temporal and changing.

However, Plato is not dismissing natural science as worthless. He is categorizing it: it occupies a genuine cognitive level, appropriate to its objects, below the mathematical sciences and the philosophy of Forms but above mere unstructured perception.

###### The Meno and the Paradox of Inquiry

The *Meno* (80d–e) raises a paradox about knowledge and time: how can you inquire after what you do not know? If you know what you are looking for, the inquiry is unnecessary (you already have the answer). If you do not know what you are looking for, you would not recognize it when you found it. Therefore inquiry is impossible.

Plato's response is the doctrine of recollection (*anamnesis*): "Learning is nothing but recollection" (*Meno* 81d, Grube trans.). The soul, being immortal, has existed before its present embodied life. In its pre-embodied state, it had direct acquaintance with the Forms. When it enters the body and undergoes temporal experience, it forgets what it knew. But the knowledge is not lost — it is dormant, latent, recoverable.

Temporal experience — seeing, touching, experiencing beautiful or just or equal things — serves as a *trigger* for recollection: it reminds the soul of the eternal Forms it once knew directly. When you see two sticks of approximately equal length and recognize that they are *almost but not quite* equal, you are recognizing them as imperfect instances of a standard — the Form of Equality itself — that you know from before your temporal existence (*Phaedo* 74b–75a).

###### Anamnesis as a Temporal-Epistemic Structure

The doctrine of recollection is a deeply interesting temporal-epistemic structure. It reverses the ordinary direction of knowledge acquisition: instead of learning things from temporal experience (as empiricists suggest), the soul *recovers* knowledge that precedes and survives temporal experience. Temporal experience is not the source of knowledge but the occasion for its recovery.

This has several philosophical implications.

**The soul's temporal and atemporal dimensions.** The soul in its full nature transcends temporal existence: it was present before this temporal life and will be present after it. Its genuine cognitive life — the life of *noêsis*, of direct acquaintance with the Forms — is atemporal. But its embodied, temporal life includes the experience of recollection: the temporal process of recovering what was anemporally known. Recollection is thus a temporal process oriented toward an atemporal content.

**The significance of temporal ignorance.** The soul's forgetting upon embodiment is not merely unfortunate; it is, within the Platonic framework, almost necessary: embodiment in the material world involves immersion in the temporal, changing, sensible realm, and this immersion naturally produces forgetfulness of the eternal. The temporal world and the eternal world are not merely ontologically distinct; they are in tension cognitively. Temporal experience pulls the soul toward the particular, the changing, the sensory; philosophical inquiry redirects it toward the eternal.

**The asymmetry between memory and recollection.** Ordinary memory is the recovery of past temporal events: I remember what happened yesterday. But *anamnesis* is the recovery of atemporal knowledge — knowledge that was never temporally acquired, because it was acquired in a pre-temporal condition. This is not temporal memory; it is a different kind of cognitive recovery. The *Meno* (82b–85e) illustrates this with the famous episode in which Socrates draws out geometrical knowledge from an uneducated slave boy through questioning: the boy did not learn the geometry from temporal experience; he recovers it through reflection prompted by the questioning.

###### Philosophical Assessment

The doctrine of recollection faces serious objections. It presupposes the pre-existence of the soul — a substantial metaphysical commitment that requires independent argument. It does not obviously explain the *content* of what is recollected: if all knowledge is recollection, how was the knowledge acquired in the first place? Aristotle raises this objection in the *Prior Analytics* (67a21–26): if all learning is recollection, you would need to have known things before knowing them, which seems impossible.

But the doctrine illuminates something philosophically genuine: the distinction between temporal acquisition and atemporal validity. Mathematical truths are not "learned" in the same sense that historical facts are learned; they are more like truths that, once understood, seem to have been always true. The *Meno*'s slave boy episode illustrates how reflection — not experience — can produce genuine understanding of necessary truths. Whatever we make of the metaphysics of pre-existence, the epistemological point stands: some knowledge is not temporal in the sense of being acquired from temporal experience, but in the sense of grasping structures that are themselves atemporal.

For the philosophy of time, Plato's account suggests a rich and complex relationship between temporal existence and temporal knowledge. We are temporal beings; our ordinary cognitive life is temporal — memory of the past, perception of the present, anticipation of the future. But we are also capable of a kind of knowing that transcends temporal limitation — knowledge of eternal mathematical and philosophical truths — and this capacity is, for Plato, the highest expression of what we are.

---

**Key texts:** Plato, *Meno* 80d–86c; *Phaedo* 72e–77d; *Republic* 509d–511e; *Symposium* 209e–212b (Cooper 1997).

### Chapter 4 Exercises

---

#### Comprehension and Analysis

**Exercise 1.** Plato describes the Demiurge as acting from goodness "without envy." Explain what this means philosophically and why it is significant for Plato's account of creation. How does the Demiurge's motivation connect to the claim that the created cosmos is genuinely good, even though it is ontologically inferior to the eternal model? Compare this to the Abrahamic doctrine of creation discussed in Chapter 2, Section 3.2.

**Exercise 2.** Analyze Plato's definition of time as "a moving image of eternity" (*Timaeus* 37d). Identify (a) the respects in which time is like eternity (the "image" aspect) and (b) the respects in which time differs from eternity (the "moving" and "temporal" aspects). What would it mean for an image to be a good image of eternity? What would it mean for it to be a poor one?

**Exercise 3.** Explain the distinction between *aion* (eternity) and *chronos* (time) as Plato uses these terms. Why does Plato say that "was" and "will be" should not be predicated of eternal being? How does Boethius's later formulation (*tota simul*) capture and extend this Platonic insight?

**Exercise 4.** Describe the Receptacle (*chora*) and explain its role in Plato's cosmogony. Why does Plato say we know it "by a kind of bastard reasoning"? What philosophical problem does the Receptacle solve, and what new philosophical problems does it introduce?

**Exercise 5.** In the *Republic*'s Divided Line, temporal things (perceptible objects) are assigned to the level of *pistis* (perception-based belief), not *episteme* (knowledge). Does this mean that natural science — physics, chemistry, biology — is merely opinion for Plato? Develop a careful response, drawing on Plato's distinction between knowledge and opinion and on the *Timaeus*'s account of a "likely story."

**Exercise 6.** Explain the Meno Paradox and Plato's response to it via the doctrine of recollection (*anamnesis*). How does the slave boy episode (*Meno* 82b–85e) illustrate recollection? Is the evidence it provides convincing? Reconstruct Aristotle's objection to the doctrine (from *Prior Analytics* 67a21–26) and evaluate it.

**Exercise 7.** Plato's *Timaeus* presents a creation myth — a "likely story" about the origin of the cosmos. The debate in scholarship is whether this is meant literally (there was an actual creation event) or metaphorically (the creation narrative describes structural features of the cosmos, not an historical event). What philosophical considerations bear on this question? Which interpretation do you find more defensible, and why?

**Exercise 8.** Compare Plato's account of the relationship between eternity and time with the Heraclitean account of the relationship between the Logos and temporal flux. Both accounts include a "rational principle" underlying the temporal world. How do they differ in their conception of this principle's relationship to time?

---

#### Critical Thinking

**Exercise 9.** Consider the following objection to Plato's ontological hierarchy: "If eternal, unchanging Forms are more real than temporal things, then mathematical truth is more real than the existence of conscious persons. But surely the existence of a conscious person is at least as real as the truth of a mathematical theorem — indeed, it seems to be the precondition of any knowledge of such truths." Construct the strongest possible Platonic response to this objection. Then assess whether the response succeeds.

**Exercise 10.** Plato's account implies that temporal passage — the movement of time — reflects a kind of incompleteness or deficiency: time spreads out sequentially what eternity holds all at once. Is this a plausible picture of temporal passage? Compare it to A-theorist accounts that treat temporal passage as an objective feature of reality (not a deficiency) and B-theorist accounts that deny that time "passes" at all. Which picture is closest to Plato's, and why?

---

#### Lab Exercises

**Lab 1: The Still Point and the Moving Image.** Find a clock with a circular face and a second hand. Observe the motion of the second hand for two minutes. Now: (a) Consider the circle that the second hand describes — a perfect, complete circle, "all at once" in a single geometrical figure. Now consider the second hand's motion, which takes 60 seconds to trace that circle. In what sense does the motion "image" the circle? In what sense is the circle "eternal" by comparison with the motion? (b) Write a one-page philosophical reflection on what this observation reveals about Plato's definition of time as a moving image of eternity. Try to identify both where the analogy is apt and where it breaks down.

**Lab 2: Recollection and Recognition.** This lab explores the difference between temporal memory (remembering past temporal events) and what Plato might call recollection (recognizing eternal truths). Take a mathematical proof that you have not seen before — a simple geometry proof from Euclid's *Elements* Book I (available freely online), such as Proposition 1 (constructing an equilateral triangle) or Proposition 5 (the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal). Work through it carefully. Then reflect: when you follow the proof and see that each step must be so — does this feel like *learning something new from experience*, or like *recognizing something you could not have not known*? Write a one-page reflection on whether your experience of mathematical understanding provides any evidence for the Platonic doctrine that mathematical knowledge is "recollection."

**Lab 3: Becoming and Instability.** Choose an object in your environment — a plant, a piece of fruit, a candle, a glass of water with ice. Observe it closely at one-hour intervals over the course of a day and record your observations in as much detail as possible: color, shape, texture, temperature (estimated), smell, apparent state. At the end of the day, reflect: has the object changed? In what ways is it "the same object"? In what ways is it different? Now consider: is there any respect in which the object's properties are *necessary* and *unchanging* — any respect in which the object genuinely exemplifies a stable Form — and any respect in which it is purely in flux? Write a one-page reflection connecting your observations to Plato's distinction between the Forms (unchanging originals) and temporal things (changing images).

### Chapter 4: Further Reading and Bibliography

---

#### Annotated Further Reading

**Cornford, F. M. 1937. *Plato's Cosmology: The Timaeus of Plato*. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner.**
The classic English translation and commentary on the *Timaeus*. Cornford's commentary is philosophically engaged and historically informed. His discussion of the distinction between *aion* and *chronos* and his analysis of "time as a moving image of eternity" are still required reading, even if some of his interpretive conclusions have been challenged.

**Leftow, Brian. 1991. *Time and Eternity*. Ithaca: Cornell University Press.**
The most rigorous contemporary philosophical treatment of the distinction between temporal and eternal modes of existence. Leftow carefully distinguishes timelessness from sempiternity, addresses the theological implications of divine eternity, and provides detailed analysis of the arguments for and against various views. Demanding but essential for anyone interested in the eternity-time distinction.

**Plotinus. *Enneads* III.7: "On Eternity and Time." In *The Enneads*, translated by Stephen MacKenna. London: Faber and Faber, 1969.**
Plotinus's most important text for the philosophy of time. He argues that eternity is the simultaneous totality of Intellect's life, while time is the restless, sequential unfolding of the World Soul's activity — a temporal image of what Intellect holds all at once. The analysis is philosophically subtle and reads as a creative development of, rather than mere commentary on, the *Timaeus*.

**Plato. *Timaeus*. Translated by Donald Zeyl. In *Complete Works*, edited by John M. Cooper. Indianapolis: Hackett, 1997.**
The standard contemporary scholarly translation. Read alongside *Timaeus* 27c–38e for the cosmogony and the account of time; 48e–52d for the Receptacle; 37c–38e for the definition of time.

**Plato. *Meno*. Translated by G. M. A. Grube. In *Complete Works*, edited by John M. Cooper. Indianapolis: Hackett, 1997.**
Essential for the doctrine of recollection. The dialogue raises the paradox of inquiry (how can you learn what you don't know?) and provides the slave boy episode as an illustration of recollection. Read especially 80d–86c.

**Plato. *Phaedo*. Translated by G. M. A. Grube. In *Complete Works*, edited by John M. Cooper. Indianapolis: Hackett, 1997.**
The fullest treatment of the soul's immortality and its implications for knowledge. Particularly important for the philosophy of time is the discussion at 72e–77d of recollection and the soul's pre-temporal knowledge of the Forms.

**Sorabji, Richard. 1983. *Time, Creation and the Continuum: Theories in Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages*. London: Duckworth.**
The definitive scholarly treatment of ancient and early medieval philosophy of time. Sorabji covers every major figure from the Pre-Socratics through Boethius with rigorous scholarship and philosophical clarity. His chapters on Plato's *Timaeus*, on the creation-eternity debate, and on Aristotelian time are each worth reading in full.

**Stump, Eleonore, and Norman Kretzmann. 1981. "Eternity." *Journal of Philosophy* 78(8): 429–458.**
The most influential contemporary philosophical analysis of the distinction between timeless eternity and temporal existence. Stump and Kretzmann argue that an eternal being exists in a mode in which all of its life is simultaneously present (ET-simultaneous with every temporal moment). Though the paper focuses on divine eternity, it illuminates the philosophical content of the *aion*-*chronos* distinction directly.

**Vlastos, Gregory. 1964. "Creation in the *Timaeus*: Is It a Fiction?" In *Studies in Plato's Metaphysics*, edited by R. E. Allen, 401–419. London: Routledge and Kegan Paul.**
The classic statement of the metaphorical/structural interpretation of the *Timaeus* creation account. Vlastos argues that "creation" in the *Timaeus* should not be read as implying a temporal first moment; rather, it is a philosophical device for displaying the structural dependence of temporal order on eternal being.

**White, Nicholas P. 1976. *Plato on Knowledge and Reality*. Indianapolis: Hackett.**
An accessible and philosophically careful account of Plato's epistemology, including the theory of Forms and the Divided Line. White's treatment of the relationship between Platonic knowledge and temporal existence is particularly useful for understanding the epistemological dimensions of Plato's philosophy of time.

Vlastos, Gregory. 1964. "Creation in the *Timaeus*: Is It a Fiction?" In *Studies in Plato's Metaphysics*, edited by R. E. Allen, 401–419. London: Routledge and Kegan Paul.

White, Nicholas P. 1976. *Plato on Knowledge and Reality*. Indianapolis: Hackett.

Zeyl, Donald. 1997. "Introduction to the *Timaeus*." In *Plato: Complete Works*, edited by John M. Cooper, 1224–1230. Indianapolis: Hackett.

### Chapter 4: Important Concepts

---

**Timaeus**
Plato's cosmological dialogue (ca. 360 BCE), in which the character Timaeus delivers an account of the creation of the universe. The *Timaeus* contains Plato's most systematic treatment of time, the Demiurge, the Forms, and the Receptacle. It was one of the most widely read and influential philosophical texts of antiquity and the early medieval period.

**Demiurge**
The divine craftsman of the *Timaeus* (*dêmiourgos* — artisan). He creates the cosmos by imposing mathematical order on pre-existing material (the Receptacle), using the eternal Living Being as his model. He is motivated by goodness and lack of envy: he wants everything to be as good as possible. He is not an omnipotent creator ex nihilo but a craftsman working within constraints.

**Living Being (Intelligible Model)**
The eternal Form that serves as the Demiurge's model for creating the cosmos. The Living Being is the most comprehensive of the Forms — an eternal, intelligible totality encompassing all the formal principles of living things. The cosmos is made as a temporal likeness of this eternal model.

**Time as a Moving Image of Eternity**
Plato's definition at *Timaeus* 37d: "a moving image of eternity, proceeding according to number." Time is an *image* (*eikôn*) of eternity — it genuinely represents eternity but imperfectly, through cyclical motion that approximates what eternity holds all at once. The motions of the celestial bodies are the specific moving images that constitute time.

**Aion (Eternity)**
The Greek term Plato uses for the eternal model's mode of existence — not endless temporal duration but timeless being, to which the predicates "was" and "will be" do not apply. Only "is" correctly applies to eternal being. Eternity is *all-at-once* (*tota simul*), not spread across temporal succession.

**Chronos (Time)**
The Greek term for ordinary, measurable time — the time of the clock and calendar, in which events have dates, durations, and positions relative to each other. In the *Timaeus*, *chronos* is the created moving image of *aion*, produced when the Demiurge orders the cosmos by the celestial motions.

**Being vs. Becoming**
Plato's fundamental ontological distinction. *Being* (*ousia*) is the eternal, unchanging realm of the Forms: stable, necessary, fully real, the object of genuine knowledge. *Becoming* (*genesis*) is the temporal, changing realm of perceptible things: unstable, contingent, imperfectly real, the object of belief or opinion. Time is the medium of becoming; eternity is the mode of being.

**Forms (Ideas)**
