The eternal, unchanging, intelligible objects of genuine Platonic knowledge. Forms are not located in time or space; they are not sensible objects; they are not particular things. The Form of Beauty is beautiful, necessarily, unconditionally, unchangingly. Particular temporal things are beautiful insofar as they participate in the Form of Beauty, but they are beautiful only imperfectly, contingently, and temporarily.

**Receptacle (Chora / Hypodoche)**
The "third kind" (*triton genos*) in the *Timaeus* — alongside Being and Becoming. The Receptacle is the characterless, all-receiving medium that underlies all temporal change. It has no positive properties of its own but receives the impressions of the Forms that appear in the temporal world. It is known "by a kind of bastard reasoning" rather than by reason or perception.

**Participation**
The relation between temporal things and the Forms: a temporal thing *participates in* (or *partakes of*) a Form insofar as it instantiates or reflects the Form's character. A beautiful face participates in the Form of Beauty; a just action participates in the Form of Justice. The participation relation is philosophically puzzling (it generates the Third Man regress) but central to Plato's metaphysics.

**Divided Line**
Plato's image in the *Republic* (509d–511e) of an epistemological and ontological hierarchy: images, perceptible objects, mathematical objects, and Forms, corresponding to four cognitive states: conjecture (*eikasia*), perception-based belief (*pistis*), hypothetical reasoning (*dianoia*), and intellectual insight (*noêsis*). Temporal things occupy the middle levels, beneath the eternal Forms.

**Episteme vs. Doxa**
Knowledge (*episteme*) versus opinion or belief (*doxa*). For Plato, genuine knowledge is of the unchanging eternal Forms; it is necessarily true, certain, and rationally justified. Opinion is of the changing temporal world; it can be accurate and justified but is fallible because its objects change. Natural science, including cosmology, produces *doxa*, not *episteme*, in the strict sense.

**Anamnesis (Recollection)**
The doctrine, developed in the *Meno* and *Phaedo*, that learning is the recovery of knowledge the soul already possesses from its pre-embodied existence with the Forms. Temporal experience — encountering beautiful, equal, or just things — triggers the soul's recollection of the corresponding Forms. Recollection is not ordinary temporal memory of past events but the recovery of atemporal knowledge.

**Likely Story (Eikos Logos)**
Plato's term for the cosmological account in the *Timaeus* (*eikôs logos* or *eikôs mythos*): a probable, plausible account rather than a strict demonstration. Because the subject matter (the temporal, material cosmos) is in the domain of becoming rather than being, the best we can achieve is a probable account. This epistemic humility is part of the philosophical content.

**Third Man Argument**
An objection to Platonic participation, raised by Plato himself in the *Parmenides* (132a–b) and by Aristotle (*Metaphysics* 990b17–991a8). If a beautiful thing is beautiful because it participates in the Form of Beauty, what makes the Form of Beauty itself beautiful? Another Form? Then a third Form is needed to explain what the first Form and the original beautiful thing have in common — and so on, in an infinite regress.

**Tota Simul (Boethius)**
Boethius's Latin formulation of divine eternity in the *Consolation of Philosophy* V.6: *interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio* — "the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of an unlimited life." This formulation captures the Platonic idea that eternity is not endless temporal duration but an all-at-once possession of complete being, without before or after. It became the standard definition of eternity in medieval Christian theology.

**World Soul**
The intelligent animating principle of the cosmos in the *Timaeus* (34b–37c), constructed by the Demiurge from mathematical ratios. The World Soul animates and governs the cosmos; it produces the celestial motions that constitute time; and it serves as the cosmic counterpart to the individual soul that inhabits each living body.

### Chapter 4: Important Researchers and Thinkers

---

**Plato (428–347 BCE)**
The central figure of the chapter. Plato founded the Academy in Athens — the first institution of higher learning in the Western tradition. His dialogues, essentially all of which survive, constitute one of the most rich and philosophically productive bodies of work in the history of thought. The *Timaeus* is his main cosmological dialogue, central to the philosophy of time; the *Republic* provides the epistemological framework (Divided Line, Allegory of the Cave); the *Phaedo*, *Meno*, and *Phaedrus* develop the doctrine of the immortal soul and recollection; the *Parmenides* and *Sophist* engage critically with the theory of Forms.

**Timaeus of Locri**
The character who delivers the cosmological account in Plato's dialogue. He is described as a Pythagorean philosopher from Locri in southern Italy, expert in astronomy and mathematics. Whether he is based on a historical person of this name is uncertain; what matters philosophically is the Pythagorean character of the account he gives — its mathematical precision, its cosmological scope, and its treatment of the cosmos as a mathematically ordered living being.

**Plotinus (204–270 CE)**
The founder of Neoplatonism. Plotinus's *Enneads*, edited by his student Porphyry, contains the most systematic and philosophically sophisticated development of Platonic philosophy in antiquity. His treatise on time and eternity (*Enneads* III.7) is one of the greatest texts in the philosophy of time: it distinguishes Eternity as the simultaneous totality of Nous's intellectual life from Time as the sequential unfolding of the World Soul's restless activity. Plotinus's influence on subsequent philosophy of time — particularly through Augustine and medieval Christian thought — was enormous.

**Boethius (ca. 480–524 CE)**
Roman philosopher and statesman, author of the *Consolation of Philosophy*, written while awaiting execution on charges of treason. Book V of the *Consolation* contains the most influential medieval treatment of divine eternity and temporal existence. Boethius's definition of eternity — *interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio* — took up the Platonic *aion* and gave it a formulation that dominated medieval theology. He also addressed the problem of divine foreknowledge and free will, arguing that God's knowledge of future events is knowledge of a timeless present, not foreknowledge in the temporal sense.

**Gregory Vlastos (1907–1991)**
American philosopher and classicist. His 1964 paper "Creation in the *Timaeus*: Is It a Fiction?" is the definitive modern treatment of the debate about whether the *Timaeus* creation account is meant literally or metaphorically. Vlastos argued for the metaphorical interpretation — that the creation narrative is a device for revealing the structural dependence of temporal order on eternal being, not a claim about a historical act of creation.

**Richard Sorabji (1934–)**
British philosopher and classicist. His *Time, Creation and the Continuum* (1983) is the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of ancient philosophy of time, covering Aristotle, Plato, and their successors in depth. Essential reading for anyone who wants to study ancient philosophy of time seriously. Sorabji's treatment of the question of temporal creation is particularly valuable.

**F. M. Cornford (1874–1943)**
British classical scholar. His *Plato's Cosmology* (1937), a translation and commentary on the *Timaeus*, was the standard English-language treatment for decades. Cornford's commentary is philosophically sensitive and his translation remains readable, though it has been superseded in some respects by more recent scholarship.

**Donald Zeyl (1940–)**
American classicist. His translation of the *Timaeus* in the Hackett *Complete Works of Plato* (1997, edited by John M. Cooper) is the current standard scholarly translation in English. Zeyl's translation is accurate, readable, and accompanied by a useful introduction that situates the dialogue in Plato's overall philosophical project.

**Julia Annas (1946–)**
British-American philosopher. Her article "Aristotle, Number and Time" (1975) and related work provide important analysis of the relationship between number, time, and the *Timaeus* in the context of Aristotle's response to Plato. More generally, her work on ancient ethics and epistemology helps situate Plato's theory of knowledge — including its temporal dimensions — in the broader framework of ancient moral philosophy.

**Harold Cherniss (1904–1987)**
American classical scholar. Author of *Aristotle's Criticism of Plato and the Academy* (1944), a magisterial defense of Plato against Aristotle's criticisms. Cherniss's work is important for understanding the relationship between Plato's cosmogony and Aristotle's natural philosophy, and for assessing the Aristotelian objections to the *Timaeus* that recur throughout the tradition.

**Brian Leftow (1956–)**
American philosopher of religion. His *Time and Eternity* (1991) is the most rigorous and comprehensive contemporary treatment of the philosophical theology of divine eternity, building on both the Platonic tradition and analytic philosophy. Leftow carefully distinguishes timeless eternity from sempiternal existence and defends a version of the timeless eternity view.

## Chapter 5: Aristotle's Physics of Time

---

### Chapter Introduction

If Plato's treatment of time is cosmological and mythological — oriented toward the big picture of creation, eternity, and the soul's relationship to eternal truth — Aristotle's treatment is systematic, analytical, and aggressively deflating of mythological pretension. Aristotle is not interested in the soul's journey toward eternity; he is interested in the question "what is time?" — and he pursues it with the patience and precision of a scientist.

Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was Plato's student for twenty years at the Academy, and then — after Plato's death and a period of travel and biological research — he returned to Athens to found his own school, the Lyceum. His philosophical relationship to Plato was one of profound respect and radical disagreement: he took Plato's problems with full seriousness while systematically dismantling the metaphysical framework in which Plato had set them. The Forms are gone; there is no realm of eternal intelligible objects beyond the world of nature; nature itself is the primary domain of philosophical inquiry. Time, change, and motion are features of the natural world, not defective images of a higher reality.

The primary text for Aristotle's philosophy of time is *Physics* Books III and IV, particularly Chapters 10–14 of Book IV (*Physics* 217b29–224a17). This passage — roughly thirty pages in modern editions — is among the most dense, careful, and philosophically productive analyses in the entire ancient corpus. Aristotle proceeds dialectically: he begins with the *aporia* (the puzzles and apparent contradictions), examines previous views, and gradually works toward his own positive account.

Here is what he argues, in brief:

Time is the *number of motion with respect to before and after* (*Physics* 219b1–2). This definition packs an enormous amount of philosophical content into a short phrase, and unpacking it occupies much of this chapter. It implies that time is not motion itself (motions differ in speed; time does not), but it also implies that time without motion is impossible (there is nothing to count). Time is continuous, because motion is continuous. Time is measured primarily by the circular motion of the celestial spheres — the most regular, the most knowable, and the most universal of all motions. Time is related to the mind: without a soul to do the counting, Aristotle suggests, there would be no time strictly speaking, though there would be what time counts.

The chapter traces these ideas through five sections. Section 1 examines the definition of time as the number of motion; Section 2 examines the concept of the Now (*to nun*); Section 3 treats temporal continuity and the response to Zeno; Section 4 takes up the famous and difficult question of whether time requires a soul; Section 5 examines Aristotle's cosmology — his defense of an eternal world and his account of the Prime Mover — and its relationship to his account of time.

Aristotle's account of time is not perfect. It faces serious difficulties, some of which Aristotle himself acknowledges. But it is the most sustained, rigorous, and philosophically rich account of time produced in antiquity, and it set the terms of the discussion for the next two thousand years.

---

*Chapter 5 comprises five sections. Chapter-end resources include exercises, further reading, key concepts, and key researchers.*

### Section 1: Time as the Number of Motion

---

#### Section Introduction

Aristotle's *Physics* is his systematic account of natural change: what motion is, what causes it, how space and time structure it. The investigation of time occurs within this broader investigation, and it cannot be understood in isolation from Aristotle's general framework.

This section sets up and explains the definition of time that is the center of Aristotle's account. The first subsection provides the context: what Aristotle is doing in *Physics* IV.10–14, and why he approaches time through the study of motion. The second subsection unpacks the definition itself, examining what "number," "motion," and "before and after" mean in Aristotle's framework. The third subsection addresses an important negative claim: Aristotle's argument that time cannot simply be identified with motion.

Three terms need preliminary clarification. *Physis* (the Greek word the *Physics* takes its title from) means "nature" — the principle of motion and rest that living things and natural objects possess in themselves. *Kinesis* means "motion" or "change" — Aristotle uses it broadly for any kind of change: locomotion (change of place), qualitative change (change in quality), quantitative change (change in quantity), and substantial change (coming to be or passing away). *Hupokeimenon* means "substrate" or "underlying subject" — the thing that undergoes change and persists through it.

These three terms are central to Aristotle's account of time, and keeping them in view will make the account easier to follow.

#### 1.1 Setting the Context: Physics IV and the Study of Nature

---

##### What Is Aristotle Doing in the Physics?

To understand Aristotle on time, you need to understand the project of the *Physics* as a whole. The *Physics* is not what we today call "physics" — it is not a mathematical theory of the behavior of matter and energy. It is closer to what we might call "philosophy of nature": a systematic investigation into the most fundamental features of natural things, the principles that make natural change possible and intelligible.

The central subject of the *Physics* is *kinesis* — motion or change. Book I investigates the principles of natural change (form, matter, privation). Book II examines the concept of nature (*physis*) and the four causes. Books III and IV analyze motion itself, together with the concepts of infinity, place, void, and time that are required to make sense of it. Books V through VIII pursue further questions about the structure of change and culminate in the argument for the Unmoved Mover — the ultimate cause of all natural motion.

Time appears in *Physics* IV.10–14 as a topic that must be treated as part of the analysis of motion. The connection is necessary: motion occurs *in* time; we measure motion *by* time; and we cannot understand what time is without understanding its relationship to motion. Time and motion are, for Aristotle, mutually implicated concepts that illuminate each other.

###### The Dialectical Method

Aristotle's philosophical method in the *Physics* is dialectical: he begins with the *aporia* — the puzzles, contradictions, and difficulties that arise from ordinary experience and from previous philosophical accounts — and then works toward a resolution that preserves what is most defensible in the competing views while eliminating their defects.

This method is explicitly stated in *Nicomachean Ethics* VII.1 (1145b2–7) and is operative throughout the *Physics*: "We must start with what is familiar to us." What is familiar includes the views of previous philosophers (his predecessors and especially Plato) and the judgments of ordinary experience. A good philosophical account must account for what is right in both, and it must do so in a principled, non-ad-hoc way.

For time, the aporiai include: Does time exist at all, since the past is gone and the future is not yet? Is there always a now? Is there one now or many? What is the relationship between time and motion? These are the puzzles that Aristotle's analysis of *Physics* IV.10–14 attempts to resolve (Aristotle, *Physics* 217b29–218b29).

###### The Place of Time in the Natural World

One way to see what Aristotle is doing is to contrast his approach with Plato's. For Plato, time is a moving image of eternity — its significance lies in its relationship to something outside and above the natural world. For Aristotle, time is immanent in the natural world: it is a feature of natural motion, not a reflection of anything beyond nature. There is no eternal model that time approximates; there is no Demiurge who created it. Time is simply what it is — the quantitative dimension of natural change — and it can be analyzed without reference to anything transcendent.

This is a characteristic Aristotelian move: naturalizing. Where Plato looked beyond nature for explanations, Aristotle looks within it. Forms are not transcendent objects; they are the immanent forms of natural things. The good is not a Form beyond all forms; it is the end at which natural and rational activities aim. Time is not an image of eternity; it is the number of motion. This naturalistic orientation shapes every aspect of Aristotle's account.

###### The Key Questions

Aristotle's analysis of time addresses a cluster of related questions:

1. What is time? (The definition)
2. Does time exist? (The aporiai about the existence of the past and future)
3. What is the Now (*to nun*)? (Its identity, its function as boundary and limit)
4. Is time continuous? (Its relationship to spatial and kinematic continuity)
5. Does time require a soul? (The problem of temporal idealism)
6. What is the best measure of time? (The relationship between time and celestial motion)

We address questions 1–3 in this section, 4 in Section 3, 5 in Section 4, and 6 in connection with the broader account of celestial motion in Section 5.

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 217b29–218b29.

#### 1.2 The Definition: Time as the Number of Motion

---

##### Unpacking the Definition

At *Physics* 219b1–2, Aristotle gives his definition of time: *touto gar estin ho chronos, arithmos kinêseôs kata to proteron kai husteron* — "This is what time is: the number of motion with respect to before and after." This is one of the most discussed definitions in the history of philosophy, and it rewards very careful analysis.

The definition has three key components: "number," "motion," and "before and after." Understanding what Aristotle means by each is the key to understanding the whole.

###### "Motion" (Kinesis)

Motion (*kinesis*) for Aristotle is not merely locomotion — spatial movement — but any kind of change. In *Physics* V.1–2, Aristotle distinguishes four kinds of change: change of place (locomotion), change of quality (alteration), change of quantity (growth and diminution), and change of substance (coming-to-be and passing-away). Any of these can be the motion whose number constitutes time.

But Aristotle also holds that time is primarily measured by the most regular, continuous, and universal motion available — and this turns out to be the circular motion of the celestial spheres (specifically the sphere of the fixed stars, the outermost sphere) (*Physics* 223b12–224a2). This motion is regular (it never varies in speed), continuous (it never starts and stops), universal (it is the measure for all other motions), and eternal (it has always been occurring and always will). The celestial rotation is the standard against which all other motions are measured.

###### "Number" (Arithmos)

The claim that time is the *number* of motion is the philosophically most distinctive feature of the definition. Aristotle is not saying that time *is* motion — he will argue against this explicitly (see subsection 1.3). He is saying that time is the *number* or *measure* of motion: what you get when you count how much motion has occurred.

But Aristotle's notion of number (*arithmos*) is subtle. In *Metaphysics* XIII.7 (1082b16–19), Aristotle distinguishes the number *by which we count* from the number *which is counted* — the counting number from the counted number. Which of these is time?

Time is the *counted* number — the number that motion *has*, the measuredness of the motion. When you count the seconds during which a ball falls, "forty-two" is the number that the ball's fall *has*; forty-two is not an abstract counting number but the number that characterizes the temporal extent of this particular motion.

This is a delicate point. Numbers, for Aristotle, do not exist independently of things that have them (unlike Platonic numbers, which exist in the intelligible realm). The number of a pile of horses is not a separate entity; it is the pile's having-a-certain-number. Similarly, the number of a motion is not a separate entity; it is the motion's having-a-certain-temporal-extent. Time is not a separate entity over and above motion; it is motion's having-a-certain-temporal-extent — its being measurable by before and after.

###### "Before and After" (To Proteron kai Husteron)

The "before and after" in the definition refers to the ordering of motion's parts. Aristotle holds that the order of points in space (the path of a motion) corresponds to an order in the motion itself (*Physics* 219a14–b1). As an object moves from A to B, the parts of its motion are ordered: there is a first part (the beginning of the motion, near A) and a last part (the end, near B), and the intermediate parts are ordered in between. This ordering of parts of the motion is the "before and after" in the motion.

Time is then the numbering of this before-and-after structure. The sequence of the motion's parts — the order in which they occur — provides the before-and-after framework; time is what results when we measure or count how much motion occurs within this framework.

Here is a helpful way to think about it. Imagine a race. The race has spatial parts (the first stretch, the second stretch, the finish) and temporal parts (the first minute, the second minute, etc.). The spatial parts give the before-and-after in *space* (which parts of the track come earlier and later in the path). The temporal parts give the before-and-after in *time* (which parts of the race occur earlier and later). These are analogous but distinct: spatial order corresponds to position on the track; temporal order corresponds to position in time. Aristotle's point is that temporal order — the before-and-after of time — is derived from and corresponds to the before-and-after of the motion itself.

###### The Definition and Aristotle's Theory of Number

The definition connects directly to Aristotle's general theory of number, which holds that number is always the number *of* something — there are no free-floating numbers that exist independently (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* 1073a17–22). This contrasts sharply with Plato, for whom numbers are eternal, independent objects. For Aristotle, numbers are always dependent on and derived from the things that have them.

Applied to time, this means: time is always the time *of* some motion. There is no pure, free-floating time independent of any motion whatsoever. This is a relational account of time: time is a feature of motions (their having-a-certain-extent), not a container in which motions occur. In this respect, Aristotle's account is much closer to Leibniz's relationism than to Newton's absolutism.

But there is a complication. Aristotle holds that time is a *single*, *universal* measure — not multiple, with different motions having their own separate times. The celestial motion provides a single universal standard against which all particular motions are measured. This suggests that time is not merely relative to each motion individually but is a unified framework within which all motions are located. How exactly to reconcile the relational character of time (as the number *of* motion) with its universal, unified character is one of the more difficult interpretive questions in Aristotle's account (Hussey 1983: xxxvi–xlii; Coope 2005: 93–116).

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 219a10–b5; *Metaphysics* 1073a17–22.

#### 1.3 Why Time Is Not Motion Itself

---

##### The Negative Argument

Before arriving at his positive definition, Aristotle clears the ground by arguing that time cannot simply be identified with motion or change. The argument is brief but important (*Physics* 218b9–219a10).

###### The Argument from Differential Speed

Aristotle's main argument for distinguishing time from motion is this (*Physics* 218b13–18):

"The motion of any individual thing is confined to that thing, or to the place and time in which the thing happens to move. But time is present equally and simultaneously everywhere and with all things. Furthermore, change can be faster or slower, but time cannot. In fact, the fast and the slow are defined by time — the fast is what moves a large amount in a small time, and the slow is what moves a small amount in a long time. But time is not defined by time." (Waterfield trans., slightly modified)

The crucial point: motions can be faster or slower, but time cannot. You can walk faster or slower; you cannot make time faster or slower (in any ordinary sense). If time were identical with some particular motion, then that motion's speed would determine time's "speed" — but this is incoherent. Time is not faster or slower; it is the standard against which speed is measured.

Moreover, different motions occur at different rates — a fast runner covers the same distance as a slow runner in less time. If time were identical with motion in general, then different motions would each have their own time, and these would differ in speed from each other. But there is only one time, not multiple times running at different rates.

###### Time and the Measure of Motion

The distinction between time and motion does not mean that time is entirely independent of motion. Aristotle is clear that time *requires* motion: "when we do not notice any change at all, time does not seem to have passed" (*Physics* 218b21–219a2). If we were somehow unaware of change — if we were anaesthetized, or like the sleepers in the myth who fall asleep in Sardinia and wake up unchanged — we would not perceive any time as having passed, even if it had.

This suggests that time is not detectable in the absence of motion, and raises the question of whether time exists in the absence of motion. Aristotle's answer is carefully formulated: time would not exist without motion (*Physics* 223a26–29), but time is not identical with motion. Time is the number of motion — the measured quantity that motion has — and this is different from motion itself.

An analogy: the weight of a stone is not the stone, and it is not the scales used to measure it. The weight is the stone's having-a-certain-heaviness — a relational property of the stone. Similarly, time is motion's having-a-certain-temporal-extent — a property of the motion, not the motion itself, and not the measuring instrument.

###### The Normative Role of Celestial Motion

One consequence of distinguishing time from any particular motion is that the question of which motion best measures time becomes open. Aristotle's answer (*Physics* 223b12–224a2) is that the circular motion of the outermost celestial sphere — the sphere of the fixed stars — is the natural measure of time, because:

1. **It is the most regular**: it never varies in speed, producing a uniform standard.
2. **It is the most knowable**: it is observable from everywhere on Earth.
3. **It is the simplest**: circular motion is the purest and most continuous form of motion.
4. **It is eternal**: it has always been occurring and always will be (on Aristotle's cosmology).

All other motions are measured against this standard. When we say a human generation is thirty years, or a day is twenty-four hours, we are using the celestial rotation as the base unit. The celestial sphere's motion is not itself *identical* with time, but it provides the best available *measure* of time.

This normative role is philosophically interesting. It presupposes that some measures of time are better than others — not merely more convenient, but more accurate — and that the celestial motion is the most accurate of the available natural measures. This is a kind of temporal realism: there is a fact about how much time has passed, and the celestial motion gives the best available access to that fact.

The claim that the celestial motion is uniquely privileged as a temporal measure was challenged by Simplicius and other ancient commentators, and the issue remains philosophically alive. In modern physics, we use atomic oscillations (the cesium atom's hyperfine transition) as our standard of time — a motion that Aristotle could not have known about but that fits his criteria of regularity, universality, and knowability. The philosophical principle he articulates — that the best temporal measure is the most regular and universal available motion — is still operative.

###### The Transition to the Now

Once Aristotle has established that time is the number of motion and not motion itself, he faces the question of *how* we count motion. The answer involves the concept of the Now (*to nun*) — the moving boundary between past and future that serves as the unit of temporal counting. This leads to Section 2.

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 218b9–219a10, 223b12–224a2.

### Section 2: The Now

---

#### Section Introduction

The concept of the Now (*to nun*) plays a central and somewhat puzzling role in Aristotle's account of time. On the one hand, the Now is indispensable: it is what makes time a unified whole rather than a disconnected heap of intervals. On the other hand, the Now raises some of the deepest puzzles in the philosophy of time: Is the Now always the same one, or always a different one? Is it a part of time, or a boundary? Does it make sense to say that the Now "moves"?

These questions are not merely technical. They bear on the relationship between time and temporal consciousness, between the mathematical structure of the time line and the phenomenological experience of a present moment. Aristotle addresses them in *Physics* 219b9–220a24, and his analysis — while dense — contains genuine philosophical insights.

This section has two subsections. The first examines the Now as a boundary: its role in unifying time and marking the distinction between past and future. The second examines the puzzle of whether the Now is always the same or always different, and assesses Aristotle's solution.

#### 2.1 The Now as Boundary

---

##### The Now and the Structure of Time

Aristotle develops the concept of the Now by analogy with a moving point on a line (*Physics* 219b9–220a4). Think of the path of a moving object. The object has a position at each moment; its position at a given moment corresponds to a point on the path. The point is both a *boundary* (it divides the path into what came before and what comes after) and a *connector* (it links the before-part and the after-part into a single, continuous path).

The Now plays the analogous role in time. It is the moving "position" of temporal process — the present moment — and it is both a boundary (dividing past from future) and a connector (holding past and future together as parts of a single, continuous temporal reality). As the object moves from earlier positions to later ones, the Now moves from earlier times to later times.

This analogy illuminates two functions of the Now that might otherwise seem contradictory.

###### The Now as Divisive (Past/Future Boundary)

The Now marks the distinction between past and future. Everything on one side of the Now is past (no longer real in the sense of no longer occurring); everything on the other side is future (not yet real). The Now is the boundary that separates what has happened from what has not yet happened.

This is the Now as we ordinarily experience it. "Now" picks out the present moment, and everything before now is past, everything after now is future. The Now is the edge of the past and the edge of the future simultaneously.

###### The Now as Connective (Temporal Continuity)

But the Now also *holds time together*. This is less obvious but equally important. Consider time as a line. A line is not merely a heap of points; it is a continuous whole. What makes it continuous — what makes it a *line* rather than scattered points — is that every point connects to adjacent points: every point is both the end of the segment before it and the beginning of the segment after it.

The Now plays this role in time. It is the "bridge" between the stretch of time that just occurred (the recent past) and the stretch that is about to occur (the near future). Without the Now, time would fall apart into disconnected pieces — the past and the future would be separate and unrelated. The Now connects them into a continuous whole.

Aristotle puts this in terms of the Now's dual role: "The 'now' connects and divides in that it is both the end of one time and the beginning of another" (*Physics* 220a4–5, Waterfield trans.). The Now is simultaneously the terminal boundary of the past interval and the initial boundary of the future interval — the same boundary from two sides.

###### The Analogy with the Moving Point

The analogy with a point on a moving object is precise. Consider a point P on the surface of a moving ball. P has a position at each moment: it is at location L₁ at time t₁ and at location L₂ at time t₂. The point is the *same* point (P), but its *position* differs from moment to moment.

Now consider the Now. The Now is the present moment — the temporal "position" of the moving present. At each moment, the Now is at a different position in time (a different moment). It is the same *kind of thing* (the present) at each moment, but it is always at a *different* moment.

This analogy suggests that the Now is not a fixed point but a *moving point*: it is the temporal position of a kind of moving boundary, not a fixed location in time. The Now is always "here" in time, but "here" keeps moving.

###### The Aporiai about the Now's Existence

Before developing this account positively, Aristotle confronts an *aporia* about whether the Now exists (*Physics* 218a8–30). The worry is: the past no longer is, the future is not yet, and the Now is a durationless instant that has no extent — it is not a period with beginning, middle, and end. So the present seems to have no real existence: it is a mere boundary between a past that is gone and a future that has not arrived.

Aristotle does not fully dissolve this worry; he holds that the Now is a genuine entity — not an interval but a genuine part of time's structure, analogous to a geometric point. The Now has no duration, but it is not nothing: it is a limit or boundary, and limits are real even if they are not themselves the things they limit.

This is not entirely satisfying, and Aristotle knows it. But the alternative — denying that the Now exists, and therefore denying that time has any present — is even more unacceptable. A time with no present would be a time with no relationship to experience, no anchor in reality. The Now must exist, even if its mode of existence is that of a limit rather than an interval.

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 219b9–220a24.

#### 2.2 The Paradox of the Now's Identity

---

##### Is the Now Always the Same, or Always Different?

Here is a puzzle that anyone who thinks carefully about the present moment runs into: the present moment is always "now." No matter when you think about it, the present is now. But surely the present moment at noon today is *different* from the present moment at 3:00 PM yesterday. These are different times; they cannot be numerically the same present. So the present changes — it is always a different now.

But if the present always changes, then in what sense is "the present" the same thing at all? Is "the present" simply a description that applies to different moments at different times, like "the current president" applies to different people in different years? Or is there a single thing called "the present" that moves through time, maintaining its identity as the present while occupying different temporal positions?

Aristotle confronts this puzzle at *Physics* 219b10–220a4 and offers a careful, if compressed, solution.

###### Aristotle's Distinction

Aristotle draws a distinction between the Now considered *as what it is* (a boundary, a present) and the Now considered *in its being* (at a particular temporal position). In what it is — as a boundary between past and future, as the present — the Now is always the same. There is only one present; "the present" refers to the same thing whenever you use it. In this sense, the Now is one.

But in its *being* — in which particular moment it occupies, which temporal position it marks — the Now is always different. The present at noon is not the same temporal position as the present at 3:00 PM. Each now occupies a different position in time, and this positional difference makes them numerically different instances of the same *kind* of thing (the present).

The analogy Aristotle uses is the point again: the moving point on the surface of a ball. "The point on this ball's leading edge" always refers to the same *kind* of thing (the leading-edge point), but the point occupies different spatial positions as the ball moves. Similarly, "the now" always refers to the same *kind* of thing (the present), but it occupies different temporal positions as time advances.

###### The Sporting Analogy

Another helpful analogy is the starting position in a running race. At any given race, there is one starting position — it is the same starting position in the sense that it is always the starting position. But the starting positions of different races are numerically different (they may be at different physical locations, or the same physical location at different times). "The starting position" is a role-description that picks out different instances in different contexts.

"The now" works similarly: it is always *the present* (same role), but it is always a *different particular moment* occupying that role (different instances). The present is a temporal role, not a fixed occupant of that role.

###### Assessment: Does This Solve the Puzzle?

Aristotle's solution is elegant and has been influential. It introduces a distinction — between type-identity (the same *kind* of thing) and token-identity (the same *particular* thing) — that is important throughout metaphysics. The Now is always type-identical (always the present) but never token-identical across different moments (each moment is a different particular now).

But does this solution fully satisfy? Several philosophers have worried that it does not (Roark 2011: 66–78; Coope 2005: 48–52).

The worry is this: if different token-nows are genuinely different particulars, then the "movement" of the now from one token-now to the next is just the replacement of one token by another — and this replacement requires a further time in which it occurs. But then there would have to be a meta-time — a second temporal dimension — in which the now moves from one position to another. This threatens an infinite regress of times.

This is essentially a version of McTaggart's argument (Unit V) applied to the Aristotelian Now. Aristotle's framework does not obviously have resources to avoid it. His solution identifies the type-identity of the present (always the same role) without fully explaining how a single "moving present" is possible without a regress.

Aristotle's account is best understood not as a complete solution to the puzzle of temporal passage but as a step toward one. He identifies the right conceptual distinction (type vs. token identity), but he does not give a full metaphysics of how the type moves through its token instances. That problem is still open.

###### Connection to Modern Debates

The puzzle about the Now's identity connects directly to the contemporary debate between A-theories and B-theories of time (Unit V). An A-theorist holds that there is a genuinely moving present — a single now that advances through time — and faces the challenge of explaining how this is possible without a regress. A B-theorist denies the moving present: there is no privileged "now" in the objective world; different moments are all equally real, and "now" is a perspectival indexical (like "here"). Aristotle is clearly more sympathetic to something like the A-theory — the Now is a genuine, moving boundary — but his account of its identity has the difficulties we have just noted.

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 219b10–220a4, 222b30–223a8.

### Section 3: The Continuity of Time

---

#### Section Introduction

Zeno's paradoxes (Chapter 3, Section 3) raised the question of whether time and motion are continuous magnitudes or compositions of discrete units. Aristotle's account of time is deeply and deliberately continuous: time, like motion and spatial extension, is a continuous magnitude — infinitely divisible, with no smallest unit, no temporal atom below which further division is impossible.

This commitment to continuity is not incidental; it is central to Aristotle's response to Zeno and to his understanding of the relationship between time, motion, and space. In *Physics* VI, Aristotle develops a systematic account of continuous magnitude that underlies his treatment of time.

This section's single subsection examines the continuity of time: what Aristotle means by it, how it relates to spatial and kinematic continuity, and how it functions as a response to Zeno. We also consider the modern challenge to temporal continuity from quantum mechanics and quantum gravity.

#### 3.1 Time as Infinitely Divisible and Continuous

---

##### What Continuity Means

For Aristotle, a magnitude is *continuous* if and only if any two adjoining parts share a common boundary (*Physics* 227a10–13). A line is continuous because any two adjacent segments share an endpoint: the right endpoint of the left segment is the same as the left endpoint of the right segment. This shared endpoint is the connecting boundary.

This is different from mere *contiguity* (things touching at a boundary but having separate endpoints) and from *succession* (things following each other with a gap or interval between them). Continuity requires genuine sharing — the boundary is one, not two.

Time is continuous in this sense. Any two adjacent temporal intervals share a common Now at their junction: the final Now of the earlier interval is the same as the initial Now of the later interval. This shared Now is what makes time a continuous whole rather than a sequence of discrete, separate periods.

###### The Relationship Between Temporal and Spatial Continuity

Aristotle holds that temporal, spatial, and kinematic continuity are intimately related — they are not three independent kinds of continuity but one underlying continuous structure expressed in three ways (*Physics* 219a10–b9).

The argument is this: motion occurs through a spatial path, and the order of positions in the path determines the order of parts in the motion. The path is spatially continuous; therefore the motion through it is kinematically continuous. And if the motion is continuous, then time — the number of that continuous motion — is temporally continuous.

This three-way relationship is expressed in *Physics* 219a10–14: "the motion corresponds to the magnitude, and the time to the motion." Just as the spatial magnitude is continuous (indefinitely divisible), so the motion is continuous (no smallest temporal unit of motion), and so time is continuous (no smallest temporal duration).

The relationship runs in both directions. Not only does the continuity of space imply the continuity of time; the continuity of time also implies the continuity of space. A time with discrete minimal units would correspond to a space with discrete minimal units — and Aristotle argues against spatial atoms in *Physics* VI.1–2 on purely geometrical grounds (any magnitude can be divided, at least conceptually, without limit).

###### Potential vs. Actual Infinity

Aristotle's continuity does not imply that time (or space or motion) is *actually* infinitely divided. It implies only that it is *potentially* infinitely divisible: at any level of division, further division is always possible in principle. But the infinite divisions are never all simultaneously actualized.

This distinction — between *potential* and *actual* infinity — is Aristotle's central tool for responding to Zeno (*Physics* 233a21–31; 263a4–b9). Zeno's paradoxes assume that completing a task with infinitely many sub-tasks requires *actually* completing infinitely many separate acts. Aristotle denies this: the journey from A to B is potentially divisible into infinitely many sub-journeys, but these sub-divisions are only potential, not actual. The journey is completed in one continuous act, not in infinitely many separate acts.

The potential/actual distinction does real philosophical work here. A continuous motion does not consist of infinitely many distinct acts; it is a single continuous process that can be analyzed (divided in thought) into as many sub-processes as we like. The analysis is always in principle extendable, but this does not mean the motion itself is composed of infinitely many actual parts.

###### Aristotle's Response to Zeno

How does temporal continuity respond to Zeno's paradoxes?

**Dichotomy and Achilles**: These paradoxes assume that to complete a journey, you must complete infinitely many sub-journeys, each requiring a positive amount of time. Aristotle's response: the sub-journeys are only *potentially* many, not *actually* many. The continuous journey is completed in a single continuous act; the infinite divisibility of the journey does not require infinitely many actual acts of traversal. The sum of potentially infinitely many sub-durations is finite, because the sub-durations converge to zero.

**Arrow**: This paradox assumes that time is composed of durationless instants, and that being "at rest" in an instant makes sense as a state of the arrow. Aristotle's response: instants are limits of temporal intervals, not parts of time. Motion is a continuous process defined over intervals; it is not composed of instantaneous states. The arrow is moving in the sense that it is *in the midst of* a continuous motion over an interval; the question "is it moving at an instant?" is malformed, because motion is defined for intervals, not points.

**Stadium**: This paradox targets discrete space and time. Aristotle's response: space and time are continuous, so there is no smallest spatial atom or temporal atom whose multiplied extent could generate a contradiction.

###### Continuity and the Real Number Line

In modern terms, Aristotle's continuity corresponds to the continuum of the real numbers: the temporal line is isomorphic to the real number line, on which between any two numbers there are infinitely many others. This is the mathematical model for Aristotelian temporal continuity, made rigorous by the development of the theory of the real line in the nineteenth century (Dedekind 1872; Cantor 1883).

However, modern physics raises a challenge. There is theoretical and some empirical evidence suggesting that at the Planck scale (ca. 10⁻⁴³ seconds), the continuum description of spacetime may break down and be replaced by something discrete. Loop quantum gravity, causal set theory, and other approaches to quantum gravity posit that spacetime has a discrete structure at the smallest scales (Penrose 2004: 961–966; Sorkin 2003). If these theories are correct, then Aristotle's (and the continuum's) account of time as infinitely divisible is an approximation that holds at the scales relevant to ordinary experience but fails at the fundamental level.

This is a philosophically interesting situation: the conceptual argument for temporal continuity (Aristotle's) seems compelling at the macroscopic scale, but quantum gravity may require a revision of the underlying ontology. The relationship between the continuous macroscopic account and the potentially discrete fundamental account remains an open problem in physics and philosophy of physics.

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 219a10–b9, 227a10–b25, 231b2–232a21, 233a21–31.

### Section 4: Time and the Soul

---

#### Section Introduction

Among the most discussed and most puzzling passages in Aristotle's account of time is a brief section in *Physics* IV.14 (223a16–29) where Aristotle raises the question: would there be time if there were no soul?

The question might sound like a contemporary debate about mind-dependence — does time exist independently of minds? But in Aristotle's context, the question is more specific and more philosophically precise. Aristotle has defined time as the number of motion. Numbers, for Aristotle, require a numbering subject — an intellect or soul that counts. If there were no soul to count, would there be any numbers, and therefore any time?

This question connects Aristotle's philosophy of time to his philosophy of mind, to the Platonic tradition's interest in the relationship between soul and time, and to the modern debate about whether time is mind-independent. The passage is brief, somewhat hedged, and admits of multiple interpretations — which is part of what makes it philosophically fertile.

#### 4.1 Does Time Require a Soul?

---

##### The Passage

Here is *Physics* 223a16–29 in Waterfield's translation:

"One might raise the question of whether without soul there could be time. If nothing can count, then nothing can be counted either; hence there can be no number, since number is either what has been counted or what can be counted. But if only soul, or intellect as a faculty of soul, naturally counts, then there can be no time without soul — although the substrate of time (i.e. that aspect of motion which can be prior or posterior) could exist without soul. But if being prior and posterior in motion is what we identify as time, then time must depend on soul."

This is a careful, hedged passage, and it admits of at least two readings.

###### The Strong Idealist Reading

The strong reading is that time is mind-dependent: without a counting soul, there is no time at all. The argument is clean: time is number; number requires a counter; a counter is a mind (soul, intellect); without a mind, there is no number, and therefore no time.

If this reading is correct, Aristotle is endorsing a form of *temporal idealism*: time is a feature of how minds represent and count motion, not a feature of mind-independent reality. This would make Aristotle's position similar to Kant's, who held that time (and space) are forms of intuition imposed by the mind on the matter of experience, not features of things-in-themselves.

###### The Weaker Realist Reading

But Aristotle himself immediately hedges. He says that the *substrate* of time — "that aspect of motion which can be prior or posterior" — could exist without soul. And he ends with a conditional: "if being prior and posterior in motion is what we identify as time, then time must depend on soul." This conditional leaves open whether we should identify time with that: perhaps we should identify time with the prior-and-posterior in motion itself, not with the counting of it.

On this weaker reading, what depends on soul is the *counting* — the actualization of time's number in a cognitive act. But the *countable* — the before-and-after structure of motion — exists independently of any soul. Time, on this reading, is like a book before it is read: the text is there, but its being *read* requires a reader. Similarly, motion's before-and-after structure is there, but its being *counted* requires a counter.

This weaker reading preserves the realism of Aristotle's account: the temporal structure of the world exists independently of any mind, even if its actualization as a counted number requires a mind.

###### Scholarly Debate

The scholarly debate about this passage is extensive and not fully resolved. Hussey (1983: lii–lvii) argues for the weaker, realist reading: what depends on soul is the *actualized* number, not the objective before-and-after structure that is countable. Coope (2005: 154–164) argues that Aristotle's account is genuinely ambiguous here and that he was not fully settled on the question of time's mind-dependence.

Sorabji (1983: 90–93) suggests a middle position: Aristotle distinguishes two senses of time — a mind-independent sense (the before-and-after ordering of motion) and a mind-dependent sense (the number actually counted). Both senses are legitimate; the definition is primarily of the second sense, but the first sense underpins it.

###### The Connection to Modern Debates

The question of time's mind-independence is one of the central issues in contemporary philosophy of time. The *A-theory* — particularly in its "moving spotlight" version — holds that there is an objective present that moves through time independently of any observer. The *B-theory* holds that the temporal ordering of events is mind-independent (the before-and-after structure exists objectively), but that the sense of a moving present is a perspectival, possibly mind-dependent feature of temporal experience (Mellor 1998; Skow 2015).

Aristotle's tentative position is closest to the B-theory in its realist dimension: the before-and-after ordering of motion is objective and mind-independent. But in suggesting that the *number* of motion (time strictly speaking) requires a counter, he anticipates the idealist tendency that will be developed more fully by Augustine and, much later, by Kant.

###### The Lesson for Philosophy of Time

This passage illustrates a general point about time: it has both objective and subjective dimensions, and it is not always clear how to separate them. The before-and-after structure of motion is objective; it does not depend on any mind to be ordered in a certain way. But the identification of this ordering as a *number* — the assignment of a quantity to the ordering — does seem to involve an act of measurement, of counting, that requires a cognitive subject.

Modern discussions of time measurement make a similar distinction: the events that constitute the temporal order (physical processes, causal relations) are objective; but the assignment of numbers to those events — the metric of time — involves a choice of standard (which clock? which physical process?) that is not simply read off the world but involves a judgment about which standard best serves our theoretical and practical purposes (Poincaré 1898; Dummett 2000).

Aristotle did not have the resources to articulate this distinction clearly, but he sensed it. The *Physics* 223a16–29 passage is evidence of a philosopher probing the limits of his own account and acknowledging, honestly, where the account becomes less secure.

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 223a16–29.

### Section 5: Eternity, the Prime Mover, and the Eternal World

---

#### Section Introduction

Aristotle's account of time is embedded in a larger cosmological picture that is, in several respects, radically different from Plato's. Where Plato's cosmos was created by a Demiurge and is a temporal image of an eternal model, Aristotle's cosmos is eternal: it has always existed, it always will exist, and there was no first moment at which it began.

This commitment to an eternal, uncreated cosmos generates a distinctive account of time's relationship to eternity. For Aristotle, there is no eternity in Plato's sense — no realm of timeless Forms over and above the natural world. But there is something eternal within the natural world: the circular motions of the celestial spheres, which are eternal and uniform, and the Prime Mover (*to prôton kinoun akinêton* — the first, unmoved mover), which is the ultimate cause of those motions.

The Prime Mover is itself unmoved and unchanged: it is the cause of eternal motion without itself being in motion, and it is therefore atemporal in a sense — not located in time, not subject to change. But it is also not "outside" the natural world in Plato's sense; it is at the limit of the natural world, the final cause of natural motion, the ultimate ground of temporal existence.

This section examines the cosmological background of Aristotle's temporal philosophy: the argument for an eternal world (subsection 1) and the paradoxical status of the Prime Mover as a timeless cause of temporal change (subsection 2).

#### 5.1 The Eternal World

---

##### Was the Cosmos Always There?

One of the sharpest disagreements between Aristotle and Plato concerns the temporal status of the cosmos. Plato, in the *Timaeus*, described the world as *created* — made by the Demiurge at a specific time (or, on the metaphorical reading, as ontologically dependent on an eternal model in a way that is analyzed as "creation"). Aristotle rejected this picture entirely: the world has no beginning and no end; it has always existed and always will. There was no creation event, no first moment.

The arguments for an eternal world are developed primarily in *Physics* VIII.1 (*Physics* 250b11–252b6) and *De Caelo* I.10–12 (*De Caelo* 279b5–283b22).

###### The Argument from Motion

The main argument in *Physics* VIII.1 proceeds from the nature of motion itself:

1. Motion is either eternal or it had a beginning.
2. If motion had a beginning, there was a first change — the transition from rest to motion.
3. But the transition from rest to motion is itself a change — which requires prior motion to explain it.
4. Therefore, if motion had a beginning, there would have to be motion before the supposed first motion. Contradiction.
5. Therefore motion has no beginning; it is eternal.

The argument is an instance of the general Aristotelian principle that every change requires something that initiates it. A transition from complete stasis to motion requires a cause; but the cause must already be in motion (or be a moved mover), which means motion was already occurring. Therefore there can be no absolute first motion.

This argument has been criticized on several grounds. The most obvious is that it assumes a causal regress: every change requires a prior cause. But why could there not be a *spontaneous* beginning — a first change with no prior cause? Aristotle's answer would appeal to the Principle of Sufficient Reason: there can be no change without a cause, because change requires an agent that changes something, and an agent acting requires a reason for acting at that time rather than another.

###### De Caelo and the Indestructibility of the Cosmos

In *De Caelo* I.10–12, Aristotle argues that the heavens (the outermost celestial sphere and its contents) are neither generated nor destructible. The argument is partly empirical — there is no evidence of any part of the heavens being generated or destroyed; "in the whole time of our life, according to tradition, no perceptible change has occurred in the whole heaven or in any of its proper parts" (*De Caelo* 270b12–16) — and partly conceptual.

The conceptual argument appeals to the relationship between natural potentiality and actuality: a naturally destructible thing is something that *can* not-be, and therefore something that has a *tendency toward* not-being. The heavens show no such tendency; there is nothing in their nature toward dissolution or destruction. Therefore they are naturally indestructible.

Moreover, Aristotle holds that the natural motion of the heavens — circular motion — has no contrary motion (locomotion can be up or down, left or right; but circular motion has no opposite direction in the relevant sense). Without a contrary, there is nothing that could "act against" the circular motion and eventually overcome it. Therefore the circular motion is eternal and the heavens are eternal.

###### The Conflict with Plato and Theology

Aristotle's eternal world is in direct conflict with Plato's cosmogony and with all versions of creation theology. For Plato, the world was made at a specific time (or in a specific metaphysical act of dependence). For the Abrahamic traditions, the world was created by God from nothing at a definite first moment.

The conflict with Christian theology was particularly important in the medieval period. The condemnation of 1277 at the University of Paris explicitly targeted (among other Aristotelian claims) the doctrine of the eternity of the world, which was seen as contradicting the doctrine of creation ex nihilo. Aquinas attempted to reconcile Aristotle and Christian theology by arguing that while revelation establishes that the world has a temporal beginning, it cannot be demonstrated by philosophical reason alone that the world could not have been eternal — Aristotle's argument for the eternity of the world is not a decisive proof (*Summa Theologica* Ia.46.1–2).

Whether Aquinas succeeded in this reconciliation is a matter of continuing debate. The philosophical issue — whether the universe must have had a temporal beginning — remains alive in modern cosmology. The Big Bang model describes an initial singularity approximately 13.8 billion years ago; whether this constitutes a genuine temporal "beginning" — whether there is any meaningful sense in which time itself began — is a question that physics and philosophy have not yet definitively resolved (Hawking 1988: 133–140; Carroll 2010: 37–55).

###### The Theological Significance of Aristotle's Position

Despite rejecting the Platonic creation narrative, Aristotle does not hold that the world is entirely without a transcendent dimension. The eternal cosmos requires an eternal cause: the Prime Mover, which is the subject of the next subsection. Aristotle's eternal world is not a world without God; it is a world with a God that is radically different from the creator-God of either Plato or the Abrahamic traditions.

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 250b11–252b6; *De Caelo* 270b12–16, 279b5–283b22.

#### 5.2 The Unmoved Mover

---

##### A Timeless Cause of Temporal Change

The argument for an eternal, continuously moving cosmos requires a solution to a pressing problem: if motion is eternal, what keeps it going? What is the ultimate cause of eternal motion?

Aristotle's answer, developed in *Physics* VIII.6 and *Metaphysics* XII.6–9, is the Prime Mover (*to prôton kinoun akinêton*) — the first mover that is itself unmoved. This is not a mover that acts by pushing or pulling — it does not exert force in a mechanical sense. It is a mover that causes motion by being the *final cause* of motion — the object of desire and thought that the celestial spheres pursue, not through deliberate rational decision, but through a kind of metaphysical attraction.

###### The Argument for a First Unmoved Mover

The argument in *Physics* VIII.5–6 is a form of the causal regress argument:

1. Every mover is either moved or unmoved.
2. If every mover is moved, there is an infinite causal regress of movers — every mover requires a prior mover.
3. An infinite causal regress is impossible (Aristotle argues this from the nature of causal efficacy: an infinite chain of intermediaries cannot transmit causal efficacy to the thing at the beginning).
4. Therefore, there is a first mover that is itself unmoved: the Prime Mover.
5. The Prime Mover causes the eternal circular motion of the outermost celestial sphere; this motion is transmitted through the sphere system to the sublunary world.

The Prime Mover is the cause of all temporal motion without itself being in motion — and therefore without itself being *in* time. As Aristotle says in *Metaphysics* XII.7: "And it produces motion by being loved" (*kinei dê hôs erômenon*: 1072b3). The unmoved mover is the object of cosmic love — the final end toward which all natural motion is ultimately oriented.

###### The Nature of the Prime Mover

What kind of thing is the Prime Mover? *Metaphysics* XII.7–9 develops the account:

The Prime Mover is pure actuality (*energeia*) without any potentiality. Potentiality implies the possibility of change (you can actualize what is potential); but the Prime Mover cannot change, since change would require it to go from one state to another, which would imply being in time. The Prime Mover is always fully actual — there is no possible state it is not yet in.

The Prime Mover is also *noêsis noêseôs* — "thought thinking itself" (*Metaphysics* 1074b34). Its activity is pure intellectual contemplation of itself. It does not think about the world or exercise providential care; it is absorbed in self-contemplation, and this activity is so perfect and so complete that it serves as the final cause — the ultimate object of attraction — for all cosmic motion. The celestial spheres move in eternal circular motion because they are, in their way, "attracted toward" the perfection of the Prime Mover's self-contemplation.

###### The Paradox of a Timeless Cause of Temporal Change

The Prime Mover is the most philosophically challenging element in Aristotle's cosmology. It is the cause of eternal temporal motion — without it, the celestial spheres would not move, and without their motion, there would be no time. Yet the Prime Mover itself is not in time: it has no before-and-after, no earlier-and-later, no duration. Its "activity" is timeless self-contemplation, not a temporal process.

How can something timeless cause temporal effects? This is a version of the problem that confronts anyone who posits a timeless ground of temporal existence — whether the Platonic Forms, Aristotle's Prime Mover, or the eternal God of Christian theology.

Aristotle's implicit answer seems to be that the Prime Mover is the *final cause* of motion, not the *efficient cause*. An efficient cause produces an effect by acting — by doing something, which takes time. A final cause produces an effect by being *the end toward which something is oriented* — and this orientation can be eternal even if the process of orientation is temporal. The celestial sphere moves in a circle because a circle is the best approximation to the Prime Mover's timeless perfection; this "because" is the relation of final causation, which does not require the Prime Mover to do anything in time.

This is a subtle but important distinction. The Prime Mover does not act in time; it does not push the celestial sphere around its orbit; it does not initiate temporal events. It is the ultimate *why* of temporal motion — the ground of its intelligibility — without being a temporal agent.

###### The Conflict with Christian Theology

Aristotle's Prime Mover differs from the Abrahamic creator-God in several important ways. First, it did not create the world ex nihilo: the world is eternal, not created. Second, it has no knowledge of the world: the Prime Mover thinks only about itself; it does not exercise providence or hear prayers. Third, it is not personal in any way that would support religious worship: it is a philosophical principle, not a God who enters into covenantal relationships.

Medieval philosophers, particularly Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Maimonides, developed sophisticated analyses of the relationship between Aristotelian and Abrahamic conceptions of God (Averroes, *Long Commentary on De Caelo*, passim; Maimonides, *Guide of the Perplexed* I.69–76). The synthesis they attempted — identifying the Aristotelian Prime Mover with the Abrahamic God while managing the differences — was one of the great intellectual projects of the medieval period.

###### The Prime Mover and the Philosophy of Time

For the philosophy of time, the Prime Mover raises a question that is still unresolved: what is the relationship between a ground of temporal existence that is itself atemporal and the temporal world it grounds?

In Aristotle's case, the answer is that the Prime Mover is the *final cause* of the eternal celestial motion, which is itself the ground (measure and standard) of time. The Prime Mover does not create time; it makes possible the eternal regularity of the celestial motions that serve as time's measure. Time, in this sense, is as eternal as the cosmos — it has no beginning and no end — but it is ultimately grounded in something that is not itself temporal.

This picture — temporal process grounded in something atemporal — recurs in very different forms in later philosophy. Plato's temporal cosmos grounded in eternal Forms, Kant's temporal phenomenal world grounded in atemporal things-in-themselves, modern physics's temporal evolution governed by atemporal laws — all exhibit the same structural feature that Aristotle's cosmology first articulates clearly: temporal reality, intelligible and ordered, must ultimately rest on something that is not itself subject to temporal change.

---

**Key texts:** Aristotle, *Physics* 258b10–259a20, 267b17–26; *Metaphysics* 1072a19–1073a13, 1074b15–35.

### Chapter 5 Exercises

---

#### Comprehension and Analysis

**Exercise 1.** Explain Aristotle's definition of time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after" (*Physics* 219b1–2). What does "number" mean in this context? What does "before and after" refer to? How is time related to motion on this account — why is time *not* identical with motion?

**Exercise 2.** Aristotle argues that time cannot be identical with motion because different motions can be faster or slower, but time cannot (*Physics* 218b13–18). Assess this argument. Does the conclusion follow? Could there be a conception of time on which "faster time" and "slower time" make sense? (Consider the B-theory: is there any B-theoretic sense in which time could go faster or slower?)

**Exercise 3.** Explain Aristotle's account of the Now (*to nun*) as a boundary. How does the Now both divide time (past from future) and connect it (as a shared boundary between intervals)? Use the moving-point analogy to illustrate your explanation.

**Exercise 4.** Aristotle says the Now is "the same in what it is but different in being" at different moments (*Physics* 219b10–220a4). What does this distinction mean? Does it solve the puzzle of whether the Now is always the same or always different? Reconstruct the worry that this solution generates a regress, and assess whether Aristotle has the resources to avoid it.

**Exercise 5.** Explain Aristotle's distinction between potential and actual infinity, and show how it is supposed to resolve Zeno's Dichotomy and Achilles paradoxes. Does this resolution succeed? Identify any philosophical residue that the distinction fails to address.

**Exercise 6.** In *Physics* 223a16–29, Aristotle asks whether time would exist without a soul. Carefully reconstruct the argument that it would not. Then present the "weaker realist" interpretation, which holds that the before-and-after structure of motion exists independently of any soul. Which interpretation do you find more consistent with the rest of Aristotle's account of time? Why?

**Exercise 7.** Explain Aristotle's argument for an eternal world in *Physics* VIII.1. What assumption does the argument rely on, and how might someone challenge that assumption? How does Aquinas attempt to reconcile Aristotle's eternal world with the Christian doctrine of creation?

**Exercise 8.** Explain the concept of the Prime Mover (*to prôton kinoun akinêton*). How does Aristotle argue for its existence? In what sense does the Prime Mover "cause" the eternal celestial motion without itself being in motion or in time? Evaluate whether the notion of a "timeless final cause" of temporal motion is philosophically coherent.

---

#### Critical Thinking

**Exercise 9.** Compare Aristotle's account of time as the number of motion with Plato's account of time as a moving image of eternity. What does each account say about: (a) the relationship between time and eternity/the eternal; (b) the relationship between time and motion; (c) the mind-dependence or mind-independence of time? Which account do you find more philosophically satisfying, and why?

**Exercise 10.** Consider the following objection to Aristotle: "The definition 'time is the number of motion' entails that without motion, there is no time. But surely it is at least conceivable that time could pass with no change at all — imagine a completely static universe in which nothing moves or changes, but time passes. Therefore Aristotle's definition is wrong." Reconstruct the strongest Aristotelian response to this objection. Then evaluate: does the possibility of "static time" (time without motion) constitute a genuine problem for Aristotle, or can it be resisted?

---

#### Lab Exercises

**Lab 1: Counting Motion.** Choose a simple, repetitive physical process: a pendulum swing, a dripping tap, a metronome, your own resting pulse. Time yourself counting 100 repetitions. Then: (a) Record the total time (in seconds) and calculate the period (seconds per repetition). (b) Now use this process as your "clock" — use it to measure the duration of another activity (e.g., reading a page of text, walking to the end of the hall and back). (c) Reflect on what you have done in Aristotelian terms: you have used "the number of motion" (the count of a regular, repeating process) to measure the duration of another motion. Write a one-page reflection on how this activity illuminates Aristotle's definition of time, including the relationship between the "clock" motion and the "measured" motion.

**Lab 2: The Now and Temporal Boundaries.** This lab explores the experience of the Now as a boundary between past and future. Find a quiet place to sit. Set a timer for five minutes. During this time, try to observe the experience of "now" as precisely as you can. When does "now" end? Can you catch the moment when "now" becomes "just past"? Is there a sense in which the present moment has any duration, or does it always seem to vanish as soon as you try to grasp it? After the five minutes, write a one-page reflection on what this observation reveals about the phenomenology of the Now, connecting it to Aristotle's claim that the Now is a boundary (not an interval) and to the puzzle about whether the present has any duration.

**Lab 3: Motion, Rest, and the Perception of Time.** This lab explores the relationship between perceived motion and perceived time. Conduct the following observations on three separate occasions: (a) Sit in a quiet room with nothing happening — no phone, no music, no activity — for five minutes. Record your estimated duration when the time is up. (b) Watch a film or engage in an absorbing activity for five minutes. Record your estimated duration. (c) Observe a complex, dynamic environment (a busy street corner, a crowded cafeteria) for five minutes without participating. Record your estimated duration. Compare your three estimates to the actual five-minute duration. Reflect: which condition produced the most accurate estimate? Which the most distorted? What does this reveal about the relationship between perceived motion (or activity) and perceived duration? Connect your observations to Aristotle's claim that time is the number of motion — and to the phenomenological tradition's distinction between clock time and lived time.

### Chapter 5: Further Reading and Bibliography

---

#### Annotated Further Reading

**Coope, Ursula. 2005. *Time for Aristotle: Physics IV.10–14*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.**
The definitive contemporary philosophical treatment of Aristotle's theory of time. Coope goes through the text systematically, addressing every major interpretive issue with rigor and clarity. Her analysis of the definition of time as the number of motion, the Now's identity, and the "time and soul" passage are all superior to anything else in the secondary literature. If you read only one scholarly work on Aristotle's theory of time, it should be this one.

**Hussey, Edward. 1983. *Aristotle's Physics Books III and IV*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.**
The standard English scholarly translation with commentary. The introduction provides a lucid overview of Books III and IV, including the account of time. The notes are detailed and philosophically engaged. Indispensable for close reading of the text.

**Sorabji, Richard. 1983. *Time, Creation and the Continuum*. London: Duckworth.**
The most comprehensive scholarly treatment of ancient and early medieval philosophy of time. The chapters on Aristotle cover the definition, the Now, continuity, and the "time and soul" passage with exceptional depth and historical range. Sorabji's survey of the ancient reception of Aristotle's theory is also valuable.

**Waterfield, Robin, trans. 1996. *Aristotle: Physics*. Oxford: Oxford University Press.**
The most readable modern English translation of the *Physics*. Waterfield's introduction and notes make the text accessible to non-specialists while remaining philosophically responsible. Used for the translations throughout this chapter.

**Annas, Julia. 1975. "Aristotle, Number and Time." *Philosophical Quarterly* 25(99): 97–113.**
A careful analytical article that explains what Aristotle means by calling time a "number" of motion. Annas distinguishes the number-by-which-we-count from the number-that-is-counted, and applies this distinction to clarify the definition of time. Essential for understanding the technical content of the definition.

**Bergson, Henri. 1889. *Time and Free Will: An Essay on the Immediate Data of Consciousness*. Translated by F. L. Pogson. London: Swan Sonnenschein, 1910.**
Bergson's first major work, in which he introduces the concept of *durée* (duration) as a qualitative, lived time that is radically different from the measurable, quantitative time of science and Aristotelian philosophy. Bergson's critique is a sustained and philosophically stimulating challenge to the Aristotelian framework; engaging with it is essential for assessing the limits of the "time as number" account.

**Bostock, David. 1988. "Time and the Continuum." *Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy* 6: 255–270.**
An analytical reconstruction of Aristotle's argument for the continuity of time and its relationship to the continuity of motion and space. Bostock assesses the logical structure of the argument and identifies its strengths and weaknesses with precision.

**Graham, Daniel W. 1999. *Aristotle: Physics Book VIII*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.**
