The Clarendon Aristotle translation and commentary on *Physics* VIII, covering the arguments for the eternity of motion, the first mover arguments, and the Prime Mover. Essential for the material covered in Section 5 of this chapter.

**Judson, Lindsay, ed. 1991. *Aristotle's Physics: A Collection of Essays*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.**
A collection of important scholarly essays on the *Physics*, including essays by Ursula Coope, Jonathan Lear, and others on topics central to the philosophy of time: change, continuity, motion, the infinite, and the Now. A useful anthology for advanced students.

**Owen, G. E. L. 1976. "Aristotle on Time." In *Motion and Time, Space and Matter: Interrelations in the History and Philosophy of Science*, edited by Peter Machamer and Robert Turnbull, 3–27. Columbus: Ohio State University Press.**
An important essay by one of the major twentieth-century Aristotle scholars, addressing the definition of time, the role of the Now, and the relationship between Aristotle's account and contemporary philosophy of time.

### Chapter 5: Important Concepts

---

**Physics (Physis)**
The Greek word *physis* (nature) gives the *Physics* its title. For Aristotle, physis is the internal principle of motion and rest that characterizes natural things (as distinguished from artifacts, which have their principles of motion imposed from without). The *Physics* is a systematic investigation of natural motion and its presuppositions, including time.

**Kinesis (Change / Motion)**
Aristotle's general term for any kind of change. In the *Physics*, Aristotle identifies four kinds of kinesis: locomotion (change of place), qualitative change (change of quality or property), quantitative change (change of size), and substantial change (coming-to-be and passing-away). Time is the number of kinesis in general, though it is primarily measured by the most regular and universal kinesis (celestial rotation).

**Time as the Number of Motion (Arithmos Kinêseôs)**
Aristotle's definition of time: "the number of motion with respect to before and after" (*Physics* 219b1–2). Time is not motion itself (different motions can be faster or slower; time cannot) but the *countable quantity* of motion — what you get when you measure how much motion has occurred. This definition makes time relational (dependent on motion) but also universal (there is one unified temporal framework for all motions).

**Before and After (Proteron kai Husteron)**
The ordering of the parts of a motion from earlier to later. This ordering in motion is what time numbers: time is the measure of how much of this before-and-after ordering has been traversed. The before-and-after in motion corresponds to the before-and-after in space (the path); the two orderings are analogous and related.

**The Now (To Nun)**
Aristotle's term for the present moment — the moving boundary between past and future. The Now is not a part of time (it has no duration) but a *limit* or *boundary* of temporal intervals, analogous to a geometric point on a line. The Now is both divisive (separating past from future) and connective (joining the past interval and future interval into a continuous whole). The Now is type-identical (always the present) but token-different (a different particular moment at each time).

**Potential vs. Actual Infinity**
Aristotle's crucial distinction for responding to Zeno. Something is potentially infinite if it can always be further extended or divided, in principle, without limit. Something is actually infinite if it is simultaneously and completely divided into or contains infinitely many parts. Aristotle holds that continuous magnitudes (space, time, motion) are potentially but not actually infinite in their divisibility. Zeno's paradoxes confuse potential divisibility (which is harmless) with actual division into infinite parts (which is impossible).

**Continuity**
For Aristotle, a magnitude is continuous when its parts share a common boundary — when adjacent parts have the same limit. Time is continuous because any two adjacent intervals of time share a common Now at their junction. Continuity implies infinite divisibility but not actual infinite division. The continuity of time is related to and supported by the continuity of spatial paths and of motion through those paths.

**Celestial Motion (Rotation of the Outermost Sphere)**
For Aristotle, the rotation of the outermost celestial sphere (the sphere of the fixed stars) is the natural measure of time. It is preferred as a temporal measure because it is the most regular (uniform speed), most continuous (never stopping), most universal (observable from everywhere on Earth), and eternal (it has always occurred and always will). All other motions are measured against this standard.

**Mind-Dependence of Time (Time and Soul)**
The question Aristotle raises in *Physics* 223a16–29: would there be time without a soul to count it? If time is the number of motion, and number requires a counter (a soul or intellect), then time seems to require a soul. Aristotle hedges: the *substrate* of time (the before-and-after ordering of motion) might exist without soul, even if the *actualized number* requires a counter. The passage anticipates later debates about temporal idealism.

**Eternal World**
Aristotle's cosmological claim that the cosmos has no beginning and no end: motion has always existed and always will, and the cosmos with it. The argument turns on the claim that a first motion would require a prior motion to cause it, generating a regress. The eternal world is in direct conflict with Platonic creation and Abrahamic theology.

**Prime Mover (To Prôton Kinoun Akinêton)**
The first unmoved mover: Aristotle's solution to the question of what causes eternal celestial motion. The Prime Mover is pure actuality (no potentiality), pure intellect thinking itself (*noêsis noêseôs*), and the final cause of all cosmic motion — it moves the celestial spheres by being the ultimate object of their "attraction," not by pushing or acting. The Prime Mover is not in time: it is atemporal, unchanging, without before-and-after in its own nature.

**Final Cause**
One of Aristotle's four causes (*aitiai*): the *telos* (end or goal) toward which a natural process is directed. The Prime Mover is the final cause of eternal celestial motion: the celestial spheres move eternally in circles because a circle (returning perpetually to itself) is the best approximation available to the timeless, perfect self-completeness of the Prime Mover. Final causation is teleological (end-directed) rather than mechanical.

**Noêsis Noêseôs**
"Thought thinking itself" (*Metaphysics* 1074b34): Aristotle's description of the Prime Mover's activity. The Prime Mover is pure intellect engaged in the highest possible intellectual activity — self-contemplation — without any admixture of lower cognitive processes or any engagement with the changing temporal world. This activity is the most complete, most perfect, and most continuous — and as such, it is the ultimate object of cosmic attraction.

**De Caelo (On the Heavens)**
Aristotle's treatise on the structure of the cosmos, the nature of the celestial bodies, and the elements. Book I establishes the eternal, unchanging nature of the celestial region; Books II–IV discuss the earth, water, air, and fire. The arguments for the eternity and indestructibility of the heavens in *De Caelo* I.10–12 are closely related to the arguments for an eternal world in *Physics* VIII.

**Hylomorphism**
Aristotle's general metaphysical framework: all natural substances are composites of *matter* (*hylê*) and *form* (*morphê* or *eidos*). Matter is the material substratum that underlies change; form is the determining structure that makes a thing what it is. Hylomorphism provides the framework for Aristotle's account of change, which requires a substratum (matter) that persists through the change and acquires a new form. It also provides the background for the account of time as the numbered form of motion.

**Aporia**
"Impasse" or "puzzle" — Aristotle's methodological starting point. In the *Physics*, Aristotle begins with the aporiai about time: puzzles about whether time exists, what the Now is, and how time relates to motion. The dialectical resolution of these puzzles is what generates the positive account. Attending to the aporiai ensures that the account addresses the genuine difficulties rather than talking past them.

### Chapter 5: Important Researchers and Thinkers

---

**Aristotle (384–322 BCE)**
The central figure of the chapter. Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy for twenty years, traveled and conducted biological research in Asia Minor and Lesbos, tutored the young Alexander of Macedon, and founded the Lyceum in Athens. His *Physics* remains one of the most important philosophical texts ever written — not merely as a historical document but as a rigorous investigation of the nature of natural change. His account of time in *Physics* IV.10–14 set the terms of the discussion for two millennia.

**Edward Hussey (1939–)**
British philosopher and classicist. His translation and commentary on *Physics* III and IV (*Aristotle's Physics Books III and IV*, 1983, Clarendon Aristotle Series) is the standard English-language scholarly treatment of the text. Hussey's introduction and notes are philosophically acute and remain essential for anyone studying Aristotle's account of time seriously.

**Ursula Coope (1969–)**
British philosopher at Oxford. Her book *Time for Aristotle: Physics IV.10–14* (2005) is the most philosophically sophisticated and up-to-date monograph on Aristotle's theory of time. Coope argues for a careful reading of the definition of time as the number of motion and addresses the major interpretive controversies with rigor and originality. Essential reading for any serious student of Aristotle's temporal philosophy.

**Richard Sorabji (1934–)**
British philosopher and classicist. Already mentioned in Chapter 4, Sorabji's *Time, Creation and the Continuum* (1983) is equally important for Chapter 5. His chapters on Aristotle's definition of time, the Now, and the continuity of time provide the fullest available scholarly treatment. His analysis of the "time and soul" passage (Chapter 8) is particularly valuable.

**Robin Waterfield (1952–)**
British translator and ancient historian. His Oxford World's Classics translation of the *Physics* (1996) is the most readable modern English translation and the one used for quotations throughout this chapter. Waterfield's introduction provides accessible context for non-specialists.

**St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274)**
Medieval Dominican philosopher and theologian. Aquinas wrote a detailed *Commentary on Aristotle's Physics* that was the standard medieval treatment of the text. He also addressed the tension between Aristotle's eternal world and Christian creation theology in the *Summa Theologica* (Ia.46.1–2), arguing that neither the eternity nor the temporality of the world can be demonstrated by reason alone — both require revelation or argument beyond pure metaphysics. Aquinas's synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Christian theology was the dominant intellectual framework of the medieval Latin West.

**Averroes / Ibn Rushd (1126–1198)**
Andalusian philosopher and physician. Averroes wrote voluminous commentaries on Aristotle — long, middle, and short commentaries on most of the corpus — and was known in the Latin West simply as "the Commentator." His defense of Aristotelian eternal world against religious objections, and his sophisticated treatment of the Prime Mover, were enormously influential on both Islamic and Latin medieval philosophy. His long commentary on the *Physics* is a major source for Aristotle's account of time in the medieval tradition.

**Richard McKirahan (1943–)**
American philosopher and classicist. In addition to his *Philosophy Before Socrates* (cited in Chapter 3), McKirahan's work on Aristotle's physics provides useful analytical reconstructions of Aristotle's arguments. His more recent work on pre-Socratic responses to Parmenides is particularly helpful for understanding the dialectical context of Aristotle's account.

**Henry Bergson (1859–1941)**
French philosopher and Nobel laureate (literature). Though not primarily an Aristotle scholar, Bergson's critiques of Aristotelian and mechanistic accounts of time in *Time and Free Will* (1889) and *Creative Evolution* (1907) are philosophically important. Bergson argued that Aristotelian (and scientific) time — time as a measurable quantity, the "number of motion" — is an abstraction from real *durée* (lived duration), which is qualitative, flowing, and not reducible to spatial measurement. Bergson's critique is the most influential twentieth-century challenge to the Aristotelian framework.

**J. L. Ackrill (1921–2007)**
British philosopher and classicist at Oxford. His essays on Aristotle's categories and metaphysics, collected in *Essays on Plato and Aristotle* (1997), provide incisive analyses of many of the concepts central to Aristotle's account of time, including actuality, potentiality, and form. His analysis of Aristotle's concept of *energeia* (actuality) is particularly useful for understanding the Prime Mover.

**Julia Annas (1946–)**
British-American philosopher. In addition to her work mentioned in Chapter 4, Annas's article "Aristotle, Number and Time" (*Philosophical Quarterly*, 1975) provides the clearest available analysis of what Aristotle means by calling time a "number" — distinguishing the number that counts from the number that is counted, and relating this to Aristotle's general philosophy of number.

# Unit III: Hellenistic, Late Ancient, and Medieval Philosophy of Time

---

## Unit Introduction

Philosophy does not move in a straight line. It spirals — returning to the same questions but from greater depth, carrying more equipment, pressing harder against the places where earlier thinkers faltered. Aristotle gave us a systematic account of time that dominated ancient thought. But Aristotle's account, brilliant as it was, left questions unanswered: What is the nature of the present moment? Does time depend on the mind or on the world? What happens to time at the boundaries of creation — if there are such boundaries? What is the relationship between time and eternity? The four centuries following Aristotle produced a series of attempts to answer these questions, attempts that were not mere commentaries on the master but genuine philosophical innovations.

The story of this unit runs from the Hellenistic schools (Chapter 6) through Plotinus (Chapter 7) and Augustine (Chapter 8) to the rich medieval tradition that culminated in Aquinas, Scotus, and Ockham (Chapter 9). These thinkers were separated by centuries and by language — Greek, Latin, Arabic, Hebrew — and they inhabited vastly different intellectual and theological frameworks. What unites them is a shared seriousness about the problem of time: not as a footnote to other concerns but as a question that forced itself onto their attention and demanded genuine answers.

The Stoics (Chapter 6) brought to the question a metaphysical framework unlike anything in Plato or Aristotle. Time, for the Stoics, was one of four "incorporeals" — real but not corporeal, subsisting rather than fully existing. Chrysippus pressed the analysis of the present moment further than anyone had before, arriving at a position that is startling in its radicalism: the present, strictly understood, is not a thing at all but a knife-edge between two modes of non-being. The Epicureans took a different route, treating time as an "accident of accidents" — a second-order property that arises from events without being a thing in its own right. And Lucretius, the great Epicurean poet, gave us in the process one of the most beautiful and philosophically serious arguments in the ancient world: the symmetry argument, which asks why we fear death when we do not fear the prenatal non-existence that precedes it.

Plotinus (Chapter 7) represents a different kind of genius. Working within the Platonist tradition but transforming it beyond recognition, he developed a three-tiered ontology — the One, Intellect, and Soul — and located time precisely at the level of Soul. Time is not, for Plotinus, a feature of the physical world that the mind then measures. It is generated by the Soul itself, as the Soul moves restlessly through its activities rather than resting in the unified, simultaneous grasp that characterizes Intellect. This is a deeply interior account of time — one that anticipates Augustine in striking ways.

Augustine (Chapter 8) is the towering figure of this unit, and arguably the most important philosopher of time before Kant. His account in Book XI of the *Confessions* is not a philosophical treatise in the technical sense; it is a meditation on creation, eternity, and the nature of God that discovers, along the way, a set of insights about time that have never been superseded. Time, for Augustine, exists in the soul as *distentio animi* — the stretching of the soul between memory and expectation. The mind measures time not by measuring the world but by measuring itself. This is phenomenology before there was a word for it.

The medieval thinkers (Chapter 9) inherited this rich tradition and added their own framework: the demands of Christian, Islamic, and Jewish theology. Questions about divine eternity, the beginning of the world, the compatibility of foreknowledge and freedom, and the ontological status of created time were not merely academic exercises. They were matters of theological urgency, which is one reason why medieval philosophy of time is both unusually precise and unusually ambitious.

Throughout this unit, a single thread runs: the growing recognition that time cannot be understood in isolation from mind. Whether mind is the generator of time (Plotinus, Augustine), the measurer of time (Aristotle, carried forward), or the interpreter of a mind-independent temporal structure (the Stoics), the relationship between temporality and consciousness moves ever closer to the center of the philosophical picture. By the end of Unit III, you will be prepared to see why that relationship became the central philosophical problem of time in the modern and contemporary periods.

---

*Unit III comprises Chapters 6, 7, 8, and 9.*

## Chapter 6: Hellenistic Schools

---

### Chapter Introduction

When Aristotle died in 322 BCE, his students and successors faced the task of inheriting one of the most systematic bodies of philosophical thought ever produced. But philosophy does not simply pass from one generation to the next like a deed of property. It transforms in the passage. The Hellenistic period — roughly from Alexander's death in 323 BCE to the rise of the Roman Empire — was one of the most creative and underappreciated eras in the history of philosophy, and its contributions to the philosophy of time deserve far more attention than they typically receive in introductory treatments.

Two schools dominate this chapter: the Stoics and the Epicureans. They were intense rivals, competing not only in the lecture rooms of Athens but for the allegiance of the educated classes across the Mediterranean world. They disagreed about physics, ethics, logic, and almost everything else. But they shared a practical orientation — philosophy was not an academic exercise for them but a way of life — and they shared a concern with the nature of time that expressed itself in ways both technically precise and existentially urgent.

The Stoics (Sections 6.1 and 6.2) developed perhaps the most sophisticated ancient ontology. Their framework divided reality into corporeal things — things that can act or be acted upon — and four incorporeals that are real but not bodies: sayables (*lekta*), void, place, and time. Understanding what it means for time to be "incorporeal" in this technical sense is the first task of this chapter, and it opens onto a much larger discussion of what "existence" means in Stoic metaphysics. From there, we examine Chrysippus's remarkably radical analysis of the present moment — an analysis that anticipates debates about presentism that are very much alive today.

The Epicureans (Section 6.3) approached time from a different direction entirely. Starting from the atomist physics inherited from Democritus and Leucippus, Epicurus arrived at a view of time as an "accident of accidents" — not a thing that exists alongside bodies and events, but a higher-order property that supervenes on them. Lucretius, the first-century BCE Roman poet whose *De Rerum Natura* is our most complete surviving source for Epicurean natural philosophy, argued for this view with arguments of striking clarity and modern resonance.

Section 6.4 examines what is perhaps the single most discussed argument about time and death in the entire history of philosophy: Lucretius's symmetry argument. If the prenatal period of non-existence causes us no concern in retrospect, why should the post-mortem period of non-existence cause us concern in prospect? The argument is elegant, counterintuitive, and philosophically serious — and the responses to it (from Thomas Nagel, Jeff McMahan, and James Warren, among others) have generated some of the best work in contemporary philosophy of death.

This chapter covers material that is often treated only briefly in histories of philosophy, partly because the primary sources are fragmentary and reconstruction is required. That fragmentation is not a defect but a kind of philosophical invitation: the work of piecing together a position from evidence, weighing the reliability of sources, and distinguishing what a philosopher actually said from what was reported of them is excellent philosophical training. Where we rely on second-hand sources, we will say so and explain why.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to: articulate the Stoic distinction between corporeal and incorporeal and explain why time was classified as incorporeal; reconstruct Chrysippus's analysis of the present and its difficulties; explain the Epicurean relational account of time and contrast it with the Stoic view; and reconstruct and critically evaluate Lucretius's symmetry argument. These are not small achievements. The Hellenistic schools thought harder about time than most subsequent philosophical traditions have given them credit for.

### Section 6.1: Stoic Metaphysics and the Incorporeals

---

#### Section Introduction

Before we can understand what the Stoics said about time, we need to understand the ontological framework within which they said it. Stoic metaphysics is unlike anything in Plato or Aristotle, and it rewards careful study in its own right. The Stoics divided everything that is real into two fundamental kinds: bodies (*somata*) and incorporeals (*asomata*). This division is not merely a taxonomic convenience; it carries deep philosophical weight.

For the Stoics, only bodies can act or be acted upon. This is their criterion for being a body: causal efficacy. Mind, for the Stoics, is itself corporeal — the soul is a special kind of air, the *pneuma* or "breath" that pervades and animates the body. Even virtues and vices are corporeal on this account, since they have genuine causal powers. This is a thoroughgoing materialism in one sense — everything with genuine causal powers is material — but it is not a reductive materialism that denies reality to non-material things. The incorporeals are real. They just have a different mode of reality: they do not exist (*hyparchein*) in the full sense but *subsist* (*hyphestanai*).

Time falls into this category of the incorporeal. It is not nothing. It cannot be dismissed. But it is not a body, and it does not exist in the same robust sense that a stone or a person exists. Understanding exactly what this means, and whether it is coherent, is the central task of this section.

The two subsections that follow examine: first, the four incorporeals and the metaphysical framework that generates the distinction (6.1.1); and second, the specific Stoic definition of time as the interval of the world's motion and the cosmological context in which that definition operates (6.1.2).

#### 6.1.1 — The Four Incorporeals: The Ontological Framework

---

##### Something and Nothing

One of the oldest temptations in metaphysics is to think that the question of what exists admits of a clean binary answer: a thing either exists or it doesn't. The Stoics resisted this temptation with unusual sophistication. They recognized that there are things that are real — that play genuine roles in the world and in our thought — without qualifying as full-blooded existents. Their framework for capturing this graduated ontology is among the most interesting in ancient philosophy.

The Stoics distinguished at the highest level between the *ti* (literally "something," the most general positive ontological category) and the *outhen* (nothing). Everything that falls under *ti* is real in some sense. Below *ti*, they drew a fundamental distinction between *somata* (bodies) and *asomata* (incorporeals). Bodies are the only things that truly *exist* (*hyparchein*) — they have the capacity to act and be acted upon. The Stoics were prepared to say that even qualities, souls, and the commanding faculty of the mind (*hegemonikon*) are corporeal. Incorporeals, by contrast, *subsist* (*hyphestanai*) — they are real but do not possess the full-blooded causal efficacy that characterizes bodies (Long and Sedley 1987: 27–28 = §27A–C).

The four incorporeals are:

1. **Lekta** (sayables): the meanings or propositional contents of utterances, distinct from both the physical utterance and the mental act of understanding
2. **Void** (*kenon*): infinite empty space surrounding the finite cosmos, occupied by nothing
3. **Place** (*topos*): the extension occupied by a body
4. **Time** (*chronos*): the interval of the world's motion

This is a carefully curated list. Each of the four incorporeals had to pass a test: it had to be genuinely real (not nothing), but it had to lack the power to act or be acted upon that characterizes bodies. Let us verify that time passes this test.

##### What "Incorporeal" Means for Time

Can time act on anything? Can anything act on time? In the ordinary sense, no. Time does not push or pull; it does not heat things or cool them; it cannot be increased or decreased by any physical operation. In this sense, time is causally inert: it is not an agent of change. Nor can physical processes alter time itself. The cosmic conflagration that periodically destroys and reconstitutes the Stoic world (on which more below) does not affect the interval within which it occurs — time frames the event rather than participating in it.

But time is not nothing. The Stoics insisted that time is real. It can be measured. Events occur *in* it and can be ordered by it. It provides the framework within which causal sequences unfold. If time were simply nothing — a mere concept with no foothold in reality — these features would be inexplicable. The Stoics were not tempted by an eliminativist view of time any more than they were tempted by an eliminativist view of meanings.

Our primary evidence here is assembled in Long and Sedley's collection. Stobaeus preserves the report that "the Stoics say there are four incorporeals: sayable, void, place, time" (Long and Sedley 1987: §51A). Arius Didymus, cited by Stobaeus, gives slightly more detail: these four "subsist" (*hyphestanai*) alongside bodies but do not themselves exist in the robust sense (Long and Sedley 1987: §27D). The philosophical task is to understand what this subsistence consists in.

##### The Distinction Between Existence and Subsistence

The Stoic distinction between existence and subsistence is not the same as modern debates about "being" and "existence" in the philosophy of logic (where, for example, Meinong's theory of objects posited non-existent objects). It is closer to the distinction some contemporary metaphysicians draw between things that are "part of the furniture of the world" and things that are "real but derivative" — ontologically second-class but not fictional.

A helpful analogy: consider the equator. The equator is not a body — it occupies no space, has no mass, cannot be seen or touched. But it is not fictitious. Ships cross it. It separates hemispheres. It plays a determinate role in geography and navigation. The equator is real without being a physical thing. It is, we might say, a real feature of the world that is not itself a constituent of the world in the way bodies are. Something similar is true, for the Stoics, of time. Time is a genuine feature of the world — the interval of the cosmic process — without itself being a body that could act or be acted upon.

This analogy has limits. The equator is defined by our conventions of mapping, while the Stoics would insist that time is mind-independent. But the analogy captures the ontological middle ground that the Stoic framework is trying to mark out.

##### Lekta and Their Significance

It is worth pausing on the *lekta* — the sayables — because they illuminate the broader logic of Stoic incorporeals. Lekta are the propositional contents expressed by utterances. When I say "Socrates walks," the sounds I produce are physical; the mental act of understanding is physical (since mind is corporeal for the Stoics); but the *meaning* — the proposition that Socrates walks, which can be expressed in different languages, understood by different people, and which can be true or false — is incorporeal. It subsists without being a body.

The importance of lekta for time is indirect but real. The Stoics were prepared to posit incorporeals whenever they had systematic theoretical reasons to do so — when eliminating the posit would leave something genuinely unexplained. Time, place, and void were posited for the same reason: because the physical world cannot be fully described without reference to the framework within which bodies operate, and that framework, while real, is not itself corporeal.

##### Bodies, Qualities, and the Cosmos

One last feature of the Stoic framework deserves mention. The Stoics held that the cosmos as a whole is a living organism — an ordered whole pervaded by *pneuma* (a fiery, vital breath) that holds everything together and gives each part its characteristic qualities. This cosmic organism undergoes periodic total conflagrations (*ekpyrosis*): the entire cosmos is consumed in fire and then reconstitutes itself identically. This cyclical cosmology has implications for the nature of time, which we will examine in the next subsection.

What matters here is that the Stoic ontological framework is not arbitrary. The distinction between bodies and incorporeals follows from the core Stoic thesis that causal power is the mark of genuine existence. Bodies are causally active and passive; incorporeals are neither. Time is incorporeal because, while it is the framework within which causation operates, it does not itself cause or undergo change. It is the interval of the world's motion — a feature of that motion — but not an agent in it.

This is a philosophically serious and defensible position. Whether it is ultimately correct is a different question, and one to which we will return. But the Stoic framework shows that the question "does time exist?" is not as simple as it sounds. How we answer depends on what we mean by existence — and getting clear on that is part of what philosophy of time is for (Long and Sedley 1987: 162–163).

#### 6.1.2 — Time as the Interval of the World's Motion

---

##### The Definition

The Stoic definition of time survives in a report preserved by Stobaeus, drawing on an early Stoic doxography that almost certainly reflects the views of Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism, and was elaborated by his successors. The report reads: "Time is the interval of motion according to which the measure of speed and slowness is spoken of" (Stobaeus, *Eclogae* I.105 = Long and Sedley 1987: §51B). A related formulation appears in the same passage: time is "the interval of the motion of the cosmos."

This is a compact definition that rewards unpacking. Let us take it phrase by phrase.

**"The interval"** (*diastema*): The Greek word *diastema* can mean extension, stretch, or interval. It is the same word used in music for the interval between notes. Time is not the motion itself but the *extent* or *measure* of the motion — the dimension along which the motion unfolds. This marks an important distinction: time is not identical with the physical process it measures; it is the framework within which that process can be measured.

**"Of the world's motion"**: The Stoics specified that this is the interval of *cosmic* motion, the overall movement of the cosmos taken as a unified whole. This is significant because it anchors time to the physical world without identifying it with any particular motion within it. The cosmic conflagration and reconstitution — the entire life-cycle of the Stoic universe — are what time primarily measures.

##### Comparison with Aristotle

The Stoic definition is clearly in dialogue with Aristotle's, and comparison is illuminating. Aristotle had defined time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after" (*Physics* IV.11, 219b1–2, trans. Hussey 1983). For Aristotle, time is what we count when we count the before-and-after of motion; it requires a counting mind, a soul capable of numbering. Plotinus will later make much of this mentalist implication in Aristotle's definition, but the Stoics had already drawn a different lesson.

The Stoic definition replaces "number" (*arithmos*) with "interval" (*diastema*). This is not a trivial substitution. Number suggests a discrete, mind-dependent counting operation. Interval suggests a continuous, mind-independent extent. For the Stoics — who, unlike Aristotle, held that time exists even if no mind is present to count it — this substitution reflects a genuine commitment to the objective, mind-independent character of time as an incorporeal framework.

There is another difference: Aristotle's definition is general — it applies to any motion, and time is defined relative to any motion whatsoever. The Stoic definition anchors time specifically to the motion of the cosmos. This gives Stoic time a distinctly cosmological flavor. Time is not the interval of any arbitrary process but of the world-process itself.

##### The Cosmic Conflagration (*Ekpyrosis*)

To fully understand the Stoic definition, we need to know something about Stoic cosmology. The Stoics held that the universe undergoes periodic total conflagrations: at the end of each cosmic cycle, everything — all the bodies that make up the cosmos — is consumed in fire, which is the primal element from which all others derive. This *ekpyrosis* is not destruction in the sense of annihilation; it is a return to the source. From this cosmic fire, the entire world reconstitutes itself, and it reconstitutes itself *identically*: every event, every person, every philosophical debate recurs in exactly the same order in the next world-cycle. This is the Stoic doctrine of eternal recurrence.

What happens to time during the ekpyrosis? This is a question on which our sources are not entirely clear, but the most plausible reading is that time, as an incorporeal framework, persists across the conflagration. The motion of the cosmos is interrupted — there is a phase of pure fire that is not articulated into the complex motions of ordinary cosmic life — but the interval that constitutes time is not destroyed. It continues to be the interval within which even the conflagration occurs. If this reading is right, time in Stoic cosmology is strictly speaking unbounded — it extends before the current cosmic cycle and will extend after it.

This has an interesting implication. The Stoic definition ties time to the world's motion, but the world's motion includes not just the orderly processes of the current cosmic epoch but the entire cyclical life of the cosmos across conflagrations and reconstitutions. Time is thus cosmic in scope in a very strong sense.

##### The Relationship Between Time and the Cosmos

Commentators have sometimes asked: is time identical with the world's motion, or merely coextensive with it? The Stoic definition says time is the *interval* of the motion — not the motion itself. This suggests the following picture: the world's motion provides the content of time, but time as interval is distinct from that content. It is the dimension along which the content is ordered, not the content itself. This is analogous to the way that spatial extension is not identical with the matter that occupies it, even though matter is what gives spatial extension its determinate character.

This analogy is imperfect, since place (not extension as such) was the Stoic incorporeal that corresponded to space, but the structural point stands: time is a real framework, not a body, within which the world's motions are ordered and measured.

##### Infinite Divisibility and the Problem of the Present

The definition of time as the interval of cosmic motion has a further implication that the Stoics were fully aware of: if time is an interval, it is divisible. And if it is divisible, then any temporal interval, however small, can be further divided. There is no smallest possible duration — no temporal atom. This is not a problem unique to the Stoics; it is a feature of any continuous conception of time.

But it creates a puzzle specifically about the present: if every duration can be divided, and if the present has some positive duration, then it can be divided into a past part and a future part, neither of which is the present. So the present, if it exists at all, must be durationless — an instantaneous knife-edge between past and future. Chrysippus pressed this point with great force, as we will see in Section 6.2. The definition established in this section sets up the problem that the next section addresses.

##### Long-Standing Resonances

The Stoic definition anticipates several features of modern relational theories of time. Like Leibniz and unlike Newton, the Stoics held that time is not an absolute container independent of the world's processes but rather an interval inherently tied to those processes. There is no time in a universe with no motion — not because time would be undetectable but because there would be nothing for time to be. Time is not a thing that could persist in a motionless universe; it is the structure of cosmic process itself.

This is a position with significant contemporary defenders. The substantivalist-relationist debate in philosophy of time — which we will examine in detail in Chapter 10 when we reach Leibniz and Newton — has Stoic roots. The Stoics were among the earliest thinkers to articulate a clear relationist intuition about time and to argue for it from metaphysical principles about what kinds of things are real. That they arrived at this position while still maintaining that time is genuinely real and not merely a mental construct marks them as careful and sophisticated metaphysicians (Long and Sedley 1987: 304–306; White 2003: 151–153).

### Section 6.2: The Present in Stoic Thought

---

#### Section Introduction

If you had to identify the single most philosophically acute contribution of Stoic thought to the philosophy of time, it would be Chrysippus's analysis of the present. This analysis is brief — it survives only in a hostile report by Plutarch — but it is extraordinarily dense, and it raises problems that philosophy has never fully resolved. The Stoics were not content to treat the "now" as a simple, obvious thing; they pressed the question of what the present actually is with a rigor that exposes deep tensions in any continuous conception of time.

The problem, in brief, is this: on any account of time as a continuous interval that is infinitely divisible, the present faces a dilemma. If the present has duration — if it lasts for any positive stretch of time — then it contains a past part (what has just occurred) and a future part (what is about to occur), and so it is not purely present. But if the present has no duration — if it is a durationless instant — then it seems to be a kind of nothing, a boundary between past and future with no thickness of its own. Chrysippus confronted this dilemma directly and arrived at a remarkable conclusion.

Section 6.2.1 reconstructs Chrysippus's position and its implications. Section 6.2.2 sets it alongside Aristotle's analysis of the Now, drawing out both the parallels and the differences, and considers what the Stoic position anticipates in contemporary debates about presentism.

#### 6.2.1 — Chrysippus on the Present

---

##### The Radical Thesis

Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280–207 BCE), the third head of the Stoic school and arguably its greatest systematic thinker, held an astonishing view about the ontological status of the present. According to a report preserved by Plutarch, Chrysippus maintained that of the three temporal divisions — past, present, and future — only the present *exists* in the strict sense, while past and future merely *subsist*. But he then went further: the present itself, when analyzed rigorously, turns out not to be a positive temporal interval with genuine duration but rather an infinitely thin boundary — a limit that has no positive extent at all.

Our primary source is Plutarch's *On Common Conceptions* (1081E–F), which Long and Sedley catalogue as §51C. The passage is hostile in intent — Plutarch is criticizing Stoic inconsistency — but it preserves the doctrine with what appears to be genuine fidelity. Plutarch reports that Chrysippus said the present time is never entire (*holon*) but is always being divided; the present is "a part neither of the past nor of the future" but is nothing more than the moving boundary between them. Chrysippus compares the present to a point — a boundary that has position but no magnitude (Long and Sedley 1987: §51C; Plutarch, *On Common Conceptions* 1081E–F).

##### The Argument for Infinite Divisibility

Why did Chrysippus think the present was infinitely divisible? The argument, as best we can reconstruct it, runs as follows.

Suppose the present has some positive duration, however small — say, one second. Then that second can be divided into two halves: the first half-second has already passed (it is now past), and the second half-second has not yet occurred (it is future). So neither half-second is wholly present. The same reasoning applies to any sub-interval we might choose as "the present." Any positive duration contains a past part and a future part and is therefore not purely present.

This is a reductio ad absurdum of the idea that the present has positive duration. If the present cannot be any positive duration, then the only candidate for the present is a durationless instant — what mathematicians call a point on the temporal line, which has position but no extension.

The Stoics were committed to the continuity of time — they had no temporal atomism, no minimum possible duration. Given this commitment, the argument is valid. If time is a continuum and we define the present as the boundary between past and future, the present has zero positive duration.

##### What Exists, What Subsists

Here the peculiarity of Chrysippus's position becomes vivid. The Stoics held that only the present exists in the full sense (*hyparchein*). But if the present is a durationless instant with zero duration, what exactly is it that fully exists? An instantaneous boundary has no extent — it is nowhere "thick" enough to contain any event, any motion, any occurrence. Events take time; even the fastest physical process lasts for some positive duration. A durationless instant cannot contain any event.

Chrysippus's response, insofar as we can reconstruct it, seems to have been to accept both horns of this strange position: the present, in the strict metaphysical sense, is indeed a durationless limit; but in common parlance, we use "the present" loosely to refer to some temporal neighborhood of that limit — "today," "this year," "this century" are all loose present-talk, not strict metaphysical claims. The strict present is an ideal boundary; the practical present is whatever temporal span is salient for the purposes at hand.

This distinction between strict and loose senses of "present" is philosophically important but also somewhat unsatisfying. It does not quite resolve the problem; it redefines it. The strict present, being durationless, cannot really be the locus of what exists, since existence requires some positive temporal extent. Chrysippus seems aware of this tension but does not have a fully worked-out response to it (Sorabji 1983: 21–23).

##### Infinite Divisibility and the Regress

There is a further difficulty. If the present is always already divisible — if any period I call "the present" can be divided into a past-half and a future-half — then there is no terminus to the analysis. I never reach a genuine present; I only ever reach smaller and smaller intervals, each of which admits the same division. The present is, in this sense, always receding. What I call "now" is really a neighborhood of now that is being constantly evacuated.

Plutarch, hostile witness though he is, puts the point with force: Chrysippus seems committed to the view that the present is being perpetually divided, so that we are always standing between a past and a future with no genuine present to stand in (*On Common Conceptions* 1081F). The present is like a mathematical limit — it can be approached arbitrarily closely but never reached.

Modern philosophers of time will recognize this as a precursor to the problem of the "specious present" — the psychologically extended "now" that William James, Edmund Husserl, and William Earle analyzed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The specious present is the temporally extended interval within which experience occurs as a unified whole, and it does not seem to be reducible to a durationless instant. Chrysippus's strict present raises the question of what grounds the specious present: how can we experience a "now" at all if the real now has no duration?

##### The Present Moment and What "Exists"

The most interesting philosophical legacy of Chrysippus's analysis is its relevance to the contemporary debate between presentism and eternalism. Presentism is the view that only the present moment exists — past and future things and events do not exist, they merely did or will exist. This sounds like a natural commonsense view, but Chrysippus's analysis reveals a problem: if the present is a durationless instant, then presentism seems committed to saying that the only things that exist are things that exist in a durationless instant — which is to say, nothing at all exists, since existence requires positive duration (Sider 2001: 11–12).

The Stoic response — that past and future subsist even if they do not exist in the full sense — is one way of addressing this problem. But it does so at the cost of complicating the ontology: we now have three modes of being rather than a simple exist/not-exist binary. Whether this is a refinement or a retreat is a question worth debating. What is clear is that Chrysippus saw the problem clearly and was not willing to paper over it with comfortable imprecision (Long and Sedley 1987: 164–165).

#### 6.2.2 — Chrysippus and Aristotle: Comparing Analyses of the Now

---

##### Common Ground

Aristotle and Chrysippus approached the present moment from different directions and arrived at positions that are, on the surface, quite different. But they shared a problem: how to give an account of the "now" — the present moment — that does not dissolve it into inconsistency. Comparing their solutions reveals both what they had in common and where they genuinely parted ways.

Aristotle, in *Physics* IV.10–14, devoted sustained attention to time and the now. His starting analysis was that time is divisible — into hours, minutes, and so on — but he resisted the idea that time is made up of discrete nows, as if a series of instantaneous moments were strung together like beads. Time is continuous (*syneches*), which means it flows smoothly rather than jumping from one now to the next. The now (*to nun*) is not a part of time but the boundary of temporal intervals — it is what separates the past from the future, and it is in this sense like a point on a line: it bounds the line without being a segment of it (Aristotle, *Physics* IV.11, 219b9–22, trans. Hussey 1983).

This is strikingly close to what Chrysippus said. Both thinkers hold that the now is not a part of time but a limit. Both hold that time is continuous and infinitely divisible. Both deny that the now has positive duration. The convergence is not coincidental: the Stoics were deeply engaged with Aristotle, and the parallels here reflect genuine philosophical inheritance.

##### Where They Diverge: Number vs. Interval

The first and most important divergence is in the definition of time itself. Aristotle defines time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after" — a definition that seems to require a counting mind. The Stoics define time as "the interval of the world's motion" — a definition that is structurally analogous but deliberately non-mentalist. As we saw in Section 6.1.2, this shift from "number" to "interval" reflects a different view of time's relation to mind: Aristotle seems to hold that time would not exist without a soul to count it; the Stoics seem to hold that time is an objective feature of the cosmos (Sorabji 1983: 73–79).

This divergence is philosophically significant. If Aristotle is right, then questions about time are inseparable from questions about consciousness. If the Stoics are right, time is objective and mind-independent — it belongs to the cosmos, not to the observer. The twentieth century's phenomenological tradition, from Husserl through Heidegger to Merleau-Ponty, tends toward the Aristotelian side; the physicalist tradition tends toward the Stoic side. The debate was already live in antiquity.

##### What Only the Present "Exists" Means for Aristotle vs. the Stoics

Aristotle does not say that only the present exists. His analysis is of time's structure, not primarily of time's ontological status. He does not develop a presentist metaphysics in the way Chrysippus does. The Aristotelian treatment of the now is part of an analysis of how continuous quantities have limits, and it does not generate a general thesis about what temporal intervals exist and what they don't.

Chrysippus, by contrast, makes existence-claims about temporal regions: only the present exists; the past and future merely subsist. This is a more explicitly ontological thesis. It anticipates what contemporary metaphysicians call *presentism* — the view that the present is the only temporal region that genuinely exists — though it differs from most contemporary presentism in holding that the present is a durationless instant rather than a temporal interval (Sider 2001: 11–15; Markosian 2004: 47–49).

The Stoic version of presentism is, in this sense, more radical than most contemporary versions. Contemporary presentists typically allow that the present has some positive extent — that it includes at least the contents of the specious present, or that "now" picks out a suitably short interval. Chrysippus's version does not allow this escape: the present is, strictly speaking, durationless, and what exists strictly speaking is nothing more than this durationless boundary.

##### What the Stoic Doctrine Anticipates

The resonances with contemporary debates are worth spelling out.

**Presentism and the growing block**: The contemporary debate between presentism (only the present exists), the growing block theory (the past and present exist, the future does not), and eternalism (past, present, and future equally exist) has structural analogies in Stoic thought. The Stoic view — only the present *exists*, past and future *subsist* — is closest to presentism but with a more nuanced ontology. The notion of subsistence plays a role analogous to the growing-block theorist's claim that the past has some kind of being even though it is not "present."

**The problem of temporal ontology**: Modern presentists face a notorious problem: how can we make true past-tensed statements ("Caesar crossed the Rubicon") if the past does not exist? One response appeals to the idea of truthmakers in the present; another appeals to the claim that past-tensed statements are made true by present facts that "trace back" to past events. The Stoic notion of the past as *subsisting* — having some mode of reality without fully existing — offers an interestingly different framework: past things are real enough to be the semantic referents of past-tensed statements but not real enough to be genuine causes.

**The specious present problem**: As noted above, Chrysippus's durationless present creates the problem of how experience is possible. Aristotle has the same problem, but he does not develop it in the direction of a phenomenology of temporal experience. That development will be Augustine's contribution, and it will require reconceiving what the present is — not as a mathematical limit but as the structure of conscious attention.

##### A Tentative Assessment

The Stoic analysis of the present is more philosophically radical than Aristotle's, and its radicalism is both a strength and a liability. The strength is clarity: if time is continuous and the present is not a part of time, then the present can only be a durationless limit. This follows rigorously from premises the Stoics are committed to, and they deserve credit for following the argument rather than fudging it.

The liability is that this clean logical result is very difficult to reconcile with the phenomenology of temporal experience. We do not experience time as a series of durationless instants. We experience it as flowing, as having a present that spans at least a brief interval. Any account of time that leaves no room for this experienced present is missing something important — even if it is hard to say exactly what. The solution, as we will see, required a more radical rethinking of the relationship between time and mind than either Aristotle or the Stoics attempted.

### Section 6.3: Epicurus and Lucretius on Time

---

#### Section Introduction

The Epicureans and the Stoics shared a world — the Hellenistic Mediterranean — and a conviction that philosophy must do practical work in human lives. But their philosophical systems could hardly have been more different. The Stoics were rationalists who believed in a providential cosmic order woven through with divine reason; the Epicureans were materialists who believed the universe was nothing but atoms falling through void, with no divine supervision and no cosmic purpose. These are not small differences, and they generated very different approaches to the philosophy of time.

For the Epicureans, the metaphysics of time followed directly from their atomism. If everything is either atoms or void, where does time fit? It is not an atom — it has no shape, size, or weight. It is not void — it is not space waiting to be filled. Epicurus's solution was to treat time as an "accident of accidents" — a property that belongs not to bodies directly but to the complex events and processes that bodies constitute. Time, on this view, is real but ontologically secondary: it supervenes on events without being a thing in its own right.

Lucretius, writing in Latin roughly two centuries after Epicurus, articulated this position with a poet's clarity in *De Rerum Natura* (On the Nature of Things). His treatment of time is brief — a few dozen lines — but philosophically precise. He offers what amounts to a conceivability argument for the relational nature of time: we cannot conceive of time apart from events and processes, and this inability reflects a genuine ontological dependence.

Section 6.3.1 examines Epicurus's original position and its philosophical basis. Section 6.3.2 turns to Lucretius and the specific argument he developed, its structure, and its modern parallels.

#### 6.3.1 — Epicurus: Time as Accident of Accidents

---

##### The Atomist Framework

To understand Epicurus's account of time, you need to begin with the atomist universe. For Epicurus — following and revising Leucippus and Democritus — the fundamental constituents of reality are atoms (*atomoi*) and void (*kenon*). Atoms are indivisible, indestructible material particles moving through infinite void. Everything that exists is composed of atoms; everything that happens is the result of atomic collisions, aggregations, and dispersions. There is no matter other than atoms, no space other than void, and no agency other than atomic motion.

Within this framework, Epicurus recognized a category of things that are real but that are not atoms and not void: what he called *symbebêkota* — properties, accidents, or attributes. Accidents are features that belong to bodies (aggregates of atoms) rather than to atoms directly. They are real in the sense that they genuinely characterize the bodies they attach to; but they do not have independent existence. Remove the body and the accident goes with it.

Epicurus's *Letter to Herodotus*, our most important source for his physics, contains the key passage on time. He writes:

> "Time is a peculiar thing: we must not say 'time is' in the same way as substances... Time is an accident of accidents — it is what accompanies the motions and rests and changes of things, and we must not seek to grasp it as if it were a substance in its own right." (Epicurus, *Letter to Herodotus* §73, in Long and Sedley 1987: §7A, trans. adapted from Inwood and Gerson)

The phrase "accident of accidents" (*symbebêkos symbebêkotôn*) is technically precise. Ordinary accidents — properties like "red" or "hot" — belong directly to bodies. Time is an accident not of bodies but of the *events* (changes, motions, rests) that bodies undergo. It is, as it were, one ontological level further removed from basic reality than ordinary accidents.

##### What "Accident of Accidents" Means

This locution deserves careful unpacking. Consider a particular event: Socrates walks across the agora. This event involves Socrates (a complex of atoms), his motion (an accident of Socrates), and a duration (the time the walk takes). Epicurus's claim is that the duration is an accident of the motion — it characterizes the motion rather than directly characterizing Socrates. And the motion is itself an accident of Socrates. So the duration is an accident of an accident: a second-order property.

This means that time, on Epicurus's account, cannot exist without events (processes, motions, changes). There is no time "left over" when all events are removed. Time is not an empty container that persists even when nothing is happening; it is a feature of what happens, and it exists only as long as there is something happening to be its subject.

This is a *relational* view of time in the strongest sense: time is constituted by the temporal relations between events, and those relations supervene on the events themselves. There is no additional "temporal substance" that exists alongside events and within which events are located.

##### The Phenomenological Starting Point

It is worth noting how Epicurus arrives at this position. He does not begin with abstract metaphysical principles and deduce the nature of time from them (though his conclusions cohere with his atomist metaphysics). He begins, characteristically, with what is evident to experience: "We must apprehend time, using an evident standard, just as we apprehend everything else — we must apprehend it by our clearest impression, which is that of days and nights, and the changes and motions and rests that we observe in things" (Epicurus, *Letter to Herodotus* §72–73, Long and Sedley 1987: §7A).

The method here is empiricist. Our concept of time is derived from experience of temporal processes — the alternation of day and night, the observation of change and motion. We do not have an experience of time itself, independent of these processes. If this is right, it suggests that time is not the kind of thing that can be independently experienced; it is always given through our experience of temporal events. This phenomenological point supports the metaphysical conclusion: if time cannot be experienced independently of temporal events, then time is not an independently existing thing.

This is an Epicurean version of an argument that appears, in different forms, in Berkeley, Hume, Leibniz, and twentieth-century relationist philosophers of physics. The argument from the conditions of temporal experience to the relational nature of time is one of the more durable threads in the history of the philosophy of time.

##### Implications for the Ontology of Time

Epicurus's account has several distinctive implications.

**Against absolute time**: If time is an accident of accidents, there is no absolute temporal container. There is no "void" of time, analogous to the void of space, within which events are located. Events are not in time the way balls are in a box. Rather, time is in events — it characterizes them, and through them, characterizes the relations between them.

**Against temporal vacuum**: On Epicurus's view, a period of time with no events occurring is strictly speaking impossible — or at least, the concept of such a period is empty. There is no time between events if no events connect them. This contrasts with Newton, for whom absolute time flows whether or not anything is happening in it.

**For temporal pluralism**: If time supervenes on events, then there is a question whether there is one unified time or many local times — one for each system of interacting events. Epicurus does not develop this implication, but it is worth noting that the modern physicist's concern about whether there is a global time for the universe (as opposed to local times relative to reference frames) resonates with an Epicurean concern, even if the physics is utterly different.

##### Comparison with Stoic Time

A comparison with the Stoic view is instructive. Both Stoics and Epicureans held that time is not an independently existing body. But they differed in how they characterized what time is. For the Stoics, time is an incorporeal — real but not corporeal, a genuine feature of the cosmos. For Epicurus, time is an accident of accidents — a second-order property that supervenes on events. These are not the same view.

The Stoic view seems more willing to accord time a kind of robust reality: time subsists, it is a genuine cosmic interval, it structures the entire life of the cosmos. The Epicurean view is more deflationary: time is not quite a thing at all, but a feature of things. The Stoics give time an objective status that the Epicureans seem reluctant to grant.

This difference matters because it bears on the question of whether time could exist in a universe with no change. The Stoic answer seems to be: yes, time would persist even in a universe with no change, as the interval of a cosmic process that was itself motionless (though this is not a scenario Stoic cosmology makes room for). The Epicurean answer is: no, time cannot exist without change, because time is constituted by change.

#### 6.3.2 — Lucretius on Time: *De Rerum Natura* I.459–463

---

##### The Poet-Philosopher

Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE) wrote one of the most ambitious poems in Latin — *De Rerum Natura* (On the Nature of Things) — as a vehicle for Epicurean philosophy. The poem is a tour de force: it presents a complete atomist physics, a philosophy of mind, an account of the evolution of civilization, and a sustained argument against the fear of death, all in the meter of Homer. It is at once a work of philosophy and a work of art, and unlike many philosophical poems (which use the verse as a thin wrapper for prose argument), Lucretius's verse actively serves his philosophical purposes. The poem is intended to be beautiful because beauty is evidence of truth, and because only beauty can hold the reader's attention long enough to deliver the philosophical medicine.

Lucretius's treatment of time in Book I, lines 459–463, is brief but philosophically pointed. It comes in the context of his general argument about what kinds of things exist. He has established that everything that can be said to exist is either a body or void. He then considers what to say about things that are clearly real but that are neither bodies nor void — such as time, events, and the past history of things. His answer is that these are *accidentia* or *eventa*: accidents and events. They are real, but their reality is derivative — they cannot exist except insofar as they belong to or characterize bodies and the interactions of bodies.

##### The Key Passage

The passage in question reads, in a literal translation:

> "Time also does not exist by itself; but from things themselves sense-experience makes clear what happened in the past, what is happening now, and what is going to follow upon that. One must admit that no one has a sense-experience of time itself apart from the motion of things, or their restful quiet." (Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* I.459–463, trans. Melville 2009, adapted)

The argument has a simple but elegant structure. It proceeds from an empiricist premise about experience to a metaphysical conclusion about existence. Let us lay it out:

1. We have no sense-experience of time itself — we only ever experience time as the time of some event or process (the pastness of what happened, the presentness of what is occurring, the futurity of what will come).
2. If we had no sense-experience of time-in-itself, this would naturally be explained by the fact that time does not exist in itself — it only exists as a feature of events and processes.
3. Therefore, time does not exist by itself.

The premise is a conceivability-cum-experiential claim: can you conceive of, or have any sensory access to, time that is not the time of something? Lucretius's answer is no. Strip away all events, motions, and processes — imagine a universe with nothing happening — and you have no grip on time at all. Time is not something over and above the events that occur in it; it is the temporal character of those events.

##### Testing the Argument

Lucretius's argument depends on the conceivability premise, and it is worth pressing on it. Can we conceive of time apart from events?

The hardest case for Lucretius is this: we can surely imagine a universe in which nothing is happening for some period, and then something begins to happen. Don't we then have a conception of time during which nothing occurred? Newton would say yes: absolute time is precisely this empty temporal container that persists even when nothing is in it. If we can coherently imagine such a period, the conceivability premise seems false.

Lucretius's response, implicit in the context, would be: what you are imagining is not time itself but the *before* and *after* of some event sequence — you are borrowing temporal structure from the events and projecting it into the gap between them. You are not really conceiving of time independent of all events; you are conceiving of time relative to events by imagining a region of the temporal framework that they define but do not fill.

Whether this response is convincing depends on how we think about the relationship between temporal vacua and relational time. Leibniz later made exactly this argument with greater technical precision: the concept of "empty time before the creation" is not coherent because temporal order is constituted by event sequences, and there is no event sequence to constitute temporal order in a period of absolute nothing (Leibniz, *Fifth Letter to Clarke* §4, in Alexander 1956: 75). Lucretius anticipates this by two millennia.

##### The Modern Parallel: Relationalism in Philosophy of Physics

The view Lucretius is defending has a direct descendant in contemporary philosophy of physics. The debate between substantivalists and relationists about the nature of spacetime is, at its core, a debate about whether spacetime is an independently existing entity (an absolute container, like Newton's absolute space and time) or merely the totality of spatiotemporal relations between events (with no "container" over and above the relata). Lucretius is clearly a relationist.

Contemporary physicists have found Machian relationism attractive in the context of general relativity, which makes spacetime geometry dynamical — the structure of spacetime is not a fixed background but is affected by the distribution of matter and energy. In this sense, Einstein's general relativity leans Leibnizean/Lucretian rather than Newtonian (Barbour 1999: 1–10; Earman 1989: 12–15). Lucretius did not, of course, anticipate the detailed physics; but he anticipated the philosophical stance that has proven most compatible with it.

##### The Rhetorical Function

It is worth noting that Lucretius's treatment of time is not primarily a contribution to metaphysics for its own sake. It is part of a larger argument aimed at removing the fear of death. If time has no independent existence — if it is merely a feature of events — then the "time after death" is not a real temporal container waiting to be empty and lonely. Death is not an event that occurs in time; it is the cessation of the events whose temporal character constitutes time for the person who dies. This metaphysical point supports the therapeutic conclusion: there is no "time after death" in which you will be absent and missing things, because there is no time for you once the events of your life have ceased. We will examine this connection more carefully in Section 6.4.
