### Section 6.4: The Symmetry Argument

---

#### Section Introduction

Philosophy at its best does double duty: it clarifies abstract metaphysical questions and it illuminates how we should live. The Epicurean tradition excelled at this double work. The metaphysics of atoms and void was not only a contribution to natural philosophy; it was the foundation of a therapeutic project aimed at liberating human beings from their most destructive fears. Of those fears, the most pervasive and the most philosophically tractable was the fear of death.

Lucretius's symmetry argument — also sometimes called the "mirror argument" — appears in Book III of *De Rerum Natura* (lines 830–842). It is brief, elegant, and philosophically challenging. The argument turns on a temporal comparison: the period after your death is structurally symmetric with the period before your birth. Since you do not regard the latter with regret or terror — since the eternity of non-existence before you existed causes you no grief — you should, by consistency, not regard the former with terror either. The pre-natal and post-mortem darknesses are the same kind of thing.

The argument seems compelling on first encounter. And yet something about it resists. Most people who hear it feel that the symmetry cannot be complete — that there is some genuine asymmetry between the prospect of one's own non-existence and the retrospect of it. The philosophical question is whether this felt asymmetry can be articulated and defended.

Section 6.4.1 reconstructs the argument carefully and examines what it actually claims. The discussion of challenges — particularly Thomas Nagel's influential response and James Warren's analysis — follows within the same section.

#### 6.4.1 — Lucretius's Symmetry Argument

---

##### The Argument in Context

Lucretius's symmetry argument appears late in *De Rerum Natura*, after he has laid out the Epicurean view that the soul is mortal — that it is, like everything else, composed of atoms, and that at death these atoms disperse, ending the person as definitively as a fire is extinguished when its fuel runs out. Death, on this account, is simply the cessation of the atomic configuration that constitutes a person. There is no afterlife, no continuation of consciousness, no shade in the underworld. Death is — exactly — nothing.

Given this picture, why do people fear death? Lucretius argues that they fear it because they implicitly conceive of their own death as a kind of deprivation — an ongoing absence of the goods they currently enjoy. They imagine themselves lying in the grave, missing the warmth of the sun, the pleasures of friendship, the satisfactions of work. This implicit picture is, Lucretius argues, incoherent: it requires imagining oneself present to experience one's own absence, which is precisely what death rules out. The famous argument, from slightly earlier in Book III (line 830), is: "Where death is, I am not; where I am, death is not." Death and the person are mutually exclusive; there is no subject of the deprivation.

The symmetry argument is a supplementary argument aimed at a different source of fear: the sheer temporal extent of non-existence that follows death. Even if death is not experienced as a deprivation, it might be feared simply because of the infinite void of non-being that it introduces. Lucretius addresses this by drawing a temporal comparison.

##### The Text

The key lines are:

> "Look back at the eternity that passed before we were born, and mark how utterly it counts to us as nothing. This is a mirror that Nature holds up to us, in which we may see the time that shall be after our death. Is there anything terrifying in it? Is there anything that looks like gloom? It is more peaceful than any sleep." (*De Rerum Natura* III.972–977, trans. Bailey, adapted)

The parallel passage that is most cited is III.830–842, in which Lucretius explicitly draws the symmetry:

> "Death, then, is nothing to us and concerns us not one jot, since the nature of mind is found to be mortal... For in the days of old we felt no anguish, when the Carthaginians came from all sides to the conflict; when all the world, shaken by the alarming tumult of war, shudderingly quaked beneath the high coasts of heaven, and mortal men were in doubt to which domain they must fall by land and sea. So, when we shall be no more — when there shall have been a separation of body and soul, out of both of which we are each formed into a single being — to us, who shall then be nothing, nothing by any hazard will happen any more at all, nothing will excite our feeling; no, not if earth shall be mingled with sea, and sea with heaven." (*De Rerum Natura* III.830–842, trans. Bailey 1910)

The formal structure of the argument is this:

1. There is a long period of non-existence before your birth (the "prenatal" period).
2. This period does not distress you — you do not regret or fear the eternity of non-existence that preceded your life.
3. The period after your death is structurally identical to the period before your birth: in both, you do not exist; in both, the world goes on without you; in both, you are present to no experiences.
4. By consistency, you should not fear the post-mortem period of non-existence any more than you regret the prenatal period.
5. Therefore, death is not to be feared.

This is a symmetry argument: if two things are structurally symmetric, they call for symmetric evaluative attitudes.

##### The Argument's Logical Force

The argument has genuine force. The prenatal period was not distressing. We do not lie awake at night regretting that we were not alive to witness the construction of the Colosseum, or that we missed the philosophical debates in Athens in the fifth century BCE. We have no felt sense of loss about the infinity of time before we existed. If this is right, and if the post-mortem period is really structurally symmetric with the prenatal period, then consistency demands that we not fear the post-mortem period either.

Philosophers who have defended the Lucretian view (roughly) include Stephen Rosenbaum (1986, 1989) and Fred Feldman (1991). They argue that the symmetry is genuine and that Lucretius's conclusion follows. The fear of death is, on this view, a kind of temporal parochialism — an irrational attachment to the near-future that would not survive clear-eyed temporal impartiality.

##### Nagel's Challenge: Why the Symmetry May Break Down

Thomas Nagel's influential essay "Death" (1979) argues that the symmetry argument fails, though he takes it seriously rather than dismissing it. Nagel's challenge operates at two levels.

At the first level, Nagel questions whether the prenatal period is really parallel to the post-mortem period. The prenatal period is one in which you did not yet exist — there was no subject to suffer deprivation. But the post-mortem period is one in which you have ceased to exist — there *was* a subject (you), and it is that subject who no longer enjoys the goods it previously did. The post-mortem period is the deprivation of a specific individual who existed; the prenatal period is not the deprivation of anyone, since the subject who would be deprived had not yet come into existence (Nagel 1979: 7–8).

At the second level, Nagel argues that what makes death bad is the deprivation of life — the goods that life contains that death forecloses. Death is bad not because dying is painful (it need not be) but because it cuts short a life that would otherwise have contained more good things: more experiences, more relationships, more achievements. This "deprivation account" of death's badness makes no direct reference to temporal direction; what matters is not *when* the non-existence occurs but whether the non-existence deprives a subject of goods they would otherwise have had (Nagel 1979: 6–7). But if that is what makes death bad, it is not obviously symmetric: the prenatal non-existence does not deprive you of goods you would have had, because there is no you prior to your birth to be deprived.

##### Warren's Analysis

James Warren (2004) offers the most careful sustained analysis of the symmetry argument in recent literature. Warren argues that the Lucretian argument is more sophisticated than it appears and that Nagel's asymmetry objection, while pointing to something real, does not fully undermine it.

Warren makes a key distinction: there is an asymmetry between pre-natal and post-mortem non-existence at the level of *personal identity* (there is no pre-natal you to be deprived), but there may be a symmetry at the level of *evaluative attitude* (what reasons do you have to care about your non-existence, in either direction?). The Lucretian point, Warren argues, is not primarily about metaphysical symmetry but about the rationality of temporal preferences: is there any reason to prefer that your non-existence occur before rather than after your life? And Lucretius's answer — that there is no such reason — may be defensible even if the metaphysical asymmetry Nagel points to is genuine (Warren 2004: 58–67).

Jeff McMahan (2002: 75–77) argues that birth and death are genuinely asymmetric: we have a strong interest in our future existence that is not matched by a corresponding interest in our past existence. This future-directedness of personal concern is not irrational; it reflects the fact that future goods are open to our agency in ways past goods are not. The asymmetry in our attitudes toward pre-natal and post-mortem non-existence may thus be rational rather than a bias to be corrected.

##### The Deeper Temporal Issue

What the symmetry argument ultimately probes is our relationship to our own temporal position. The argument asks: why does it matter *when* one's non-existence occurs? Why is non-existence after life worse than non-existence before life? The various responses to Lucretius have converged on the view that temporal position matters because of what it means for personal identity, narrative, and agency: the goods of life are not timeless goods that can be redistributed across time indifferently, but are goods of a specific kind of temporal existence — of being a persisting subject with a past and a future.

This is a profound point about the philosophy of time. Time is not merely a neutral container in which goods and ills are located; it structures what goods and ills *are* for beings like us. The Stoic insight that the present has a special ontological status, the Epicurean insight that time supervenes on events, and the Lucretian argument about temporal symmetry all converge on the same deep theme: time is not separable from what it means to be the kind of being we are.

---

### Chapter 6: Exercises

---

#### Comprehension and Analysis

**Exercise 6.1**
In your own words, explain the Stoic distinction between bodies and incorporeals. Why does time qualify as incorporeal rather than corporeal? In your response, make sure to specify what the Stoics understood as the criterion for being a body.

**Exercise 6.2**
Reconstruct Chrysippus's argument for the claim that the present moment is a durationless instant. What premise about time generates this conclusion? Do you think the conclusion is correct? If not, where does the argument go wrong?

**Exercise 6.3**
Compare the Stoic definition of time as "the interval of the world's motion" with Aristotle's definition of time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after." What philosophical difference does the substitution of "interval" for "number" signal? Which definition do you find more defensible, and why?

**Exercise 6.4**
Epicurus describes time as an "accident of accidents." Explain in detail what this means. In what sense is time "ontologically secondary" on this account? How does this view differ from both the Stoic view and a view that treats time as an independently existing substance?

**Exercise 6.5**
Reconstruct Lucretius's symmetry argument in your own words. Present it as a formal argument with numbered premises and a conclusion. Then identify the premise you think is most vulnerable to challenge and explain why.

**Exercise 6.6**
Nagel argues that there is a genuine asymmetry between prenatal and post-mortem non-existence. Explain his argument. Then write a response defending Lucretius against Nagel's objection. Does Lucretius have an adequate reply?

**Exercise 6.7**
The Stoics held that only the present exists, while past and future *subsist*. How does this position relate to contemporary presentism? Is the Stoic position a version of presentism, or is it importantly different? Explain your answer.

**Exercise 6.8**
James Warren argues that the symmetry argument may be defensible even if Nagel's metaphysical asymmetry is correct. Explain Warren's distinction between metaphysical symmetry and evaluative symmetry. Is this distinction tenable?

---

#### Observational and Experimental Exercises

**Lab Exercise 6.A — The Shrinking Present**

Try to identify the duration of "the present moment" through careful introspection. Start with a broad present ("this afternoon"), then narrow: this hour, this minute, this second, this half-second, this tenth of a second. At each step, ask yourself: is this interval purely present, or does it contain a "just-passed" part and a "just-coming" part? Keep narrowing until you cannot reliably distinguish present from immediate past. Record the smallest interval you can identify as "clearly present" and reflect: does your experience support or challenge Chrysippus's claim that the strict present is durationless?

**Lab Exercise 6.B — Time Without Events**

Find a quiet place and spend five minutes trying to attend to time itself — not to events, sensations, or thoughts, but to pure time. Keep a brief journal of what you find. Then consider: Is Lucretius's claim that "no one has a sense-experience of time itself apart from the motion of things" confirmed or disconfirmed by your experiment? Report your findings, and discuss what methodological limitations affect this kind of introspective experiment.

**Lab Exercise 6.C — The Mirror Argument in Ordinary Life**

The Lucretian symmetry argument has an everyday version: we regularly look back at periods of our past with equanimity that we do not extend to the corresponding future periods (for example: you don't regret being asleep for the last eight hours, but you might fear being in a coma for the next eight hours). Identify three examples of this temporal asymmetry in your own experience or observation. For each example, ask: is the asymmetry rational? Does it support or challenge Lucretius's argument? Write up your findings as a brief philosophical reflection.

---

#### Essay Questions

**Exercise 6.9 (Essay)**
Is Chrysippus's account of the present self-defeating? If the present is a durationless instant, can anything be said to "exist" strictly in the present? Write an essay of 800–1000 words exploring this question, drawing on both the Stoic text and at least one contemporary discussion of presentism.

**Exercise 6.10 (Essay)**
The Epicurean relational account of time holds that there is no time without events. Newton held that time flows even in a universe with no events. Write an essay of 800–1000 words evaluating these competing views. Consider the following question: if a universe with no events is coherently conceivable, what follows for the Epicurean view?

**Exercise 6.11 (Essay)**
How does the fear of death relate to one's conception of time? Drawing on Epicurus, Lucretius, and at least one contemporary philosopher (Nagel, Warren, or McMahan), write an essay of 1000–1200 words arguing for a position on whether Lucretius's symmetry argument should lead us to revise our attitudes toward death.

#### Annotated Suggestions for Further Reading

**Long, A. A., and D. N. Sedley. *The Hellenistic Philosophers*. 2 vols. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1987.**
The indispensable resource for primary texts. Volume 1 contains translations organized by topic; Volume 2 contains the original Greek and Latin with commentary. Chapter 51 ("Time") contains the key Stoic sources; Chapter 7 contains the Epicurean sources. Any serious study of Hellenistic philosophy of time begins here.

**Sorabji, Richard. *Time, Creation and the Continuum*. London: Duckworth, 1983.**
The most thorough scholarly treatment of ancient and early medieval theories of time. Sorabji combines meticulous textual scholarship with genuine philosophical acuity. The chapters on the Stoics and Epicureans are particularly valuable for establishing the relationship between their positions and Aristotle's. Highly recommended for any student who wants to go beyond the introductory level.

**Warren, James. *Facing Death: Epicurus and His Critics*. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 2004.**
The best contemporary treatment of Epicurean arguments about death, including the fullest analysis of the symmetry argument available. Warren is both careful about the ancient sources and genuinely engaged with the contemporary philosophical debates. Essential for Exercise 6.11.

**Nagel, Thomas. "Death." In *Mortal Questions*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1979.**
The most influential modern engagement with the Epicurean view of death. Short (about 10 pages) but dense. Nagel takes the Epicurean position seriously rather than dismissing it, which is one reason the essay has been so important. Accessible to undergraduates.

**Long, A. A. *Hellenistic Philosophy: Stoics, Epicureans, Sceptics*. 2nd ed. London: Duckworth, 1986.**
A readable introduction to Hellenistic philosophy as a whole, with good coverage of the metaphysical and physical views of both schools. A good starting point before tackling the primary sources directly.

**Sedley, David. *Lucretius and the Transformation of Greek Wisdom*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.**
A detailed study of how Lucretius adapted and transformed Epicurean philosophy in his poem. Essential for understanding what Lucretius adds to Epicurus and what he changes. Particularly good on the structure of *De Rerum Natura* as a philosophical argument.

**White, Michael J. "Stoic Natural Philosophy." In *The Cambridge Companion to the Stoics*, edited by Brad Inwood. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003.**
A reliable survey of Stoic physics and cosmology, including the cosmological framework within which the Stoic theory of time was developed. Accessible to undergraduates and a good reference for the ekpyrosis doctrine.

**Brunschwig, Jacques. *Papers in Hellenistic Philosophy*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1994.**
A collection of sophisticated essays by one of the leading historians of Hellenistic philosophy. The essay on the supreme genus and Stoic ontology is directly relevant to understanding the incorporeal/corporeal distinction.

**Feldman, Fred. "Some Puzzles About the Evil of Death." *Philosophical Review* 100 (1991): 205–227.**
A useful complement to Nagel, examining the deprivation account of death's badness in more detail and with more philosophical rigor. Accessible and clear.

**McMahan, Jeff. *The Ethics of Killing*. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2002, chap. 2.**
McMahan's analysis of death's badness in relation to personal identity and time is among the most sophisticated available. Though the broader book is not primarily about the philosophy of time, Chapter 2 on death and deprivation rewards careful study.

**Caston, Victor. "Something and Nothing." *Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy* 17 (1999).**
A careful philosophical analysis of Stoic ontology, focused on the status of universals and concepts but illuminating for the broader question of what "subsistence" means in the Stoic framework. Best for students with some background in contemporary analytic metaphysics.

**Markosian, Ned. "A Defense of Presentism." *Oxford Studies in Metaphysics*, vol. 1 (2004).**
One of the best contemporary defenses of the view that only the present exists. Reading this alongside the Stoic material helps to identify both the anticipations of contemporary presentism in ancient thought and the ways in which the positions differ.

### Chapter 6: Important Concepts

---

**Incorporeal** (*asomaton*)
In Stoic metaphysics, an incorporeal is something that is real but lacks the capacity to act or be acted upon — the defining characteristic of bodies (*somata*). The four Stoic incorporeals are lekta (sayables), void, place, and time. Being incorporeal does not mean being nonexistent; incorporeals *subsist* rather than fully *exist*.

**Subsistence** (*hyphestanai*) vs. **Existence** (*hyparchein*)
The Stoics drew a distinction within the category of "the real" between things that fully exist (bodies, which can cause and be caused) and things that merely subsist (incorporeals, which are real but causally inert). This is not the same as the distinction between the real and the fictional; it is a distinction within the real itself, based on degree or mode of ontological robustness.

**Lekta** (Sayables)
The propositional contents of statements — the meanings expressed by utterances. Lekta are incorporeal because they are not bodies and cannot act on or be acted upon. They belong to a class of "subsisting" things that play genuine roles in reasoning and communication without being material constituents of the world.

**Time as Interval** (*diastema*)
The Stoic definition of time as the interval of the world's motion. Unlike Aristotle's definition in terms of "number" (which implies a counting mind), the Stoic "interval" is meant to be objective and mind-independent. The interval is not the motion itself but the extent or dimension along which motion unfolds.

**Ekpyrosis** (Cosmic Conflagration)
The Stoic cosmological doctrine that the universe periodically undergoes total dissolution into fire, from which it reconstitutes itself identically. This cycle of conflagration and reconstitution is the cosmic process whose "interval" constitutes time; time on this view is coextensive with the entire cyclical life of the cosmos.

**Eternal Recurrence**
The Stoic cosmological thesis that each cycle of the cosmos is an exact repetition of every previous cycle, down to the smallest detail. Every philosophical argument, every person, every event recurs in exactly the same order in every cosmic cycle. This doctrine is importantly different from Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, which has ethical rather than cosmological import.

**Durationless Instant**
Chrysippus's conclusion about the nature of the strict present: because any positive temporal duration can be divided into a past part and a future part, the present can only be a durationless limit between past and future, analogous to a mathematical point on a line. This is a rigorous consequence of combining temporal continuity with the demand that the present be "purely" present.

**Presentism (Ancient Version)**
The Stoic view that only the present fully exists, while past and future merely subsist. This anticipates the contemporary metaphysical position called presentism (the view that only present entities and events exist), but with the important difference that Stoic presentism involves a graduated ontology (full existence vs. subsistence) rather than a simple binary between existing and not existing.

**Accident of Accidents** (*symbebêkos symbebêkotôn*)
Epicurus's description of the ontological status of time. Ordinary accidents (properties) belong directly to bodies; time is an accident that belongs to events (motions, changes, rests), which are themselves accidents of bodies. This makes time ontologically second-order — real but doubly derivative.

**Relational Theory of Time**
The view, held in different forms by the Epicureans and later by Leibniz, that time is not an independently existing container but is constituted by the temporal relations between events. There is no time "left over" once all events are removed; time is a feature of the event-structure of the world, not a background within which events occur.

**The Symmetry Argument**
Lucretius's argument (*De Rerum Natura* III.830–842) that the post-mortem period of non-existence is structurally symmetric with the prenatal period, and that since we do not regret or fear the latter, consistency requires that we not fear the former. The argument aims to liberate readers from the fear of death by revealing it as a temporal inconsistency.

**Deprivation Account**
The view (defended by Nagel and others) that death is bad primarily because it deprives a person of the goods they would otherwise have enjoyed — further experiences, relationships, achievements. On this account, death's badness is not about the experience of dying (which may be painless) but about the foreclosed future. This account motivates Nagel's challenge to Lucretius: the prenatal period does not deprive anyone of anything, while death deprives a specific existing person.

**Temporal Asymmetry of Attitudes**
The widely observed phenomenon that people are more distressed about future non-existence than about past non-existence, and generally more future-directed in their personal concerns than past-directed. Whether this asymmetry is rational or a bias to be corrected is one of the central questions raised by Lucretius's symmetry argument.

**Specious Present**
The psychologically extended "now" of conscious experience — the temporal interval within which experience presents itself as unified and simultaneous, even though it has positive duration. The specious present was analyzed by William James and Edmund Husserl and is relevant to the Stoic problem of the present: how can consciousness have a present if the strict present is durationless?

**Temporal Atomism vs. Temporal Continuity**
Temporal atomism is the view that time is composed of indivisible minimal units — temporal atoms that cannot be further divided. The Stoics and Epicureans both rejected temporal atomism in favor of temporal continuity (the view that any temporal interval, however small, can be further divided). This commitment to continuity is what drives Chrysippus's analysis of the durationless present.

### Chapter 6: Important Researchers

---

**Zeno of Citium** (c. 334–262 BCE)
The founder of Stoicism, who taught at the Stoa Poikile ("painted porch") in Athens. Zeno established the basic Stoic ontological framework, including the distinction between bodies and incorporeals and the classification of time among the incorporeals. His original writings survive only in fragments preserved by later authors, principally Stobaeus and Diogenes Laertius. The definition of time as "the interval of the world's motion" is attributed to Zeno's circle, though it was elaborated by later Stoics, particularly Chrysippus.

**Chrysippus of Soli** (c. 280–207 BCE)
The third head of the Stoic school and by all ancient accounts the philosopher who gave Stoicism its mature systematic form. He wrote prolifically — ancient sources credit him with over 700 books — but nothing survives intact. His analysis of the present moment as a durationless limit is preserved only in Plutarch's hostile report in *On Common Conceptions*. Chrysippus was also central to Stoic logic and ethics; his breadth and rigor made him the dominant intellectual figure of the Hellenistic period.

**Epicurus** (341–270 BCE)
The founder of the Epicurean school, who established his community ("the Garden") in Athens. Epicurus's philosophical project was explicitly therapeutic: philosophy should liberate humans from fear, above all the fear of death and divine punishment. His physics — atomism derived from Democritus but revised — was the theoretical basis for this therapy. The *Letter to Herodotus* is our best source for his philosophy of time; it survives in Diogenes Laertius's *Lives of the Eminent Philosophers*.

**Titus Lucretius Carus** (c. 99–55 BCE)
Roman poet and philosopher, author of *De Rerum Natura* (On the Nature of Things), the most complete surviving exposition of Epicurean philosophy. Lucretius's distinctive contribution was not only to preserve and transmit Epicureanism in Latin but to make it vivid and compelling through brilliant poetic imagination. His treatment of time in Book I and his symmetry argument in Book III are philosophically precise as well as aesthetically powerful. Almost nothing is known of his life.

**A. A. Long** (b. 1937)
British philosopher and classicist, now Emeritus Professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and one of the foremost authorities on Hellenistic philosophy. His collaborative work with David Sedley, *The Hellenistic Philosophers* (2 vols., 1987), is the indispensable scholarly resource for primary texts on Stoic and Epicurean philosophy, including the philosophy of time. Long's earlier study *Hellenistic Philosophy* (1974) remains an accessible introduction to the period.

**David Sedley** (b. 1947)
British classicist and philosopher, Laurence Professor of Ancient Philosophy at Cambridge University. Co-author with Long of *The Hellenistic Philosophers*, Sedley has done extensive work on Epicurean atomism, Stoic philosophy, and the reception of ancient philosophy in later periods. His book *Lucretius and the Transformation of Greek Wisdom* (1998) is essential for understanding Lucretius's philosophical project.

**Richard Sorabji** (b. 1934)
British philosopher and historian of ancient philosophy. His book *Time, Creation and the Continuum* (1983) is one of the most thorough studies of ancient and medieval theories of time, covering Aristotle, the Stoics, Plotinus, Augustine, and their medieval successors. Sorabji's patient reconstruction of arguments from fragmentary sources is an exemplary model of historical philosophy.

**Thomas Nagel** (b. 1937)
American philosopher at New York University, known for contributions to philosophy of mind, ethics, and political philosophy. His essay "Death" (in *Mortal Questions*, 1979) is the most influential modern response to the Epicurean and Lucretian view that death is not bad for the person who dies. Nagel argues that death is bad as a deprivation and challenges the Lucretian symmetry argument by pointing to an asymmetry between pre-natal and post-mortem non-existence.

**James Warren**
British philosopher and classicist at Cambridge University, author of *Facing Death: Epicurus and His Critics* (2004), the most careful recent analysis of Epicurean arguments about death, including Lucretius's symmetry argument. Warren carefully distinguishes the philosophical logic of the Lucretian argument from the historical and philological questions about what Lucretius intended, and he defends the argument more fully than most contemporary philosophers are willing to do.

**Jeff McMahan** (b. 1954)
American philosopher at Oxford University, known for his work in ethics, political philosophy, and the ethics of killing. His *The Ethics of Killing: Problems at the Margins of Life* (2002) contains an extensive analysis of the nature and degree of death's badness, including a careful discussion of the Lucretian symmetry argument and the grounds for temporal asymmetry in our attitudes toward past and future goods.

## Chapter 7: Plotinus

---

### Chapter Introduction

Plotinus (204–270 CE) is one of those philosophers who is enormously influential and remarkably underread. His influence on Augustine, on medieval Islamic, Jewish, and Christian philosophy, and on subsequent mystical and idealist traditions in Western thought is incalculable. Yet he is rarely taught in introductory philosophy courses — partly because his system is demanding, partly because it resists easy summary, and partly because modern philosophy has largely moved in directions that make his concerns seem remote. This is unfortunate. Plotinus is one of the most original and subtle philosophers of time who ever wrote, and his account anticipates features of phenomenological and idealist accounts of time that would not be fully developed for another seventeen centuries.

Plotinus worked in the tradition he received from Plato and the Platonists, but he was not merely a commentator. The *Enneads* — the six groups of nine treatises that his student Porphyry compiled and edited — contain sustained, difficult, original philosophical work. The treatise *On Eternity and Time* (*Enneads* III.7) is widely regarded as one of the greatest philosophical treatments of time in the ancient world, and it repays close study.

The organizing structure of Plotinus's philosophy is the doctrine of the three *hypostases* — the three fundamental levels of reality: the One, Intellect (*Nous*), and Soul (*Psychê*). Understanding these three levels is the prerequisite for understanding his account of time, because time, for Plotinus, is not a feature of the physical world but a feature of Soul's activity. Time is not something the world has; it is something Soul does. This is a revolutionary claim, and it requires careful unpacking.

Chapter 7 proceeds as follows. Section 7.1 introduces the three hypostases and explains the ontological structure within which time is located. This includes the concept of *aion* (eternity) as the mode of being of Intellect — a mode that is atemporal and simultaneous rather than temporal and successive — and the contrast between the "complete, simultaneous life" of Intellect and the "stretched-out, discursive" life of Soul. Section 7.2 examines the central claim of *Enneads* III.7: that time is the life of the Soul in a movement of passage from one way of life to another. What does this mean? How does it generate the time that we experience? And does it make time subjective in a problematic way? Section 7.3 considers Plotinus's critique of his predecessors — particularly Aristotle — and assesses whether his critique is successful.

Two cautions for readers new to Plotinus. First, the *Enneads* are not easy reading. Plotinus writes in a way that is simultaneously abstract and intensely personal — the prose has a quality of reaching toward something that resists full articulation. Second, Plotinus is not simply repeating Plato. While he draws heavily on Plato's *Timaeus* (which introduced the idea of time as the "moving image of eternity"), he transforms Plato's account in ways that Plato himself would not have recognized. The relationship between Plotinian eternity and Platonic eternity is important and philosophically interesting.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to explain the three Plotinian hypostases and their temporal characteristics; articulate Plotinus's account of time as the life of Soul; and assess whether time on Plotinus's view is objective, subjective, or something in between.

### Section 7.1: The Three Hypostases

---

#### Section Introduction

Every account of time is embedded in a broader metaphysical vision of what reality is and how it is structured. For Plotinus, the relevant metaphysical vision is a tiered ontology of three fundamental levels — the One, Intellect, and Soul — each of which "proceeds" from the level above it and each of which has a distinctive relationship to time.

The word "hypostasis" (*hypostasis*) means something like "underlying reality" or "what stands beneath" — a substrate of being. Plotinus uses it for each of the three fundamental levels of his ontology. What is important is that the three hypostases are not equal in reality or in dignity: they form a strict hierarchy, with the One at the apex as the source of all being, Intellect as its first emanation, and Soul as the emanation from Intellect. Each level proceeds from the one above it by a kind of overflow or emanation, not through deliberate creation but through a metaphysical necessity analogous to the way light proceeds from a luminous source.

This hierarchical structure is the key to understanding time: time belongs to the lowest of the three hypostases, Soul, and not to the two higher ones. Understanding why the One and Intellect are outside time — and precisely what "outside time" means in each case — requires understanding what they are. That is the work of Section 7.1.

#### 7.1.1 — The One, Intellect, and Soul: The Procession Structure

---

##### The One (*to Hen*)

At the apex of Plotinus's ontology sits the One — the absolutely simple, undifferentiated, self-sufficient source of all being. The One is not a being among beings; it is beyond being (*epekeina tes ousias*), beyond thought, beyond any determination whatsoever. If you predicate anything of the One — that it is good, that it exists, that it is one — you have already compromised its absolute simplicity, because predication involves a kind of duality (the thing said and the thing of which it is said). The One is strictly beyond all predication; what we say about it is said not to characterize it but to gesture toward it (Plotinus, *Enneads* V.3.13–14, trans. Armstrong 1984).

The One is beyond time in the most radical sense: time does not even arise as a question with respect to the One. The One does not persist through time, does not endure, is not "at" any moment. It simply is — absolutely and without temporal qualification. This is not eternity-as-endless-duration; it is being that is not even the right kind of thing to have a duration, endless or otherwise.

The metaphysical relationship between the One and everything else is one of *emanation* (*prohodos*): everything that is proceeds from the One as light proceeds from a luminous body, not by deliberate creation (which would require a prior intention and thus temporal priority) but through the sheer superabundance of the One's being. The One does not lose anything in this emanation; it remains what it is. But from it, Intellect proceeds.

##### Intellect (*Nous*)

Intellect is the first emanation from the One. It is also called Nous, Mind, or Pure Intelligence. Intellect is the level at which being and thought first coincide: Intellect is pure thinking thinking itself, where the thinker and the thought are identical (Plotinus, *Enneads* V.1.4, trans. Armstrong 1984). It is the realm of the Platonic Forms — the eternal, perfect archetypes of which sensible things are imperfect copies — and it grasps all the Forms in a single, simultaneous act of thought.

This simultaneity is crucial for Plotinus's account of time. Intellect does not move from one Form to another sequentially, considering them one at a time. It contemplates all the Forms at once, in a single atemporal act of comprehension. Its "life" (if we can call it that) is complete and entire at every "moment" — though "moment" is the wrong word, because Intellect is not in time. This mode of being is what Plotinus means by *aion* — eternity. We will examine the concept of *aion* in more detail in Section 7.1.2.

The important point for now is that Intellect is outside time not merely in the sense that it lasts forever but in the more radical sense that the categories of before and after, earlier and later, do not apply to it at all. It is atemporal through and through. As Plotinus writes: "Eternity [*aion*] belongs to the things around Intellect and has its being there" (*Enneads* III.7.3, trans. Armstrong 1967).

##### Soul (*Psychê*)

Soul is the second emanation — it proceeds from Intellect as Intellect proceeded from the One. Soul has a complex status in Plotinus's system. On the one hand, Soul is ontologically dependent on Intellect and the One; it is "lower" in the hierarchy. On the other hand, Soul is the principle that generates the physical world and animates it; it is, in a sense, the creative force responsible for everything below Intellect.

Most importantly for the philosophy of time: Soul is where time originates. Unlike Intellect, which grasps everything simultaneously, Soul cannot hold all its knowledge and activity in a single act. It must move through its knowledge discursively, considering one thing after another, passing from one state to another. This sequential, discursive character of Soul's activity is the source of time (Plotinus, *Enneads* III.7.11, trans. Armstrong 1967).

Soul is also the principle of life in the physical cosmos. The physical world is ordered and animated by Soul, which is why the cosmos is not dead matter but a living, rational whole. The temporal succession that characterizes the physical world is an expression of Soul's own temporal character — the physical world is temporal because Soul, which animates it, is temporal.

##### The Procession Structure and Time

The structure of procession — from One to Intellect to Soul to the physical world — is thus also a structure of increasing temporality. The One is beyond time; Intellect is outside time but within eternity; Soul is within time as the generator of time; the physical world is within time as Soul's temporal expression.

This is a profoundly original metaphysical picture. Time, for Plotinus, does not come "from outside" to attach itself to a pre-existing world. It is generated from within — from the nature of Soul itself. Understanding why Soul generates time requires understanding what Soul is trying to do, and why it cannot do it all at once. That is the subject of Section 7.2.

It is worth noting a contrast with Plato here. In the *Timaeus*, Plato says that the Demiurge created time as "a moving image of eternity" — time was made by an external divine craftsman to be an imperfect copy of eternal being (Plato, *Timaeus* 37d5–7, trans. Zeyl 2000). For Plotinus, time is not an artifact made by a demiurgic mind; it is the natural expression of Soul's own activity. This is a genuine departure from Plato, not merely a commentary on him (Armstrong 1967: 301–302).

#### 7.1.2 — Eternity (*Aion*) and the Life of Intellect

---

##### What Eternity Is Not

Before we can say what Plotinian eternity (*aion*) is, it helps to say what it is not. Two misunderstandings are common.

The first misunderstanding is to think that eternity is just time stretched to infinity — a temporal duration without beginning or end. This conception of eternity, sometimes called "sempiternity," describes something that has always existed and will always exist — something that endures through time but does so without limit. A God who has existed since before the Big Bang and will exist after the heat death of the universe would be sempiternal, not eternal in Plotinus's sense. Sempiternity is a property of things that are *in* time; it just says something about how long they are in it.

The second misunderstanding is to think that eternity is a frozen instant — a single timeless "now" that is somehow outside the flow of time but is nevertheless a kind of temporal position. This is closer to the truth but still not quite right.

Plotinus's eternity is neither of these. It is the mode of being of a life that is *complete, all at once, and without succession* — a life whose entire reality is present simultaneously, without any part of it being "not yet" or "no longer." This life is Intellect's life.

##### The Definition of Eternity in *Enneads* III.7

The key text is *Enneads* III.7.3, where Plotinus defines eternity (*aion*) as "the life which belongs to that which exists and is in being, all together and full, completely without extension or interval" (Plotinus, *Enneads* III.7.3.7–8, trans. Armstrong 1967). He continues: eternity is "what was and is and will be — not what 'was' and 'will be' as if these referred to different things — but what always is, all together, without any division" (*Enneads* III.7.3.16–18, trans. Armstrong 1967).

Several features of this definition deserve attention.

**"Life"**: Eternity is not a static, dead timelessness. It is a *life* — a complete, active, self-aware existence. The analogy might be to the experience of understanding something with perfect clarity, all at once: not working through it step by step but grasping the whole simultaneously. Intellect's life is like that, except that what is grasped simultaneously is not a theorem but the entire intelligible universe.

**"All together"** (*homou*): The characteristic mark of eternity for Plotinus is simultaneity. Everything that Intellect is and knows is present to it all at once. There is no "first I think of the Form of Beauty, then I think of the Form of Justice" — Intellect comprehends all Forms in a single, undivided act.

**"Without extension or interval"**: Eternity has no temporal parts. It is not a long time; it is no time at all. The spatial metaphor of interval (*diastema*) is precisely what is absent in eternity, even though interval is exactly what characterizes time.

##### Contrast with Platonic Eternity

Plato introduced the concept of eternal Forms in the *Phaedo*, *Republic*, and *Timaeus*, and he used the language of eternity (*aei*) to characterize them. For Plato, the Forms are eternal in the sense that they do not change — they are always what they are, without beginning or end. But Plato does not develop a sophisticated concept of eternity as a mode of being in the way Plotinus does.

Plotinus's *aion* is a significant elaboration of the Platonic idea. What Plotinus adds is the emphasis on *simultaneous completeness*: not just that the Forms persist without change, but that they are grasped by Intellect in a single undivided act that has no temporal parts. Eternity is not just unchangingness; it is the positive character of a life that is complete without succession.

This concept of eternity becomes enormously influential. Boethius (Chapter 9) will adapt it to characterize God's eternal mode of being: "the complete, simultaneous, and perfect possession of unlimited life" (*Consolation of Philosophy* V, prose 6) — a formulation that is almost certainly indebted to Plotinus. Augustine (Chapter 8), though he does not follow Plotinus directly, arrives at a structurally similar notion of the divine *nunc stans* — the eternal standing now — that echoes Plotinian eternity.

##### The Priority of Eternity over Time

For Plotinus, eternity is not derived from time; time is derived from eternity — or rather, time arises when the completeness and simultaneity of eternity are "stretched out" into succession. Time is what eternity looks like when it is encountered by a nature (Soul) that cannot hold it all at once.

This priority of eternity over time is metaphysical, not merely temporal. Eternity is not "earlier" than time (that would be a temporal relationship); it is the ontological model of which time is an imperfect realization. Time is the moving image of eternity — Plotinus endorses Plato's phrase (*Timaeus* 37d) but interprets it more deeply: the "movement" is not physical motion but the movement of Soul's discursive activity, and the "image" is a genuine ontological image, not merely a resemblance.

##### Why This Matters for Philosophy of Time

Plotinus's account of eternity is important for the philosophy of time for two reasons.

First, it provides a genuine alternative to the view that time is simply the most fundamental feature of reality. If time is derived from something deeper — from the nature of Soul's activity, which is in turn a realization of Intellect's eternal life — then time is not ontologically basic. This is a significant departure from any view that treats time as an irreducible feature of the universe.

Second, it raises the question of what it would mean to "get outside" time — to experience time from the perspective of eternity. For Plotinus, this is not merely an abstract possibility; it is the highest form of human activity. In moments of genuine philosophical or mystical insight, the soul may briefly share the atemporality of Intellect, grasping something entire and complete rather than moving through it sequentially. Whether this is psychologically possible — and what it would feel like — are questions that Plotinus takes seriously, and that later thinkers from Augustine to Boethius to the medieval mystics will pursue.

### Section 7.2: Time as the Life of Soul

---

#### Section Introduction

We have seen that for Plotinus, eternity is the mode of being of Intellect: complete, simultaneous, without succession. Time, by contrast, is the mode of being of Soul. But this is a strange claim. We are accustomed to thinking of time as a feature of the physical world — something measured by clocks, something that flows regardless of whether any mind is attending to it. Plotinus is saying that time is, in some sense, a product of Soul's activity — that Soul generates time rather than merely being in it.

This claim requires very careful handling. It does not mean that time is merely subjective — a hallucination or a convenient fiction. It means that time has the kind of reality that belongs to Soul's activity: genuine, structured, ordered, but dependent on Soul in the way that a performance depends on a performer. The physical world is temporal because Soul animates it, and Soul's temporal character derives from its own nature as a discursive, sequential mode of intellection.

Section 7.2.1 examines the central passage in *Enneads* III.7 where Plotinus articulates this view. Section 7.2.2 explores its implications, including the comparison with Augustine's later *distentio animi* and the question of whether Plotinus's account makes time subjective in a troubling sense.

#### 7.2.1 — Time Generated by Soul: *Enneads* III.7

---

##### The Central Passage

The most important passage in Plotinus's philosophy of time is *Enneads* III.7.11, where he offers his own positive account of what time is, after critiquing the alternatives. The key sentence is: "Time is the life of the Soul in a movement of passage from one way of life to another" (*Enneads* III.7.11.43–45, trans. Armstrong 1967). This sentence is compressed but precise, and unpacking it takes us to the heart of Plotinus's view.

The sentence does not say that time is measured by Soul, or that Soul is aware of time, or that time depends on Soul for its measurement. It says that time *is* the life of Soul in its particular mode of activity — the mode of "passage from one way of life to another." Time is not a container in which Soul lives; it is the form of Soul's living. Soul does not move through time as a fish moves through water; Soul *is* temporal because its mode of being is essentially sequential and transitional.

##### Why Soul Generates Time

To understand why Plotinus thinks Soul generates time, we need to understand what Soul is trying to do and why it cannot do it all at once.

Soul proceeds from Intellect and in some sense aspires to be like Intellect — to grasp all things in a single, undivided act. But Soul cannot do this. Its mode of being is discursive (*dianoêtikos*): it must move from thought to thought, from one activity to another, building up its understanding sequentially. Where Intellect knows all Forms simultaneously and completely, Soul knows them one after another — or rather, it presents them to itself in a sequence that is the temporal unfolding of what Intellect grasps all at once.

Plotinus uses the image of a restless soul that cannot remain still: "Soul was not willing to remain with Intellect but wanted to possess all it had in itself in another manner" (*Enneads* III.7.11.16–18, trans. Armstrong 1967). This "wanting to possess in another manner" is the root of time. Soul, by its nature, generates a series — it cannot hold everything at once, so it unfolds everything in succession. That unfolding is time.

##### The Analogy of the Seed and the Tree

Plotinus offers an analogy that illuminates this account. Consider a seed: it contains, in some sense, the entire structure of the tree it will become — roots, trunk, branches, leaves, fruit. But this content is not all present simultaneously in the seed in the way it will be present in the mature tree. The seed "unfolds" what is implicit in it through a process of temporal development. 

Intellect is like the tree: its entire content is present simultaneously, completely actualized. Soul is like the seed in the process of growing: its content is genuine, but it can only be actualized sequentially, through a temporal process. Time is the "growing" by which Soul actualizes what it contains (*Enneads* III.7.11.1–15, trans. Armstrong 1967).

This analogy makes clear why Plotinus's account is neither a simple idealism (time as a product of individual human minds) nor a simple realism (time as an independently existing feature of the physical world). Time is a feature of Soul — the cosmic Soul, not any individual human mind — and the physical world is temporal because it is animated by this cosmic Soul. Individual human temporal experience is a participation in the cosmic Soul's temporal activity.

##### The Character of Soul's Temporal Life

What exactly is the "movement of passage from one way of life to another" that Plotinus identifies with time? Soul moves through its activities — its discursive thinking, its administration of the physical world, its care for individual souls — in a sequential manner. This sequencing is not arbitrary but ordered: each state of Soul follows from the previous state according to the rational principles (*logoi*) that govern Soul's activity. The sequence is thus the temporal "image" of the rational structure that Intellect grasps all at once.

This is an important feature of Plotinus's account. Time is not merely arbitrary succession; it is ordered succession, a rational sequence. The temporal order reflects the logical and ontological order that Intellect holds in its eternal grasp. Time is, in this sense, the temporal expression of the rational structure of being — it is what the logos looks like when it is encountered by a nature that must unfold it step by step.

##### The Cosmic Dimension

Plotinus is not describing the time of individual human consciousness, though individual temporal experience is a participation in what he describes. He is describing the temporal life of the cosmic Soul — the principle that animates and orders the entire physical universe. Time, for Plotinus, is cosmic before it is personal.

This is different from what some readers expect when they first encounter Plotinus's phrase "time is the life of Soul." They expect a theory of temporal consciousness — a phenomenology of how time is experienced by individual minds. And Plotinus's account does have implications for individual temporal experience; but it is primarily a cosmological claim about the source and nature of time as a feature of the universe, not a phenomenological claim about how time appears to a particular subject.

Augustine will later do something closer to a pure phenomenology of time — attending to how individual consciousness structures temporal experience. Plotinus's account is both grander in scope (it covers the cosmic Soul, not just individual minds) and less phenomenologically fine-grained than Augustine's.

#### 7.2.2 — Implications: Subjectivity, Augustine, and the Difference from Aristotle

---

##### Is Plotinian Time Subjective?

The first question a philosophically alert reader will ask about Plotinus's account is: if time is "the life of Soul," does this make time merely subjective? Does Plotinus's position collapse into the view that time is a feature of minds — that the physical world, in itself, is not really temporal at all?

Plotinus does not think so, and his reasons are important. The Soul in question is not any individual human soul but the cosmic Soul — the principle that animates and orders the entire physical universe. The physical world is temporal not merely because you or I experience it temporally but because the cosmic Soul generates temporal succession in the very act of animating the world. Individual temporal experience is real, but it is a participation in a more fundamental temporal reality that belongs to the cosmos as a whole.

This means Plotinus's account is not a simple subjectivism. The temporal order of the physical world — the fact that causes precede effects, that the sun rises and sets in a regular sequence, that organisms go through stages of development — is a genuine feature of the world, not merely a feature of how we represent it. It is a feature of the world, however, because the world is animated by a Soul whose nature is essentially temporal (Emilsson 2017: 125–127).

There is a genuine tension here, though. If we were to abstract away from Soul entirely — if we imagined the physical world without any animating soul — would there be any time left? On Plotinus's account, presumably not. The atoms of Democritus and Epicurus, if they fell through void with no soul animating them, would produce a world with no genuine temporal order. Time requires Soul. This is a substantial dependence of time on mind, even if it is not a simple subjectivism.

##### The Relationship to Augustine's *Distentio Animi*

Augustine's account of time in *Confessions* XI (Chapter 8) is the most famous inner-directed account of time in Western philosophy. Augustine argues that time is a "distension of the soul" (*distentio animi*) — the soul's stretching between memory and expectation, with the present as the moment of attention connecting them. This is a thoroughly psychological account: time is located in the soul's structure, not in the world.

Plotinus and Augustine are connected but not identical. Their similarities are real: both locate the source or nature of time in soul or mind rather than in the external world; both see temporal succession as a consequence of the sequential, discursive character of mental activity; both contrast temporal succession with the eternal simultaneity of a higher mode of being.

The differences are equally significant. Plotinus is talking about the *cosmic* Soul; Augustine is talking about the *individual human* soul. Plotinus's account is primarily ontological (what is time?); Augustine's is primarily phenomenological (how do we experience time? what do we measure when we measure time?). Plotinus sees the temporal character of Soul as a metaphysical necessity that follows from Soul's place in the hierarchy of being; Augustine sees the temporal structure of the soul as a feature of *creaturely* existence — time is the mode of being of creatures, as opposed to the eternal mode of being of the Creator.

Despite these differences, Augustine's account is intelligible as a further development and internalization of themes already present in Plotinus. Plotinus says time is the life of Soul; Augustine goes further and asks what the structure of *individual* temporal experience is, and how that structure relates to measurement and language. Plotinus gives the cosmological picture; Augustine provides the phenomenological close-up.

##### How Plotinus Differs from Aristotle

The surface similarities between Plotinus and Aristotle are misleading. Both thinkers connect time to motion and to soul. But they mean very different things by these connections.

For Aristotle, time is "the number of motion with respect to before and after." Aristotle's soul enters the picture because *counting* — the activity that reveals time — requires a soul to do the counting. But the motion that is counted is real and objective: celestial motion, the rotation of the heavens, the physical processes of the world. Time is, for Aristotle, primarily a feature of the physical world that the soul then measures.

For Plotinus, this gets things exactly backwards. Time is not a feature of the physical world that Soul measures; time is a feature of Soul that is expressed in the physical world. Soul does not number the world's motion; Soul generates the temporal succession that the world exhibits. Time flows from Soul downward into the physical world, not from the physical world upward into Soul's awareness.

Plotinus makes this inversion explicit in *Enneads* III.7.9, where he argues that Aristotle's definition puts the cart before the horse: you cannot understand what time is by starting from physical motion, because the temporal character of physical motion is itself dependent on Soul. To define time through motion is to explain the explanandum by the phenomenon that itself needs explaining (Sorabji 1983: 98–100).

Whether Plotinus's inversion is correct is a deep question. One way to assess it: consider a physical universe without any animating soul. Would it have temporal succession? Common sense says yes — the stars would still rise and set, causes would still precede effects. Plotinus says no — in the absence of Soul, there would be no genuine temporal order, only the appearance of such order from the perspective of a soul that projects it. This is a strong metaphysical claim, and it is not obviously right. But it is not obviously wrong either, and the question it raises — whether temporal order is genuinely objective or depends on minds — is one of the deepest in the philosophy of time.

### Section 7.3: Plotinus's Critique of Earlier Accounts

---

#### Section Introduction

Plotinus's positive account of time as the life of Soul emerges from a sustained critique of his predecessors. *Enneads* III.7 begins not with Plotinus's own position but with a survey and criticism of earlier views: those who identified time with motion, with the measure of motion, with the sphere of heaven, and — most importantly — those in the Aristotelian tradition who defined time as the number of motion. Plotinus's critique of Aristotle is philosophically important in its own right and illuminates his own positive view.

The central critique is that defining time through motion puts the explanatory relationship backwards. Motion is temporal; but that means motion's temporal character is what needs explaining, not what does the explaining. Any definition of time in terms of motion takes for granted what it should be explaining: namely, what makes motion temporal in the first place. For Plotinus, the answer is that motion is temporal because it is an expression of Soul's activity, and Soul's activity is temporal because of Soul's nature. You cannot explain time by appealing to motion; you must explain time's presence in motion by appealing to what underlies motion — and that is Soul.

#### 7.3.1 — Against Aristotle: The Critique of *Enneads* III.7.9

---

##### Aristotle's Position Revisited

To understand Plotinus's critique of Aristotle, we need to be clear about what Aristotle actually said. Aristotle's definition of time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after" (*Physics* IV.11, 219b1–2) involves two components: the *numerical* character of time and its connection to *motion*.

On the numerical side: Aristotle says that time is what we count when we count the before-and-after of motion. If you count the number of complete rotations of the heavens, you are counting time. Time is not the same as the motion — the celestial sphere moves spatially, while time is a quantity. Time is the number — the measure — that we impose on motion by counting it.

On the motion side: time, for Aristotle, is specifically connected to motion. Rest has no time of its own; a body at rest is still located in time, but its location in time is defined by the motion of other things (including the heavens). Motion is the "substrate" of time — the material in which time exists, as it were.

Aristotle also makes the famous comment that "if there were no soul, there would be no time" (*Physics* IV.14, 223a25–28, trans. Hussey 1983). This is because time requires counting, and counting requires a soul. This comment opens the door to a mind-dependent account of time, though Aristotle did not develop it in that direction.

##### Plotinus's Critique: Motion Cannot Number Itself

The central argument in *Enneads* III.7.9 runs as follows. Suppose we define time as the measure of motion (following Aristotle). What does the measuring? Not the motion itself — motion is what is measured, not the measurer. It must be something external to the motion. But what is that external thing?

If it is another motion, then we have a regress: what measures the second motion? Another motion? And what measures that? This regress cannot be stopped by positing an infinite series of measuring motions; that just pushes the problem back without solving it. We need something that can measure motion without itself being measured by another motion — something that is the standard rather than the thing to be measured.

Plotinus's answer is Soul. Soul provides the standard against which motion is measured. But if Soul provides the standard, then the real ground of time is not motion but Soul. Motion is what is measured; Soul is what measures; and time is the measure itself — which is a feature of Soul's activity, not of motion.

Plotinus makes this argument at *Enneads* III.7.9.69–79: "If time is the measure of movement, how is it a measure? One can say 'this much movement corresponds to this length of time,' but what is 'this length of time'? It is nothing other than the Soul's extension of itself... the motion is measured by the Soul, which has time as its own extension, and time is not the number of motion but the form by which Soul extends itself" (trans. Armstrong 1967, paraphrased).

##### The Regress Problem

The regress argument is important, and it is worth spelling out more carefully. The problem is not just that motion is measured by Soul but that any definition of time in terms of motion seems to generate a regress.

Suppose time = the measure of motion. What is the measure? Call it M. What is M? If M is itself a motion or a temporal process, then M itself takes time, and we need M to be measured by some prior measure M'. But M' also takes time... and so on. There is no non-question-begging way to halt the regress within a purely motion-based account of time.

Plotinus's proposal is that the regress is stopped by Soul: Soul's activity is temporal in a way that does not require any further measurer, because time just *is* the form of Soul's activity. Soul does not measure time the way a ruler measures length; Soul generates time in the very act of its sequential activity. The measuring is not a further operation on something else; it is what Soul is and does.

Whether this response is fully satisfying is debatable. One might ask: if Soul's activity is temporal, what makes it temporal? Does that not require another level of explanation? Plotinus's answer would presumably be that Soul's temporality is primitive — it is not explained in terms of something else but is just the character of what Soul is. This is not evasion; it is the claim that Soul is the *explanatory terminus* for temporality. Time traces back to Soul, and Soul's temporal character is a brute feature of Soul's nature, not a further phenomenon requiring explanation.

##### The Soul Must Number, Not Motion

A closely related point: Aristotle's definition says time is the *number* of motion, where "number" implies an act of counting. Plotinus agrees that counting is involved, but draws the implication that Aristotle downplays: if time requires counting, and counting requires a soul, then time depends essentially on Soul. Not just for its measurement but for its existence.

This is a stronger claim than Aristotle intended. Aristotle meant to say that time would not exist "for us" without a counting soul — that time is what we count, and counting requires a soul. He seems to have thought that the before-and-after character of motion is mind-independent, even if time as an explicit count requires a counter. Plotinus argues that the before-and-after character itself is not mind-independent — it is a feature of motion *as experienced or generated by Soul*.

If Plotinus is right, then Aristotle's definition is confused: it appeals to counting but then tries to locate time in the world rather than in the counting subject. Aristotle noticed the mind-dependence implication ("if there were no soul, there would be no time") but did not follow it to its conclusion. Plotinus follows it to its conclusion and arrives at the view that time is genuinely a feature of Soul.

##### Lingering Difficulties

Plotinus's critique of Aristotle is powerful but not without difficulties of its own.

The most pressing is: if time is a feature of Soul, and Soul is a metaphysical principle that animates the cosmos, what is the relationship between cosmic time (Soul's time) and the time measured by physical processes (clocks, seasons, planetary motions)? Plotinus seems to think that physical temporal order is an expression of Soul's time — that the regularity of the heavens reflects the regularity of Soul's activity. But this relationship is not fully developed in *Enneads* III.7, and it raises questions about how we are to understand the physical processes that we actually use to measure time.

A second difficulty: if Soul's temporal activity is the ground of physical time, what happens when individual souls are out of sync with the cosmic Soul? If I am deeply absorbed in thought and lose track of time — or if my sense of duration is distorted by emotion — does this alter the temporal order of the cosmos? Plotinus's answer would presumably be no: individual soul's distortions do not affect the cosmic Soul's regular activity, which sets the objective temporal framework. But this response reveals that Plotinus's "time as the life of Soul" is really "time as the life of the *cosmic* Soul," not any individual mind. Individual temporal experience is participation, not generation.

### Chapter 7: Exercises

---

#### Comprehension and Analysis

**Exercise 7.1**
Explain the three Plotinian hypostases: the One, Intellect, and Soul. What is the relationship between them? How does each hypostasis relate to time and eternity?

**Exercise 7.2**
Plotinus defines eternity (*aion*) as the "complete, simultaneous, and full life" of Intellect. Explain what each part of this definition means. How does this differ from the concept of sempiternity (endless time)?

**Exercise 7.3**
Plotinus says that "time is the life of the Soul in a movement of passage from one way of life to another" (*Enneads* III.7.11). What does this mean? In what sense is time the "life" of Soul rather than a container in which Soul lives?

**Exercise 7.4**
Explain Plotinus's critique of Aristotle's definition of time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after." What is the regress problem that Plotinus identifies? Is this criticism successful?

**Exercise 7.5**
Compare Plotinus's account of time with the Stoic account (from Chapter 6). Identify at least three significant differences. Which account do you find more philosophically defensible, and why?

**Exercise 7.6**
Does Plotinus's account make time "merely subjective"? Is the cosmic Soul a sufficiently objective foundation for time's reality? Write a 400-word response defending or challenging the view that Plotinus's account avoids problematic subjectivism.

**Exercise 7.7**
How does Plato's account of time in the *Timaeus* (time as the "moving image of eternity") relate to Plotinus's account? In what ways does Plotinus transform the Platonic material rather than simply repeating it?

**Exercise 7.8**
Plotinus connects his account of time to a critique of motion-based accounts: motion cannot number itself; something outside motion must do the measuring. Formulate a response that an Aristotelian might give to this critique. Then evaluate whether Plotinus's position can accommodate this response.

---

#### Observational and Experimental Exercises

**Lab Exercise 7.A — The Simultaneous vs. Sequential Grasp**

Choose a piece of music you know well — something you can sing or recall mentally. Try two different ways of "having" the piece in mind. First, recall it sequentially: sing or hum through it from beginning to end, experiencing each section as it comes. Then try to hold the entire piece in mind *simultaneously* — not as a sequence but as a single unified whole. (You might try imagining seeing the musical score all at once, or thinking of the piece "as a whole" rather than "as a sequence.") Which is easier? What does the difference between these two modes of attention tell you about Plotinus's contrast between the sequential life of Soul and the simultaneous grasp of Intellect? Write a brief reflection.

**Lab Exercise 7.B — Absorption and Time-Loss**

Identify an activity that regularly causes you to "lose track of time" — deep reading, creative work, exercise, conversation. After your next such experience, note: how long did the absorbed state last? How different was your felt sense of duration from the clock time? Plotinus says that when the soul is most engaged with Intellect, it approaches atemporal existence. Does your experience of absorption provide any phenomenological support for the idea of degrees of temporal engagement? What are the limits of using such experiences as evidence for Plotinus's account?

**Lab Exercise 7.C — Drawing the Hierarchy**

Create a visual diagram of Plotinus's three hypostases, showing: (1) the relationship between them (procession from above, return from below); (2) the temporal characteristics of each level (beyond time / atemporal eternity / temporal succession); (3) where individual human experience fits in the diagram. Write a brief explanatory caption for each element of the diagram. Then discuss: does the diagram help or distort understanding of Plotinus's account?

---

#### Essay Questions

**Exercise 7.9 (Essay)**
Plotinus says that time is generated by Soul; Aristotle says that time is measured by soul. Are these two different positions or are they closer than they appear? Write an essay of 800–1000 words comparing the two accounts and assessing which is more defensible.

**Exercise 7.10 (Essay)**
Plotinus anticipates what later became the central question in the phenomenology of time: is time a feature of the world that consciousness measures, or a feature of consciousness that is projected onto the world? Write an essay of 1000 words tracing this question from Plotinus through Augustine (previewing Chapter 8 if you have read ahead) and assessing whether phenomenological or realist accounts of time are more plausible.

**Exercise 7.11 (Essay)**
Is the concept of a "timeless" entity coherent? Plotinus holds that the One and Intellect are outside time entirely. But contemporary philosophers often argue that the concept of a timeless entity faces serious problems (how can a timeless entity act in time? know temporal truths?). Write an essay of 800–1000 words assessing whether Plotinus's atemporal hypostases are philosophically defensible.
