#### Annotated Entries

**Mellor, D. H. 1998. *Real Time II*. London: Routledge.**
The definitive statement of a sophisticated, technically rigorous B-theory. Mellor distinguishes the meaning of tensed claims from their truth conditions, gives a careful token-reflexive analysis, and engages thoroughly with the best A-theoretic objections. Begin with Chapter 1 for the overview; work through Chapters 4–6 for the detailed analysis of tensed language.

**Sider, Theodore. 2001. *Four-Dimensionalism: An Ontology of Persistence and Time*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.**
The standard contemporary reference on worm theory and B-theoretic metaphysics. Chapters 3–5 develop worm theory and stage theory in detail. The book is technically demanding but written with exceptional clarity; the introductory and concluding chapters are accessible to readers without background in formal metaphysics.

**Smart, J. J. C. 1949. "The River of Time." *Mind* 58 (232): 483–494.**
The foundational statement of the mid-twentieth-century B-theory, accessible and engagingly written. Smart's argument against temporal passage has been discussed continuously since its publication. Essential reading for understanding the historical development of the debate.

**Williams, Donald C. 1951. "The Myth of Passage." *Journal of Philosophy* 48 (15): 457–472.**
A classic defense of the block universe that develops the "temporal-as-spatial" analogy with great rhetorical force. Williams argues that the idea of temporal passage is a confusion — a category error — and that the block universe is the only coherent picture of temporal reality. Essential alongside Smart as a statement of the classical B-theory position.

**Putnam, Hilary. 1967. "Time and Physical Geometry." *Journal of Philosophy* 64 (8): 240–247.**
The philosophical statement of what is now called the Rietdijk-Putnam argument. Short, clearly written, and philosophically important. Putnam's version of the argument is more focused on the metaphysics of existence than Rietdijk's, and his engagement with the A-theorist's possible responses is instructive.

**Maudlin, Tim. 2012. *Philosophy of Physics: Space and Time*. Princeton: Princeton University Press.**
An excellent introduction to the philosophy of spacetime physics, written by one of the most important philosophers of physics working today. Particularly valuable for connecting the block universe debate to the actual content of special and general relativity. Chapters 3 and 4 are directly relevant to this chapter's material.

**Lewis, David. 1986. *On the Plurality of Worlds*. Oxford: Blackwell. Chapter 4.**
Lewis's worm theory of temporal persistence is embedded within his broader modal realism, but Chapter 4's discussion of the distinction between spatial and temporal extent is accessible on its own. Lewis's prose is among the most enjoyable in analytic philosophy, and his argument is a model of clarity.

**Hawley, Katherine. 2001. *How Things Persist*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.**
A balanced and careful examination of the endurantism/perdurantism debate, with careful attention to stage theory as a distinct alternative. Hawley's approach is to take the ordinary cases seriously and ask which theory gives the best account of them. A good companion to Sider's more theoretical treatment.

**Craig, William Lane. 2000. *The Tensed Theory of Time: A Critical Examination*. Dordrecht: Kluwer.**
An extensive and passionate critique of B-theory from the perspective of a committed A-theorist. Craig's objections are forceful, though his own positive view is sometimes underargued. Reading this alongside Mellor gives an excellent sense of what is at stake in the debate.

**Dainton, Barry. 2000. *Stream of Consciousness: Unity and Continuity in Conscious Experience*. London: Routledge.**
A rich and carefully argued account of temporal consciousness that engages directly with the phenomenological objection to B-theory. Dainton defends a version of extensionalism about temporal experience — the view that the specious present is genuinely temporally extended — and his book is the best place to start on the empirical and philosophical psychology of temporal experience.

### Chapter 14 Important Concepts

---

**Block Universe**
The metaphysical thesis that all past, present, and future events exist with equal ontological status in a four-dimensional manifold. On this view, there is no "front edge" of reality advancing from past to future; the temporal dimension is fully extended and complete.

**Eternalism**
The view that objects and events at all times exist; past and future entities are as real as present ones. Eternalism is the ontological corollary of the block universe thesis. It contrasts with presentism (only present things exist) and the growing block view (only past and present things exist).

**Tenseless Statement**
A statement whose truth value does not vary with the time of its utterance — for example, "Event A is earlier than Event B." Tenseless statements express B-series facts and are permanent: they are true, or false, at every time.

**Indexical Expression**
An expression whose reference depends on the context of utterance. "I" refers to whoever is speaking; "here" refers to where the speaker is; "now" — on the B-theory — refers to when the speaker is. Indexicals do not pick out metaphysically special objects; they pick out contextually specified objects.

**Token-Reflexive Analysis**
A B-theoretic strategy for giving truth conditions of tensed statements in terms of relations between events and the token utterance (or the time of the utterance). "It is raining now" (uttered at t) = "It is raining at t." The analysis eliminates reference to objective A-properties.

**Perdurantism (Worm Theory)**
The view that objects persist through time by having temporal parts at each moment of their existence, just as they have spatial parts at each region of their spatial extent. A person is a four-dimensional temporal worm; the person "now" is a temporal stage of that worm.

**Temporal Stage**
An instantaneous or brief time-slice of a four-dimensional temporal worm. On perdurantism, temporal stages are the fundamental bearers of temporal properties; on stage theory, they are what we refer to when we use ordinary object terms.

**Stage Theory**
A variant of four-dimensionalism holding that ordinary objects are instantaneous temporal stages, and persistence is constituted by temporal counterpart relations among stages rather than by a four-dimensional worm of which stages are parts. Associated with Sider and Hawley.

**Temporal Counterpart Relation**
On stage theory, the relation that holds between temporal stages in virtue of which they are "the same object" at different times. Modeled on Lewis's modal counterpart relation; grounded in physical continuity, psychological continuity, and causal ancestry.

**Problem of Temporary Intrinsics**
The problem that one and the same object seems to instantiate incompatible properties at different times (a leaf is both green and yellow). Worm theory resolves it by attributing the incompatible properties to different temporal stages rather than to the numerically identical object simpliciter.

**Rietdijk-Putnam Argument**
An argument from the relativity of simultaneity in special relativity to the conclusion that all events — past, present, and future — are equally real. If there is no privileged present, then events cannot "become" real at a particular time; hence all events exist timelessly.

**Relativity of Simultaneity**
In special relativity, the fact that events simultaneous in one inertial reference frame are not simultaneous in all inertial reference frames. This follows from the constancy of the speed of light and is central to the argument against objective presentness.

**Truthmaker Principle**
The principle that for every true proposition, there exists something in reality that makes it true. The truthmaker argument for eternalism holds that truths about past events require truthmakers, and the most natural candidates are the past events themselves — which must therefore still exist.

**Passage Problem**
The objection to B-theory that it cannot account for the passage of time, because the block universe is a static four-dimensional structure and nothing "moves" through it. The B-theorist's response is either to deny that genuine passage exists or to explain it in terms of the B-series structure.

**Four-Dimensionalism**
The metaphysical view that objects have both spatial and temporal parts, and that the correct way to understand persistence is in terms of temporal extension rather than strict identity across time. Four-dimensionalism is the natural ontological complement to the block universe view.

### Chapter 14 Important Researchers

---

**J. J. C. Smart (1920–2012)**
Jack Smart was an Australian philosopher at the Australian National University who was one of the earliest and most influential defenders of the B-theory of time in the analytic tradition. His 1949 paper "The River of Time" argued that the passage of time is a metaphysical illusion and that all temporal facts are B-series facts. Smart was also a prominent defender of physicalism in the philosophy of mind and of utilitarianism in ethics, and his work consistently exemplifies the virtues of analytic clarity and theoretical parsimony.

**D. H. Mellor (1938–2020)**
Hugh Mellor was a British philosopher at Cambridge whose *Real Time* (1981) and *Real Time II* (1998) are the most sustained and technically rigorous defenses of B-theory in the philosophical literature. Mellor developed the token-reflexive analysis of tensed language in careful detail, argued that the existence of causation is compatible with a B-series ontology, and engaged with A-theoretic positions from a position of genuine respect for their motivations. His work is a model of how to argue for a controversial metaphysical position with rigor and fairness.

**Ted Sider (born 1966)**
Ted Sider is an American metaphysician whose *Four-Dimensionalism* (2001) is the standard contemporary reference work for worm theory and B-theoretic metaphysics. Sider argues comprehensively for perdurantism over endurantism (the view that objects persist by being wholly present at each time), defends the block universe against A-theoretic objections, and connects the debate about persistence to broader questions in ontology. His later *Writing the Book of the World* (2011) develops a metaontological framework in which B-series relations are among the most natural and fundamental features of reality.

**David Lewis (1941–2001)**
David Lewis was arguably the most influential analytic metaphysician of the twentieth century. His worm theory of persistence, developed in *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986), is one of the most elegant and comprehensive developments of the four-dimensionalist picture. Lewis also made foundational contributions to the analysis of counterfactual conditionals, possible worlds semantics, and the philosophy of mind. His work on the asymmetry of time and the "past hypothesis" is discussed in Chapter 18.

**Katherine Hawley (born 1970)**
Katherine Hawley is a Scottish philosopher whose *How Things Persist* (2001) is one of the most careful and balanced examinations of the persistence debate. Hawley defends a version of stage theory while engaging seriously with the alternative positions, and her work is distinguished by its attention to what the various theories actually predict about ordinary cases. She is also known for work on knowledge and evidence, and her philosophical writing exemplifies clarity and precision.

**Hilary Putnam (1926–2016)**
Hilary Putnam was one of the most versatile and influential philosophers of the twentieth century, making major contributions to philosophy of language, philosophy of mind, mathematics, and metaphysics. His 1967 paper "Time and Physical Geometry" argued for the block universe on the basis of the special theory of relativity, developing what is now called the Rietdijk-Putnam argument. Putnam's later career involved a significant revision of many of his earlier positions, but his work on time and relativity remains highly influential in the philosophy of physics.

**C. W. A. Rietdijk (1932–2009)**
Cornelis Wietze Rietdijk was a Dutch physicist and philosopher who, independently of Putnam and in the same year, published the argument from special relativity to the reality of all times. His paper "A Rigorous Proof of Determinism Derived from the Special Theory of Relativity" (1966) argued that special relativity entails determinism and the equal reality of all events. Though less well known than Putnam, his formulation of the argument was clear and influential.

**Hans Reichenbach (1891–1953)**
Hans Reichenbach was a German-American philosopher of science who made foundational contributions to the philosophy of time, space, and probability. His token-reflexive analysis of tensed language in *Elements of Symbolic Logic* (1947) anticipated the full B-theoretic semantics developed by later philosophers. His work on the conventionality of simultaneity (discussed in Chapter 16) and on the direction of time (discussed in Chapter 18) established the terms of debate for subsequent generations. Reichenbach was a pioneer of logical empiricism and a rigorous analyst of the philosophical implications of modern physics.

## Chapter 15: A-Theory — Presentism, Growing Block, and the Moving Spotlight

---

### Chapter Introduction

If you find the block universe unsatisfying — if the thought that all times are equally real, that the present is merely a perspectival indexical, and that temporal flow is either illusory or redundant strikes you as missing something essential — you are in good philosophical company. A-theory is the name for a family of views that insist on the reality and metaphysical importance of the distinction between past, present, and future. For A-theorists, the present is not just one more position in a static four-dimensional manifold; it is the site of what is *actually happening*, the locus of genuine reality.

But A-theory is not a single view. It is a family of positions that differ in precisely what they say about the ontological status of the past and future, and in how they handle the difficulties that come with the territory. This chapter examines three major members of that family.

**Presentism** is the most radical: only present things exist. The past has ceased to exist; the future does not yet exist. Reality is constituted entirely by what is presently the case. This view has an immediate appeal — it matches the common intuition that the past is gone and the future has not arrived — but it faces serious difficulties, especially regarding the truthmakers for past-directed claims and the challenge from special relativity.

**The growing block view**, developed by C.D. Broad, holds a middle position: the past and present exist, but the future does not. The universe is literally growing as new events occur, with the present as the leading edge of an ever-accumulating reality. This view captures something of the presentist's intuition about the openness of the future while preserving the existence of the past.

**The moving spotlight theory** accepts the full four-dimensional block of events (like the B-theory) but adds to it an objectively moving present — a "spotlight" that singles out one time as genuinely present, a spotlight that advances through the manifold. This view preserves the objective reality of A-series properties while acknowledging the block structure that physics seems to support.

Each view faces distinctive difficulties, and this chapter examines those difficulties honestly. The goal is not to tell you which A-theory is correct — that remains contested — but to give you the tools to evaluate them yourself.

---

*Chapter 15 comprises Sections 15.1 through 15.4.*

### Section 15.1: Presentism

---

#### Section Introduction

Presentism is, in one sense, the most natural view of time. Ask anyone on the street whether the past still exists, and most people will say no — it's gone. Ask whether the future exists yet, and most will say no — it hasn't happened. Only the present is real. Presentism elevates this common intuition into a metaphysical thesis and defends it rigorously.

This section develops presentism through three subsections. We begin with the thesis itself and the arguments in its favor. We then examine the truthmaker problem — the challenge of grounding past-directed truths when the past no longer exists. Finally, we confront the challenge from special relativity, which many philosophers regard as the most serious obstacle to any presentist view.

---

*Section 15.1 comprises subsections 15.1.1, 15.1.2, and 15.1.3.*

#### 15.1.1 — Presentism: The Thesis and Its Motivations

---

Presentism is defined by a single, stark claim: only present things exist. The past has ceased to exist — not merely ceased to be present, but ceased to exist altogether. The future does not yet exist — not merely the future is not present, but the future is literally nothing. Reality is exhausted by what is happening now.

##### Formulating the View

A precise formulation is important, because presentism is easily confused with weaker claims. It is not the view that the present is the most important or salient time — that is a claim about value, not ontology. It is not the view that we have more knowledge of the present than of the past or future — that is a claim about epistemology. It is the claim that only present *entities* — present events, present objects, present states of affairs — genuinely *exist*. The unrestricted existential quantifier, in a correct ontology, ranges only over present things.

Dean Zimmerman gives a clean formulation: presentism is the view that "everything is present" — or equivalently, that there are no non-present things (Zimmerman 2008: 211). Compare this with eternalism (everything — past, present, and future — exists) and with the growing block view (past and present things exist, future things do not).

##### Arguments for Presentism

Several considerations motivate presentism.

**The commonsense argument.** Presentism is what the pre-theoretic conception of time actually says. When we talk about "what exists," we mean what exists *now*, not what existed in the past or will exist in the future. If someone asks "does the dodo exist?," the correct answer is "no" — even though dodos once existed. The dodo no longer exists because it is no longer present. Presentism simply takes this commonsense view seriously (Markosian 2004: 48–49).

**The flow of time argument.** If time genuinely flows — if the present is the dynamic site of what is actually happening — then it is natural to think that only present things are real in the fullest sense. The past is what *has* happened: it is over, no longer happening, no longer real. The future is what *will* happen: it has not yet arrived, is not yet real. Presentism captures the intuitive sense in which the present is uniquely actual.

**The causal relevance argument.** What causes what happens now? Causal influence flows from the present and the past into the present. The future does not cause anything that is happening now; the future has no causal power over present events. This causal asymmetry suggests a corresponding ontological asymmetry: the causally efficacious is real; what has no causal power has at best a secondary or derived existence. But the future has no causal power over the present. Hence the future does not exist.

**The epistemological argument.** We have direct access — through perception — to what is present. We have indirect, inferential access to what is past (through memory, records, traces). We have only predictive, uncertain access to what is future. This epistemological asymmetry tracks an ontological asymmetry: what we are directly acquainted with is real; what we must infer from traces is gone.

None of these arguments is decisive on its own, and each has been challenged. But together they constitute a genuinely attractive case for taking presentism seriously.

##### The Presentist's Distinctive Picture

The presentist picture is dramatically different from the block universe. Think of reality as a spotlight that illuminates a single time — the present — against a background of complete darkness. The past is not "in storage" somewhere; it does not exist. The future is not "waiting in the wings"; it does not exist. There is only what is present.

This means that presentism is committed to a dynamic, non-static conception of reality. Reality is not the complete four-dimensional manifold; it is the momentary cross-section that constitutes the present. As time passes, this cross-section is replaced by another — not added to, not revealing what was already there, but genuinely new. The universe grows, event by event, not in the sense of accumulating into an ever-larger block, but in the sense of constituting itself moment by moment.

There is something deeply appealing about this picture. It captures the sense that what is *happening* — what is *going on right now* — is real in a way that what has happened and what will happen are not. It preserves what may be the deepest A-series intuition: that reality has a present, and the present is where life is being lived.

---

###### References

- Markosian, Ned. 2004. "A Defense of Presentism." In *Oxford Studies in Metaphysics*, vol. 1, edited by Dean Zimmerman, 47–82. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
- Zimmerman, Dean. 2008. "The Privileged Present: Defending an 'A-theory' of Time." In *Contemporary Debates in Metaphysics*, edited by Theodore Sider, John Hawthorne, and Dean Zimmerman, 211–225. Oxford: Blackwell.

#### 15.1.2 — The Truthmaker Problem for Presentism

---

The most persistent difficulty for presentism is the truthmaker problem. True statements about the past seem to require truthmakers — something in reality that makes them true. But if the past no longer exists, there is nothing left to be the truthmaker. The presentist faces the challenge of explaining how past-directed truths are grounded without appealing to past entities.

##### The Problem Stated

Consider the proposition: "The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event occurred approximately 66 million years ago."

This proposition is true. It is true now, and it was true before anyone thought about it, and it will be true long after anyone cares. What makes it true? What is its truthmaker?

The natural answer: the extinction event itself. The event occurred; its having occurred makes propositions about it true. But the presentist says the event no longer exists. It is not a past entity lurking in some temporal attic; it has simply ceased to be. If it no longer exists, how can it make anything true now?

John Bigelow noted that this problem has deep roots: the challenge of grounding truths about the past without appeals to past entities was recognized, in different forms, by Lucretius and other ancient philosophers (Bigelow 1996: 35–36). In its modern form, it is one of the main objections to presentism.

##### Proposed Solutions

Presentists have offered several strategies for dealing with the truthmaker problem.

**Haecceitism / Ersatzism about the past.** One strategy posits *abstract representations* of past events — "ersatz" past events that exist in the present as abstract entities or as theoretical posits. The present reality includes not just concrete objects and events but also abstract representations of past states of affairs. The proposition "the extinction event occurred" is made true by a present abstract fact to the effect that a past extinction event is represented in the abstract record of reality.

This strategy faces the objection that it multiplies ontology uncomfortably (we now need abstract entities corresponding to every past event) and that it is unclear what grounds the abstract facts themselves.

**Lucretianism.** Another strategy holds that the universe contains certain features that depend on past events — dispositional properties, for instance, that encode a causal history. The present-day universe has properties that it would not have had if the extinction event had not occurred, and these properties serve as truthmakers. "The extinction event occurred" is made true by the present world's having these trace-properties.

This strategy faces the "Cambridge change" worry: the properties serving as truthmakers are relational, not intrinsic, and it seems odd to say that a proposition about a specific historical event is made true by the contemporary world's having certain dispositional or trace-properties. The truthmaker seems too weak or too remote from what the proposition is about.

**Presentist haecceities.** A third strategy, developed in various forms, posits *individual essences* or *haecceities* of past objects as abstract entities that persist into the present. The haecceity of Julius Caesar — the property of being-Caesar — exists now, even though Caesar does not. Propositions about Caesar are made true by this haecceity together with facts about what that haecceity was "like" in the past.

This is clever, but critics argue it amounts to a covert form of the growing block view: if haecceities of past objects persist into the present, then something associated with past objects exists now — and one might reasonably ask what distinguishes this from simply saying that past objects themselves exist in some (perhaps diminished) form.

**Primitivism.** Some presentists bite the bullet: they deny the truthmaker principle, at least in its unrestricted form. It is a primitive, ungrounded fact that certain propositions about the past are true. There is no deeper explanation — no truthmaker — for why "the extinction event occurred" is true. It just is. This is a philosophically uncomfortable response, but it is not obviously wrong; the truthmaker principle is a theoretical commitment, not a self-evident truth (Cameron 2008: 327–342).

##### Assessment

No response to the truthmaker problem fully satisfies. The haecceity strategy and the abstract-entity strategies multiply ontology without obvious benefit. The primitivism response gives up a plausible theoretical principle. The Lucretian strategy seems to misidentify the truthmaker.

The challenge is this: the more robust the past-directed truth — the more specific and concrete the claim about what happened — the less plausible it is that anything present can serve as its truthmaker. "There was a time when no humans existed" seems groundable in present evolutionary and geological facts. "Julius Caesar's last words were 'Tu quoque, Brute?'" seems not groundable in anything presently existing.

This is a serious difficulty for presentism, and it motivates both the growing block view (which preserves the existence of past events) and the block universe view (which preserves the existence of all events). Presentists are aware of the difficulty and continue to develop responses, but a fully satisfying resolution has not yet appeared.

---

###### References

- Bigelow, John. 1996. "Presentism and Properties." *Philosophical Perspectives* 10: 35–52.
- Cameron, Ross P. 2008. "How to Be a Presentist and Believe in the Past." *Philosophia* 36 (3): 327–342.
- Markosian, Ned. 2004. "A Defense of Presentism." In *Oxford Studies in Metaphysics*, vol. 1, edited by Dean Zimmerman, 47–82. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

#### 15.1.3 — The Challenge from Special Relativity

---

Beyond the truthmaker problem, presentism faces what many philosophers regard as the most serious challenge from contemporary physics: the challenge from special relativity. The challenge is not merely that special relativity makes things complicated; it is that, on a standard reading, special relativity is *inconsistent* with presentism — at least in its naive form.

##### The Problem: No Global Present

Presentism requires a global, objective present: a three-dimensional "slice" of the universe that constitutes the present moment, with the past below it and the future above it. This is the ordinary picture of presentism.

But special relativity, as we saw in Chapter 14.2.1, denies that there is an observer-independent, privileged simultaneity relation. In Minkowski spacetime — the spacetime of special relativity — there is no global, frame-independent "now." For any pair of spacelike-separated events (events that could not be connected by a light signal), there exist reference frames in which the events are simultaneous, frames in which one is earlier, and frames in which the other is earlier. None of these frames is privileged.

If presentism requires that there be a determinate global present — a fact about what is simultaneous with what that holds independently of any reference frame — and if special relativity says there is no such fact, then presentism is incompatible with special relativity. That is a significant problem.

Hilary Putnam made this point forcefully: "I shall argue that the problem of the reality of the future and the problem of the status of 'future' have been in principle solved by the Special Theory of Relativity" (Putnam 1967: 240). His conclusion was that special relativity establishes eternalism.

##### The Neo-Lorentzian Response

The most influential presentist response is the **neo-Lorentzian strategy**, associated with philosophers like Dean Zimmerman and physicists like John Bell. The strategy is to note that special relativity is *empirically* compatible with the existence of a privileged rest frame — a frame that corresponds to "absolute rest" — even though we cannot empirically detect which frame it is. The Lorentz ether theory is empirically equivalent to special relativity: it makes all the same experimental predictions, but it posits an underlying preferred frame that defines absolute simultaneity.

If the correct metaphysics is neo-Lorentzian, then there is an objective fact about what is simultaneous, even though our experiments cannot tell us which simultaneity relation is the correct one. The presentist's global present would correspond to the simultaneity relation of the privileged frame. The fact that we cannot identify which frame is privileged is an epistemological limitation, not an argument against the metaphysics.

Zimmerman argues that this is a coherent and defensible strategy: "The presentist should simply accept that the physics we have doesn't tell us which foliation of spacetime corresponds to objective simultaneity, while insisting that one of them does" (Zimmerman 2008: 213).

The objection to this strategy is that it seems ad hoc: we are positing a feature of reality (the privileged frame) specifically to save presentism, with no independent evidence for it. The neo-Lorentzian replies that this is the standard structure of underdetermination in science: empirical equivalence does not establish that the alternative is false, only that we cannot confirm it empirically. If independent metaphysical reasons support presentism — including the arguments of Section 15.1.1 — then the neo-Lorentzian strategy is not ad hoc but a principled reconciliation of metaphysics and physics.

##### The Relativized Presentism Response

A second response, more revisionary, is **relativized presentism**: the claim that what is present is relative to a reference frame, and there is no frame-independent present. This is a deflationary move: rather than defending an objective global present, the presentist accepts that "what is present" is always relative to some frame, just as B-theorists say "what is present" is relative to an observer.

The difficulty is that this response may give away too much. If what exists is relative to a frame, then the ontological distinction between existence and non-existence is also relative to a frame. And if existence is relative to a frame, it is unclear in what sense the view is still presentist — rather than a version of the eternalism it was meant to oppose.

##### Sklar's Strategy

Lawrence Sklar has argued that the challenge from special relativity is less decisive than it appears, because the metaphysics of time is not straightforwardly derivable from the kinematics of spacetime. The equations of special relativity describe the transformations between reference frames and the invariances of physical quantities; they do not, by themselves, entail an ontology. Whether one adopts a Minkowski or a Lorentzian interpretation of those equations is a further metaphysical choice (Sklar 1974: 267–271). The physics underdetermines the metaphysics, and there is space — though tight space — for the presentist to maneuver.

##### Assessment

The challenge from special relativity is genuine and serious. The neo-Lorentzian response is coherent but requires positing undetectable metaphysical structure. Relativized presentism threatens to collapse into a form of eternalism. Sklar's strategy buys breathing room but does not provide a positive account of the global present.

The state of the debate is this: presentism in its naive form is incompatible with special relativity. Sophisticated versions can be made compatible, at a metaphysical cost. Whether that cost is worth paying depends on how strongly one is committed to the presentist intuitions — and on how seriously one takes the physics.

---

###### References

- Putnam, Hilary. 1967. "Time and Physical Geometry." *Journal of Philosophy* 64 (8): 240–247.
- Sklar, Lawrence. 1974. *Space, Time, and Spacetime*. Berkeley: University of California Press.
- Zimmerman, Dean. 2008. "The Privileged Present: Defending an 'A-theory' of Time." In *Contemporary Debates in Metaphysics*, edited by Theodore Sider, John Hawthorne, and Dean Zimmerman, 211–225. Oxford: Blackwell.

### Section 15.2: The Growing Block Universe

---

#### Section Introduction

The growing block view occupies a distinctive middle position in the ontology of time. It shares with presentism the intuition that the future is not yet real — that there is something genuinely open about what has not yet happened. It shares with eternalism the recognition that the past, once real, does not simply vanish — that there is something wrong about saying that Caesar and the dinosaurs are just nothing.

The result is a view in which reality grows: what exists is the totality of past and present events, and this totality is always expanding as new events occur. The present is the leading edge of this ever-accumulating reality. What is future does not yet exist — but what is present and past exists permanently, preserved in the growing block.

This section examines Broad's original formulation and the most pressing epistemological objection to the view.

---

*Section 15.2 comprises subsections 15.2.1 and 15.2.2.*

#### 15.2.1 — The Growing Block: Broad's Formulation

---

C.D. Broad introduced the growing block view in *Scientific Thought* (1923), in the context of a general examination of the nature of time. His formulation is simple but pregnant with philosophical consequence: "Nothing has happened to the present by becoming past except that fresh slices of existence have been added to the total history of the world" (Broad 1923: 59).

##### The View Stated

On the growing block view, the ontological inventory of the universe at any given time includes:

- All *past* events (everything that has occurred up to and including the present)
- All *present* events (whatever is occurring now)
- No *future* events (whatever has not yet occurred does not exist)

The universe is, in this sense, a growing block: it has a fixed "bottom" (the earliest events, whatever they are) and a constantly advancing "top" (the present), and the block grows as new events occur. Past events do not cease to exist when they are superseded by newer events; they remain in the block, their positions simply receding from the leading edge.

##### Advantages over Presentism

The growing block view solves the truthmaker problem that bedevils presentism. Because past events genuinely exist — they are real parts of the block — they can serve as truthmakers for past-directed propositions. "The extinction event occurred 66 million years ago" is made true by the extinction event itself, which exists at its position in the growing block. The growing block theorist does not need to posit abstract representations, haecceities, or trace-properties; they can appeal directly to the events themselves.

The growing block also preserves one of the presentist's most important intuitions: the future is not yet real. This means that the universe has a genuinely open future — an ontological openness that the block universe denies. On the growing block view, there is no block corresponding to future events, because future events do not yet exist. What will happen is not yet settled in the sense of being already real.

##### The Phenomenological Appeal

There is something phenomenologically satisfying about the growing block view. It captures the way in which the past feels permanent and the future feels open. When you remember yesterday's events, they feel genuinely past — not just "earlier in the manifold" but *actually gone, not happening any more*. When you anticipate tomorrow, it feels genuinely open — not "later in the manifold, already there," but *genuinely undetermined, not yet real*.

The growing block formalizes these intuitions. The past has happened and is preserved in the block; it is real, fixed, and not subject to change. The future has not happened; it is not yet real, and therefore genuinely open. This seems to match the ordinary experience of time better than either presentism (which eliminates the past) or eternalism (which eliminates the ontological distinction between past, present, and future).

##### The Direction of Growth

One feature of the growing block that requires comment is the direction of growth. Why does the block grow "upward" — from the past toward the future — rather than "downward"? This is not a trivial question. If the block is real and growing, there must be something about reality that explains why it grows in the direction from earlier to later rather than the reverse.

Broad's answer is that the direction of growth *is* what the future direction of time consists in. Time's direction is the direction of ontological accretion — the direction in which new events come to be. This gives the growing block view a natural account of the direction of time that neither presentism nor eternalism possesses: for the growing block, the future direction is the direction in which reality is expanding.

This connects to the broader debate about the arrow of time, examined in Chapter 18. Some philosophers have argued that the growing block provides the most natural ontological ground for the asymmetry of time.

---

###### References

- Broad, C. D. 1923. *Scientific Thought*. London: Kegan Paul. Chapter 2.
- Bourne, Craig. 2006. *A Future for Presentism*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.

#### 15.2.2 — The Epistemological Problem for the Growing Block

---

The growing block view has the resources to handle the truthmaker problem and preserves an ontologically open future. But it faces a distinctive and deeply unsettling epistemological problem, first articulated clearly by Craig Bourne: how do you know you are at the edge of the block?

##### The Problem Stated

On the growing block view, the present is the leading edge of reality — the most recently formed layer of the block. Past events exist in the block, but they are not the present; the present is specifically the newest, most recently real events.

Now here is the problem. From the inside — from the perspective of a conscious agent embedded in the block — the experience of being at the "leading edge" of the growing block would be indistinguishable from the experience of being embedded somewhere in the *middle* of a completed block.

Consider: if you are a temporal stage located in the year 2026, your experience consists of perceptions of your immediate environment, memories of past events, and anticipations of future events. This experiential profile — memory of the past, anticipation of the future — is exactly what you would have if you were:

(a) A person at the leading edge of the growing block in 2026, with the real future genuinely open.
(b) A person embedded in a completed block universe in 2026, with all times equally real.
(c) A person in a growing block in 2027, looking back at a "past" that includes a 2026-temporal-stage with no genuine future.

You cannot distinguish these scenarios from the inside. Your experience in each case is exactly the same: you are conscious, you have memories, you anticipate a future. But in scenario (c), the "you" in 2026 is not at the leading edge of the block; you are already in the past of the 2027-observer, a fixed and completed portion of the block. Your sense that you are "at the edge" is illusory.

Bourne formulates the challenge precisely: "If the growing block theory is true, how do any of us know that we are located at the edge of the block rather than embedded somewhere in its interior?" (Bourne 2006: 19–21).

##### The Implications

The problem is more serious than it might initially appear. The growing block view is supposed to capture the intuition that we are genuinely at the "living edge" of reality — that we are experiencing real becoming, that the future is genuinely open to us. But if we cannot know that we are at the edge, then for all we know the future is already real (we are in the middle of a completed block), and the "openness" of the future is illusory.

This is a strange epistemic predicament. The growing block view is motivated partly by the phenomenological sense that we are at the edge of reality, that the future is open, that becoming is real. But the view itself cannot guarantee that this phenomenology is accurate. It allows for the possibility — indeed, it cannot rule out the possibility — that our sense of being at the "living edge" is an illusion produced by being embedded in the middle of an already-completed block.

##### Responses

**The indexical response.** Some growing block theorists argue that "I am present" is like "I am here" — it is automatically true of anyone who asserts it, wherever (or whenever) they are located. If I am a temporal stage located at time t, then I am present *relative to t*, whatever the ontological status of later times. This response makes "being present" perspectival rather than objective — but then it seems to collapse into a form of B-theory.

**The primitive present response.** Others argue that the present is a primitive, mind-independent feature of reality — not merely the "leading edge" in a geometrical sense but something genuinely metaphysically distinguished. If the present is objectively marked as such — not just as the latest time in the block but as having a distinctive metaphysical property — then an agent at the leading edge would have *non-inferential access* to the fact that they are present. The problem with this response is that it seems to require positing A-properties of exactly the kind that McTaggart's regress targets.

**The acceptance response.** Perhaps the most honest response is to accept that the growing block view, unlike presentism, does not give us epistemic access to the openness of the future. Whether we are at the edge or in the middle is not something we can determine from the inside. The growing block theorist may simply accept this and argue that the view is nonetheless the best metaphysical account of temporal ontology — whatever our epistemic limitations.

##### Assessment

The epistemological problem is a genuine difficulty for the growing block. It reveals that the view's phenomenological motivation — the sense of being at the living edge of reality — cannot be secured from within the view itself. A thoughtful growing block theorist must either introduce additional metaphysical machinery (a primitive present, an irreducible A-property) or accept the epistemological cost.

---

###### References

- Bourne, Craig. 2006. *A Future for Presentism*. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Chapter 2.
- Broad, C. D. 1923. *Scientific Thought*. London: Kegan Paul.
- Forrest, Peter. 2004. "The Real but Dead Past: A Reply to Braddon-Mitchell." *Analysis* 64 (4): 358–362.

### Section 15.3: The Moving Spotlight Theory

---

#### Section Introduction

The moving spotlight theory represents an attempt to combine the ontological comprehensiveness of the block universe with the A-theorist's insistence on an objective, moving present. On this view, all times exist — the four-dimensional manifold is real and complete — but there is, in addition, an objectively moving "spotlight" of the present that singles out one time at a time as genuinely present. The present is not merely perspectival; it is a primitive, mind-independent, non-relational feature of reality.

The view is intellectually attractive but faces distinctive difficulties, including a notorious problem about the rate of the spotlight's movement and a regress that parallels McTaggart's. This section examines the view's formulation and its problems.

---

*Section 15.3 comprises subsections 15.3.1 and 15.3.2.*

#### 15.3.1 — The Moving Spotlight: Formulation

---

The moving spotlight theory has a long lineage. McTaggart himself seems to have something like it in mind when he formulates the A-series within the context of a complete temporal manifold. Its most rigorous recent defense is Bradford Skow's *Objective Becoming* (2015), which develops the view in careful detail and responds to the major objections.

##### The Core Idea

The moving spotlight theorist accepts the four-dimensional block: all times exist, all events are real in the manifold. In this respect, the view agrees with the block universe. But — and this is the essential addition — the moving spotlight theorist also holds that there is an objective, mind-independent fact about which time is *present*. This is not merely the indexical fact that a particular observer is located at a particular time; it is a feature of the temporal structure of the world itself. One time, and only one time at a time, is genuinely, objectively, non-relationally present.

The "spotlight" metaphor captures the idea: imagine the four-dimensional manifold as a darkened theater, and the present as a spotlight moving along the timeline from past to future. Each position is equally there, equally real, equally part of the manifold — but only the position illuminated by the spotlight is *now*. The spotlight moves, advancing through the manifold, and what it illuminates is what is genuinely present.

Bradford Skow describes the core commitment as follows: "On the moving spotlight theory... there is an objective fact about which time is present, and which time is present changes" (Skow 2015: 71). The present is not just a position that each temporal stage occupies relative to itself; it is a primitive property that exactly one time possesses at any given moment of "second-order" time.

##### Motivations for the View

The moving spotlight theory is motivated by a specific combination of commitments that neither the block universe nor the pure A-theories can fully satisfy.

**Against presentism:** The moving spotlight theorist is uncomfortable with the apparent ontological discontinuity of presentism — the idea that as the present moves forward, entities literally come into and go out of existence. On the moving spotlight view, nothing comes into or goes out of existence; the four-dimensional manifold is complete. Change consists in the present moving through the manifold, not in the manifold itself growing or shrinking.

**Against the pure block universe:** The moving spotlight theorist is equally uncomfortable with the B-theory's treatment of the present as merely indexical. The sense that there is something objectively special about the present — not just "special for me" but special in itself — is, the moving spotlight theorist insists, tracking a real feature of reality. The block universe, by making the present merely perspectival, misses something genuine.

**For a comprehensive A+B-theory:** The moving spotlight view attempts to have the ontological comprehensiveness of the block universe and the metaphysical dynamism of the A-series. It is, in a sense, the most ambitious A-theory: it says that the A-series is real and adds nothing to the temporal manifold that the A-series requires, while preserving all the advantages of the block universe approach to ontology.

##### The Non-Relational Present

A crucial feature of the moving spotlight view is that the property of being present — the property that the spotlight illuminates — is **non-relational** and **intrinsic**. It is not "present relative to me" or "present relative to this utterance." It is just present — a primitive property that the present moment has and no other moment has, independent of any perspective.

This distinguishes the view sharply from the B-theory's indexical treatment of "now." For the moving spotlight theorist, "now" picks out the time that has the objective property of being present. The reference of "now" shifts with the speaker's temporal location not because presentness is relative, but because the speaker is (we hope) at the same time as the objective present, and as the objective present moves, the speaker's temporal location (and hence the reference of their "now") also advances.

---

###### References

- Skow, Bradford. 2015. *Objective Becoming*. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
- McTaggart, J. M. E. 1908. "The Unreality of Time." *Mind* 17 (68): 457–474.

#### 15.3.2 — Problems for the Moving Spotlight

---

The moving spotlight theory faces several serious difficulties, two of which are especially penetrating: the problem of the rate of change, and the regress problem. Both suggest that the view's attempt to combine the block universe with a dynamic present is unstable.

##### The Rate Problem

If the spotlight moves — if the present advances through the temporal manifold — then it moves at some rate. But what rate? The natural answer is "one second per second" — the present advances one second for every second that passes. But this is trivially true and profoundly uninformative. It is like saying a car moves one kilometer per kilometer.

The problem is that measuring a rate requires two distinct variables: the quantity changing (position) and the parameter against which it changes (time). The present's "movement" through the temporal manifold would need to be measured against something. Movement in space is change of spatial position over time. But movement of the present through time would be change of temporal position over *what*? Over a second-order time?

This is the regress worry: if the present moves through first-order time at some rate, then it takes some amount of second-order time for the first-order present to advance. But then the second-order time needs a present of its own, and the second-order present would need to move through third-order time, and so on without end. The moving spotlight view seems to require a hierarchy of times, which is difficult to make sense of without generating a vicious regress (see Prosser 2012 for a careful development of this objection).

Skow's response in *Objective Becoming* (2015: Ch. 6) is to argue that the rate problem does not generate a vicious regress, because the "rate" of the spotlight's movement is not a real rate in the problematic sense. Rather, the movement of the present is a brute, primitive feature of temporal reality that does not admit of a further analysis in terms of a rate. Just as we do not ask at what rate space extends through some "meta-space," we should not ask at what rate the present moves through some meta-time. The movement is primitive.

This response may be coherent, but it is not entirely satisfying. The accusation that "one second per second" is trivial is precisely that it provides no information about the nature of the movement. If the movement is primitive and unanalyzable, what distinguishes a world with a moving present from a world with a static present? What does the "movement" amount to, if not a change that can be characterized in terms of some parameter?

##### The Extra Structure Problem

A related difficulty is that the moving spotlight view postulates a feature of reality — the objective present — that makes no difference to the physical description of the world. The four-dimensional block manifold of events, with all its B-series relations, remains exactly the same whether or not there is a moving spotlight. The spotlight adds no physical structure; it does not affect the causal relations between events or the distribution of matter and energy.

This means the moving spotlight view posits something physically epiphenomenal: the objective present is real, but it makes no testable difference. Critics argue that such a posit violates the principle of parsimony (see Chapter 14.2.3) and raises the suspicion that the "objective present" is a metaphysical addition with no genuine explanatory work to do.

Moving spotlight theorists reply that the objective present is metaphysically required even if it is physically epiphenomenal: it grounds the truth of A-series statements, it explains why the present feels genuinely special, and it vindicates the intuitions that motivated A-theory in the first place. Parsimony in physics does not equal parsimony in metaphysics; the metaphysics may require features that the physics does not describe.

##### The Regress Problem

The most serious objection is a regress that parallels McTaggart's original argument. If the present is an objective, non-relational property that one time has and all others lack, and if this present "moves" — so that yesterday's present is today's past — then we need to account for this change. The present moves from time t₁ to time t₂ to time t₃... but how are we to characterize this movement without invoking a second-order temporal structure? And doesn't that second-order structure require its own moving present?

Skow's response is to deny that the movement of the spotlight requires characterization in terms of a higher-order temporal structure. The movement is simply the fact that at one time t₁ the property of being present belongs to t₁, and at another time t₂ it belongs to t₂. This is a perfectly well-defined fact about a four-dimensional manifold with an additional primitive property, and no second-order time is required.

Whether this response is adequate depends on whether one accepts that a property can "move" through a manifold without that movement being analyzable in terms of some further structure. The intuition that motivates the regress worry is that any genuine change requires a parameter against which it is measured. The moving spotlight theorist says: not so — some changes are primitive. This is a defensible position, but it requires accepting a degree of primitiveness in the account of temporal change that many philosophers find unsatisfying.

##### Assessment

The moving spotlight theory is the most ambitious A-theory, but it purchases its ambitions at a high philosophical cost. The rate problem, the extra structure problem, and the regress problem together suggest that the combination of block universe ontology and a dynamic present is not as stable as it initially appears. The view has defenders — Skow's treatment is the most serious — but the problems are genuine.

If you are drawn to the moving spotlight view, the key question to answer is: what does the movement of the present consist in, if not a rate measurable against some second-order time? If you cannot answer that question satisfactorily, you may be pushed toward either the pure block universe (which eliminates the objective present) or toward presentism or the growing block (which makes the present ontologically, not merely formally, distinctive).

### Section 15.4: The Open Future and Aristotle's Sea Battle

---

#### Section Introduction

Running through all forms of A-theory is a concern with the openness of the future: the sense in which what is future is genuinely undetermined, genuinely open, genuinely available to be otherwise. This section examines the connection between this metaphysical intuition and the logical question of bivalence — the question of whether every proposition has a determinate truth value. Aristotle's famous discussion of the sea battle in *De Interpretatione* 9 is the classical locus for this question, and it remains philosophically productive.

---

*Section 15.4 comprises subsection 15.4.1.*

#### 15.4.1 — Aristotle's Sea Battle: Bivalence and the Open Future

---

In *De Interpretatione* chapter 9, Aristotle raises what is perhaps the earliest philosophical puzzle about the metaphysics of the future. The problem is known as the *sea battle argument*, and its core is a collision between two principles that both seem compelling:

1. **The principle of bivalence:** Every proposition is either true or false; there is no third option.
2. **The principle of the open future:** Future contingent events — events that could go either way — are not yet determined; the future is genuinely open.

Aristotle argues that if both principles hold, an absurdity follows.

##### The Argument

Consider the proposition: "There will be a sea battle tomorrow."

By the principle of bivalence, this proposition is either true or false — now, before tomorrow arrives. Suppose it is true. Then it is already settled that a sea battle will occur tomorrow. But if it is already settled, then the sea battle is necessary — it cannot fail to happen. And if the sea battle's occurrence is necessary, then there seems to be nothing anyone can do to prevent it. The generals' plans, the captains' decisions, the individual sailors' choices are all irrelevant: the battle will happen.

Suppose instead that the proposition is false. Then it is already settled that no sea battle will occur tomorrow. In that case, again, the outcome is necessary: the non-battle is inevitable.

Either way, if bivalence holds for future contingent propositions, the future is already fixed — not just known by some omniscient being, but *logically* fixed by the truth of present propositions about future events. This is the fatalistic conclusion: the future is as settled as the past (Aristotle, *De Interpretatione* 9, 18a28–18b25).

##### The Threat of Fatalism

The worry here is not exactly determinism. Determinism is the thesis that the laws of nature and the current state of the universe necessitate every future state — a physical/metaphysical thesis. Fatalism is stronger: it holds that the future is fixed *logically*, independently of causal structure. Even in an indeterministic universe, if bivalence holds for future contingent propositions, fatalism follows: the truth of the proposition fixes the outcome independently of causal processes.

A.N. Prior (1967: 113–127) was particularly attentive to this distinction and argued that the threat of logical fatalism is a genuine problem, not dissolved by appeal to indeterminism. In a tense logic framework, the question is whether future tensed propositions have determinate truth values, and this is independent of whether the processes that determine future states are deterministic.

##### Aristotle's Response: Rejecting Bivalence for Future Contingents

Aristotle's own response is radical: he denies that bivalence applies to future contingent propositions. "There will be a sea battle tomorrow" is neither true nor false right now. It is, we might say, *indeterminate*: it will become either true or false as the future unfolds, but it does not currently have a truth value. Future contingents occupy a middle status: they are not yet determined.

This position is logically controversial. It requires restricting bivalence — a principle that many logicians regard as a fundamental theorem of classical logic. How can a proposition be neither true nor false? Aristotle seems to think it can: the proposition is neither fixed-as-true nor fixed-as-false, because the underlying facts that would fix it do not yet exist.

##### Supervaluationism

A more technically sophisticated version of Aristotle's response is **supervaluationism**, developed in the philosophy of language by Bas van Fraassen and applied to the logic of time by Kit Fine and others. Supervaluationism holds that future contingent propositions are *indeterminate* — their truth value is not yet fixed — but this indeterminacy is compatible with the validity of the law of excluded middle ("P or not-P") while blocking the inference to a fixed truth value for P alone.

The idea is this: a proposition P is *supertrue* if it is true in all admissible precisifications (all ways of making the indeterminate future determinate), *superfalse* if it is false in all, and indeterminate if it is true in some and false in others. "There will or won't be a sea battle tomorrow" is supertrue (it is true in every precisification), but "there will be a sea battle tomorrow" is indeterminate (true in some and false in others). This preserves excluded middle while blocking fatalism (Fine 1975: 281–293).

Supervaluationism is technically elegant but philosophically controversial. It requires accepting a three-valued (or more) logic for future-directed propositions, which has consequences for many standard inferences.

##### The Connection to A-Theory

The open future debate connects directly to A-theory. If the future is genuinely open — if future contingent propositions lack determinate truth values — then the future is not "already there" in the block. The open future view is naturally allied with presentism and the growing block: if future events do not yet exist, then there are no facts about them that could fix truth values of future-directed propositions.

The block universe view, by contrast, straightforwardly supports bivalence for future contingents: there is a fact about whether a sea battle occurs tomorrow, because tomorrow's events exist in the four-dimensional manifold. The B-theorist is comfortable with a fixed future precisely because all times are equally real.

##### Assessment

Aristotle's sea battle argument remains philosophically productive because it isolates the tension between two deep commitments: our conviction that the future is open and our conviction that meaningful propositions have truth values. Any theory of temporal ontology must take a stance on this tension.

If you accept bivalence, you are pushed toward either accepting fatalism (and working out what that means) or explaining how bivalence is compatible with genuine openness (and the block universe offers one such explanation). If you reject bivalence for future contingents, you face the technical challenge of developing a logic that handles the resulting indeterminacy.

The debate has not been resolved, but it has been clarified: we now understand much better what the options are and what each costs.

---

###### References

- Aristotle. *De Interpretatione*. Translated by J. L. Ackrill. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1963. Chapter 9, 18a28–18b25.
- Fine, Kit. 1975. "Vagueness, Truth and Logic." *Synthese* 30 (3–4): 265–300.
- Prior, Arthur N. 1967. *Past, Present and Future*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.

### Chapter 15 Exercises: A-Theory and Its Variants

---

#### Comprehension and Analysis

**1.** State the three A-theoretic positions — presentism, growing block, moving spotlight — in your own words, identifying exactly what exists on each view. Make a table comparing them on four dimensions: (a) do past events exist?, (b) do present events exist?, (c) do future events exist?, (d) is the present metaphysically special?

**2.** What is the truthmaker problem for presentism? Identify the three main presentist responses and explain why none is entirely satisfying. Which do you find most promising, and why?

**3.** The growing block view faces an epistemological problem: how do you know you are at the edge of the block? Why is this a problem specifically for the growing block view and not equally for presentism? Does presentism avoid the problem, or merely sidestep it?

**4.** The moving spotlight theory holds that the present is an objective, non-relational property of one time. Reconstruct the "rate problem" as a formal argument. Then assess Skow's response that the movement is primitive and requires no further analysis.

**5.** Reconstruct Aristotle's sea battle argument. Identify the exact premise that leads to fatalism. Does supervaluationism successfully block the fatalistic inference? What does it cost?

---

#### Synthetic and Argumentative

**6.** Among presentism, growing block, and moving spotlight, which is most compatible with special relativity? Rank the three views in terms of how serious the relativity challenge is for each, and explain your ranking.

**7.** The truthmaker problem seems to favor eternalism over all forms of A-theory. But the A-theorist might argue that eternalism has its own "truthmaker problem" — for propositions about what is not the case. Develop this counter-argument as carefully as you can, then evaluate it.

**8.** "Presentism matches common sense better than any other theory of temporal ontology, but common sense is a poor guide to metaphysics." Evaluate this claim, distinguishing between (a) the methodological point about common sense, (b) whether presentism actually matches common sense, and (c) whether 'matching common sense' is a genuine virtue in metaphysics.

---

#### Lab and Observational Exercises

**9. Lab — The Growing Block Diary.** For three days, keep a brief daily diary. At the end of each day, write: "What now exists, that did not exist this morning?" Think about the growing block view: new events have occurred, and they have been added to the real. How does it feel to think of the day's events as *permanent additions* to the block of the real, rather than as "gone"? Write a half-page reflection at the end of the three days.

**10. Lab — The Open Future Exercise.** Make a list of five things you plan to do tomorrow. Now, for each item, consider: is the proposition "I will do X tomorrow" true or false right now? Try to hold in mind the experience of genuine uncertainty — not just epistemic uncertainty about what will happen, but *ontological* openness, the sense that what will happen is genuinely not yet real. Does this experience feel different from the experience of not knowing what has already happened? Write 150–200 words on what you notice.

**11. Lab — News as Ontology.** Listen to a news broadcast and pay attention to how reports use tense. Pick five past events reported in the news. For each, ask: on presentism, what makes this report true? On the growing block, what makes it true? On the block universe, what makes it true? Which account feels most natural for each type of report? Do different types of past-directed claim (recent vs. distant past, physical vs. historical) call for different ontological treatments?

---

#### Reflection

**12.** Consider the phenomenological experience of the future as "open" — the way in which upcoming decisions feel genuinely undetermined, as if the future genuinely awaits constitution. Does this phenomenological datum provide strong evidence for A-theory over B-theory? Or can it be explained within a B-theoretic framework? Write a half-page reflection on whether phenomenology is the right kind of evidence for metaphysical claims about temporal ontology.
