What this diagram elegantly captures is the double character of temporal experience: at any given "now," I have access both to the sequence of nows (represented horizontally) and to the depth of the just-past still present in retention (represented diagonally). Every now is simultaneously the source-point of new experience and the beginning of a sinking into the past.

The diagram also illustrates a key feature of retention that Husserl calls "retention of retention." The moment just before the current now is retained. But that moment was itself retaining its own just-past. So when I retain the previous moment, I also retain, in a kind of second-order way, what that moment was retaining — and so on back through the chain. Retention thus carries a whole "tail" of the past, with each retained moment being itself a retaining of earlier moments, but with diminishing phenomenal intensity as we move further back.

##### The Absolute Flow

The most enigmatic aspect of Husserl's account is his notion of the "absolute flow" (*absoluter Fluss*) of consciousness. The structure of retention-primal impression-protention is not simply a property of individual acts of experience; it is the form of consciousness as such, the manner in which consciousness flows. But this raises a question: if we are analyzing the time-consciousness of individual acts, what is the time-consciousness of consciousness itself? What makes the flow of consciousness temporal?

Husserl's answer is that the absolute flow is "self-constituting" — it constitutes its own temporality without needing a higher-level temporal structure to make it intelligible. The flow is not in time in the ordinary sense; it is what constitutes the experience of time. This is why Husserl describes it as "absolute": it is not relative to any further temporal framework. The flow flows, and in flowing, it constitutes both objective time (the time of clocks and events) and the subjective experience of time (the temporal character of experience itself).

This is one of the most difficult passages in Husserl's work, and commentators disagree sharply about how to interpret it. Dan Zahavi, in his careful study *Husserl's Phenomenology* (2003), argues that the absolute flow should be understood as the ultimate pre-reflective self-awareness of consciousness — the way in which consciousness is aware of its own flowing without this requiring a separate act of reflection (Zahavi 2003: 71–90). On this reading, the absolute flow is not a mysterious metaphysical entity but the structure of consciousness's basic self-intimation.

##### Difficulties in Husserl's Account

Despite its extraordinary depth and rigor, Husserl's account faces several significant difficulties that have occupied subsequent phenomenologists and philosophers of mind.

The first is the problem of **regress**. If consciousness constitutes time through its flowing structure, what constitutes the temporality of the flow itself? Husserl's answer — that the flow is self-constituting — seems to risk either circularity (the flow constitutes itself) or an infinite regress (the flow requires a meta-flow to be temporal, and so on). Zahavi's defense of the self-constituting character of the flow is plausible, but the worry is not fully dissolved (Zahavi 2003: 83–87).

The second difficulty is the problem of **individuation**. Retention is supposed to hold the just-past as still phenomenally present but as past. But what distinguishes the retained moment from any other moment that might be "present" in memory? Husserl's answer — that retention is a distinct mode of intentionality — is correct in identifying the distinction, but it does not fully explain how retention is possible. What is the phenomenological difference between the retained tone and a momentarily imagined tone, both of which are "present" only as mental objects?

A third difficulty concerns the **applicability of the analysis** to complex temporal objects. Husserl's account works most naturally for short temporal sequences — a five-note melody, a brief spoken word. It is less clear how it accounts for our temporal grasp of longer temporal wholes — a symphony, a conversation, a day. Secondary retention (memory) must play a larger role here, but Husserl does not fully develop the relationship between primary retention and the higher-level temporal synthesis required for grasping extended temporal structures.

##### Husserl's Lasting Achievement

Despite these difficulties, Husserl's analysis stands as one of the deepest and most important investigations of temporal experience in the philosophical tradition. He identifies with precision a feature of consciousness — its intrinsic temporal structure, the way in which the living present stretches across retention and protention — that no empirical science of the time was in a position to study, and that remains centrally important for philosophy of mind today.

The diagram is not merely a pedagogical tool. It is a theoretical instrument that captures the topology of temporal experience: the way in which the past is genuinely present (in retention) while being genuinely past (as the object of a retentional act), and the way in which the future is genuinely present (in protention) while being genuinely future (as the object of a protentional act directed toward what has not yet arrived). This topology — the extended, three-part structure of the living present — is Husserl's enduring contribution to our understanding of temporal consciousness.

### Section 3: Heidegger and the Temporality of Existence

Martin Heidegger was Husserl's student and, for a time, his closest philosophical collaborator. But when Heidegger published *Being and Time* in 1927, it became clear that he had moved in a fundamentally different direction. Where Husserl had analyzed time-consciousness — the temporal structure of the acts of an experiencing subject — Heidegger argues that this analysis, however careful, begins in the wrong place. The problem is not to explain how a consciousness constitutes temporal objects or how a mind structures its experience of time. The problem is to understand what it means for a human being — what Heidegger calls *Dasein* ("being-there") — to exist at all, and to show that the answer to this question is irreducibly temporal.

For Heidegger, we are not minds that happen to experience time. We are beings whose very mode of existence is temporal — beings who are always already thrown into a past they did not choose, projecting themselves toward a future they cannot fully anticipate, in a present constituted by their commitments and encounters with the world. Temporality, on Heidegger's account, is not a feature of experience; it is the "ontological meaning of care," the deep structure of what it means to be a human being in the world.

This is a radical reorientation. To follow it, we must be willing to approach time not as an object for the gaze of a detached theorist, but as the structure of existence from the inside — from within a life that is always already engaged, always already concerned, always already finite.

#### Authentic Temporality: The Three Ecstases

##### Care and Its Temporal Meaning

Heidegger's *Being and Time* (1927) is organized around a fundamental question: what is the being of *Dasein* — of the kind of being that we are? In Division I, Heidegger argues that the fundamental structure of *Dasein* is *care* (*Sorge*): we are beings who are always already ahead of ourselves (in projection toward possibilities), always already thrown into a factical situation (a past we did not choose), and always already engaged with things and others in the world (falling into concernful dealings). Care, in Heidegger's technical sense, encompasses this entire structure: *ahead-of-itself-already-in-having-always-already-been-alongside*.

In Division II, Heidegger asks: what makes this structure possible? What is its ultimate ground? His answer is *Zeitlichkeit* — temporality. The three structural moments of care (ahead-of-itself, already-in, alongside) correspond to the three fundamental "ecstases" of temporality: the future (*Zukunft*), the having-been (*Gewesenheit*), and the present (*Gegenwart*). To say that care is grounded in temporality is to say that *Dasein* exists in a manner that is constituted by its orientation toward the future, its inheritance of the past, and its engagement in the present — and that these three orientations form a unified, mutually implicating structure (Heidegger 1962: 374–380).

##### Running Ahead Toward Death: The Future Ecstasis

The primary ecstasis of authentic temporality, for Heidegger, is the future — specifically, the future understood as one's ownmost possibility: death. Heidegger argues, notoriously, that *Dasein* is always "being-toward-death" (*Sein-zum-Tode*): death is not merely an event that will eventually occur but a structural possibility that shapes the whole of existence. Being-toward-death means existing in the awareness that one's possibilities are finite, that time is not unlimited, that one cannot indefinitely postpone commitment.

Authentic temporality involves what Heidegger calls "anticipatory resoluteness" (*vorlaufende Entschlossenheit*): running ahead (*Vorlaufen*) to one's own death, not in the sense of obsessing about dying, but in the sense of living with a clear-eyed awareness of one's finitude, and thereby taking ownership of one's possibilities rather than drifting through a life organized by what "one" (*das Man*) — the anonymous, public, average self — expects and does.

When *Dasein* runs ahead to its death, it "individualizes" itself — it becomes aware that its existence is uniquely its own, not exchangeable with anyone else's. This individualizing is also a confrontation with one's thrownness: I am not thrown into possibilities in general but into this particular set of possibilities, this particular situation, this particular life.

##### Taking Over Thrownness: The Having-Been Ecstasis

The second ecstasis of authentic temporality is the having-been (*Gewesenheit*). Note that Heidegger uses "having-been" rather than simply "past," and this is deliberate. The past, in ordinary temporal language, is simply what has occurred and is now over. But the having-been, in Heidegger's sense, is not over: it is the thrownness (*Geworfenheit*) that I am, the factical situation into which I have been thrown and which I carry with me.

Authentic existence involves "taking over" one's thrownness — not accepting it passively or denying it, but owning it as one's own. This is what Heidegger means by "authentic repetition" (*Wiederholung*): not nostalgic return to the past, but a resolute appropriation of the possibilities that one's historical situation makes available. I inherit a language, a culture, a set of relationships, a set of limitations and affordances — and authentic existence means taking responsibility for what I make of this inheritance rather than pretending it isn't there or that I could have been otherwise.

The having-been ecstasis also makes clear why Heidegger describes temporality as having "ecstases" — literally, "standing-outside-of-oneself" (*Ekstasen*). I am not simply a point in time that has a past; I am always already "outside myself" toward my past, always shaped by what I have been, always carrying my thrownness with me.

##### The Moment of Vision: The Present Ecstasis

The third ecstasis of authentic temporality is the present — but not the present conceived as the "now" of ordinary clock time. Heidegger's term for the authentic present is the *Augenblick* — usually translated as "moment of vision" or "the moment." The *Augenblick* is the present as it appears within anticipatory resoluteness: the moment in which, having run ahead to death and taken over one's thrownness, one makes a resolute decision about how to exist in one's situation.

The *Augenblick* is not the present as a fleeting instant in a series of nows. It is the present as the moment of action and commitment, the present that is constituted by one's having-been and one's running-ahead, the present that has existential weight because it is owned. It is "the moment of vision" because, in it, *Dasein* can see its situation clearly: it can see what genuinely matters and what is merely noise, what possibilities are genuinely its own and what are merely "what one does."

##### The Unity of the Ecstases

A crucial feature of Heidegger's account is that the three ecstases are not three separate faculties or three separate times. They are moments of a single, unified temporal structure. Authentic temporality is the "simultaneous" (in a non-temporal sense) holding-together of future, having-been, and present. Running ahead to death is only possible on the basis of taking over one's thrownness, and both together make possible the moment of vision in the present. Neither the future nor the having-been nor the present is primary in isolation; they co-constitute each other (Heidegger 1962: 380–382).

This unity distinguishes Heidegger's account sharply from ordinary conceptions of time as a linear sequence in which future, present, and past succeed one another. For Heidegger, authentic temporality is not a sequence at all; it is a structure. It is the structure of existence as a unified whole that reaches backward into its thrownness and forward into its possibilities, while being concretely engaged in its situation. Time, at this level, is not something that happens to *Dasein* from the outside; it is what *Dasein* is.

#### Vulgar Time and Originary Temporality: Heidegger's Critique

##### The Ordinary Conception of Time

The time we are most familiar with in everyday life — clock time, calendar time, the time of schedules and appointments and deadlines — is what Heidegger calls "vulgar time" (*vulgäre Zeit*) or "the ordinary conception of time." This is time understood as an infinite, homogeneous sequence of "now-points," stretching from the indefinite past through the present into the indefinite future. Any moment in this sequence is as real as any other; none is intrinsically privileged; time moves steadily and uniformly forward, indifferent to who is living in it.

This ordinary conception has deep roots in the history of philosophy. Aristotle's account of time as the measure of motion with respect to before and after presents time as something available to any observer who can register change and count it. Augustine's puzzlement about time — if the past is no longer and the future is not yet, what is the "present"? — is also conducted within the framework of the "now-series." And Husserl's analysis of time-consciousness, however sophisticated, still takes as its starting point the analysis of *how a consciousness experiences time* — it remains, Heidegger argues, within a framework that treats time primarily as an object of experience (Heidegger 1962: 472–480).

##### Time as Available and Leveled-Off

For Heidegger, the ordinary conception of time has a specific existential root: it is time as experienced from the standpoint of inauthentic *Dasein*, absorbed in the world of everyday concern. In everyday life, we relate to time primarily as a resource to be managed: there is time "for" doing this, time "until" that deadline, time "since" something happened. Time is the field within which tasks are distributed and scheduled.

This practical engagement with time produces a characteristic leveling-off and publicizing of temporality. Time becomes "public time" — the time that "everyone" shares, that is measured by clocks that everyone can read, that is indifferent to any particular individual. The "now" of public time is a position in the sequence available to anyone, not the *Augenblick* of a particular *Dasein* making a resolute decision. This is what Heidegger means by calling it "vulgar": not morally low, but ordinary, common, averaged-out, and anonymous.

##### Originary Temporality as Prior

Heidegger's critical point is that vulgar time is a *derived* mode of time — derived from originary temporality by a process of leveling-off and abstraction. Originary temporality is the authentic temporal structure of *Dasein* analyzed above: the unified ecstatic structure of future-having-been-present. Vulgar time is what you get when you strip away the existential character of this structure — when you detach the ecstases from their connection to death, thrownness, and resolute existence, and treat them as mere positions in a neutral sequence.

The derivation works roughly as follows. Inauthentic *Datability*: every "now" in originary temporality is "now that I am doing this," or "now that this situation is in play." This "datability" (the fact that temporal moments are indexed to situations) gets leveled off into mere abstract positions on a timeline when time becomes public. Inauthentic *Significance*: every originary now has significance — it matters in a particular way relative to a particular existence. Public time strips away significance, treating all moments as equivalent. Inauthentic *Extension*: originary temporality has a span or stretch that reflects the existential scope of *Dasein*'s projects; public time treats extension as purely quantitative measure (Heidegger 1962: 460–465).

##### Connections to Augustine and Husserl

The relationship to Augustine is interesting. Heidegger explicitly discusses Augustine's analysis of time in the *Confessions* (Book XI), where Augustine famously argues that past, present, and future are all modifications of the present soul: the present of the past (memory), the present of the present (attention), and the present of the future (expectation). Heidegger finds in Augustine a genuine insight: that time is not simply "out there" in the world but is rooted in the structure of a particular kind of being. But Augustine remains within a framework of the soul's relation to eternity, which is quite different from Heidegger's analysis of temporality as the structure of a finite, mortal existence.

The relationship to Husserl is more complex and more critical. Heidegger acknowledges that Husserl's analysis of time-consciousness is more sophisticated than any previous account, and he credits Husserl with showing that consciousness has an intrinsic temporal structure that cannot be reduced to a series of punctual nows. But Heidegger argues that Husserl's analysis remains at the level of the intentional acts of a transcendental subject — a subject whose being has not been adequately questioned. By beginning with consciousness and its constituting acts, Husserl presupposes a subject whose mode of being is already implicitly that of a "worldless" mind, rather than a being-in-the-world whose very existence is temporal.

For Heidegger, the analysis of time-consciousness is derivative of — and depends on — a more fundamental ontological analysis of *Dasein*'s temporal existence. Husserl asks: how does consciousness constitute temporal experience? Heidegger asks: what does it mean to be the kind of being that has, or can have, such experiences? The second question is prior.

##### The Significance of Heidegger's Critique

Heidegger's distinction between vulgar and originary temporality has profound consequences for how we think about time more generally. It suggests that the time of physics — homogeneous, universal, available to any observer — is not the most fundamental kind of time but a highly abstract and derived representation that has its roots in the leveling-off of originary temporality. The physicist's time is, in a sense, a social and cognitive achievement, not a primal datum.

It also challenges us to ask what it means to take time seriously in the way that Heidegger suggests. If authentic temporality is the structure of a life that genuinely owns its finitude, then a great deal of ordinary temporal experience — hurrying through the present, avoiding thought of death, treating time as a neutral resource — represents a kind of flight from what we essentially are. Heidegger is not moralizing here; he is making an ontological point. But the ontological point has, unmistakably, an ethical resonance: to live inauthentically in time is to miss something essential about what we are.

### Section 4: Merleau-Ponty and Embodied Time

Maurice Merleau-Ponty's *Phenomenology of Perception*, published in 1945, is among the most important works in the phenomenological tradition. Its central claim — that the perceiving subject is not a pure consciousness but an embodied being, a "motor intentionality" that engages with the world through the body — transforms every major topic that phenomenology had addressed, and the analysis of time is no exception.

Merleau-Ponty's critique of Husserl is not as radical as Heidegger's, but it is in some ways more concrete. Where Heidegger argues that the analysis of consciousness must be replaced by an analysis of *Dasein*'s mode of being, Merleau-Ponty argues that the analysis of consciousness must be replaced by — or at least grounded in — an analysis of the lived body (*corps propre*). Temporal experience, on Merleau-Ponty's account, is not constituted by a transcendental subject performing acts of retention and protention; it is lived through a body that is always already oriented in a practical situation, shaped by habits and motor patterns that reach back into the past and forward into anticipated action.

This is a claim that deserves to be felt before it is analyzed. Sit quietly and notice how your body is already positioned in time: the slight anticipatory lean in your muscles as you wait for something; the way a habitual gesture carries the history of a thousand repetitions; the way an unfamiliar posture feels temporally disorienting. The body is not merely a vehicle for a temporal mind — it is itself a temporal organization, a living archive of past experience and a practical orientation toward the future.

#### Temporal Experience and the Motor Body

##### The Inadequacy of Pure Consciousness Accounts

In Part III, Chapter 2 of *Phenomenology of Perception* (1945), Merleau-Ponty takes up the analysis of time after a long development of his central thesis about the primacy of the lived body. His point of departure, as so often, is a diagnosis of what goes wrong in both empiricist and rationalist accounts — here, specifically, in the attempts to analyze temporal experience as either the effect of external causal processes (empiricism) or the product of a constituting consciousness (idealism, including, implicitly, Husserl).

The empiricist account fails because it cannot explain the genuine unity of temporal experience. If time-experience were simply the sum of present sensations plus associative connections to remembered ones, it would not have the structured, intentional character it in fact has: the character of a *field* in which past, present, and future are organized relative to a subject with a perspective.

The idealist or Husserlian account is more sophisticated but, Merleau-Ponty argues, ultimately still one-sided. Husserl analyzes temporal constitution as the work of a transcendental consciousness performing acts of retention and protention. But this leaves the body out of the account, or treats it as one object among others that consciousness constitutes rather than as the very ground of constitution. For Merleau-Ponty, this is a fundamental mistake: consciousness does not hover over the body and constitute time; consciousness is embodied, and its temporal character is shaped by the body's engagement with the world.

##### The Motor Body as Temporal Archive

Merleau-Ponty's most striking contribution to the phenomenology of time is his account of how the body itself is a temporal organization (Merleau-Ponty 2012: 410–420). Consider what it means to have a habit. A pianist who has practiced a Chopin étude for years can play it without consciously recalling how the notes go. The fingers "know" the music in a way that is not a matter of recollection or deliberate attention. This bodily knowledge is a form of sedimented past — the history of thousands of repetitions encoded in the motor schema of the hands.

What this shows, for Merleau-Ponty, is that the past is not merely something we mentally represent and retain (as in Husserl's account of retention). It is also — and perhaps more fundamentally — something that the body carries in its habits, its dispositions, its practical orientations. The lived body is a temporal being not because it occupies successive positions in objective time but because it is organized by its history of engagement with the world.

Similarly, the future is not merely something that consciousness protends. The motor body is always already oriented toward future action: the body of a practiced athlete is a body that has been shaped by training to anticipate certain kinds of challenges and respond to them. This anticipatory orientation is not a mental representation of future events; it is a bodily readiness, a motor intention that is already reaching forward into the space of potential action.

##### Temporal Habit as Foundational

The concept of habit (*habitude*) is central to Merleau-Ponty's temporal analysis. Habit is the way in which the past persists in the present, not as a mental trace but as a practical disposition. A habit is a past pattern of engagement that has been incorporated into the body's current way of being in the world. To have the habit of playing the piano is not to remember playing the piano; it is to be the kind of body that, when placed before a keyboard, moves in certain organized ways.

This means that temporal experience is, at its most basic level, not an affair of mental acts at all but of the body's practical engagement with its situation. The "now" of bodily experience is the moment of action — not the abstract instant of Aristotelian physics or even the primal impression of Husserl's analysis, but the moment of the body's engagement with its task. And the "past" of bodily experience is not a retained content but the accumulated history of the body's practical dealings with the world.

Merleau-Ponty supports this analysis with careful attention to cases of motor disability and disruption. A patient with certain neurological conditions may lose specific motor habits without losing the corresponding memories. Such cases suggest that bodily habit is not simply a subspecies of memory but a distinct form of temporal organization. Conversely, patients with certain kinds of memory loss may retain motor habits intact — further suggesting that the temporal sedimentation of habit and the temporal representation of memory are different, if related, phenomena.

##### Temporal Experience as Fundamentally Practical

One of the most important implications of Merleau-Ponty's account is that temporal experience is fundamentally practical and action-oriented, not primarily theoretical or observational. We do not primarily experience time by observing the succession of events from a detached standpoint. We experience it in the midst of our practical engagement with the world: in the urgency of an imminent deadline, in the reluctance of a task we are dreading, in the swift passage of time when we are absorbed in an activity we love.

This practical character of temporal experience connects Merleau-Ponty to Heidegger, who also insists that originary temporality is the time of care and concern, not the time of theoretical observation. But Merleau-Ponty's account is more specific: the "practical subject" whose temporal experience he analyzes is not the abstract *Dasein* of *Being and Time* but the concrete, fleshy, habituated, situated body — the body of a particular person in a particular environment, shaped by a particular history.

This specificity is both a strength and a challenge. It is a strength because it makes the phenomenological analysis more concrete and more connected to what we actually know from psychology and neuroscience. It is a challenge because it raises the question of how to account for the universal features of temporal experience — the structure of retention and protention, the unity of past, present, and future — if that experience is so thoroughly shaped by the particularities of individual bodily history.

##### The Intersubjective Dimension

Merleau-Ponty also gestures toward the intersubjective dimension of temporal experience, which neither Husserl nor Heidegger had fully developed. The body is not merely a private temporal organization but a social one: our bodily habits are shaped by our cultural environment, our linguistic practices, our shared rhythms and rituals. The time of a shared meal, of a conversation, of a musical performance with others — these are temporal experiences that are constituted partly by the bodily coordination of multiple subjects, not merely by the temporal structure of any single consciousness.

This social and intersubjective dimension of temporal experience opens onto questions about cultural variation in temporal experience that empirical psychology has begun to investigate — questions that we will encounter in Chapter 27. Merleau-Ponty does not pursue these questions in detail, but his analysis of the motor body as the ground of temporal experience provides a framework within which they make sense.

#### The Field of Presence: Extending and Correcting Husserl

##### Beyond the Point-Like Present

One of Merleau-Ponty's most suggestive contributions to the phenomenology of time is his concept of the "field of presence" (*champ de présence*). The idea emerges from his dissatisfaction with any account — including Husserl's — that treats the subject's temporal experience as organized around a punctual or even a structured "now" that is then extended through retention and protention. For Merleau-Ponty, this picture still implicitly treats the present moment as the anchor point from which experience radiates outward, forward, and backward. But this misses something important: I do not experience myself as a point that has retentional and protentional "rays"; I experience myself as always already within a temporal field that surrounds me (Merleau-Ponty 2012: 415–425).

The metaphor of a "field" is deliberate and important. A field is not organized around any single privileged point; it is an extended space in which various elements are present in different relations to one another. Merleau-Ponty proposes that temporal experience is field-like in this sense: I am not at a point in time with retention trailing behind me and protention reaching ahead. Rather, I am in a temporal field that has horizons — a "near past" and "near future" that are genuinely present to me as temporal context, a "more distant past" that fades into memory, and a "more distant future" that dissolves into anticipation.

##### Embodied Orientations as Pre-Given

What is especially important about the field of presence is that it is not constituted by my conscious acts of retention and protention. It is pre-given by my embodied situation. When I sit down to work on a project, the temporal field of that situation is already laid out before my conscious acts begin: the project has a history that I bring with me bodily — in my habits, my accumulated knowledge, my practical skills — and it has a future that my body is already oriented toward in its posture, its alertness, its readiness for certain kinds of demands.

Merleau-Ponty captures this with the observation that the future is not merely anticipated — it is already anticipated in my embodied orientations toward the world. A skilled driver does not explicitly anticipate the curve in the road; the body is already preparing for it before the driver consciously registers that it is coming. The anticipatory structure of temporal experience is, at this level, a feature of the body's practical engagement with its environment, not of the mind's explicit projection toward possibilities.

This claim extends and corrects Husserl in a specific way. Husserl's protention is an intentional act directed toward the about-to-come; it is a mode of consciousness's temporal structure. Merleau-Ponty's pre-given temporal orientation is a feature of the body's motor engagement; it is not an intentional act in Husserl's sense at all, but a practical readiness that underlies and enables such acts. In this sense, the Husserlian analysis of protention is, for Merleau-Ponty, an analysis of what temporal experience looks like from the perspective of a reflective, observing consciousness — but this perspective is built on a deeper foundation of embodied temporal engagement.

##### The Temporal Structure of Perception

This analysis has important implications for the phenomenology of perception more broadly. When I perceive an object, I do not perceive it as a static snapshot. I perceive it with an implicit temporal depth: I see the far side of the cup though I cannot currently see it, because I perceive the cup as an object with a back as well as a front. This "hidden" presence of the unseen side is a kind of temporal horizon: it reaches back to my past encounters with similar objects, which have established the practical expectation that cups have backs, and it reaches forward to the possible experience of turning the cup around.

Merleau-Ponty generalizes this: perception as such has a temporal horizon structure. The temporal field of presence is not merely a context for perception; it is a structural feature of perception itself. To perceive is always to perceive within a temporal field — to perceive something as having been and as about to continue, as located within a practical context that stretches backward and forward in time.

##### Correction of Husserlian Account

Merleau-Ponty's most direct correction of Husserl concerns the order of explanation. For Husserl, temporal constitution runs from the subjective to the objective: consciousness performs acts of retention and protention, and through these acts, it constitutes the experience of objective temporal sequence. The body's temporal character, on this account, is something that consciousness constitutes along with everything else.

For Merleau-Ponty, this order is reversed. The lived body is the primary locus of temporal experience; it is the motor body's engagement with the world that first establishes the basic temporal orientations — backward into habituated past, forward into anticipated action — within which conscious acts of retention and protention are then possible. Consciousness does not constitute the body as a temporal object; the body, as a living temporal subject, is the condition of possibility for conscious temporal experience.

This reversal has far-reaching implications. It suggests that the deepest analysis of temporal experience will not be found by reflection on the acts of a transcendental consciousness but by careful attention to the concrete, habituated, practically engaged body in its situation. And it suggests that the temporal disorientation we experience in illness, injury, or extreme fatigue — when the body's habitual engagements are disrupted — is not a distortion of a primarily mental temporal experience but a disruption of the bodily ground on which all temporal experience rests.

##### What Merleau-Ponty Achieves

Merleau-Ponty's analysis of embodied time and the field of presence offers three major contributions to the phenomenological tradition. First, it grounds temporal experience in the lived body rather than in pure consciousness, making the analysis more concrete and more connected to the facts of embodied existence. Second, it introduces the concept of the temporal field, which captures the way in which temporal experience extends around the subject rather than being organized around a central "now." Third, it opens the phenomenological analysis of time to the intersubjective and cultural dimensions of experience, which Husserl and Heidegger had largely left undeveloped.

At the same time, Merleau-Ponty's account raises questions of its own. If temporal experience is fundamentally bodily, how do we account for the explicitly reflective and conceptual dimensions of temporal experience — planning, regretting, narrating? These require something more than motor habit, more than pre-given bodily orientation. The resources of narrative — of the stories we tell about our lives and the lives of others — may be needed to complete the phenomenological analysis. This is the insight that Paul Ricoeur will develop.

### Section 5: Ricoeur, Narrative, and the Configuration of Time

Paul Ricoeur occupies a unique position in the phenomenological tradition. Deeply versed in Husserl, Heidegger, and the hermeneutical tradition, he is also a careful reader of narrative theory, literary criticism, and historiography. His three-volume *Time and Narrative* (1984–1988) is the most sustained attempt in twentieth-century philosophy to ask what human beings do with time — not merely how we experience it, but how we configure it, give it shape, make it livable.

Ricoeur begins from an observation that the preceding phenomenological accounts share: each of them runs into what he calls the "aporia of time" — the puzzling character of time that cannot be fully resolved by any phenomenological analysis alone. Augustine shows that time is in the soul; Husserl shows that time-consciousness has a tripartite structure; Heidegger shows that temporality is the meaning of care. But each of these analyses runs into difficulties that send us back to the question. Time remains, in some sense, resistant to full understanding.

Ricoeur's response is not to try yet another phenomenological analysis from scratch, but to look to a different region of human practice for what phenomenology alone cannot provide: narrative. We are, Ricoeur argues, story-telling animals. We configure time by telling stories — about ourselves, about our communities, about the world. And narrative does something for temporal experience that neither the analysis of consciousness nor the analysis of existence had been able to achieve: it gives time a human shape.

#### Time and Narrative: The Aporia and the Response

##### The Aporia of Time

In the first chapter of *Time and Narrative*, Volume 1 (1984), Ricoeur confronts what he calls the fundamental "aporia of time." The aporia is not a single puzzle but a family of related difficulties that arise whenever we try to give a complete philosophical account of time. Ricoeur illustrates it through a careful reading of two foundational texts: Augustine's *Confessions*, Book XI, and Aristotle's *Physics*, Book IV.

Augustine's analysis reveals that time, insofar as it is experienced, is a "distension of the soul" (*distentio animi*). Past, present, and future are not external realities but modes of the present soul: the "present of the past" (memory), the "present of the present" (attention), and the "present of the future" (expectation). This is a profound phenomenological insight: time is not merely "out there" in the world but is constituted in and through the experiencing subject. But Augustine's analysis generates an aporia: if time is a distension of the soul, what is the relationship between this subjective time and the objective time of the world — the time of the sun's course, of decay, of history? Augustine finds himself drawn in two directions at once, and the tension is never fully resolved.

Aristotle's analysis in the *Physics* moves in the opposite direction: time is the "number of motion with respect to before and after." This is a cosmological account: time is a feature of the world, measured by the regular motions of the heavens. But Aristotle's account generates its own aporia: number requires a counter, and a counter requires a soul. So even the cosmological account of time seems to require reference to a subjective experience of counting and registering before-and-after (Ricoeur 1984: 7–22).

The lesson Ricoeur draws is that these two perspectives — the subjective/phenomenological and the objective/cosmological — are both indispensable and irreducible to each other. Every attempt to give a complete account of time from one perspective alone runs into difficulties that can only be addressed by reintroducing the other perspective. The aporia of time is not a problem to be solved but a tension to be negotiated.

##### Narrative as Response

Ricoeur's central claim is that narrative is the primary way in which human beings negotiate this aporia. We cannot resolve the tension between subjective and objective time by philosophical analysis, but we can *configure* time — give it a human shape — through the act of story-telling. Narrative is the medium through which we make time livable (Ricoeur 1984: 52).

The key concept is *mimesis* — a term Ricoeur borrows from Aristotle's *Poetics*, where it means the imitation or representation of action in narrative. Ricoeur argues that mimesis is not a single operation but a threefold one, and that the three phases of mimesis correspond to three different relationships between narrative and temporal experience.

**Mimesis I** (*prefiguration*): Before any narrative is constructed, experience is already "pre-figured" — it is already structured in ways that make it amenable to narrative representation. Human action has a temporal character (before and after), a symbolic dimension (meanings that actions carry in their cultural context), and a narrative pre-understanding (we already implicitly understand action in terms of plots, motives, consequences, and so on). Experience is already, in this sense, "proto-narrative": it has the structural features that narrative will articulate more explicitly.

**Mimesis II** (*configuration*): Narrative proper begins with what Ricoeur calls the *configurational act* — the operation of "emplotment" (*mise en intrigue*). Emplotment is the act by which a narrative takes a diversity of events and characters and weaves them into a unified, intelligible whole with a beginning, middle, and end. The plot is not merely a sequence of events but a transformation: it draws together heterogeneous elements — events, characters, circumstances, consequences — and configures them into a narrative whole that is "followable," that makes sense as a story (Ricoeur 1984: 54–77).

The act of configuration is, Ricoeur argues, a response to the aporia of time: it does not resolve the tension between subjective and objective time but holds them together in a new synthesis. A narrative is both objective (it follows a sequence of events) and subjective (it is a configured interpretation from a particular perspective). It is both temporal (it unfolds in time) and atemporal (it grasps a temporal sequence as a whole, in a single act of comprehension). In narrative, time becomes human time — time organized according to human concerns, shaped by human meaning, and directed toward the future that the ending of the story discloses.

**Mimesis III** (*refiguration*): The narrative does not end when the story is told. It continues in the act of reading or hearing — what Ricoeur calls the "intersection of the world of the text and the world of the reader." When a reader engages with a narrative, their own lived experience is *refigured* — reorganized, enriched, challenged — by the temporal configuration that the narrative offers. This is why stories matter: not merely as entertainment or as information, but as configurations of temporal experience that re-shape how the reader understands and lives their own time.

##### The Claim Assessed

Ricoeur's account of the threefold mimesis is among the most influential ideas in late twentieth-century philosophy and literary theory. It establishes a principled connection between narrative and temporal experience: not merely the claim that we enjoy stories, but the deeper claim that narrative is the primary medium through which human beings configure time in a humanly intelligible way.

Several questions arise. First, how does the narrative configuration of time relate to the individual's lived temporal experience? Ricoeur's account seems to operate at the level of cultural products — stories, histories, novels — rather than at the level of the individual's ongoing self-understanding. The connection between the two levels requires further development, which Ricoeur provides in *Oneself as Another* (1992) and which we take up in the next section.

Second, is narrative truly necessary for the configuration of time, or is it merely one way among others? One might argue that music, ritual, and practical projects also configure time in humanly meaningful ways. Ricoeur does not deny this, but he insists that narrative has a special status because it is the form in which the relation between event-level time and life-level time is most explicitly and reflexively articulated.

Third, what of the aporia? Ricoeur is explicit that narrative does not resolve the aporia of time but provides a practical response to it: it allows us to live with the tension rather than eliminating it. This may seem like a disappointing conclusion, but Ricoeur argues that it is the most honest and most adequate conclusion available: the aporia of time is not a philosophical failure but a permanent feature of the human condition, to which narrative is the appropriate human response.

#### Narrative Identity: The Self as Story

##### The Problem of Personal Identity Through Time

Who are you over time? This question might seem to belong to metaphysics — to the debates about personal identity that we will examine in Unit IX. But Ricoeur argues, in *Oneself as Another* (1992), that the question of personal identity through time cannot be answered by purely metaphysical analysis alone, because it is not merely a question about the persistence of an object but about the unity of a life as lived and understood from the inside.

The metaphysical question — what makes you now the same person as you were ten years ago? — typically invites answers in terms of psychological continuity, physical continuity, or some combination. These are important questions. But they do not, by themselves, address the question of what it means for a person to have a life that hangs together — to be someone with a coherent self-understanding, capable of making and keeping commitments, capable of being held responsible for past actions, capable of having genuine projects that extend over time. These are features of a self that is not merely numerically identical over time but that has a kind of qualitative unity — a unity of character, commitment, and self-understanding. This is what Ricoeur calls the problem of *narrative identity* (Ricoeur 1992: 140–168).

##### Idem-Identity and Ipse-Identity

Ricoeur draws a fundamental distinction between two senses of the word "same" — or, since he is writing in French, between two senses of *idem* and *ipse*. 

**Idem-identity** is sameness in the sense of numerical identity and qualitative identity: the same entity, the same properties, the same substance. When we ask whether the ship in harbor today is the same ship as the ship that left last year, we are asking for idem-identity. When we ask whether you are the same person as you were ten years ago in the sense of being numerically identical, we are also asking for idem-identity.

**Ipse-identity** is selfhood — the identity of a self that consists not in remaining the same in the sense of idem, but in remaining true to itself in the sense of a promise or commitment. When you make a promise, you commit your future self to an action. The grounds for keeping the promise are not that your future self will be numerically identical to you (though it presumably will be) but that you — this self, this person — have given your word, and keeping your word is part of what it means to be who you are. Ipse-identity is the identity of the self as a subject of commitments (Ricoeur 1992: 121–125).

The distinction matters because the two kinds of identity can come apart. A person in the advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease may retain idem-identity (they are the same biological organism) while losing much of their ipse-identity (they can no longer maintain the commitments, projects, and self-understanding that constituted who they were). Conversely, a person can undergo radical change in personality and character — becoming, as we sometimes say, "a different person" — while retaining full idem-identity.

##### Narrative as Mediating Idem and Ipse

Ricoeur's central claim is that narrative identity mediates between idem and ipse: it is the form in which the self achieves a unity that is neither the brute numerical identity of a thing nor the pure formal selfhood of a promise, but something richer — the coherence of a life story.

To have a narrative identity is to be able to tell a story of one's life that is both truthful (in the sense of conforming to the facts of one's history) and intelligible (in the sense of hanging together as a coherent narrative with discernible patterns, transitions, and significance). Narrative identity is not a fixed essence but an achievement — something constructed and reconstructed over time through the ongoing act of self-interpretation (Ricoeur 1992: 147–151).

This account captures something that purely metaphysical accounts miss: the fact that personal identity through time is not merely a matter of what obtains independently of one's self-understanding, but is partly constituted by one's ongoing interpretive relationship to one's own history. I am, in part, the person who tells this story about this life. Different stories about the same sequence of events can constitute different identities — not because the events change, but because narrative identity involves selection, emphasis, interpretation, and the attribution of meaning, all of which are acts of the interpreting self.

##### The Narrative Self and Ethics

The concept of narrative identity has direct ethical implications, which Ricoeur develops at length in *Oneself as Another*. If personal identity is narrative identity, then the ethical life — the life of commitments, responsibilities, and ongoing concern for oneself and others — is not an optional addition to identity but constitutive of it. To be the kind of self that can make and keep promises is to be the kind of self that has a narrative: a past that carries commitments forward and a future toward which those commitments reach.

This connects the phenomenology of time directly to ethical philosophy. Heidegger had argued that authentic existence involves taking over one's thrownness and projecting toward the future with resolution. Ricoeur agrees that the temporal structure of selfhood is connected to authentic self-ownership, but he insists that this temporal structure is fundamentally narrative in form — it requires the kind of explicit self-interpretation that narrative enables. A merely biological or psychological account of continuity cannot explain why I am responsible for my past actions, or why I should care about my future self. Narrative identity can explain this, because it shows that the self who made the promise and the self who must keep it are unified by a shared story that makes both intelligible.

##### Connections to the Preceding Analysis

Ricoeur's concept of narrative identity completes the arc of the phenomenological analyses we have traced in this chapter. Husserl shows how the living present is structured by retention and protention. Heidegger shows how temporal existence is the structure of care — the unified reaching of *Dasein* toward its future, its past, and its present situation. Merleau-Ponty shows how temporal experience is grounded in the embodied, habituated body. Ricoeur shows how these different levels of temporal experience are integrated, at the level of a human life, by the practice of narrative self-interpretation.

Each analysis is partial, and each requires supplementation by the others. The lived present of Husserl is the ground-level temporal structure that makes any experience possible. Heidegger's temporality is the structure of a whole human life oriented toward its end. Merleau-Ponty's embodied time is the concrete, habituated body that carries the past into the present through motor engagement. Ricoeur's narrative identity is the interpretive synthesis that draws all of these levels together into the intelligible unity of a life.

To understand temporal experience in its full richness, we need all four levels — and perhaps more. What this chapter has aimed to show is that time, as experienced, is not a simple or transparent datum. It is a complex, multi-layered structure that phenomenological analysis can illuminate layer by layer, revealing at each level something that was hidden at the previous level. The phenomenology of time-consciousness is not finished; it is one of the most active areas of philosophical inquiry, and each of the thinkers we have studied has contributed essential resources for its continued development.

### Chapter 26 Exercises: The Phenomenology of Time-Consciousness

#### Analytical Exercises

**1. Brentano vs. Husserl on the Just-Past**
Brentano argues that past tones persist in consciousness in a "modified" mode — as just-now tones with a quality of pastness attached. Husserl argues that this account confuses the content of the present impression with the intentional act directed at the past. In your own words, reconstruct this disagreement as precisely as you can. Which account do you find more persuasive, and why? Your answer should engage with the specific phenomenological datum at issue: the experience of hearing a melody.

**2. The Three Structures of the Living Present**
Husserl distinguishes three phases of the living present: primal impression, retention, and protention. For each phase, explain (a) what it is, (b) what it is directed toward, and (c) why it is necessary for the experience of temporal objects. Then explain Husserl's crucial claim that retention is not memory. What exactly is the difference, and why does it matter?

**3. Interpreting Husserl's Diagram**
Describe Husserl's time-diagram in your own words, explaining what each axis represents and what the diagonal "sinking" of past moments represents. What feature of temporal experience does the diagram capture that could not be captured by a simple horizontal timeline? What, if anything, does the diagram fail to capture?

**4. Heidegger's Ecstases**
Heidegger describes authentic temporality as involving three "ecstases": running ahead toward death (future), taking over thrownness (having-been), and the moment of vision (present). Explain each ecstasis and then explain why Heidegger insists that these three are not three separate things but three moments of a unified structure. How does this differ from simply saying that life involves a past, present, and future?

**5. Vulgar vs. Originary Temporality**
Heidegger argues that "vulgar" time — the ordinary sequence of nows available to anyone — is derived from, and less fundamental than, originary temporality. Is this an empirical claim or a conceptual/ontological one? What would it mean for the claim to be false? Evaluate the argument.

**6. Merleau-Ponty and Embodied Habit**
Merleau-Ponty argues that the body carries the past in its habits, not merely in its memories. Using an example of a specific skill or habit you have developed, explain what Merleau-Ponty would say about the temporal structure of that habit. How does this account differ from Husserl's account of retention? How does it enrich or challenge it?

**7. Ricoeur's Threefold Mimesis**
Explain the three phases of mimesis in Ricoeur's account: prefiguration, configuration, and refiguration. Then apply the framework to a specific narrative you know well — a novel, a film, a historical account, or a story from your own life. What does the analysis reveal about how that narrative configures temporal experience?

**8. The Aporia of Time**
Ricoeur argues that the "aporia of time" — the tension between subjective and objective time — cannot be resolved by phenomenological analysis but can be negotiated through narrative. Is this a satisfying conclusion? Is it a form of philosophical defeat, or is it a genuine philosophical achievement? Defend your view with reference to the specific aporias Ricoeur identifies.

#### Comparative Essay Exercises

**9. Husserl and Heidegger on the Present**
Compare Husserl's concept of the "primal impression" with Heidegger's concept of the *Augenblick* (moment of vision). Both are accounts of the present, but they are very different accounts. What does each capture that the other misses? Is there a way to integrate them, or are they fundamentally incompatible?

**10. Embodiment and Temporal Constitution**
Merleau-Ponty argues that temporal experience is grounded in the motor body rather than in pure consciousness. Critically evaluate this claim. Are there aspects of temporal experience — such as the experience of regret, anticipation of death, or narrative self-understanding — that seem to require more than the motor body can provide? What does your assessment imply about the relationship between Merleau-Ponty's account and those of Husserl and Ricoeur?

#### Observational and Experiential Lab Exercises

**11. The Melody Experiment (Lab)**
This exercise requires approximately 20 minutes and a recording of a short piece of music — preferably something unfamiliar.

First, listen to the piece once with your eyes closed. After listening, write a paragraph describing your experience. Try to capture: Did you hear the piece as a unified musical object, or as a series of separate sounds? Were you aware, while hearing any given note, of what came before it? Was there a sense of forward momentum, of the music "going somewhere"?

Second, listen again, but this time try to attend specifically to the phenomenological structure Husserl describes: as each note sounds, notice the "trailing" presence of the previous notes (the retention), the freshness of the current note (the primal impression), and the forward lean toward what is coming (the protention). Write a paragraph describing whether you can identify these three structures in your actual experience.

Third, reflect: does Husserl's analysis match your experience? What aspects does it capture well? What aspects does it miss or distort?

**12. Embodied Temporal Habit (Lab)**
Choose a physical skill you have practiced enough to perform habitually — typing, playing an instrument, riding a bicycle, cooking a familiar dish, or any comparable activity. Perform the activity for five to ten minutes. Then answer the following questions:

(a) During the activity, were you consciously recalling how to do it, or was the knowledge "in your hands"? What is the difference?
(b) Merleau-Ponty says that a habit is the past "sedimented" in the body. Can you identify the sense in which your past practice is present in your current performance — not as memory, but as practical disposition?
(c) Was there a sense in which your body was anticipating the next movements before you consciously directed it? Describe this as precisely as you can.
(d) Now compare your experience with Husserl's account of protention. Are these the same phenomenon? Are they related? How?

**13. Temporal Field of a Waiting Experience (Lab)**
Find an occasion when you are genuinely waiting for something — waiting for an important email, waiting in a waiting room, waiting for a result to come in. During the wait, pay close attention to your temporal experience and take notes (or write them up immediately afterward) addressing the following:

(a) Describe the "temporal field" of the waiting experience. Is the future narrowed to a point (the awaited event), or does it have a broader structure?
(b) Is your experience of the past different during the wait than at other times? Do past events seem more or less present? More or less distant?
(c) Merleau-Ponty describes the "field of presence" as a feature of embodied experience. Does your body seem to be involved in the waiting — not just your mind? Describe any bodily dimensions of the temporal experience.
(d) Does the experience of waiting confirm, challenge, or complicate any of the phenomenological analyses in this chapter? Explain.

#### Annotated Entries

**Husserl, Edmund. *On the Phenomenology of the Consciousness of Internal Time (1893–1917)*. Translated by John Barnett Brough. Dordrecht: Kluwer, 1991.**
The primary source for Husserl's analysis of time-consciousness, containing the famous 1905 lectures together with supplementary texts from across Husserl's career. Translator Brough's introduction is an indispensable guide to the complexities of the text. Required reading for anyone who wants to engage seriously with phenomenological approaches to time.

**Zahavi, Dan. *Husserl's Phenomenology*. Stanford: Stanford University Press, 2003.**
The most accessible and rigorous secondary guide to Husserl's thought currently available in English. Chapter 4 (on internal time-consciousness) and Chapter 5 (on the absolute flow and self-awareness) are directly relevant to this chapter. Zahavi's interpretive framework — understanding the absolute flow as the structure of pre-reflective self-awareness — is one of the most influential approaches to Husserl's most difficult claims.

**Heidegger, Martin. *Being and Time*. Translated by John Macquarrie and Edward Robinson. New York: Harper and Row, 1962.**
The central text for Heidegger's account of temporality, developed in Division II (§§54–83). The analysis of authentic temporality and its ecstases is in §§65–68, and the account of vulgar time and its derivation is in §§78–83. Heidegger's writing is dense and requires patience; a good secondary guide (such as Dreyfus 1991 or Blattner 2006) is recommended alongside the primary text.

**Merleau-Ponty, Maurice. *Phenomenology of Perception*. Translated by Donald A. Landes. London: Routledge, 2012.**
Merleau-Ponty's analysis of time appears in Part III, Chapter 2. The Landes translation (2012) is considered more accurate than the earlier Routledge translation by Colin Smith. Reading Part II (on the body) before the temporal analysis is strongly recommended, as the temporal analysis presupposes the account of motor intentionality developed there.

**Ricoeur, Paul. *Time and Narrative*, Vol. 1. Translated by Kathleen McLaughlin and David Pellauer. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984.**
The foundational text of Ricoeur's project. Chapter 1 (on the aporia of time in Augustine and Aristotle) and Chapter 3 (on emplotment and the threefold mimesis) are the most directly relevant to this chapter. Ricoeur's style is demanding but rewarding; the argument builds across all three volumes, and readers who engage seriously will be richly rewarded.

**Ricoeur, Paul. *Oneself as Another*. Translated by Kathleen Blamey. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1992.**
This later work develops the concept of narrative identity and the distinction between idem-identity and ipse-identity. Chapters 5–6 (on personal identity and narrative identity) are most relevant. The book as a whole is Ricoeur's major contribution to ethics and the philosophy of action, and it shows how the phenomenology of time connects directly to questions about selfhood, responsibility, and moral life.

**Gallagher, Shaun, and Dan Zahavi. *The Phenomenological Mind*. 3rd ed. London: Routledge, 2021.**
An excellent introductory and intermediate survey of phenomenological philosophy of mind, with a chapter on time-consciousness that surveys the major positions. Gallagher and Zahavi are attentive to the connections between phenomenological and cognitive scientific approaches, making this a useful bridge text for readers coming from psychology or neuroscience backgrounds.

**Sokolowski, Robert. *Husserlian Meditations*. Evanston: Northwestern University Press, 1974.**
An older but still valuable guide to Husserl's thought, with particularly clear expositions of the structure of time-consciousness and the relationship between retention, recollection, and imagination. Sokolowski's style is unusually clear for Husserl scholarship, and his chapters on temporal consciousness remain among the best available introductions to the topic.

**Blattner, William. *Heidegger's Being and Time: A Reader's Guide*. London: Continuum, 2006.**
A clear and reliable guide to *Being and Time*, organized to follow the text's structure. The chapters on authentic temporality and the derivation of vulgar time are particularly useful for navigating Heidegger's dense analysis. Blattner's interpretation is one of the most analytically careful in the secondary literature.

**Dreyfus, Hubert. *Being-in-the-World: A Commentary on Heidegger's Being and Time, Division I*. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1991.**
Though focused on Division I, this remains one of the most influential English-language readings of Heidegger, and Dreyfus's background chapters on Husserl and the relationship between Heidegger and the phenomenological tradition are invaluable for understanding the context of Heidegger's temporal analysis.

**Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences** (journal, 2002–present). The leading journal for work at the intersection of phenomenology and cognitive science, regularly publishing research on temporal experience from both philosophical and empirical perspectives. An essential resource for readers who want to follow the ongoing dialogue between phenomenology and empirical temporal cognition.

**Stern, Daniel. *The Present Moment in Psychotherapy and Everyday Life*. New York: Norton, 2004.**
A psychoanalytic and developmental psychologist's engagement with the phenomenological concept of the present moment. Stern draws on Husserl's analysis of the living present and connects it to empirical findings about the "specious present" and the temporal structure of interpersonal interaction. A valuable bridge between phenomenology and clinical psychology.

**Wood, David. *The Deconstruction of Time*. Evanston: Northwestern University Press, 2001.**
A sophisticated engagement with the phenomenological tradition on time, with particular attention to Heidegger and Derrida. Wood is attentive to the aporias and difficulties within the phenomenological tradition itself, and his analysis of the relationship between Heidegger's authentic temporality and the "deconstruction" of linear time is illuminating.

### Important Concepts: Chapter 26

**Absolute Flow** (*absoluter Fluss*): Husserl's term for the self-constituting flow of consciousness that underlies all temporal experience. The absolute flow is not in time in the ordinary sense; it is what constitutes temporal experience from the inside, without requiring a further temporal framework to explain its own temporality. Its self-constituting character makes it the ultimate ground of all time-consciousness.

**Aporia of Time**: Ricoeur's term for the fundamental tension in philosophical accounts of time between the subjective (phenomenological, Augustinian) perspective and the objective (cosmological, Aristotelian) perspective. This tension cannot be definitively resolved by philosophical analysis alone but can be "negotiated" through narrative configuration. The aporia is a permanent feature of the human condition, not a solvable problem.

**Authentic Temporality** (*eigentliche Zeitlichkeit*): Heidegger's term for the originary temporal structure of *Dasein* as it exists in anticipatory resoluteness — running ahead toward death, taking over its thrownness, and making resolute decisions in the moment of vision. Authentic temporality is not a sequence of nows but a unified ecstatic structure in which future, having-been, and present are co-constitutive.

**Augenblick** (Moment of Vision): Heidegger's term for the authentic present — the present as it is constituted within anticipatory resoluteness. The *Augenblick* is not the neutral "now" of public time but the moment in which *Dasein*, clear-eyed about its finitude and resolute about its possibilities, sees its situation and acts. It has weight and significance that ordinary clock-time lacks.

**Care** (*Sorge*): Heidegger's term for the fundamental structure of *Dasein*'s being: being-ahead-of-itself (projection), already-in (thrownness), and alongside (falling). Care is the unified structure that authentic temporality makes possible. The analysis of temporality in Division II of *Being and Time* is an analysis of the ontological ground of care.

**Ecstases of Temporality**: Heidegger's term for the three fundamental "standing-outside-of-oneself" moments that constitute authentic temporality: future (running ahead), having-been (thrownness), and present (moment of vision). "Ecstasis" (literally: standing outside) captures the idea that *Dasein* is always already "outside itself" toward its past and future, not enclosed in a punctual now.

**Emplotment** (*mise en intrigue*): Ricoeur's term for the configurational act at the heart of narrative — the operation by which a narrator weaves together diverse events, characters, and circumstances into a unified, followable story with a beginning, middle, and end. Emplotment transforms a mere sequence of events into a narrative whole. It is Ricoeur's answer to the aporia of time: by configuring events into a plot, narrative gives time a human shape.

**Field of Presence**: Merleau-Ponty's term for the extended temporal field within which embodied experience is always already situated. Rather than being organized around a central "now" that radiates outward through retention and protention, temporal experience is field-like: I am in a temporal context that surrounds me, constituted by my bodily habits and practical orientations. The field of presence is pre-given by embodiment, not constructed by conscious acts.

**Ipse-Identity**: Ricoeur's term for the identity of selfhood — the kind of identity that consists in remaining true to oneself in the sense of keeping commitments and promises. Ipse-identity is distinct from idem-identity (numerical or qualitative sameness) because it is not a static property of an object but a dynamic achievement of a self that persists through time by honoring its commitments.

**Living Present** (*lebendige Gegenwart*): Husserl's term for the experienced now, understood as an extended, three-part structure rather than a punctual instant. The living present encompasses the primal impression of the current moment, the retention of the just-past, and the protention of the about-to-come. It is the most fundamental structure of time-consciousness and the ground of any possible experience of temporal objects.

**Mimesis**: Ricoeur's term (borrowed from Aristotle's *Poetics*) for the threefold process by which narrative mediates between lived temporal experience and its configuration into humanly intelligible form. The three phases — prefiguration (mimesis I), configuration (mimesis II), and refiguration (mimesis III) — describe the circular relationship between lived experience and narrative that gives time its human character.

**Modification** (Brentano): Brentano's term for the transformation that past sensations undergo in consciousness: rather than being recalled by a separate act of memory, just-past sensations persist in the present moment in a modified form — as "just-now" tones with a quality of pastness. Husserl appropriates the concept of modification but argues that the modification must be of the intentional act, not of the perceived content.

**Narrative Identity**: Ricoeur's concept of personal identity over time as constituted by the coherence of a life story. Narrative identity mediates between idem-identity (numerical sameness) and ipse-identity (selfhood as commitment). It is not a fixed essence but an ongoing interpretive achievement — the self is the self that tells and retells this story about this life.

**Originary Temporality**: Heidegger's term for the authentic, ecstatic temporal structure of *Dasein*, as opposed to "vulgar time" (the ordinary sequence of nows). Originary temporality is prior to, and is the source of, vulgar time: public, clock time is a derived and leveled-off version of the existential temporal structure of finite human existence.

**Primal Impression** (*Urimpression*): Husserl's term for the phase of the living present in which something is given as strictly and genuinely now — the source-point of temporal experience. The primal impression is the moment of direct contact with the present, but it never exists in isolation: it is always already surrounded by retention (just-past) and protention (about-to-come).

**Protention**: Husserl's term for the intentional phase of the living present directed toward the about-to-come. Protention is not a conscious expectation or prediction but a pre-reflective forward anticipation built into the structure of every moment of experience. It is the "empty" intentionality that reaches toward what has not yet occurred, and it is fulfilled when the anticipated event arrives and becomes a primal impression.

**Retention**: Husserl's term for the intentional phase of the living present that holds the just-past within the current experience. Retention is not memory: it involves no separate representational act, no re-presentation of a past event. Rather, the just-past is directly given in a retentional mode — present as just-having-been, with a phenomenal quality of pastness that distinguishes it from the primal impression.

**Thrownness** (*Geworfenheit*): Heidegger's term for the factical situation into which *Dasein* has been cast without its choice — including one's historical period, culture, language, body, family, and circumstances. Thrownness is not merely the past; it is the weight of the past as it shapes and constrains current existence. Authentic temporality involves "taking over" one's thrownness — not passively accepting or actively denying it, but appropriating it as genuinely one's own.

**Vulgar Time**: Heidegger's term for the ordinary, public conception of time as an infinite sequence of indifferent "now-points" — the time of clocks, calendars, and schedules available to anyone. Vulgar time is not illusory but derivative: it is what originary temporality looks like when the existential significance of temporal ecstases is stripped away through the leveling-off and publicizing characteristic of inauthentic existence.

### Important Researchers and Thinkers: Chapter 26

**Franz Brentano (1838–1917)**: Austrian philosopher and psychologist whose lectures in Vienna in the 1890s identified the puzzle of temporal consciousness that would occupy phenomenologists for the next century. Brentano's account of how past sensations persist in consciousness in a "modified" mode — as just-now sensations with a quality of pastness — was the direct precursor of Husserl's analysis of retention. Husserl studied under Brentano and acknowledged his debt while arguing that Brentano's account confused the modification of content with the modification of the intentional act. Brentano's broader project of descriptive psychology — the rigorous, systematic description of mental phenomena — was the methodological foundation on which phenomenology built. His most important works are *Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint* (1874) and the posthumously reconstructed *Philosophical Investigations on Time, Space, and the Continuum* (1988).

**Edmund Husserl (1859–1938)**: German philosopher and founder of the phenomenological movement. Husserl's analysis of time-consciousness, developed in lectures delivered around 1905 and reworked over subsequent decades (published as *Lectures on the Phenomenology of the Consciousness of Internal Time*, 1991), is one of the most systematic and influential investigations of temporal experience in the history of philosophy. His identification of the three-part structure of the living present — primal impression, retention, protention — provides a transcendental analysis of the conditions of possibility for any experience of temporal objects. His later work on the "absolute flow" and the "time-constituting consciousness" extends this analysis into some of the deepest and most contested regions of phenomenological inquiry. Husserl's influence on the entire phenomenological tradition — on Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, Sartre, Ricoeur, and Zahavi, among many others — is difficult to overstate.

**Martin Heidegger (1889–1976)**: German philosopher and Husserl's most prominent student, whose *Being and Time* (1927) transformed the phenomenological analysis of time by embedding it within a fundamental ontology of human existence. Heidegger argues that temporality (*Zeitlichkeit*) is the "ontological meaning of care" — the deep structure of what it means to be a human being in the world. His distinction between authentic temporality (with its three ecstases) and vulgar time (the derived sequence of public nows) remains one of the most influential frameworks for thinking about the relationship between lived time and objective time. Heidegger's later work on the "history of being" and the question of "being and time" at a cosmic scale extends these concerns in ways that continue to be debated. His political association with National Socialism in 1933–1934 remains a source of ongoing scholarly and ethical controversy.

**Maurice Merleau-Ponty (1908–1961)**: French phenomenologist whose *Phenomenology of Perception* (1945) developed a comprehensive analysis of embodied experience that transformed every major topic in phenomenology, including the analysis of time. Merleau-Ponty's insistence that consciousness is irreducibly embodied — that the perceived world is constituted not by a transcendental ego but by a "motor intentionality" rooted in the lived body — grounds temporal experience in bodily habit, practical engagement, and the "field of presence" rather than in the acts of a disembodied consciousness. His concept of the motor body as a "temporal archive" — carrying the past in its habits and reaching forward toward anticipated action — anticipates and connects with contemporary work in embodied cognition and enactivism. His untimely death at 53 cut short a philosophical career that was deepening in its later phases.

**Paul Ricoeur (1913–2005)**: French philosopher whose three-volume *Time and Narrative* (1984–1988) and *Oneself as Another* (1992) constitute the most ambitious attempt in twentieth-century philosophy to connect the phenomenology of time with the human practice of narrative. Ricoeur's concepts of threefold mimesis, narrative identity, and the distinction between idem-identity and ipse-identity have been profoundly influential across philosophy, literary theory, theology, and the social sciences. Ricoeur's method — patient, rigorous, open to dialogue with traditions and disciplines beyond phenomenology — exemplifies a philosophical temperament that is at once analytic in its precision and continental in its scope. He was awarded the Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy in 1999.

**Dan Zahavi (born 1967)**: Danish phenomenologist and one of the most important interpreters of Husserl's work on time-consciousness. His *Husserl's Phenomenology* (2003) provides the most accessible and rigorous guide to the architecture of Husserl's thought, including its temporal dimensions, currently available in English.
