Or we can accept both on their own terms: maintain that physics and phenomenology are describing different aspects of reality, and develop an account of how they relate.

This section develops the third option — the "two-level" account — in some detail, while acknowledging the trade-offs of all three positions. It is the position the author finds most defensible, but the goal is to present the alternatives fairly enough that you can reach your own considered judgment.

#### The Two-Level Account: Physics, Phenomenology, and Their Relationship

##### The Three Options Restated

The tension between the block universe of physics and the experienced passage of time has generated three broad strategies of response.

**Option (a): Debunk the phenomenology.** Accept that physics gives us the correct picture of temporal reality: a static four-dimensional manifold with no objective passage. The experienced passage is an illusion — generated by the memory-anticipation asymmetry, the self-model system, or the changing neural states of the brain. The phenomenological tradition has systematically misdescribed the character of experience, or has correctly described experience but incorrectly concluded that experience is tracking an objective feature of the world.

**Option (b): Revise the physics.** Accept that the phenomenology is tracking something real — that temporal passage is objectively real — and revise the physics accordingly. This means adopting some form of A-theory of time: presentism, the growing block theory, or the moving spotlight theory. The physics of the block universe is incorrect, or at least incomplete, as a description of temporal reality.

**Option (c): Accept both levels.** Maintain that physics and phenomenology are describing different levels of reality — or different aspects of the same reality — without either trumping or eliminating the other. Physics describes the objective, observer-independent structure of spacetime. Phenomenology describes how conscious beings with specific cognitive architectures process and experience that structure. Both descriptions are valid within their respective domains, and the relationship between them is a subject for further investigation.

##### The Case for Option (c)

The two-level account (option c) has several significant advantages over the alternatives.

**Against option (a)**: The debunking strategy faces the problem of phenomenological residue. Even granting that passage is generated by cognitive asymmetry or neural dynamics, the fact that it is vivid, pervasive, and seemingly ineliminable from experience suggests that it is tracking something real about the character of consciousness — even if not about the objective structure of time. The analogy with color is instructive: we accept that "red" does not correspond to an objective physical property of surfaces, but we do not conclude that the redness of red as experienced is an illusion. It is a real phenomenal property, though its relation to physics is mediated and complex. The same may be said of temporal passage: it is a real phenomenal property of experience, even if its relation to physics is mediated (Chalmers 1996; Callender 2017: 150–165).

More importantly, the debunking strategy threatens to undermine the very notion of perceptual access to the world. If we can dismiss the most vivid and universal feature of temporal experience — its flowingness — as a mere cognitive illusion, what principle prevents us from dismissing other features of experience in the same way? The debunking strategy requires a principled account of when and why cognitive construction diverges from reality that does not extend to the elimination of all phenomenal properties.

**Against option (b)**: The physics-revision strategy faces serious challenges from relativity. As noted above, A-theoretic passage requires a privileged foliation of spacetime — a global "present" — that is not available in the standard formulation of special relativity. While philosophers like Skow have argued that this does not make A-theory incoherent, the cost in terms of undetectable physical structure is significant. Moreover, if we revise physics to accommodate passage, we need an account of how the posited passage-facts connect with the physical facts we can measure. This account has not yet been developed to a satisfactory level.

##### The Two-Level Account in Detail

The most defensible position, as we develop it here, holds that physics and phenomenology are legitimately autonomous domains of inquiry with different subject matters and different methods, and that the apparent conflict between them arises from a category mistake: treating phenomenological claims as if they were physical claims, or physical claims as if they settled phenomenological questions.

**Physics describes objective temporal structure.** The four-dimensional spacetime manifold of physics is the best current description of the objective, observer-independent structure of time. The block universe picture — in which all times are equally real and there is no objective "now" — is supported by an enormous body of evidence. It tells us the geometric structure of time as a physical dimension.

**Phenomenology describes the structure of temporal experience.** The phenomenological tradition, from Husserl through Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, and Ricoeur, is in the business of describing the structure of experience as experience — the way in which temporal objects are given to a conscious subject. This is a different enterprise from physics. Phenomenology is not making claims about the objective temporal structure of the physical world; it is describing the a priori structures of any possible temporal experience. The "living present," the "ecstases of temporality," the "field of presence" — these are structures of experience, not features of the physical manifold.

**The sense of passage belongs to phenomenology, not to physics.** The sense that time is passing — that the present is moving, that we are being carried from past to future — is a phenomenological feature of experience. As a phenomenological feature, it is real: it is genuinely present in experience, and phenomenological analysis can describe its character, its variations, and its conditions. As a phenomenological feature, it does not need to correspond to any objective physical property of the temporal manifold to be "real." Just as the redness of red is a real phenomenal property even if there is no objective physical "redness," the flowingness of experience is a real phenomenal property even if there is no objective physical "flow."

**The relationship between levels requires investigation.** Accepting that physics and phenomenology operate at different levels does not mean that they have nothing to say to each other. The relationship between the physical description of time (objective temporal structure, causal asymmetry, entropic asymmetry) and the phenomenological description of temporal experience (living present, sense of passage, temporal self-location) is a genuine and important question — perhaps the central question for a complete account of time. The cognitive science of temporal experience (Chapter 27) is one part of the answer: it shows how specific cognitive mechanisms implement temporal experience in creatures with specific neural architectures embedded in a physically asymmetric world.

##### Trade-offs and Remaining Questions

The two-level account is not without costs. Its main vulnerabilities are:

**The relationship problem**: Saying that physics and phenomenology operate at different levels leaves the relationship between them underspecified. A complete account requires not just that the two levels are different but an account of how they connect — how physical temporal structure gives rise to (or supports, or constrains) the phenomenological structures of temporal experience. This "bridge" account is not yet available in satisfactory form.

**The integration question**: If physics provides no objective passage and phenomenology describes passage as real, we face the question of how to integrate these two descriptions into a single coherent picture of the world. The two-level account risks leaving us with two incommensurable pictures: a physical world without passage and an experiential world full of it. How are these two worlds the same world?

**The normativity of physics**: There is a persistent temptation to regard physics as the arbiter of what is real — the "gold standard" for ontological commitment. On this view, if physics does not describe passage, then passage is not real. The two-level account resists this temptation, but it needs to offer a principled reason for doing so rather than merely asserting that phenomenology has independent standing.

Despite these challenges, the two-level account is the most defensible available position, for the following reason: it is the only position that takes both the physics and the phenomenology seriously, without prematurely debunking one or revising the other in ways that are not yet adequately supported. The question of how the two levels relate remains genuinely open — and sitting with an open question honestly is sometimes the most intellectually responsible position available. The philosophy of time is not the only domain in which mind and world face each other across a gap that cannot yet be fully bridged; but it is one of the domains where that gap is most sharply felt, and most philosophically instructive.

### Chapter 28 Exercises: The Passage of Time

#### Analytical Exercises

**1. The Rate-of-Passage Argument**
Reconstruct the rate-of-passage argument (Williams 1951; Smart 1949) as carefully as you can. Then evaluate: is the argument sound? Does it show that temporal passage is incoherent, or merely that the phrase "rate of passage" requires careful handling? Consider the response that "one second per second" is an adequate answer (since time is its own standard of measurement) and the response that Skow proposes (that rate of passage is a primitive). Which, if any, succeeds?

**2. The Indexicality Response**
Explain the indexicality response to the rate-of-passage problem: the view that "now" is an indexical term, and the "movement" of the now is simply the fact that different times are picked out by "now" at different times of utterance. (a) Does this response dissolve the problem or merely relocate it? (b) Does it adequately account for the phenomenological experience of passage — the sense that we are being carried along by time? Defend your view.

**3. The No-Passage View**
Callender (2017) argues that the sense of temporal passage is generated by the asymmetry between our representations of the past and future, together with other cognitive factors, without any need for objective passage in the physical world. (a) Explain this view as precisely as you can. (b) Does it provide a satisfying explanation of the phenomenological experience of passage, or does it leave something out? (c) What is the relationship between the "cognitive illusion" of passage and the "genuine experience" of passage? Are these compatible?

**4. Skow's Moving Spotlight Theory**
Bradford Skow (2015) defends the moving spotlight theory: there is an objective property of being present that genuinely "moves" along the temporal sequence. (a) Explain the theory. (b) How does Skow respond to the rate-of-passage problem? Is his response convincing? (c) What is the cost of the theory in terms of undetectable physical structure (the preferred foliation), and is this cost acceptable?

**5. Primitive Passage and the Analogy with Consciousness**
The primitive passage thesis holds that temporal passage is irreducible — not explicable in terms of anything more fundamental, just as phenomenal consciousness may not be reducible to functional or physical properties. (a) Explain the analogy between temporal passage and phenomenal consciousness. (b) Does the analogy support the primitive passage thesis, or does it merely show that both phenomena are puzzling? (c) What would it mean to "accept" that passage is primitive? Does this amount to explaining anything?

**6. The Two-Level Account**
The "two-level" account proposed in this chapter holds that physics and phenomenology are legitimate autonomous domains of inquiry that describe different aspects of reality. (a) Explain the account. (b) What are its main advantages over the debunking strategy (option a) and the physics-revision strategy (option b)? (c) What are its main vulnerabilities, and how might they be addressed? (d) Do you find the account persuasive? Explain.

**7. The Phenomenology of Passage and Its Variations**
The experience of temporal passage varies across different states: it is barely noticeable in flow states, oppressively salient in depression and severe anxiety, and dramatically altered in fear. What does this variability tell us about the nature of the passage experience? Does it support the view that passage is a cognitive construction (since constructions can be disrupted) or is it compatible with the view that passage is real (since real features of the world can be perceived more or less clearly)?

**8. Temporal Passage and the A-Theory**
The A-theory holds that the distinction between past, present, and future is a genuine, objective, irreducible distinction — not analyzable in terms of the B-theory's earlier-later relations. How does the A-theory bear on the question of temporal passage? Does accepting A-theory commit one to objective temporal passage? Does accepting B-theory commit one to the no-passage view? Examine the relationship between these metaphysical positions and the question of passage.

#### Observational and Experiential Lab Exercises

**9. Phenomenology of Flow (Lab)**
Set aside thirty to forty-five minutes for a structured experience of temporal passage. Divide your time as follows:

*First period* (ten to fifteen minutes): sit quietly with nothing to do and no phone. Pay close attention to the experience of time passing. Note: Is there a felt "movement" to the experience? In what direction? Does the present feel special in comparison to the past moments you remember and the future you anticipate? Try to describe the phenomenological texture of temporal passage as precisely as you can.

*Second period* (ten to fifteen minutes): engage in something you find genuinely absorbing — a puzzle, music, drawing, or reading something interesting. Try to continue paying attention to whether you experience temporal passage.

*Third period* (five minutes): sit quietly again. Compare your experience in the three periods.

Write a paragraph characterizing the differences. Does the absorbed state diminish the sense of passage, or merely relocate attention away from it? Does the return to the quiet state bring a strong sense of passage back? What does this variability suggest about the nature of the passage experience?

**10. The "Nowness" of the Present (Lab)**
Find a moment when you have a few minutes of quiet, undisturbed attention. Focus on the present moment — not on any thoughts about the past or future, but simply on what is occurring right now: sounds, sensations, the quality of the moment.

Try to identify, as specifically as possible, what gives this moment the quality of being "now" as opposed to being merely a remembered moment or an anticipated moment. Is there a felt quality of actuality, of "this is happening," that distinguishes the present from the past and future? Can you sustain attention on this quality? Does it fade when you try to focus on it directly?

Write a reflection on what you found. Connect your observations to the philosophical accounts of the phenomenology of passage discussed in this chapter. Does your experience support the view that "nowness" is a vivid feature of experience, or does it suggest that "nowness" is more elusive than it seems?

**11. Imagining the Block Universe (Lab)**
Philosophical thought experiments can be enriched by attempting to inhabit them phenomenologically. Try the following:

Attempt to imagine the world as described by the block universe view: a four-dimensional "block" of events, all equally real, none objectively more present or more actual than any other. All the moments of your life — past, present, and future — are equally real "parts" of you in this block. There is no flowing, no becoming, no special present; just an extended pattern of events arranged along the time dimension.

Now try to imagine inhabiting this world as a conscious being. What would experience be like if the block universe description were complete? Would experience feel the same as it does, or would something be missing? Can you even fully imagine experience from "within" the block universe, or does the imaginative exercise always reintroduce the sense of passage?

Write a reflection on what you found. Does the thought experiment support or challenge the two-level account? Does it suggest that the sense of passage is ineliminable from experience even when one intellectually accepts the block universe?

#### Annotated Entries

**Williams, Donald C. "The Myth of Passage." *Journal of Philosophy* 48, no. 15 (1951): 457–472.**
The locus classicus for the no-passage view and the rate-of-passage argument. Williams argues with admirable clarity that the "passage" of time is literally incoherent and that the appearance of flow is a myth generated by confused thinking. Even readers who reject his conclusion will benefit from confronting the argument in its sharpest form. Essential reading.

**Smart, J. J. C. "The River of Time." *Mind* 58, no. 232 (1949): 483–494.**
An independent statement of the rate-of-passage argument, slightly earlier than Williams's, with particularly clear treatment of the regress problem. Smart's paper also connects the no-passage view to a broader scientific realism about the physical world and a skepticism about metaphysical excess. An important companion to Williams.

**McTaggart, J. M. E. "The Unreality of Time." *Mind* 17, no. 68 (1908): 457–474.**
The foundational paper for the A-series/B-series distinction that structures the entire debate. McTaggart's argument that the A-series is both necessary for time and incoherent is famously contested, but the analytic framework he introduces remains the standard conceptual vocabulary of the field. Should be read by anyone who wants to understand the debate about temporal passage.

**Callender, Craig. *What Makes Time Special?* Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2017.**
The most comprehensive and accessible recent defense of the no-passage view, with a positive account of what makes time different from space without requiring objective A-theoretic passage. Callender's treatment of the cognitive sources of the sense of passage is particularly valuable, and his engagement with both physics and philosophy is exemplary. Required reading for the contemporary debate.

**Skow, Bradford. *Objective Becoming*. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2015.**
The most careful recent defense of objective temporal passage, developing the moving spotlight theory and responding to the rate-of-passage objection. Skow's treatment is honest about the costs of his view (the undetectable preferred foliation) and rigorous in its engagement with physics. Required reading for anyone who wants to understand the best case for objective passage.

**Prosser, Simon. *Experiencing Time*. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2016.**
A systematic philosophical treatment of the relationship between temporal experience and temporal metaphysics. Prosser argues with care and rigor that no objective feature of the world could produce the specific phenomenological character of temporal passage, and provides a positive account of why we experience passage without any objective reality underlying it. An important and underread contribution to the debate.

**Le Poidevin, Robin. *The Images of Time: An Essay on Temporal Representation*. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007.**
An excellent treatment of temporal representation — how we mentally represent time, past, present, and future — with close attention to the relationship between temporal representation and temporal metaphysics. Le Poidevin navigates carefully between phenomenological and metaphysical considerations, making this a valuable bridge text.

**Maudlin, Tim. *The Metaphysics Within Physics*. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007.**
Contains one of the most serious contemporary defenses of temporal passage from a physicist-philosopher, arguing that temporal passage is a real and fundamental feature of the physical world that standard physics fails to capture adequately. Maudlin's view that temporal passage is primitive and irreducible — like the laws of nature themselves — is developed with characteristic rigor and boldness.

**Dainton, Barry. *Stream of Consciousness: Unity and Continuity in Conscious Experience*. 2nd ed. London: Routledge, 2006.**
A comprehensive treatment of the phenomenological structure of conscious experience, including extended discussion of temporal experience and its relationship to temporal metaphysics. Dainton defends the reality of the experienced flow of consciousness and connects this to debates about personal identity and the unity of experience. An important contribution from a philosopher who takes both phenomenology and metaphysics seriously.

**Metzinger, Thomas. *The Ego Tunnel: The Science of the Mind and the Myth of the Self*. New York: Basic Books, 2009.**
An accessible introduction to Metzinger's self-model theory of consciousness and its implications for the phenomenology of selfhood, including the temporal dimension of self-experience. Metzinger argues that the "self" is a model the brain constructs — the "tunnel" through which we experience reality — and that the sense of temporal passage is part of this constructed self-model. More accessible than *Being No One*, and an excellent starting point for Metzinger's work.

### Important Concepts: Chapter 28

**A-Theory of Time**: The family of views holding that the distinction between past, present, and future is a genuine, irreducible feature of temporal reality — not analyzable in terms of the B-theory's earlier-later relations. A-theories include presentism (only the present exists), the growing block theory (the present and past exist, but the future does not), and the moving spotlight theory (all times exist, but the present has a special property of "NOW"). The A-theory provides natural accommodation for objective temporal passage, which is why defenders of passage typically endorse some version of it.

**B-Theory of Time**: The view that the only genuine temporal facts are facts about the earlier-than, later-than, and simultaneous-with relations between events. The A-series properties (being past, present, or future) are either eliminable (purely eliminativist B-theory) or reducible to facts about the temporal relations events bear to the context of utterance. The B-theory is naturally associated with the block universe picture and with the no-passage view. The "B" stands for "B-series," McTaggart's term for the temporal series of before-and-after relations.

**Block Universe**: The metaphysical picture, suggested by four-dimensional spacetime physics, in which all times are equally real and the temporal dimension is, in this respect, like the spatial dimensions — just another direction in which events are distributed. In the block universe, there is no ontologically privileged "present," no objective "now," and no temporal passage: the universe "just is," spread out across all four dimensions. The block universe is the natural home of the B-theory and is the primary target of A-theory objections.

**Category Mistake**: An error that arises from applying a concept or framework to a domain for which it is inappropriate. Skow's response to the rate-of-passage problem appeals to this notion: asking "at what rate does the present move?" commits a category mistake because the concept of "rate" (requiring a second dimension against which to measure the first) does not apply to the moving of the spotlight, which is a primitive fact rather than a ratio of quantities.

**Cognitive Illusion of Passage**: The view, associated with no-passage theorists like Callender and Prosser, that the sense of temporal passage is not a veridical representation of an objective feature of the world but an artifact of cognitive architecture — specifically, of the asymmetry between how the brain represents the past (via memory traces) and how it represents the future (via anticipation). The illusion is systematic and explicable, not random or anomalous.

**Growing Block Theory**: The A-theory view that the past and present are real (as the "growing block" of already-actualized events) but the future does not yet exist. On this view, the present is the leading edge of the growing block — the moment at which new events are continually being "added" to reality. The growing block theory accommodates both the passage of time (events are continuously becoming part of the block) and the asymmetry between past and future (the past is fixed, the future is open) in a natural way.

**McTaggart's A-Series and B-Series**: J. M. E. McTaggart's distinction (1908) between two ways of ordering events in time: the B-series (ordering by earlier-than, later-than, simultaneous-with) and the A-series (ordering by past, present, and future). McTaggart argued that the A-series is more fundamental because it incorporates the passage of time — events move from future to present to past — but that the A-series is also incoherent, generating a vicious regress. This argument has generated the central debate between A-theorists and B-theorists.

**Moving Spotlight Theory**: The A-theory view, developed by Bradford Skow, that all times exist (as in the block universe) but that a special property — being "NOW" or being present — moves along the temporal sequence. The "spotlight" of the present illuminates each moment in turn, and this movement is what constitutes objective temporal passage. The theory attempts to accommodate both the reality of temporal passage and the four-dimensional structure of spacetime.

**No-Passage View**: The position, defended by Callender (2000, 2017) and Prosser (2016), among others, that there is no objective temporal passage: time does not flow, the present does not move, and the sense of passage is generated by cognitive features of temporally embedded creatures rather than by any objective feature of the temporal manifold. The no-passage view accepts the block universe picture and provides a positive cognitive explanation of why passage seems so vivid and real.

**Nowness**: The phenomenal quality that distinguishes the experienced present from experienced past or future — the quality of "this is happening now," of actuality, of what is occurring as opposed to what has occurred or will occur. The philosophical debate about temporal passage largely concerns whether this quality of nowness corresponds to an objective property of the present moment (as A-theorists hold) or whether it is a feature of the perspective of a temporally located observer (as B-theorists hold).

**Objective Becoming**: Skow's term for the genuine, non-perspectival fact that events come to be present and then recede into the past. Objective becoming is what the moving spotlight theory is designed to capture: the transition from future to present to past is not merely a change in how events are described from different perspectives but a genuine objective change in the temporal status of events.

**Phenomological Passage vs. Objective Passage**: A distinction crucial to the debate. Phenomenological passage is the felt experience of time flowing — the vivid sense that the present is moving, that the future is approaching, that we are being carried along. Objective passage would be an observer-independent feature of the world corresponding to this experience. The no-passage view accepts the reality of phenomenological passage (as a feature of experience) while denying objective passage (as a feature of the world).

**Preferred Foliation**: A specific way of slicing the four-dimensional spacetime manifold into a family of spacelike hyperplanes — a global "present" and its successive "futures." A preferred foliation is required by A-theories that posit an objective present. The problem is that preferred foliations are not detectable by any measurement (since special relativity says there is no preferred reference frame), so positing one amounts to adding undetectable structure to physics.

**Presentism**: The A-theory view that only the present moment exists — the past has ceased to exist and the future has not yet come to exist. Presentism gives the most radical ontological interpretation to temporal passage: at each moment, the present is the totality of what exists, and its passage involves the constant replacement of one moment's entities with the next moment's. Presentism faces serious challenges from special relativity's relativity of simultaneity.

**Rate of Passage**: The supposed rate at which time flows or the present moves — the target of the Williams-Smart objection. If time flows, it should flow at some rate. But "one second per second" is a tautology; a genuine rate requires two dimensions; and providing a second temporal dimension generates a vicious regress. Defenders of passage respond either that the rate is primitive (Skow) or that the question involves a category mistake.

**Two-Level Account**: The position that physics and phenomenology are legitimate autonomous domains that describe different aspects of temporal reality — the physical temporal structure of the world (objectively, without passage) and the structure of temporal experience (with its vivid sense of passage) respectively. On this account, neither level is reducible to the other, and the relationship between them is a subject for further investigation. The two-level account avoids debunking the phenomenology and avoids revising physics, at the cost of leaving the relationship between the two levels underspecified.

### Important Researchers and Thinkers: Chapter 28

**J. M. E. McTaggart (1866–1925)**: British idealist philosopher whose 1908 paper "The Unreality of Time" introduced the distinction between the A-series (ordering events as past, present, and future) and the B-series (ordering events as earlier-than, later-than, simultaneous-with) that has structured the debate about temporal passage ever since. McTaggart argued that the A-series is necessary for genuine time but that it is incoherent — generating a vicious regress — and therefore that time is unreal. Most subsequent philosophers have rejected his idealist conclusion while accepting his analytic framework.

**Donald C. Williams (1899–1983)**: American philosopher whose 1951 paper "The Myth of Passage" stated the rate-of-passage problem with unusual clarity and force. Williams argued that the "passage" of time — the idea of a flowing "now" — is a myth, generated by a confusion between the temporal dimension (real) and movement through the temporal dimension (a contradiction in terms). His paper is one of the most important contributions to the B-theory tradition and is still required reading in the philosophy of time.

**J. J. C. Smart (1920–2012)**: Australian-British philosopher who, in "The River of Time" (1949) and later work, developed the B-theory position and the objection to objective temporal passage. Smart's 1949 paper independently anticipated Williams's argument and connected the no-passage view to scientific realism. His contributions to the debate were wide-ranging, covering temporal language, temporal experience, and the relationship between common sense and scientific ontology.

**Bradford Skow (born 1975)**: American philosopher of physics whose *Objective Becoming* (2015) is the most careful recent defense of the moving spotlight theory and of the reality of objective temporal passage. Skow's treatment is notable for its rigorous engagement with both the philosophical literature and the physics, and for its careful response to the rate-of-passage problem. He accepts that the moving spotlight requires a preferred foliation of spacetime (an empirically undetectable physical structure) and argues that this cost is worth paying for a theory that accurately captures the reality of temporal passage.

**Craig Callender (born 1968)**: American philosopher of physics and one of the most prominent defenders of the no-passage view. His book *What Makes Time Special?* (2017) is a comprehensive treatment of what makes time different from space, arguing that most of the apparent "specialness" of time — including the sense of passage, the special status of the present, and the directionality of experience — is explained by the specific way in which temporally embedded creatures process information about a causally and thermodynamically asymmetric world, without any need for objective A-theoretic features of time.

**Simon Prosser**: British philosopher whose *Experiencing Time* (2016) provides the most systematic philosophical treatment of the relationship between temporal experience and temporal metaphysics. Prosser argues that no objective feature of the world could produce the specific phenomenological character of the passage experience, and provides a positive account of why we experience passage without it being real. He is a careful and rigorous defender of the no-passage view who takes the phenomenology seriously even while rejecting its apparent ontological implications.

**Thomas Metzinger (born 1958)**: German philosopher of mind whose work on the "phenomenal self-model" (PSM) — the brain's representation of itself — provides a framework for understanding how the sense of temporal passage is embedded in the broader sense of being a self in the world. Metzinger's account in *Being No One* (2003) and *The Ego Tunnel* (2009) offers a cognitive-scientific grounding for the phenomenological sense of passage without committing to its objective reality. His work is notable for its combination of rigorous philosophical analysis and deep engagement with neuroscience.

**C. D. Broad (1887–1971)**: British philosopher who, in *Scientific Thought* (1923), developed one of the earliest systematic analyses of temporal passage and argued that objective becoming — the genuine coming-into-existence of events at the "cutting edge" of time — is a real and fundamental feature of the world that cannot be captured by any static representation of temporal structure. Broad's growing block theory (in which the past and present exist but the future does not) remains one of the most influential A-theory positions.

# Unit IX: Time, Identity, and Persistence

Every object in the world exists in time, and most objects undergo change. The chair in which you sit has existed for years; it has been scratched, perhaps re-painted, possibly repaired. The river you cross today is the same river you crossed last week, though none of the water molecules are the same. You yourself are — or so we ordinarily say — the same person you were ten years ago, though you have changed in appearance, in knowledge, in belief, in circumstance, and perhaps in character. How is this possible? What makes a thing at one time the same thing as a thing at another time? And what makes you, in particular, the same person across the arc of your life?

These questions may sound like puzzles for specialists in metaphysics, and in some respects they are. But they have stakes that extend well beyond academic philosophy. The question of personal identity over time is implicated in our practices of holding people responsible for past actions, in our capacity to make and keep promises, in our concern for our future selves, and in the meaning we attach to our lives as wholes rather than as disconnected sequences of moments. If personal identity is, as Parfit argues, not what matters — if what matters in survival is some form of psychological continuity that can come apart from strict numerical identity — then large parts of our moral psychology may need revision. If personal identity is constituted by narrative, as MacIntyre and Ricoeur argue, then the coherence of a life is not given but achieved, and the philosophical stakes of how we tell our stories are immediately practical.

Chapter 29 examines the metaphysics of persistence more broadly — how any object persists through time and change. It begins with David Lewis's problem of temporary intrinsics, which is perhaps the sharpest formulation of the underlying puzzle, and then examines the two main competing theories: endurantism (the view that objects are wholly present at each time they exist) and perdurantism (the view that objects persist by having distinct temporal parts at different times). It also examines Ted Sider's stage theory as a variant of the perdurantist approach, and concludes with the Ship of Theseus as a test case for all three theories.

Chapter 30 turns to the special case of persons. Beginning with Locke's classical memory theory of personal identity and the objections raised by Reid and Butler, the chapter traces the development of the debate through Hume's bundle theory, the neo-Lockean psychological continuity views of Shoemaker and Parfit, and the animalist/biological view of Olson. It concludes with Parfit's revolutionary argument that identity is not what matters in survival, and with the narrative identity views of MacIntyre and Ricoeur that offer a richer and more humanistic framework for understanding what it means to be the same person over time.

Throughout both chapters, the goal is to combine analytical rigor with a clear sense of the human stakes of the questions. These are not merely technical puzzles about the persistence of ordinary objects; they are questions about what it means to be us — extended in time, shaped by a past we inherit and oriented toward a future we can only partly anticipate.

## Chapter 29: Persistence Through Time

Think of your favorite piece of furniture — something old that has been through a lot. Perhaps a wooden table that has been scratched, re-finished, had one leg replaced after a mishap, and been moved from house to house over thirty years. Is it the same table? Of course it is — or so we say without hesitation. But what makes it the same? It looks different than it did thirty years ago, is partly made of different matter, and has been in different places. And yet we count it as the same table. What underwrites this judgment?

This question — the question of persistence — applies to all objects that endure through time: rocks, rivers, organisms, institutions, and persons. Any object that exists at two different times potentially looks different, is in a different state, and has undergone change. How can it be the same object? There seem to be only a limited range of possible answers, and each comes with significant philosophical commitments.

This chapter begins with David Lewis's elegant formulation of the problem in terms of "temporary intrinsics" — properties that an object has at one time but not another, which seem to threaten the very coherence of change. Lewis's formulation is philosophically precise and serves as a useful anchor for the subsequent discussion of endurantism and perdurantism. After examining these two main competing views and their objections, the chapter turns to Ted Sider's stage theory as a third option, and concludes with a detailed examination of the Ship of Theseus puzzle — a thought experiment so simple that children find it immediately compelling, and so philosophically rich that it has been discussed for two and a half millennia.

### Section 1: Change and Temporary Intrinsics

The problem of persistence can be approached from many angles, but David Lewis's formulation in terms of "temporary intrinsics" is among the sharpest and most illuminating. It focuses our attention on a specific logical difficulty that arises whenever an object has incompatible intrinsic properties at different times, and it forces us to choose between a small number of philosophical options.

The power of Lewis's formulation is that it is not immediately about persons or ships or trees — objects about which we have rich intuitions and competing interests — but about intrinsic properties in the abstract. This level of generality helps to reveal the underlying logical structure of the problem and to evaluate the competing solutions on their merits before bringing them back to the cases that matter most.

#### The Problem of Temporary Intrinsics

##### Setting Up the Problem

David Lewis, in *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986), identifies a puzzle that he takes to be central to any adequate metaphysics of persistence. The puzzle concerns what he calls "temporary intrinsics" — intrinsic properties that an object instantiates at one time but not another.

An **intrinsic property** is a property an object has in virtue of itself alone, not in virtue of any relations it bears to other things. Being spherical is intrinsic (a sphere is spherical in itself, regardless of what is around it). Being taller than the Eiffel Tower is not intrinsic — it is a relational property that depends on what other things exist and what sizes they have. Being a sibling is not intrinsic — it depends on the existence of a sibling. Being shaped like an S is intrinsic — an S-shaped wire has that shape in virtue of its own structure.

Now consider a simple case. I am sitting right now. Sitting is an intrinsic property: I am bent into a sitting posture in virtue of how my own body is arranged, not in virtue of any relation to other things. An hour ago, I was standing. Standing is also an intrinsic property. I was then straight; I am now bent. These are incompatible properties. The straightness and the bentness cannot both be true of the very same thing — that would be a contradiction.

But both are true of me — of the same person, who exists both now and an hour ago. How is this possible? This is the problem of temporary intrinsics (Lewis 1986: 203–204).

##### Why This Is a Genuine Problem

The problem might seem trivially easy: "I was straight at one time and bent at another." But Lewis argues that this easy answer already presupposes one of the three solutions he is about to evaluate, and that the presupposition needs to be examined carefully.

The difficulty is this. If both properties — being straight and being bent — are genuinely instantiated by me, and if they are genuinely incompatible, then for them both to be true there must be something that relativizes them, something that explains why they do not contradict each other. What plays that role?

Three options are available. First, the properties could be relativized to times — "being straight *at t₁*" and "being bent *at t₂*" are not incompatible because they are different properties that include temporal qualifications. Second, the properties could be understood adverbially — I instantiate straightness *simpliciter* in a "t₁-way" and bentness *simpliciter* in a "t₂-way," with the adverb doing the relativizing work rather than the property itself. Third, the incompatible properties are instantiated by different things — not by me-over-time as a whole, but by different temporal parts of me, each of which instantiates only one of the incompatible properties.

Lewis argues that only the third option — temporal parts — is fully satisfactory (Lewis 1986: 204). The first two options face serious difficulties, and the third, while it requires accepting the existence of temporal parts (and thus a perdurantist metaphysics), is the cleanest and most principled solution.

##### The Stakes

Why does this matter? The problem of temporary intrinsics is not just an abstract puzzle. It is the underlying metaphysical issue that separates endurantists from perdurantists about persistence. Endurantists hold that objects are wholly present at each time they exist — that there are no temporal parts; the whole object is there at each moment. But if the whole object is present at each moment, and it has incompatible intrinsic properties at different moments, then the object seems to instantiate contradictory properties, which is impossible.

Perdurantists hold that objects persist by having temporal parts at each time — that what is present at any given moment is not the whole object but a temporal part (a "stage") of it. Different stages have different intrinsic properties, and there is no contradiction because the same whole object does not instantiate both properties; rather, different temporal parts instantiate them.

The problem of temporary intrinsics thus motivates one of the central debates in the metaphysics of time and persistence. But as we will see, the endurantist position is not without resources, and the debate turns on questions about what properties really are, how they are instantiated, and what it means for an object to be "wholly present" at a time.

#### Three Solutions to the Problem of Temporary Intrinsics

##### Solution One: Adverbialism

The first solution to the problem of temporary intrinsics is **adverbialism**: the idea that when an object instantiates a temporary intrinsic property, the instantiation itself should be understood adverbially — as qualifying the mode or manner of instantiation rather than the property instantiated.

On the adverbial view, it is not that I instantiate the property "being bent" at time t₂ and the property "being straight" at time t₁ as if these were genuinely incompatible properties both held by the same thing. Rather, I instantiate "bentness" in a t₂-manner and "straightness" in a t₁-manner. The adverbs "in a t₂-manner" and "in a t₁-manner" do the logical work of preventing the incompatibility: the two instantiation facts are not about the same mode of instantiation, so they do not conflict.

The term "adverbialism" comes from a parallel strategy in the philosophy of perception. In perception, we sometimes seem to experience objects with properties they don't have (a red apple that looks pink in certain lighting, a straight stick that looks bent in water). The adverbialist about perception proposes that we should analyze "seeing a pink apple" not as perceiving an object with the property pinkness, but as perceiving pinkly — where "pinkly" is an adverb modifying the act of perceiving.

In the persistence case, the adverb modifies the instantiation of the property by the object. I instantiate bentness at-t₂-ish-ly, and I instantiate straightness at-t₁-ish-ly. These are not contradictory because the mode of instantiation differs.

Lewis objects to adverbialism on the grounds that it is mysterious. What exactly is it to instantiate a property "in a t₁-manner" versus "in a t₂-manner"? The adverb seems to smuggle back in a temporal relativization that we were supposed to have avoided, and it is not clear that adverbialism offers any genuine analysis of what is happening when a single object has different intrinsic properties at different times. At best, Lewis argues, adverbialism is a way of redescribing the problem rather than solving it (Lewis 1986: 204).

##### Solution Two: Relativization to Times

The second solution is to **relativize properties to times**: instead of treating "being bent" as a monadic property that an object either has or lacks, we treat "being bent" as a binary relational property that relates objects to times. "I am bent" becomes "I am bent at t₂" — where "bent-at" is a two-place relation between me and the time t₂, not a monadic property I instantiate.

On this view, there are no intrinsic properties in Lewis's sense — no genuine monadic properties that objects simply have or lack. Instead, all apparently intrinsic properties are really disguised relations to times (or to temporal stages of the world). The apparent contradiction dissolves because "I am bent at t₂" and "I am straight at t₁" are not incompatible — they are simply different relational facts.

This view is sometimes called "temporal relativism" or "three-dimensionalism with relativized properties." It has the advantage of being simple and natural: of course being bent is relative to a time; there is nothing mysterious about saying that I am bent at some times and straight at others.

Lewis's objection is that this solution changes the subject. If "being bent" is really a relation to a time, then it is not an intrinsic property at all. And the intuition behind the problem was that properties like "being bent," "being spherical," "having a certain shape" are intrinsic — they are about how the object is in itself, not about its relations to other things (including times). Relativizing them to times treats them as relational and thereby denies that there are any genuine intrinsic properties, or at least that any intrinsic properties can change.

This is a cost. Intrinsic properties seem to play an important role in our understanding of the world — in distinguishing what an object is like "from the inside" versus how it is situated in relation to other things. If the relativization strategy eliminates intrinsic properties, it thereby eliminates something that seems to be real and important about the world.

##### Solution Three: Temporal Parts

Lewis's preferred solution is the **temporal parts** view: objects persist by having numerically distinct temporal parts at different times, and each temporal part has its own intrinsic properties. When I was straight at t₁, my temporal part at t₁ was straight. When I am bent at t₂, my temporal part at t₂ is bent. My temporal part at t₁ and my temporal part at t₂ are distinct parts of me — just as my left hand and my right hand are distinct spatial parts of me. The incompatible properties are instantiated by distinct entities (distinct temporal parts), so there is no contradiction.

On this view, the "me" that was straight and the "me" that is bent are both genuine parts of me, related by the same kind of mereological composition that relates my left arm and my right leg to me. Just as my left arm is straight while my right arm is bent without any contradiction (because they are distinct spatial parts), my t₁-stage is straight while my t₂-stage is bent without any contradiction (because they are distinct temporal parts).

Lewis argues that this solution preserves the genuine intrinsicality of properties: being bent is a genuine monadic property, not a relation to a time. It is just that the thing that instantiates the property is not me-as-a-whole but my temporal part at the relevant time. There is no contradiction because the two properties are instantiated by two different things.

The main cost of the temporal parts solution is ontological: it requires accepting the existence of temporal parts as genuine entities in the world. Most philosophers who accept temporal parts regard them as entities "of the same ontological type as spatial parts" (Lewis 1986: 204) — no more mysterious than spatial parts, but also no less real. Endurantists, however, argue that temporal parts are a philosophically problematic posit — that there is no good reason to believe in them, and that the problem they are invoked to solve can be handled by less costly means.

##### Lewis's Argument for Temporal Parts

Lewis's argument for preferring the temporal parts solution has a specific logical structure. He argues that adverbialism and relativization are both, in different ways, unsatisfactory. Adverbialism is mysterious and does not genuinely analyze the instantiation of properties at times. Relativization denies the genuine intrinsicality of apparently intrinsic properties, which conflicts with intuitions that are at least as strong as the intuition that objects persist through change.

The temporal parts solution, by contrast, preserves the genuine intrinsicality of properties and gives a principled account of how an object can have incompatible properties at different times: by having distinct parts that instantiate them. This is analogous to the uncontroversially acceptable case of spatial incompatibility: an object can be red on the left and blue on the right without contradiction, because "the left" and "the right" are distinct spatial parts with different properties. The temporal case should be handled the same way.

This argument is not airtight. As we will see in the following sections, endurantists have developed sophisticated responses that do not simply accept Lewis's verdict. But Lewis's formulation has the great advantage of making the stakes of the debate precise and of showing exactly what must be defended or surrendered on each side.

### Section 2: Endurantism (Three-Dimensionalism)

Endurantism — the view that ordinary objects are wholly present at each moment of their existence, without being composed of temporal parts — is the view that matches most naturally with ordinary, pre-theoretical thinking about objects and their persistence. When you see a friend across the street, you see your whole friend, not a temporal stage or a temporal part. When your friend grows older and changes, it is not the case that different "parts" of your friend exist at different times; it is the very same person who is different. Endurantism takes this common-sense intuition seriously and tries to defend it against Lewis's challenge.

The name "three-dimensionalism" reflects the view that objects have only three spatial dimensions, not four. Objects extend through space (three dimensions) but they do not extend through time in the way that perdurantists hold; they persist through time by being wholly present at each moment, not by having temporal parts.

Defending this view requires responding to the problem of temporary intrinsics, which Lewis presents as a knock-down argument for temporal parts. In this section we examine the endurantist response and assess its strengths and weaknesses.

#### Endurantism: Objects Wholly Present Through Time

##### The Core Endurantist Claim

Endurantism holds that objects persist through time by being **wholly present** at each moment of their existence. There is no sense in which only a part of an object is present at a given time; the whole object is there. This is why endurantism is sometimes called "three-dimensionalism": ordinary objects have three spatial dimensions, and they exist in time, but they do not have a fourth, temporal dimension in the way that perdurantism claims.

This is not merely a claim about everyday appearances — about how objects *seem* to be wholly present. It is a metaphysical claim about the ultimate constitution of objects: there are no temporal parts; there is no "temporal worm" composed of distinct stages; there is simply the object, wholly present whenever it exists.

Consider a simple analogy. Your coffee mug exists in space: it has spatial extent, spatial parts (the handle, the rim, the base), and spatial properties (its height, its width, its volume). But does it also have temporal extent — a "temporal height" or "temporal depth" in the way it has spatial height and depth? The endurantist says no. The coffee mug is wholly present now; it is not merely the present temporal stage of a four-dimensional "temporal mug" that extends from its manufacture to its eventual breaking. The mug simply is, as a fully three-dimensional object, present at each moment it exists.

##### Handling Temporary Intrinsics: Relativization

The endurantist must respond to Lewis's problem of temporary intrinsics. The standard endurantist response is some form of relativization — either of properties to times, or of instantiation to times.

The most developed endurantist response holds that properties like "being bent" and "being straight" are not genuinely monadic properties but are what we might call "time-indexed properties" — properties whose instantiation is always relative to a time. When I say "I am bent," what I really mean is "I am bent at this time." Being-bent-at-t is a perfectly coherent property that I can have while also having being-straight-at-t', because these are different properties relativized to different times.

The endurantist must handle Lewis's objection that this relativization eliminates genuine intrinsic properties. The standard response is to distinguish between two notions of intrinsicality. There is "intrinsic" in the narrow sense that Lewis intends: a property an object has independently of all relations to other things, including relations to times. But there is also a broader notion: a property an object has in virtue of how it is in itself, as opposed to how it is in relation to other objects (where "objects" does not include times). Endurantists can maintain that being-bent-at-t is intrinsic in the second sense — it is about how the object is arranged at t — even if it is not intrinsic in Lewis's strict sense (Johnston 1987; Haslanger 1989).

##### Advantages of Endurantism

Endurantism has several significant advantages over perdurantism.

**Ordinary talk and thought**: We ordinarily say that it is *you* who was a child, not a temporal stage of you. We hold *you* responsible for what you did last year, not a temporal part of you. We say that *this* tree has grown, not that the current temporal stage of a tree-worm has different height properties from earlier stages. Endurantism's claim that objects are wholly present fits naturally with ordinary discourse about objects, their properties, and their persistence.

**Simpler ontology**: Endurantism does not require positing temporal parts. It acknowledges the temporal dimension in which objects exist without claiming that objects are literally composed of temporal stages in the way they are composed of spatial parts. This parsimony is philosophically attractive: we should not multiply entities beyond what is necessary to account for the phenomena.

**Causal efficacy**: Some philosophers argue that only wholly present objects can be genuine causal agents. If you help a friend move house, it is you — wholly present — who is lifting boxes; not your current temporal stage, which might be causally connected to but is numerically distinct from the stage that agreed to help. Causal responsibility seems to require the causal agent to be wholly present in the relevant situation, not merely to have a present stage there.

##### The Persistence Criterion Problem

Endurantism faces a challenge that perdurantism handles more easily: the problem of specifying a criterion of persistence. What makes the object present at t₁ the same object as the object present at t₂? For perdurantism, the answer is clean: they are connected as parts of the same temporal worm. For endurantism, the identity relation holds between the whole object-at-t₁ and the whole object-at-t₂, but what grounds this identity?

The endurantist typically appeals to continuity conditions of various kinds — causal continuity, material continuity, functional continuity — as criteria for persistence. The right criterion varies with the kind of object: the persistence of a river depends on continuity of water source and flow; the persistence of an organism depends on biological continuity; the persistence of a person depends on (according to different views) physical or psychological continuity. These criteria are well-developed in the literature, but they introduce their own complexity into the endurantist picture.

#### Objections to Endurantism

##### Lewis's Objection: Relativization Fails

Lewis's primary objection to the endurantist strategy of relativizing properties to times is that it fails to preserve genuine intrinsicality. If "being bent" is not a genuine monadic property but always a relational property (being-bent-at-t) that involves a relation to a time, then there are, strictly speaking, no intrinsic properties that change over time. And if there are no genuine intrinsic properties, a large part of what we thought we were saying about objects turns out to be false or systematically misleading.

The worry is this. When I say that my friend is happy, it seems as if I am saying something about how she is — about her intrinsic state, not her relational situation. When I say she used to be sad, I am saying something about her intrinsic state at that earlier time. These seem like genuine intrinsic characterizations. But if endurantism requires treating happiness and sadness as time-indexed relational properties rather than genuine intrinsic states, then the simple, intuitive picture that objects have intrinsic states that change over time is replaced by a more complex picture in which everything is a relation — and this seems like a significant departure from intuition (Lewis 1986: 204–205).

The endurantist response, as noted above, is to distinguish between two notions of intrinsicality. But Lewis's point stands at one level: the relativization strategy cannot preserve intrinsicality in the narrow, strict sense that he intends. Whether this sense of intrinsicality is important enough to motivate rejecting endurantism is what the debate turns on.

##### The Problem of Parthood Relations

A more specific objection to endurantism concerns parthood relations. Suppose that at t₁, my body includes my appendix; at t₂ (after appendectomy), it does not. If I am wholly present at both times, then at t₁ I have an appendix as a part, and at t₂ I do not. But if I am the very same wholly present object at both times, how can I have different parts?

This is sometimes called "the problem of temporary parthood." It is a version of the problem of temporary intrinsics applied to parts rather than properties. If having a certain part is intrinsic (and it seems to be: whether you have a part is a fact about how you are constituted, not about your relations to external things), then having and not having the same part seems to involve having incompatible intrinsic properties.

The endurantist can again respond by relativizing: I have-my-appendix-at-t₁ and I lack-my-appendix-at-t₂, and these are compatible because they are different relational facts. But the regress of objections and responses suggests that endurantism consistently purchases its account of change at the cost of treating all apparently intrinsic properties as relational.

##### Van Inwagen's Objection

Peter van Inwagen (1990) raises a different and powerful objection to endurantism. If objects persist by being wholly present at each time, then the relation between the object at t₁ and the object at t₂ is strict numerical identity — they are the very same object. But van Inwagen argues that numerical identity is problematic as a relation between objects at different times, because it seems to require that there be genuine entities "at times" to be identified — and what would such entities be, if not temporal stages?

The worry is that endurantism, in trying to avoid temporal stages, ends up with an account in which the persistence relation between objects at different times is identity, but where the relata of the identity relation are not clearly specified. Perdurantism, by contrast, has a clear account of the relata: temporal stages are genuine, particular entities, and the persistence relation between them is the overlap or "worm-overlap" relation of mereology.

##### The Problem for Ordinary Language

A final challenge for endurantism comes from ordinary language and thought. We do not ordinarily say that "the very same thing" is both sitting and standing; we say "she was sitting before and is standing now." The temporal qualification seems built into the way we describe change. Endurantism must explain why this temporal qualification is necessary — if the same whole object is present at both times, why does ordinary language resist saying "she is both sitting and standing" without a temporal qualification?

This challenge does not by itself refute endurantism, but it suggests that the ordinary picture of persistence is more complex than straightforward endurantism acknowledges. The temporal qualification in ordinary language suggests that we are, at some level, already thinking in terms of time-indexed property attributions — which is the relativization strategy that endurantism endorses, but which Lewis criticizes as a departure from genuine intrinsicality.

The debate between endurantism and perdurantism is thus a debate about what we are committed to when we say, without qualification, that an object has a property — and about how much metaphysical work the temporal qualifications we add (when we say "she was sitting") are doing.

### Section 3: Perdurantism (Four-Dimensionalism)

Perdurantism — the view that objects persist through time by having distinct temporal parts at different times — is a view that initially strikes most people as strange. What does it mean to say that the "you" who is reading this page is a temporal stage of a four-dimensional "worm" that extends from your birth to your death? The picture invites resistance: surely you are a person, not a worm; surely you are here, not a stage.

But the resistance is worth examining. We are, after all, happy to say that you extend through space: you have spatial parts — a left side and a right side, a top and a bottom, a front and a back. Each of these spatial parts is a different part of you at any given moment. Perdurantism simply proposes that you also extend through time: you have temporal parts — an earlier part and a later part, a yesterday-part and a today-part — and these temporal parts are as genuinely distinct as your left hand and your right hand.

This section examines perdurantism in detail: what it claims, how it handles the problem of temporary intrinsics, and what it costs.

#### Four-Dimensionalism: Objects as Temporal Worms

##### The Core Perdurantist Claim

Perdurantism holds that objects persist through time by having distinct **temporal parts** (also called temporal stages or time-slices) at each time during their existence. An object does not exist wholly at any single time; rather, it extends through time as it extends through space. What exists at any given moment is not the whole object but a temporal part of it — a "slice" of the four-dimensional extended object.

The four-dimensional object itself — what we ordinarily call "the person" or "the car" or "the river" — is a "temporal worm" composed of all its temporal parts from beginning to end. Just as a spatial worm (a snake, say) is extended through space and composed of different spatial parts (head, middle, tail), a temporal worm is extended through time and composed of different temporal parts (the Monday-slice, the Tuesday-slice, and so on).

The picture aligns naturally with the four-dimensional block universe of physics: in the spacetime manifold, objects occupy regions of four-dimensional spacetime, and temporal parts are the portions of those regions at particular times. The ontology is elegant and fits naturally with the scientific picture: objects are four-dimensional extended entities, just as physical theory describes.

##### How It Handles Temporary Intrinsics

Perdurantism handles the problem of temporary intrinsics cleanly and without any need for the relativization strategies that Lewis finds objectionable. On the perdurantist account, when I was straight yesterday and am bent today, these incompatible properties are not instantiated by the same thing. They are instantiated by numerically distinct temporal parts: my yesterday-stage was straight, and my today-stage is bent. There is no contradiction, because the two stages are different entities — as different as my left hand and my right hand.

The crucial feature of this solution is that "being bent" is a genuine intrinsic property — not a relation to a time, not an adverb on an instantiation relation, but a genuine property an object has in virtue of how it is in itself. My today-stage is bent in virtue of how it is arranged, period. My yesterday-stage was straight in virtue of how it was arranged, period. The problem of temporary intrinsics dissolves because the apparent incompatibility was always between distinct entities (distinct temporal stages), not between incompatible properties of the same entity.

##### Change as Difference Between Stages

On the perdurantist account, change is not a process that happens to a single entity but a matter of numerical difference between successive stages. When I "change" from straight to bent, what happens is that my straight yesterday-stage is succeeded by my bent today-stage. These stages are distinct, and the succession of stages with different properties is what we describe (loosely but effectively) as "change."

This account of change is efficient and precise. It does not invoke any mysterious "persisting substratum" that underlies the change — the changing thing does not need to be anything over and above its temporal stages. The persistence through change is just the existence of a connected series of stages, bound together by the appropriate relations (causal continuity, overlapping chains of qualitative similarity, spatiotemporal continuity).

##### Temporal Parts and Spatial Parts: The Analogy

Lewis emphasizes the analogy between temporal parts and spatial parts: "temporal parts, like spatial parts, are genuine parts of objects, of the same ontological type as spatial parts" (Lewis 1986: 204). This analogy is both the most intuitive defense of temporal parts and a source of objections.

The spatial case is uncontroversial: we accept without difficulty that a long snake is composed of spatial parts, that different spatial parts can have different colors, and that this does not generate any contradiction. The snake is not contradictorily colored just because its head is red and its tail is blue; the head and tail are different parts. Similarly, the perdurantist argues, a persisting person is not contradictorily shaped just because an early temporal part is straight and a later temporal part is bent; the stages are different parts.

The analogy breaks down, however, in one significant respect: we can perceive spatial parts simultaneously, but we cannot perceive temporal parts simultaneously. When I look at the snake, I see its spatial extent. When I look at you, I do not see your temporal extent — I see your current temporal stage. This asymmetry between our epistemic access to spatial and temporal parts is one source of resistance to the perdurantist picture.

The perdurantist response is that our epistemic limitations do not reflect ontological structure. We cannot see radio waves, but they exist. We cannot see the insides of opaque objects, but they exist. Our inability to perceive temporal extent simultaneously does not show that temporal parts do not exist; it shows that our sensory systems are calibrated to present temporal cross-sections rather than temporal wholes.

#### Worm Theory: Mereology, Gains, and Costs

##### The Mereology of Temporal Parts

Lewis's perdurantism, developed in *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986) and *Parts of Classes* (1991), employs a mereological framework in which temporal parts are genuine parts of objects, governed by the same principles as spatial parts. Mereology is the formal theory of parthood and composition: it specifies the principles by which parts relate to wholes, and when a collection of parts composes something.

Lewis endorses **unrestricted mereological composition**: any collection of objects has a mereological sum, however gerrymandered or scattered. This is a strong claim that has controversial implications even in the purely spatial case. But the key application to temporal parts is this: for any region of spacetime, there exists a mereological sum of the portions of matter or stuff occupying that region. Temporal parts are simply the occupants of temporal slices of these four-dimensional spacetime regions.

The mereology of temporal parts works as follows. A complete persisting object — a person, say — is the mereological sum of all its temporal parts. Each temporal part is an entity that exists at exactly one time (or more precisely, that is wholly confined to a particular temporal region). The whole person is the sum of all these instantaneous (or short-duration) stages, connected by appropriate relations of psychological continuity, physical continuity, or whatever the appropriate persistence criterion for persons is.

This mereological framework has the advantage of being clean and formally precise: we can say exactly what kind of thing a temporal worm is (a mereological sum of temporal stages), how it relates to its parts (by mereological composition), and when two worms are identical (when they have exactly the same temporal parts). The framework inherits all the virtues of formal mereology: clarity, precision, and the absence of mysterious irreducible wholes over and above their parts.

##### What Perdurantism Gains

Perdurantism resolves the problem of temporary intrinsics without requiring the relativization strategies that Lewis criticizes. It preserves genuine intrinsic properties — being bent, being straight, being spherical — as monadic properties of temporal stages, not as relations to times. And it accounts for change in a natural way: change is the difference in properties between successive temporal stages.

Perdurantism also handles the problem of **vagueness in persistence** with a distinctive elegance. Many ordinary persistence questions have no determinate answer: "Is this the same club after all the members have been replaced?" "Is this the same car after all the parts have been replaced?" Perdurantism handles these cases by noting that the identity of a temporal worm is in principle always determinate — it is the mereological sum of its temporal parts. Ordinary persistence questions seem to have no determinate answer because we use terms like "club" and "car" in ways that are vague about which temporal parts they pick out, not because there is any genuine indeterminacy in the underlying mereological facts.

Furthermore, perdurantism handles cases of **fission and fusion** that puzzle endurantists. If an amoeba divides into two amoebae, what happened to the original? On the perdurantist view, the original temporal worm simply branches: there are two post-fission worms, each sharing the pre-fission temporal parts, but diverging after the division point. There need be no identity crisis; we simply have two overlapping worms.

##### What Perdurantism Costs

The main cost of perdurantism is one that strikes many philosophers as unacceptably high: **it complicates ordinary talk of identity over time**.

When I say "I will be at the party tomorrow," I seem to be saying something about myself — the person who is presently here — being at a future location. But on the perdurantist view, the entity that will be at the party is not identical to the entity that is here now; they are distinct temporal stages of a single worm. The worm will have a stage at the party, but "I" (if "I" refers to my current stage) will not be there.

This seems to conflict with ordinary usage. We say "I will be there" and mean it sincerely. Perdurantism seems to force the conclusion that this sincere utterance is, literally, false — that I (my current stage) will not be at the party, though my worm will have a stage at the party. Lewis is aware of this difficulty and handles it by arguing that when we use terms like "I" over time, we are typically referring to the whole temporal worm rather than to the present stage. But this requires a systematic reinterpretation of ordinary temporal language that many philosophers find ad hoc.

A related problem is **moral responsibility**. We hold people responsible for past actions. But on the perdurantist view, the person who performed the past action is a distinct temporal stage from the person who is now being held responsible. Do we have the right to punish or reward a temporal stage for what a different temporal stage did? Lewis's answer is that the whole temporal worm is responsible for the actions of all its stages, but this answer, while not obviously wrong, requires careful development.

A final cost concerns the **phenomenology of persistence**. We experience ourselves as wholly present, as persisting through time as unified subjects of experience. The perdurantist picture — in which at any moment only a stage of the temporal worm is present — seems to conflict with this phenomenological datum. The perdurantist response is that this is an artifact of our epistemic position: we can only directly experience our current stage, and this stage represents itself as the whole person, just as a spatial part of a mirror cannot "see" the whole mirror. But this response, while logically adequate, does not eliminate the phenomenological resistance.

### Section 4: Stage Theory

Stage theory, developed by Ted Sider in *Four-Dimensionalism* (2001), represents a fascinating hybrid position that accepts the ontological framework of four-dimensionalism (temporal stages as the basic entities) but modifies the semantic framework to avoid the counterintuitive consequences of worm theory about ordinary talk and practical concerns.

The key move is to shift what ordinary terms like "I," "this cat," and "the river" refer to. Worm theory says they refer to four-dimensional worms. Stage theory says they refer to instantaneous stages, with persistence talk understood in terms of counterpart relations between stages. This semantic shift preserves the ontological economy of four-dimensionalism while making ordinary temporal language come out literally true in a more natural way.

#### Sider's Stage Theory: Instantaneous Stages and Temporal Counterparts

##### The Basic Idea

Ted Sider's stage theory, presented in *Four-Dimensionalism: An Ontology of Persistence and Time* (2001, Chapter 5), makes a crucial distinction that worm theory overlooks: the distinction between **what things there are** (the ontology) and **what our ordinary terms refer to** (the semantics).

Stage theory agrees with worm theory that the fundamental ontology includes four-dimensional spacetime and temporal stages (instantaneous or short-duration slices of four-dimensional worms). But it disagrees about which of these entities our ordinary object-terms refer to. Worm theory says "the cat" refers to the whole four-dimensional worm. Stage theory says "the cat" refers to the **current temporal stage** — the instantaneous (or short-duration) stage that exists at the present moment.

The natural objection is immediate: if "the cat" refers to the current stage, and the current stage is instantaneous (or very brief), then "the cat has existed for ten years" comes out false — the current stage is only a moment old. Stage theory handles this objection with the concept of **temporal counterparts**.

##### Temporal Counterparts

The concept of temporal counterparts is borrowed, with modification, from Lewis's counterpart theory in modal logic. In Lewis's modal counterpart theory, when we say "I could have been a doctor," this is true because there is a possible-world counterpart of me — a qualitatively similar individual in another possible world — who is a doctor. I myself am not in that other world; it is my counterpart who is.

Sider's temporal counterpart theory applies the same move to temporal contexts. When we say "I will be at the party tomorrow," this is true because there is a temporal counterpart of me — the tomorrow-stage of the worm to which I belong — who will be at the party.
