#### 31.1.2 Aristotle's Sea Battle and the Open Future

---

*De Interpretatione* Chapter 9 is one of the most commented-upon passages in the entire Aristotelian corpus, and with good reason. In fewer than two pages, Aristotle formulates what remains one of the central puzzles in the philosophy of logic and time: what is the truth value of a statement about a contingent future event? The example he reaches for has lodged itself permanently in philosophical vocabulary: a sea battle that may or may not take place tomorrow.

##### The Problem

Aristotle begins from the principle of bivalence: every affirmative statement is either true or false (*De Interpretatione* 9, 18a28–34). This seems unobjectionable — it is part of what it means for something to be a genuine statement rather than, say, a question. But Aristotle notices that if bivalence holds universally, it seems to collapse contingency.

Consider the statement "There will be a sea battle tomorrow." If this statement is true now, then the sea battle is already determined to happen — anything else would make the statement false, contrary to the assumption. But if the statement is false now, then the sea battle is already determined not to happen. Either way, the outcome appears necessary, not contingent. And this applies to every future-tense statement about contingent events. The logic of bivalence seems to entail that the future is already fixed.

Aristotle's argument for this conclusion runs approximately as follows. Take any future-tense statement S. Either S is true or S is false (bivalence). If S is true, then whatever S describes must occur; if it were going to fail to occur, S would be false, contradicting the assumption. If S is false, then whatever S describes must not occur. In either case, the outcome is necessitated. Since this reasoning applies to every future-tense statement, every future event is necessitated. Deliberation, planning, and the entire apparatus of human agency become performative illusions.

##### Aristotle's Response: Denying Bivalence for Future Contingents

Aristotle's solution is radical. He denies that the principle of bivalence applies to future contingent statements. A statement like "there will be a sea battle tomorrow" is, he suggests, neither determinately true nor determinately false at the time of utterance. It is *indefinite* — poised between truth and falsity in a way that mirrors the genuine contingency of the event it describes.

This move has a certain elegance. If statements track reality, and reality includes genuinely open possibilities, then statements about open possibilities should themselves be "open" — not yet settled in their truth value. The logic of statements should respect the ontology of the world they describe.

Aristotle is careful about what he is and is not claiming. He does not deny that *either* the battle will happen *or* it will not (the law of excluded middle might still hold in some form). He denies that the disjunction distributes so that *one particular disjunct* is already determinately true. The statement "there will or will not be a sea battle tomorrow" may be true, while neither "there will be" nor "there will not be" is determinately true individually.

##### The Open Future Semantics

Aristotle's position has been developed in the twentieth century into a systematic semantic framework, often called "open future semantics" or "indeterminist semantics." The key move is to extend the Kripke-style possible-worlds semantics for modal logic to temporal contexts.

In standard possible-worlds semantics, a statement is true if it is true at the actual world. In open-future semantics, we do not treat the future as a single actual "branch" but as a tree of possibilities — many branches extend from the present, and only one will be actualized. A future-tense statement is true at a branch-time pair if the event occurs on that branch, false if it does not. The statement is *settled true* at the present if it is true on every branch extending from the present, *settled false* if false on every branch, and *unsettled* if it is true on some branches and false on others.

This framework, developed formally by Prior (1967), Thomason (1970), and Belnap et al. (2001), provides a precise logical account of the open future. It makes room for genuine contingency without abandoning classical logic entirely. Future contingent statements receive neither classical truth nor classical falsity; they receive the status of genuinely unsettled possibilities.

##### Philosophical Implications

The open future semantics has immediate implications for free will. If future contingent statements are not yet determinately true or false, then there is no *fact of the matter* now about what you will choose tomorrow — and the fatalistic inference from "true now" to "necessary now" cannot get started. The future is ontologically open in the sense that matters for agency.

But this solution carries costs. It requires revising classical logic, which is not a small concession. Many logicians and metaphysicians consider bivalence a non-negotiable feature of any serious logical system. If we give up bivalence for future contingents, we commit ourselves to a kind of logic that many find technically awkward and philosophically surprising.

Moreover, there is a tension between the open future view and eternalism about time (the block universe). If all temporal positions are equally real, and the future "exists" just as much as the past and present, then there would appear to be facts about future events — and bivalence would hold for future-tense statements. Aristotle's solution requires, at minimum, that the future is ontologically different from the past in some relevant way. A-theorists will find this natural; B-theorists will find it harder to accommodate.

##### Bivalence vs. Determinism

It is important to notice that the fatalist argument in *De Interpretatione* 9 is distinct from the problem of causal determinism. Aristotle's argument does not assume that events are causally necessitated by prior events; it assumes only that statements about them are determinately true or false. The problem is logical, not physical. This is why Aristotle's solution is a logical one — revise the logic — rather than a physical one — posit indeterminism.

Contemporary philosophers have been divided about whether the two problems are really independent. Tooley (1997: 45–68) argues that the open future view and causal indeterminism naturally fit together. Others, including Horwich (1987: 24–30), argue that the semantics can be evaluated independently of causal questions. What is clear is that Aristotle opened a line of inquiry that has proved inexhaustible: the relationship between truth, time, and the openness of the future remains one of the liveliest areas of work in analytic philosophy.

##### Legacy and Contemporary Relevance

The sea battle example continues to generate scholarly work. The branching-time framework of Belnap, Perloff, and Xu (2001) in *Facing the Future* provides the most sophisticated formal development of Aristotle's intuitions. The ockhamist tradition (explored in Section 31.2) provides an alternative response that preserves bivalence by distinguishing what is true from what is *now fixed as necessary*. MacFarlane (2003; 2014) has developed a relativist semantics on which the truth of future contingents is assessor-relative — true or false depending on when one evaluates them. Each of these approaches is a descendant of the sea battle.

What Aristotle achieved in *De Interpretatione* 9 was to show that time is not a neutral backdrop for the evaluation of statements. The temporal location of an utterance, and the temporal direction of its reference, affect its logical behavior. Logic and the philosophy of time are not separate disciplines; they illuminate each other at every turn.

---

*See also: Section 31.2 on theological fatalism and Ockham; Chapter 13 on McTaggart's A-series; Chapter 17 on growing block views.*

### Section 31.2: Theological Fatalism

---

#### Section Introduction

Logical fatalism, as Aristotle presented it, rests on the structure of truth and time alone. Theological fatalism adds a further element: an omniscient God whose knowledge of the future seems to guarantee that the future is fixed in a way that eliminates human freedom. If God knew yesterday, with perfect and infallible knowledge, that you would perform action A today, then how could you possibly do otherwise? The question is not whether God forces you — nothing in the argument requires coercion. The question is whether God's infallible foreknowledge is compatible with your having had a genuine alternative.

This section examines two major responses to theological fatalism. The first, associated with William of Ockham, accepts that God has genuine foreknowledge of contingent events but denies that this forecloses alternatives. The key move is a distinction between different kinds of facts about the past: "hard" facts, which concern only what happened at that past time, and "soft" facts, which have essential reference to other times (including the future). God's past knowledge is a soft fact — it has future-directed content — and so it does not fall under the principle that past facts are necessary. Our past freedom to do otherwise is therefore intact.

The second response, associated with Boethius, denies the premise that God's knowledge is a form of *foreknowledge* at all. God does not know the future from within time; God exists outside time and apprehends all moments simultaneously in an eternal present. On this view, the problem of foreknowledge is dissolved by relocating God outside the temporal framework in which the problem arises.

Both responses have their defenders, and both face serious objections. What this section aims to show is that the theological fatalism problem is philosophically substantive — not merely a theological curiosity, but a window into deep questions about necessity, temporal direction, and the nature of the past.

---

*Section 31.2 comprises Readings 31.2.1 and 31.2.2.*

#### 31.2.1 Foreknowledge and Freedom

---

##### The Basic Argument

The problem of theological fatalism can be stated with disarming simplicity. Suppose that God is omniscient — knowing all truths, past, present, and future, infallibly and necessarily. Suppose you freely perform action A at noon today. Then yesterday God knew that you would perform A at noon. But if God knew yesterday that you would perform A, then it seems you cannot refrain from performing A. For if you were to refrain, God's yesterday-knowledge would be false. But God's knowledge cannot be false — it is infallible by definition. Therefore you cannot refrain. But if you cannot refrain from performing A, then you do not perform it freely.

The argument can be stated more formally. Let K be the proposition "God knew at time t₋₁ that person S would perform action A at time t₀." Let the following premises be granted:

(P1) God knew at t₋₁ that S would do A at t₀. (foreknowledge claim)
(P2) Necessarily, if God knew at t₋₁ that p, then p is true. (infallibility)
(P3) If p was true at t₋₁, and t₋₁ is in the past relative to t₀, then it is now necessary (at t₀) that p. (necessity of the past)
(P4) What is now necessary is not something one could refrain from. (ability principle)

From (P1), (P2), and (P3), it follows that it is now necessary that S does A at t₀. By (P4), S cannot refrain from doing A. Therefore S does not do A freely.

The argument is valid. The question is which premise to deny.

##### Distinguishing Types of Necessity

Before examining the responses, it is worth distinguishing the different senses of "necessity" that appear in the argument. This distinction is not merely terminological; different senses of necessity interact with the argument differently.

*Logical necessity* holds of propositions that are true in all possible worlds — "all bachelors are unmarried" is logically necessary. *Temporal necessity* (or "accidental necessity") holds of propositions simply in virtue of being about the past — what happened, happened, and nothing can change it. This is the necessity captured in premise (P3). *Causal necessity* holds of events that were determined to occur by prior causal conditions.

The theological fatalism argument invokes temporal necessity, not causal necessity. God's foreknowledge doesn't *cause* you to act as you do; it merely tracks what you will do. This is why the argument is not simply a version of the determinism problem: it does not claim that your action was causally inevitable. It claims that the existence of infallible past knowledge of your action makes it temporally necessary that you perform it.

##### Fischer's Analysis and the Hard/Soft Distinction

John Martin Fischer (1989: 11–44) provides a rigorous examination of the theological fatalism argument that draws on a distinction originating with William of Ockham. The distinction is between *hard facts* about the past and *soft facts* about the past.

A hard fact about the past is a fact that concerns *only* what happened at that past time — it has no essential reference to what will happen at later times. "It rained in London on July 4, 1066" is a hard fact about that date: its truth conditions are entirely confined to that day.

A soft fact about the past is a fact that appears to be about the past but has *essential* reference to what will happen at later times. Consider: "In 1990, Jones was sitting two miles from where the first person to walk on the moon in 2050 would eventually stand." This fact is about 1990, but its truth conditions reach forward to 2050. Soft facts are, in a sense, partially about the future, even though they are expressed in the past tense.

Fischer's claim is that God's foreknowledge is a soft fact about the past. The proposition "God knew at t₋₁ that S would do A at t₀" essentially refers to t₀, since "knowledge" is factive — to know that p is to know a truth, and what makes this knowledge true is what S does at t₀. The truth conditions of God's past knowledge essentially involve S's future action.

If divine foreknowledge is a soft fact, then premise (P3) — the necessity of the past — does not apply to it. The necessity of the past applies to hard facts. Soft facts, even though they are "about" the past in a grammatical sense, do not carry the same modal weight. S can retain the ability to do otherwise, because the past fact that God knew S would do A is not a hard constraint on S's options.

##### Evaluating the Hard/Soft Distinction

The hard/soft distinction is elegant but has faced challenges. Wierenga (1991: 19–34) argues that God's foreknowledge, properly understood, should be classified as a hard fact, because God's knowing is a mental state that fully occurred at the earlier time, not a disposition that waits on future events. There is a difference, Wierenga suggests, between what makes a fact *true* and what the fact *is*: God's knowing at t₋₁ is a temporally located event, even if its accuracy depends on later events.

Fischer responds that what matters for the necessity-of-the-past principle is whether the fact *could have been different* in a world where S acts differently at t₀. Since God is infallible, God's past belief would have been different if S's future action were different. This counterfactual dependence is what makes the foreknowledge fact a soft one — it is counterfactually dependent on the future in a way that genuine hard facts are not.

This debate reaches a stalemate that reveals something important: the distinction between hard and soft facts, however intuitively compelling, does not have a fully precise characterization that all parties accept. The dispute about divine foreknowledge exposes a genuine ambiguity in our concept of "facts about the past" and their modal status.

##### The Ability Principle

Premise (P4) — that necessity forecloses ability — also deserves scrutiny. Free will requires more than mere ability in some minimal sense; it requires the ability to do otherwise in a sense that is compatible with all actual past facts being held fixed. If we hold fixed God's past foreknowledge as a hard fact, and if that foreknowledge entails S's action, then S lacks the relevant kind of ability. But if foreknowledge is a soft fact, the "fixed past" does not include it, and S's ability is intact.

The debate therefore turns on precisely what we hold fixed when we assess "ability to do otherwise." Fischer and Ravizza (1998: 55–86) develop an account of guidance control — the kind of control sufficient for moral responsibility — that does not require the ability to do otherwise in the strong sense implicated by theological fatalism. On this compatibilist approach, moral responsibility requires that one's action be produced by one's own reasons-responsive mechanism, not that one could have acted differently given an absolutely fixed past.

##### The Deeper Issue

The problem of foreknowledge and freedom illustrates a deep tension that recurs throughout the philosophy of time. Past facts bear on the present in a way that future facts (apparently) do not. We feel that the past constrains us; the future is ours to shape. But if there are — or were — facts about the future embedded in past knowledge-states, then this asymmetry is harder to maintain.

What theological fatalism forces us to examine is the precise relationship between the *fixity* of the past, the *openness* of the future, and the ground of *ability*. These are not merely theological questions; they are questions about the temporal structure of practical agency. And they cannot be answered without taking a stand on some of the deepest issues in the metaphysics of time.

---

*See also: Section 31.2.2 on Boethius; Section 31.1.2 on Aristotle's sea battle; Fischer (1989) in Further Reading.*

#### 31.2.2 Boethius and the Eternal Present

---

Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius wrote *The Consolation of Philosophy* in 524 CE while awaiting execution on charges of treason — charges he denied. The circumstances lend the work a peculiar urgency; its calm, methodical examination of providence, fate, and human freedom is the work of a man who had every personal reason to find the arguments either compelling or devastating. Book V of the *Consolation* contains what has become the most celebrated single response to the problem of divine foreknowledge and human freedom: the doctrine of God's eternity as simultaneous apprehension of all times.

##### The Problem as Boethius Frames It

Lady Philosophy, Boethius's interlocutor, articulates the tension clearly: if God's foreknowledge is certain, there can be no contingency in human affairs; if there is contingency, there can be no foreknowledge. These two claims seem to exclude each other. Yet Christian theology requires both: an omniscient God and genuine human freedom that grounds moral responsibility.

Boethius's solution depends on rejecting a hidden assumption in the foreknowledge problem: the assumption that God's knowledge of the future is *foreknowledge* — knowledge acquired from a position within time, looking forward. This assumption seems natural, but Boethius argues it is mistaken. God does not exist in time at all.

##### God's Eternity

For Boethius, *eternity* does not mean "existing for an infinite time" — an endless temporal duration stretching before and after the present. That would make God sempiternal, everlasting, but still temporal. True eternity is qualitatively different: it is the *simultaneous and complete possession of unlimited life* (*Consolation* V, Prose 6). God apprehends all moments of time not successively but all at once, in a single, timeless present.

The model Boethius offers is of a person standing on a high hill who can see the entire plain below simultaneously, while travelers on the plain can see only the stretch immediately before them. God's perspective on time is like the hilltop view: all moments are visible at once, laid out before a timeless gaze. Human perspective is like the traveler's: we see only the present and remember the past, while the future remains hidden.

On this account, what looks from our perspective like *foreknowledge* is, from God's perspective, simply *knowledge* — simultaneous, timeless apprehension of events that occur at different times. God does not *predict* your action from a position in the past; God *observes* your action in the eternal present, even though your action occurs at a particular time.

##### Does This Resolve the Problem?

The question of whether Boethius's solution genuinely resolves the problem has occupied philosophers for fifteen centuries, and the debate has not converged. The solution's proponents argue as follows. The problem of foreknowledge arises because God's past knowledge seems to fix the future — since the past is necessary, and God's past knowledge entails your future action, your future action is necessary. But if God is outside time, there is no past knowledge; there is only eternal knowledge. And eternal knowledge, being outside time, does not fall under the principle that *past* facts are necessary. The necessity of the past has no grip on a timelessly eternal being.

Moreover, Boethius argues, there is a distinction between *conditional* and *absolute* necessity. Even if God eternally knows that you will do A, this amounts only to: *given that you do A, God eternally knows it*. Your doing A is not absolutely necessary; it is necessary only given the conditional fact that God's knowledge tracks what you do. The truth of God's knowledge is conditioned on what you freely do, not the other way around. God's eternal perception is like a human witness observing an event: the observer's seeing that you do something does not make your doing it necessary — it merely tracks the contingent event.

##### The Relocation Objection

The most persistent challenge to Boethius is that his solution does not resolve the problem but *relocates* it. Even if God is outside time, God's eternal knowledge stands in a relationship to your action: God eternally knows that you will do A. If this eternal knowledge is true, and if the truth of an eternal proposition cannot be altered, then it seems your action is necessitated by the eternal truth, not by a past temporal fact.

Pike (1965: 36–46) pressed this objection with particular force. Suppose God exists outside time but knows eternally that Jones does A at noon on Monday. Is it "in Jones's power" to refrain from A? If Jones were to refrain, God's eternal knowledge would be false — which is impossible. Therefore Jones cannot refrain, whether or not God's knowledge is "foreknowledge" in a temporal sense. The impossibility does not depend on the temporal location of God's knowledge.

Boethius's supporters (Stump and Kretzmann 1981: 429–458) argue that "at the same time" and "before" are temporal relations that do not apply to a timeless God, and therefore the inference from eternal knowledge to necessity is blocked. But this response invites the question: if God is genuinely outside time, in what sense does God "know" your present action at all? The relationship between a timeless being and a temporal event needs to be characterized with great care, and many philosophers have found existing characterizations incomplete.

##### Philosophical Assessment

The Boethian solution illuminates something important even if it does not ultimately succeed. It shows that the problem of foreknowledge is, at its core, a problem about the relationship between the *modal status* of facts and their *temporal location*. The reason past facts seem to constrain the present is that they are "fixed" — outside the range of present agency. But what exactly makes them fixed? Is it their pastness as such, or is it some more fundamental feature — their being outside the causal reach of the present agent?

If the latter, then a timeless God's eternal knowledge might indeed be analogously "fixed" from a human perspective, reinstating the problem. If the former, then Boethius's appeal to divine atemporality blocks the fixity argument, but at the cost of making divine knowledge harder to understand.

Contemporary philosophy of religion has explored these questions with considerable sophistication. Hasker (1989: 150–186) argues that neither Ockhamism nor the Boethian solution adequately preserves genuine freedom, and that the only coherent theism compatible with libertarian free will is *open theism* — the view that God voluntarily limits foreknowledge of free human actions. Whatever one thinks of that conclusion, the Boethian discussion remains indispensable: it forces precision about eternity, necessity, and the temporal structure of divine cognition that illuminates the philosophy of time as much as the philosophy of religion.

---

*See also: Section 31.2.1 on the foreknowledge argument; Chapter 6 on Hellenistic philosophy of time; Chapter 7 on Plotinus and eternity.*

### Section 31.3: Determinism and the Block Universe

---

#### Section Introduction

The block universe — the view that past, present, and future events are all equally real, arranged in a four-dimensional spacetime manifold — is one of the most important metaphysical positions in the philosophy of time, and one that many students find immediately threatening to free will. If the future is already "there," already fixed in the four-dimensional structure of spacetime, then in what sense is it open to our choices? Does the block universe entail fatalism?

This section argues that the inference from block universe to fatalism rests on a conflation. The block universe is a thesis about ontology — about what exists — not a thesis about causation or determination. A block universe is compatible with causal determinism (every event is determined by prior events) and equally compatible with causal indeterminism (some events are not so determined). The mere existence of future events does not imply that they were causally inevitable from any earlier time.

Once this is clear, the real question about free will and determinism can be put properly. That question concerns not the ontological status of the future, but the causal structure of the world and its relationship to agency. This is the terrain of the compatibilism debate. Compatibilists argue that free will and determinism are not merely compossible but that free will *requires* a certain kind of deterministic connection — between one's reasons and one's actions. Incompatibilists argue that genuine freedom requires the genuine ability to do otherwise, which determinism forecloses.

---

*Section 31.3 comprises Readings 31.3.1 and 31.3.2.*

#### 31.3.1 The Block Universe and Human Agency

---

##### The Block Universe Recapped

The block universe view — also called eternalism or four-dimensionalism — holds that temporal reality is not confined to the present moment or to the past and present together. All times are equally real: the year 1066 and the year 2350 exist just as much as 2024, though of course only 2024 is present *now*, in the indexical sense. The entire four-dimensional manifold of spacetime events exists as a single, unified whole. Time is like space in one crucial respect: the fact that I am not currently in Paris does not mean Paris does not exist; similarly, the fact that the Battle of Hastings is not current does not mean it does not exist. It exists at its own time.

This view has strong support from physics. Special relativity establishes that simultaneity is relative to reference frame — different inertial observers will disagree about which events are "simultaneous" and hence about what counts as "the present." If the present were privileged in the way presentism requires, the relativity of simultaneity would generate troubling ambiguities. The block universe treats all times as equally real and thereby sidesteps these complications (Sider 2001: 42–52; Putnam 1967).

##### The Apparent Threat to Freedom

It is easy to see why the block universe might seem threatening to free will. If future events exist — if your decision tomorrow is already "there" in the four-dimensional structure — then in what sense is it up to you what happens? The future seems as fixed as the past. The person who will make a choice tomorrow is already, in a sense, making it: that choice-event is already part of the eternal furniture of the universe.

This line of thought can be formulated more precisely. On the block universe, for any future event E, there exists an event-location L in spacetime, and E is located at L. The proposition "E occurs" is true simpliciter — not "true now" or "true at some times and not others," but just true, as a timeless fact. If it is just true that you will choose option A tomorrow, then there is a sense in which the outcome is settled — it is part of the eternal structure of reality.

##### The Conflation of Ontology and Causation

Here is where careful diagnosis is needed. The argument above conflates two distinct claims:

(i) Future events exist (ontological claim).
(ii) Future events were causally determined by prior events (causal claim).

The block universe establishes (i). It does *not* by itself establish (ii). A block universe is compatible with a world in which some events are not causally determined by prior events — a world with genuine quantum indeterminism, for instance, or one with genuinely chance events at the macro-level. In such a world, the future events still "exist" in the block universe sense; they are just not the inevitable products of prior causes. Their existence is a feature of the four-dimensional structure, but their occurrence relative to prior events is not causally necessary.

To put this differently: the block universe tells us about the *ontological structure* of time — which times and events exist. It does not by itself tell us about the *causal structure* — which events are necessitated by which prior events. These are separate questions, and conflating them generates a spurious fatalism.

Mellor (1998: 127–130) makes this point clearly: the block universe "says nothing about causation" — it is a thesis about what exists, not about the relationships of necessitation between events. Similarly, Sider (2001: 42–52) notes that eternalism is compatible with a wide range of causal stories.

##### The Block Universe and Compatibilism

If the block universe does not by itself generate fatalism, what does it imply for free will? The most natural answer is: relatively little, directly. The question of free will is not "are future events real?" but "are our choices the right kind of cause of our actions?" This is the terrain of the compatibilism debate.

A compatibilist can accept the block universe without difficulty. In the four-dimensional manifold, there are events of deliberation, events of action, and causal relationships between them. The deliberation events causally influence the action events; the agent reasons, weighs options, and acts on the basis of that reasoning. Whether this constitutes genuine freedom is a question about the nature of the causal relationship between deliberation and action — a question that is independent of whether future events exist timelessly.

It is worth noting that the block universe might even be a *friendly* framework for compatibilism about agency. In the block universe, there is no "open future" that agents can influence; what there is, instead, is a rich causal structure in which some event-types (deliberations, reasons-responses) are systematically related to subsequent event-types (actions). The agent's freedom consists in being the right kind of node in this causal network — a node whose outputs are sensitive to reasons-inputs. This is exactly what sophisticated compatibilists like Wolf (1990: 30–35) and Fischer and Ravizza (1998: 36–41) have argued.

##### The Residual Problem

There is, however, a more subtle way in which the block universe might create difficulty for free will, beyond the naive fatalism critique. This concerns the relationship between the *direction of explanation* and the *direction of time*.

In the block universe, temporal relations are just relations among events; the "direction" of time is not built into the fundamental ontology but emerges from asymmetries in the causal structure (as discussed in Chapter 21). In such a framework, the agent's deliberation and the resulting action are both equally real events, related by causal and explanatory connections. But there may be a question about whether the agent's deliberation genuinely *explains* the action in the sense required for genuine agency — or whether the explanation runs the other way (from action back to deliberation) just as legitimately, given the symmetry of the underlying ontology.

This is a deep worry, but its resolution does not obviously favor fatalism. The asymmetry of causation — that causes precede their effects, and that explanations typically run forward in time — is compatible with the block universe once we recognize that causal asymmetry is an additional feature of the world beyond temporal asymmetry (Price 1996: 155–162). Free will requires the right kind of causal relationship; the block universe does not foreclose having such relationships.

The upshot is that the block universe is genuinely neutral with respect to free will. Students who feel threatened by the picture of a four-dimensional universe in which the future is "already there" should resist the inference to fatalism. The future is "already there" in the sense that it exists, not in the sense that it was preordained by prior causes. Whether our choices are genuinely free depends on the causal structure of the world and the nature of our agency — not on which theory of temporal ontology is correct.

---

*See also: Chapter 14 on B-theory and eternalism; Chapter 21 on the direction of time; Section 31.3.2 on compatibilism.*

#### 31.3.2 Compatibilism, the Consequence Argument, and Hard Incompatibilism

---

##### The Compatibilist Tradition

Compatibilism is the view that free will and determinism are not only logically compatible but that free will can be fully analyzed within a deterministic framework. The tradition is old — Hume and Hobbes are classical compatibilists — but its contemporary development is considerably more sophisticated than the classical versions.

The classical compatibilist claimed that free will simply means acting in accordance with one's desires, without external compulsion. If I do what I want to do, without physical restraint or coercion, I act freely — regardless of whether my desires were themselves causally determined by prior events. But this simple analysis faces the obvious objection: what if your desires themselves were determined by factors outside your control? You may act in accordance with your desires and yet feel that those desires are not genuinely *yours* — they were, say, the product of manipulation, addiction, or psychological conditioning that bypassed your rational agency.

Frankfurt (1971: 5–20) proposed a hierarchical response to this objection that transformed the debate. The key distinction is between *first-order desires* (desires to act in some way) and *second-order desires* (desires about one's first-order desires). A free agent is one whose first-order desires *conform to* their second-order desires — who wants to want what they in fact want. The addict who desperately wishes they did not want drugs has a first-order desire (for drugs) that conflicts with their second-order desire (not to want drugs). Their action is therefore unfree, not because it is caused, but because it is driven by a desire that is not endorsed at the higher level.

Frankfurt's account has two virtues. First, it provides a principled distinction between free and unfree action that does not invoke indeterminism — freedom is about the *structure* of motivation, not about the *absence* of causal determination. Second, it shows why mere absence of external coercion is insufficient: a manipulated agent who acts without external compulsion, but whose motivations have been engineered without their endorsement, does not act freely.

Later developments refined the hierarchical model. Wolf (1990: 67–85) argued that free will requires the ability to act in accordance with *Reason* — to recognize and respond to moral and practical reasons. Fischer and Ravizza (1998: 38–87) developed the concept of *reasons-responsiveness*: a mechanism is reasons-responsive if it would produce different outputs in response to different reasons-inputs. An agent acts freely when the mechanism producing their action is their own (appropriately) and is reasons-responsive in the right way. Neither account requires indeterminism.

##### The Consequence Argument

The most powerful challenge to compatibilism is Peter van Inwagen's Consequence Argument (1983: 55–105). The argument aims to show that no compatibilist account of free will can succeed, because the very notion of "ability to do otherwise" is incompatible with determinism.

The argument runs as follows. Let P₀ be a complete description of the state of the world at some time in the distant past (before any living human existed), and let L be the conjunction of all the laws of nature. Determinism is the thesis that P₀ and L together entail every subsequent state of the world, including your action A at time t. Now:

(1) No one has, or ever had, any choice about P₀. (It is in the past, before we existed.)
(2) No one has, or ever had, any choice about L. (Laws of nature are not up to us.)
(3) Therefore, no one has any choice about anything that is a consequence of P₀ and L.
(4) But our actions are consequences of P₀ and L (determinism).
(5) Therefore, no one has any choice about their actions.

The argument deploys a transfer principle: if you have no choice about X, and X entails Y, then you have no choice about Y. Van Inwagen defends this principle against objections. The consequence argument has generally been regarded as one of the most compelling arguments in contemporary philosophy of action.

Compatibilists have contested the argument at the level of the transfer principle. McKenna (2008: 177–192) argues that the principle, while intuitively compelling, cannot be formulated precisely without either being false or presupposing incompatibilism. Fischer (2006: 177–200) develops an account of "semi-compatibilism" that accepts the incompatibility of free will (in the sense of "could have done otherwise") with determinism, while maintaining that *moral responsibility* is compatible with determinism — and that moral responsibility is what really matters.

##### Hard Incompatibilism

Hard incompatibilism is the view that neither compatibilism nor libertarianism is correct: genuine free will does not exist, because neither determinism nor indeterminism provides the conditions required. Derk Pereboom (2001: 1–8; 2014: 1–35) is the most systematic advocate of this position.

Pereboom argues that the manipulated-agent cases show that compatibilism fails: a deterministically produced action and a manipulated action are relevantly similar in all the ways that matter for free will, yet we clearly hold that manipulated agents do not act freely. If we accept that intuition, we must accept that deterministically produced actions are equally unfree. And libertarian alternatives — agent causation, quantum indeterminism — fail to provide a metaphysically coherent account of the special causal power they require.

The implications for moral responsibility are significant. Pereboom argues that reactive attitudes — praise, blame, resentment, indignation — that presuppose libertarian free will should be revised or abandoned. But he maintains that a "forward-looking" conception of moral responsibility is still available: we can hold people accountable for pragmatic reasons (deterrence, protection, rehabilitation) without presupposing they "could have done otherwise" in the libertarian sense.

The difficulty with hard incompatibilism is not only philosophical but existential. Our self-understanding as agents, our practices of holding each other responsible, and our experience of deliberation all seem to presuppose something like libertarian free will. Pereboom is aware of this; he argues that we can revise our practices without catastrophic loss. Whether that revision is psychologically or socially achievable is a further question that philosophy cannot answer alone.

##### Time and the Responsibility Question

One further connection between temporal metaphysics and the free will debate deserves mention. The incompatibilist worry about the "fixed past" is, in a sense, a worry about the asymmetry of time. What makes the past constraining is precisely that it is *past* — outside the range of present agency. The future, by contrast, can be "influenced" by present action. If the block universe collapses this asymmetry, and future events are no more "influenceable" than past ones, then the worry resurfaces at the level of the entire temporal manifold.

But as we noted in Section 31.3.1, the asymmetry that matters for agency is causal, not merely temporal. Causes precede their effects; deliberation precedes action; reasons influence outcomes in a forward-directed way. This causal asymmetry is fully compatible with the block universe. The free will debate is ultimately a debate about the nature of causation and agency, not about which theory of temporal ontology is correct.

---

*See also: Section 31.4 on agent causation and libertarianism; Chapter 21 on temporal asymmetry; Frankfurt (1971) and van Inwagen (1983) in Further Reading.*

### Section 31.4: Libertarianism and the Open Future

---

#### Section Introduction

Libertarianism about free will is not a political position but a metaphysical one: it holds that genuine free will requires the ability to do otherwise in the strongest, indeterminist sense, and that human beings (at least sometimes) exercise such freedom. The libertarian agrees with the incompatibilist that determinism forecloses free will, but disagrees with the hard incompatibilist: rather than concluding that free will does not exist, the libertarian concludes that the world is not deterministic in the relevant ways, or that human agency involves something beyond ordinary physical determination.

Libertarianism is the position that takes the openness of the future most seriously as a metaphysical and ethical requirement. For the libertarian, the future is not merely epistemically uncertain; it is ontologically open in a way that is necessary for genuine freedom. This connects directly to the themes of the previous sections: A-theories of time, presentism, and the growing block all have natural affinities with libertarian free will, while the block universe sits more naturally with compatibilism.

This section examines the most developed and philosophically serious form of libertarianism — agent causation — and confronts the hardest challenge it faces: showing that genuinely free choices are neither predetermined nor merely random.

---

*Section 31.4 comprises Reading 31.4.1.*

#### 31.4.1 Agent Causation and the Open Future

---

##### The Libertarian Requirement

The intuition behind libertarianism is simple and powerful. When you deliberate about what to do, you experience alternatives as genuinely available — not just as things you are uncertain about, but as things that are *up to you* to bring about or not. You feel that the deliberation has a point: by reasoning carefully, by weighing the considerations, you are doing something that genuinely matters for the outcome, not merely observing a process whose result is predetermined. This experience of open alternatives is central to our self-understanding as agents.

Libertarianism takes this experience at face value and argues that it is veridical. For the experience to be veridical, two conditions must hold. First, the future must be genuinely open: at the moment of decision, more than one outcome must be causally possible given everything that has happened so far. This requires indeterminism at some level relevant to human action. Second, the agent must be the source of the determination of outcomes: among the genuinely open possibilities, the agent's choice is what actualizes one rather than another.

The second condition is the hard one. Quantum indeterminism exists — elementary particles behave probabilistically — but this provides at best the *space* for libertarian freedom, not freedom itself. If my neural processes are quantum-indeterminate, the outcome might be random rather than chosen. A coin flip is indeterminate but not free. Libertarianism needs something that bridges the gap between mere indeterminism and genuine agency.

##### The Randomness Problem

This is sometimes called the "luck objection" or the "randomness problem": if determinism forecloses free will, and if indeterminism just introduces randomness, then neither determinism nor indeterminism yields freedom. The libertarian appears stuck.

The force of this objection should not be minimized. Van Inwagen (1983: 126–150) articulated it sharply: if the laws of physics determine that an agent will either choose A or choose B, with each having some probability, then the actual choice appears to be a matter of luck — the agent did not determine which possibility was actualized. The agent's reasons may have influenced the probabilities, but they did not settle the outcome. And a choice that is partly a matter of luck — of which quantum event happens to fire — is not obviously the kind of robust, reason-sensitive agency that matters for moral responsibility.

Various responses have been developed. Kane (1996: 115–140) argues that genuine indeterminism can be free if the reasons that influence the probabilities are themselves the agent's own — if the agent's character, values, and deliberative processes shape the probability distribution over outcomes, then even a probabilistically-determined choice is an expression of the agent's self. The outcome may be undetermined, but which outcome is more likely is shaped by who the agent is.

This is a significant advance, but critics find it unsatisfying. If the reasons set the probabilities and the physics determines the outcome, the agent seems to be in a position analogous to a gambler who has influenced the odds but not fixed the result. The result that falls out may not be attributable to the agent in the strong sense that moral responsibility seems to require.

##### Agent Causation

The most philosophically ambitious libertarian response is the theory of *agent causation*, developed in contemporary analytic philosophy above all by Timothy O'Connor (2000; 2009). Agent causation holds that persons are a distinctive kind of causal entity — they are not merely part of the event-causal nexus, passive transmitters of causal influence from antecedent events. Persons are *substances* that initiate causal sequences, and their initiating of a causal sequence is not itself caused by prior events in the standard way.

O'Connor's account distinguishes two modes of causation. *Event causation* is the familiar kind: one event (a neural firing, a physical impact) causes another event. *Agent causation* is irreducible to event causation: the agent herself — as a substance, not merely as a collection of events — is the cause of her action. The agent's causing is not mediated by a prior event that caused her to cause; the agent is the causal origin.

This is an ontologically heavy commitment. It requires that agents are genuine substances with irreducible causal powers, not fully describable or analyzable in terms of the physical events that constitute them. It requires, in short, that persons are not just physical systems. O'Connor is explicit about this: agent causation implies a modest dualism about persons — not a substance dualism of Cartesian minds and physical bodies, but a recognition that persons as wholes have causal properties that are not reducible to properties of their physical parts.

##### Agent Causation and Open Time

The connection to the philosophy of time is direct. Agent causation naturally fits with an A-theory of time in which the present is ontologically privileged and the future is genuinely open. If the future is not "already there" — if presentism or the growing block view is correct — then there is genuine openness in the world, and the agent's causal initiative is what determines which of the genuinely open possibilities is actualized. The agent does not merely select from a range of predetermined options; the agent *brings into existence* the state of affairs that actualizes.

By contrast, agent causation sits uneasily with the block universe. If the future is just as real as the past and present, and if the agent's action at time t is already "there" in the four-dimensional manifold, then it is harder to make sense of the agent's causal initiative as *genuinely open*. The block universe does not make the action unfree — as we argued in Section 31.3.1 — but it does make the metaphysics of agent causation harder to formulate clearly.

##### Objections to Agent Causation

O'Connor's view has attracted significant criticism. Pereboom (2014: 65–87) argues that agent causation, even if coherent, does not help with moral responsibility: if the agent's act of causing is itself undetermined by anything — not by prior events, not by the agent's character or reasons — then the choice is arbitrary at the deepest level. Moral responsibility requires that choices be appropriately connected to the agent's reasons and values; an uncaused causal initiation seems to sever this connection.

A different objection concerns the coherence of the concept of substance causation. Hume's analysis of causation as constant conjunction between event-types is the background assumption of most scientific and philosophical work on causation. On event-causal models, to say that A caused B is to say something about regularities between event-types, or about counterfactual dependence between event-tokens. Substance causation does not fit naturally into either analysis: what is the regularity or the counterfactual relationship that characterizes agent causation?

O'Connor (2000: 45–68) responds that agent causation is a genuinely irreducible explanatory category — it explains events in terms of agents, not in terms of prior events. This is a real explanatory kind, not a disguised version of event causation. The demand that it be analyzed in event-causal terms begs the question against agent causation.

##### The Irreducibility of Agency

What is most interesting about the libertarian debate, in the context of a philosophy of time course, is what it reveals about the relationship between the temporal structure of the world and the nature of agency. Libertarians take seriously the phenomenology of deliberation — the experience of genuine openness — and attempt to provide an ontological basis for it. The basis they appeal to — genuinely open possibilities, agent causation — requires taking the openness of the future seriously at a metaphysical level.

Whether libertarianism succeeds is genuinely uncertain. The view is difficult to make coherent and faces powerful objections. But it is not obviously wrong, and dismissing it without engagement would be philosophically incurious. The questions it raises — about the kind of causal power persons possess, about the relationship between physical indeterminism and freedom, about the ontological requirements of genuine agency — are among the most important in philosophy. Their resolution, or failure to be resolved, says something deep about what we are.

---

*See also: Section 31.3.2 on compatibilism and the consequence argument; Chapter 17 on the growing block universe; O'Connor (2000) in Further Reading.*

### Chapter 31 Exercises: Time and Free Will

---

#### Conceptual Exercises

**1. Reconstructing the Master Argument**
Reconstruct Diodorus Cronus's Master Argument in your own words, stating the three premises clearly. Then identify which premise you find most vulnerable to rejection, and give your best argument for rejecting it. Does your rejection have consequences for other areas of philosophy that you are willing to accept?

**2. Bivalence and the Sea Battle**
Aristotle's response to logical fatalism is to deny bivalence for future contingent statements. Write a one-page analysis addressing the following: (a) What exactly does Aristotle deny — that future contingent statements have truth values at all, or that they have the same kind of truth values as other statements? (b) Is the law of excluded middle affected by this denial? (c) What would a logician who insists on classical two-valued logic say in response?

**3. Hard and Soft Facts**
Fischer's distinction between hard and soft facts about the past is central to the Ockhamist response to theological fatalism. Apply this distinction to the following three cases, determining whether each is a hard or soft fact, and justifying your classification:
- (a) "In 1980, Smith was the teacher of the first person to cure cancer."
- (b) "In 1980, Jones was five feet tall."
- (c) "In 1990, Brown believed that the president elected in 2000 would be a Republican."
Does your classification affect whether these facts fall under the "necessity of the past"?

**4. Boethius and the Relocation Objection**
State Pike's objection to Boethius as precisely as you can. Then write Boethius's best possible response, drawing on the distinction between conditional and absolute necessity. Is the response successful? What would you need to believe about the nature of God and time for it to work?

**5. The Block Universe and Fatalism**
A student argues: "If the block universe is true, my breakfast choice tomorrow is already 'there' in spacetime. So I can't really choose; the choice is already made." Write a careful response to this student explaining the distinction between ontological completeness and causal necessitation, and showing why the block universe does not entail fatalism. What, if anything, does the block universe imply for free will?

**6. Frankfurt Cases**
Consider Frankfurt's (1971) famous case: Black wants Jones to vote for a particular candidate. Black has implanted a device in Jones's brain that will cause Jones to vote for the candidate if Jones shows any inclination to vote otherwise. In fact, Jones decides to vote for the candidate on his own, and Black's device plays no role. Is Jones's vote free? Does it matter that Jones "could not have done otherwise" (in the sense that the device would have intervened)? What does this case show about the relationship between freedom and the ability to do otherwise?

**7. The Consequence Argument**
Van Inwagen's Consequence Argument is one of the most powerful arguments in philosophy of action. State the argument precisely, identifying the transfer principle it relies on. Then present the strongest compatibilist response you can find (using at least one source from the Further Reading), and evaluate whether it succeeds in blocking the argument.

**8. Agent Causation and the Randomness Problem**
The randomness problem for libertarianism holds that if an agent's choice is not determined by prior events, then it is merely random — no better than a coin flip, and not the kind of thing for which agents deserve credit or blame. Evaluate Kane's (1996) response: that indeterminism can be free if the agent's reasons shape the probabilities of outcomes. Does this response show that the choice is genuinely *the agent's*, or does it merely show that the agent has influence over the odds?

---

#### Discussion and Essay Questions

**9. Comparative Analysis**
Compare and contrast three different strategies for dealing with the problem of divine foreknowledge: (a) Ockham's hard/soft facts distinction; (b) Boethius's eternal simultaneous apprehension; (c) Open theism (the view that God voluntarily refrains from knowing future free actions). Which approach requires the least revision of our ordinary concepts? Which requires the least revision of traditional theological commitments?

**10. A-Theory and Libertarianism**
Some philosophers argue that libertarian free will fits most naturally with an A-theory of time in which the future is genuinely open, while compatibilism fits most naturally with the block universe. Critically evaluate this claim. Is the connection between temporal metaphysics and the free will debate as tight as this suggests, or can one hold any combination of positions?

---

#### Lab and Observational Exercises

**11. Deliberation Diary**
Over the course of three days, keep a "deliberation diary." On at least five separate occasions when you face a genuine decision (not a trivial habitual choice), pause and record: (a) what alternatives you experience as genuinely available; (b) what considerations seem to influence you; (c) whether you experience yourself as "settling" something, or merely discovering what you were always going to do. After three days, analyze your diary: does the phenomenology of deliberation support libertarianism, compatibilism, or neither? What features of the deliberative experience bear most directly on the philosophical positions?

**12. Historical Case Study**
Research one historical trial in which the defense of the accused included claims about diminished control or determinism (examples: the 1924 Leopold and Loeb case in which Clarence Darrow appealed to determinism; recent cases involving neuroscience evidence). Prepare a two-page analysis examining: (a) what theory of free will is implicit in the defense; (b) how the court and prosecution responded; (c) what philosophical issues the case illuminates. Does the legal treatment of responsibility track any of the philosophical positions discussed in this chapter?

**13. Interdisciplinary Investigation**
Quantum mechanics introduces genuine indeterminacy at the sub-atomic level. Investigate the following question empirically and philosophically: Do contemporary neuroscientists or physicists believe that quantum indeterminacy "scales up" to the level of neural decision-making in a way that could ground libertarian free will? Find at least two sources — one from neuroscience and one from physics or philosophy of physics — and write a summary of what they say. Does the empirical evidence support the view that quantum indeterminacy plays a role in human choices? What would it take for quantum indeterminacy to ground genuine freedom rather than mere randomness?

#### Annotated Entries

**Aristotle, *De Interpretatione* 9**
The locus classicus for the problem of future contingents. Aristotle's argument and proposed solution have generated two millennia of commentary. Ackrill's translation is reliable and the introduction to the Clarendon Press edition is excellent. Begin here for the historical origins of the problem.

**Belnap, Perloff, and Xu, *Facing the Future* (2001)**
The most technically sophisticated development of Aristotle's branching-time semantics for future contingents. Introduces the framework of "agent stit" ("sees to it that") logic, which connects temporal branching with a formal theory of agency and action. Essential for those interested in the logic of free will and time.

**Fischer, *God, Foreknowledge, and Freedom* (1989)**
An indispensable anthology containing the major classical and contemporary readings on theological fatalism. Includes Pike's original paper, Ockham's texts in translation, Stump and Kretzmann on eternity, and Fischer's own analysis of hard and soft facts. The introductory essay is especially helpful.

**Fischer and Ravizza, *Responsibility and Control* (1998)**
The most comprehensive contemporary compatibilist account of moral responsibility. Develops the concept of reasons-responsiveness and the notion of "guidance control." Clear, careful, and responsive to the major objections. Required reading for anyone working on compatibilism.

**Frankfurt, "Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person" (1971)**
A short, beautifully written paper that transformed the free will debate. The hierarchical account of free will and the Frankfurt cases have generated an enormous secondary literature. Read the original before the secondary literature.

**Kane, *The Significance of Free Will* (1996)**
The most systematic contemporary defense of libertarian free will that does not appeal to agent causation. Kane attempts to show that quantum indeterminism at the neural level can ground the kind of self-forming actions required for ultimate moral responsibility. Richly argued and historically informed.

**O'Connor, *Persons and Causes* (2000)**
The most developed contemporary version of agent causation. O'Connor argues for the irreducibility of agent causation and defends a non-reductive naturalist picture of persons as genuine substances with emergent causal properties. Technically demanding but rewarding.

**Pereboom, *Living Without Free Will* (2001)**
The most influential contemporary defense of hard incompatibilism. Pereboom argues through a series of manipulation cases that compatibilism fails, then addresses the existential implications of living without free will. Honest and philosophically serious about the human stakes.

**Pike, "Divine Omniscience and Voluntary Action" (1965)**
The article that launched the modern debate about theological fatalism. Pike argues that Boethius's solution fails — the problem resurfaces at the level of eternal knowledge — and that the only available solution is to deny divine foreknowledge, which is theologically unacceptable. Still the best statement of the problem.

**Prior, *Past, Present and Future* (1967)**
The foundational text of tense logic. Prior develops formal logical systems for reasoning about time and uses them to address philosophical problems including future contingents. Difficult in places but historically important; tense logic begins here.

**Stump and Kretzmann, "Eternity" (1981)**
The most rigorous contemporary defense of Boethius's doctrine of divine eternity. Introduces the concept of "ET-simultaneity" — a relation holding between eternal and temporal existence — to make sense of God's timeless knowledge of temporal events. A model of careful analytic philosophy of religion.

**van Inwagen, *An Essay on Free Will* (1983)**
One of the most important books in philosophy of action. Develops the consequence argument for incompatibilism with great precision and care. Van Inwagen is admirably clear about what he takes to be proved and what remains uncertain. Required reading for anyone working on free will.

### Chapter 31 Important Concepts: Time and Free Will

---

**Agent Causation**
The view that persons as substances (not merely as collections of events) initiate causal sequences in a way that is irreducible to event causation. Associated with O'Connor (2000), agent causation holds that the agent herself — not a prior event — is the cause of her action. The view requires that persons have irreducible causal powers not fully analyzable in physical terms.

**Bivalence**
The logical principle that every declarative statement is either true or false, with no third option. Classical logic accepts bivalence universally. Aristotle's response to the sea battle problem requires denying bivalence for future contingent statements — those describing events that are genuinely open and might or might not occur.

**Compatibilism**
The philosophical position that free will and causal determinism are logically compatible. Compatibilists analyze free will in terms of the right kind of causal relationship between an agent's reasons, desires, and actions — not in terms of the absence of prior causes. Historical compatibilists include Hume and Hobbes; contemporary versions include hierarchical accounts (Frankfurt) and reasons-responsiveness accounts (Fischer and Ravizza).

**Consequence Argument**
Van Inwagen's (1983) argument that determinism is incompatible with free will. Since no one has a choice about the laws of nature or the remote past, and since our actions follow necessarily from these, no one has a choice about their actions. The argument deploys a transfer principle: if you have no choice about X, and X entails Y, then you have no choice about Y.

**Diodorean Modality**
The modal logic associated with Diodorus Cronus, on which "possible" means "true now or at some future time." This collapses unrealized possibilities into impossibilities: if something never happens, it was never genuinely possible. Contrasts with the standard Leibnizian notion of possibility as truth in some possible world.

**Fatalism**
The view that what will happen is in some sense already settled, irrespective of what agents do. Logical fatalism grounds this in the logic of truth; theological fatalism grounds it in divine foreknowledge; physical fatalism grounds it in the causal structure of the universe. Distinct from determinism: fatalism does not require that outcomes are causally determined, only that they are in some sense fixed.

**Frankfurt Cases**
Thought experiments introduced by Frankfurt (1971) designed to show that the ability to do otherwise is not necessary for moral responsibility. In the standard case, a counterfactual intervener would have prevented the agent from doing otherwise, but the agent acts on their own without needing the intervention. If the agent is responsible, then responsibility does not require the ability to do otherwise.

**Hard and Soft Facts**
A distinction due to Ockham, formalized by Fischer (1989). A hard fact about the past concerns only what happened at that time; a soft fact about the past has essential reference to what will happen at later times. God's foreknowledge of a future action is a soft fact: its truth conditions essentially involve the future action. Soft facts do not fall under the principle that past facts are necessary, and so foreknowledge does not foreclose future freedom.

**Hard Incompatibilism**
The position that neither determinism nor indeterminism is compatible with genuine free will and moral responsibility. Pereboom (2001) argues that compatibilist accounts fail because manipulated agents and deterministically produced agents are relevantly similar, and libertarian accounts fail because they cannot coherently characterize the special causal power required. The implication is that praise and blame based on desert are unjustified.

**Hierarchical Account of Free Will**
Frankfurt's (1971) analysis on which free will involves a harmony between first-order desires and second-order desires (desires about desires). An agent acts freely when their first-order motivating desire is one they endorse at the level of second-order volition. This account preserves the significance of freedom without requiring indeterminism.

**Incompatibilism**
The view that free will and causal determinism are logically incompatible — that the truth of determinism would imply the absence of genuine freedom. Incompatibilists divide into hard incompatibilists (who conclude that free will does not exist) and libertarians (who conclude that the world is not deterministic in the relevant way).

**Libertarianism (about Free Will)**
The metaphysical position that genuine free will exists and requires indeterminism. The libertarian holds that human agents sometimes make choices that are not causally determined by prior events, and that these choices are genuinely attributable to the agent rather than being merely random. Contemporary libertarian theories include agent causation and event-causal probabilistic theories (Kane 1996).

**Logical Fatalism**
The argument that future-tense statements, if determinately true or false, entail that the future is necessary. If "there will be a sea battle tomorrow" is true today, then the battle must happen; if it is false today, the battle cannot happen. Either way, the outcome is necessitated. Logical fatalism does not depend on causal determination but only on the logic of truth and time.

**Necessity of the Past**
The principle that true propositions about the past are necessary — not in the sense of logical necessity, but in the sense of being outside the range of present agency. What happened, happened; nothing can make it otherwise. This principle is central to both logical fatalism and theological fatalism. Its precise scope — whether it applies to hard facts only, or also to soft facts — is contested.

**Open Future Semantics**
A family of semantic frameworks, developed by Prior (1967), Thomason (1970), and Belnap et al. (2001), that represent the future as a branching tree of possibilities rather than a single determined sequence. Future contingent statements are true at a branch-time pair but may be "unsettled" at a time — neither settled true nor settled false — because they are true on some branches and false on others. Implements Aristotle's intuition that the future is genuinely open.

**Reasons-Responsiveness**
Fischer and Ravizza's (1998) criterion for the kind of control sufficient for moral responsibility. A mechanism (such as a deliberative process) is reasons-responsive if it would produce different outputs in response to different reasons-inputs — if a good reason to act otherwise would, in some circumstances, lead the agent to act otherwise. Responsibility requires that the mechanism be "one's own" and reasons-responsive in the right way.

**Temporal Necessity**
Also called "accidental necessity" or "necessity per accidens." The type of necessity that past truths acquire simply by becoming past — not because they are logically necessary, but because the past is fixed and unchangeable. Contrasts with logical necessity (truth in all possible worlds) and with causal necessity (determination by prior causes). Central to the fatalism arguments examined in this chapter.

**Theological Fatalism**
The argument that divine foreknowledge is incompatible with human freedom. If God infallibly knew yesterday that you would do A today, then you cannot refrain from doing A without making God's knowledge false — which is impossible. The problem arises because divine foreknowledge combines temporal necessity (the past is fixed) with infallibility (God cannot be wrong) in a way that seems to foreclose alternatives.

### Chapter 31 Important Researchers: Time and Free Will

---

**Aristotle (384–322 BCE)**
The most influential philosopher in the Western tradition, Aristotle's contribution to the free will and time debate is centered on *De Interpretatione* 9 and its treatment of future contingents. By diagnosing the threat of logical fatalism and proposing the denial of bivalence for future contingent statements, Aristotle framed an alternative to fatalism that has influenced logicians, philosophers, and theologians for over two thousand years. His solution — the "open future" semantics — remains a live option and has been developed into sophisticated formal systems in the twentieth century. The discussion of contingency in *De Interpretatione* connects with his broader treatment of potentiality and actuality in the *Metaphysics* and the analysis of deliberation in the *Nicomachean Ethics*.

**Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 CE)**
Roman philosopher, statesman, and theologian whose *Consolation of Philosophy*, written while awaiting execution, stands as one of the masterpieces of late antique philosophy. Book V contains the definitive formulation of the eternal-present solution to theological fatalism: God is outside time and apprehends all temporal events simultaneously, so divine "foreknowledge" is not foreknowledge at all but timeless simultaneous perception. This solution has shaped Christian theology and philosophy of religion ever since. Boethius also translated Aristotle's logic into Latin, ensuring its transmission to medieval Europe.

**Diodorus Cronus (c. 340–280 BCE)**
Megarian logician famous for the Master Argument, which shows that three apparently compelling claims about possibility, necessity, and the past cannot all be true simultaneously. Diodorus resolved the tension by collapsing the possible into the actual: only what is or will be true is genuinely possible. His influence on Stoic logic was considerable, though almost none of his work survives in direct form. We know the argument primarily from Epictetus and later commentators. Despite the fragmentary evidence, his contribution to modal logic is of the first rank.

**John Martin Fischer (b. 1952)**
Contemporary analytic philosopher at the University of California Riverside whose work on free will, moral responsibility, and theological fatalism has been among the most influential of the past four decades. Fischer's analysis of hard and soft facts clarified the Ockhamist response to theological fatalism; his development of reasons-responsiveness compatibilism (with Ravizza) provides one of the most rigorous accounts of guidance control in the literature. His "semi-compatibilism" — the view that moral responsibility is compatible with determinism even if free will strictly construed is not — represents a significant methodological advance. He has also written on death, immortality, and the value of finite life (see Chapter 32).

**Harry Frankfurt (b. 1929)**
American philosopher whose 1971 paper "Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person" is one of the most cited and discussed papers in twentieth-century philosophy. Frankfurt's hierarchical model of free will — distinguishing first-order desires from second-order volitions — transformed the debate by showing that freedom is about the structure of motivation, not the absence of causal determination. The Frankfurt cases, designed to show that the ability to do otherwise is not necessary for moral responsibility, have generated an extensive secondary literature and remain controversial. Frankfurt has also written importantly on love, necessity, and the ethics of care.

**Robert Kane (b. 1938)**
Contemporary philosopher at the University of Texas whose work represents the most systematic and sustained defense of libertarian free will from within a broadly naturalist framework. Kane's key contribution is the concept of "self-forming actions" (SFAs) — moments of decision in which an agent's character and values are being formed, not merely expressed. Kane argues that quantum indeterminism at the neural level, shaped by the agent's reasons and values through their influence on probability distributions, can ground the kind of openness required for ultimate responsibility. His *The Significance of Free Will* (1996) is the definitive statement of this position.

**Timothy O'Connor (b. 1965)**
Contemporary philosopher at Indiana University whose work on agent causation represents the most technically developed version of that theory in the contemporary literature. O'Connor argues that persons are substances with irreducible causal powers — they are genuine initiators of causal sequences, not merely nodes in an event-causal network. His *Persons and Causes* (2000) defends a non-reductive naturalism about agent causation and responds systematically to the main objections. O'Connor has also worked on emergence and the metaphysics of mind.

**Derk Pereboom (b. 1957)**
Contemporary philosopher at Cornell University and the leading contemporary advocate of hard incompatibilism. Pereboom's four-case argument (the "manipulation argument") contends that compatibilism fails because manipulated agents and deterministically produced agents are relevantly similar in the ways that matter for free will, and his critique of libertarianism argues that agent causation and quantum-indeterminist theories both fail to provide the required metaphysical foundation. His *Living Without Free Will* (2001) and *Free Will, Agency, and Meaning in Life* (2014) work out the implications of hard incompatibilism for moral responsibility and practical life with unusual honesty and depth.

**Peter van Inwagen (b. 1942)**
Contemporary philosopher at Notre Dame whose *An Essay on Free Will* (1983) contains the Consequence Argument, one of the most carefully worked-out arguments in contemporary philosophy. Van Inwagen argues that no compatibilist account can succeed and that the only alternative to hard incompatibilism is libertarianism — but he regards the prospects for libertarianism as unpromising, leaving him in the uncomfortable position of being unable to accept any satisfying account of free will. His candor about this predicament is philosophically admirable. He has also written extensively on the metaphysics of material constitution and persistence.

**William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347)**
Medieval English Franciscan friar and logician whose distinction between "hard" and "soft" facts about the past provides one of the most influential tools in the theological fatalism debate. Ockham argued that God's foreknowledge, while a genuine past fact in a grammatical sense, is a "soft" fact with forward-directed content, and therefore does not fall under the principle that past facts are necessary. This move preserves both divine foreknowledge and human freedom. Ockham's broader logical work — including his development of terminist logic and his nominalism — makes him one of the most important figures in medieval philosophy.

## Chapter 32: Time, Death, and Mortality

---

### Chapter Introduction

No feature of our temporal existence is more certain or more consequential than the fact that we will die. We are beings who exist for a limited time — who come into existence, develop and change through time, and then cease to exist. This is not merely a biological fact; it is a constitutive feature of the kind of beings we are. Our projects, our relationships, our sense of urgency and value are all shaped by the awareness that time is finite. The philosophy of death is, in this sense, a philosophy of time as it applies to the structure of a life.

Yet the philosophical analysis of death is extraordinarily difficult. The central puzzle is this: death seems bad — we fear it, we mourn the dead, we treat the prolongation of life as a basic good. But if we take seriously the claim that experience is what matters, then death, which involves no experience at all, seems incapable of being bad *for the person who dies*. After all, once you are dead, there is no subject of harm. You are not suffering; you are not being deprived; you simply are not. Epicurus saw this clearly and concluded that death is not an evil. The difficulty is that this conclusion, though logically compelling, seems to miss something important.

This chapter traces the main lines of the philosophical debate. Section 32.1 examines the Epicurean challenge in both its formulations: the argument from the absence of experience (Epicurus himself) and the symmetry argument from pre-natal non-existence (Lucretius). Section 32.2 develops the "deprivation account" of death's badness — the view that death is bad not because it involves any harm to the dead person, but because it deprives them of future goods — and examines the notorious "location problem" this account generates: *when* is death bad, if the subject no longer exists to be harmed?

Section 32.3 returns to Epicurean territory with a sharper focus: the "existence requirement" for welfare and whether it can be defended against the deprivation account.
